text:
#Srikrishna_Stories 
Soon after Krishna was born, his father quietly took the newborn infant out of the evil King Kamsa’s palace in Mathura in the middle of the night, by hiding him in a wicker basket, crossed the mighty river Yamuna and left him at his sister Yashoda’s house in Vrindavan. When Kamsa came to know that Krishna had escaped, he sent many demons to kill the small child. However, each of these demons was slayed at the hands of Krishna, who was an incarnate of Lord Vishnu. The fiercest of these demons was Arishtasura, the bull demon. But for Krishna, slaying Arishtasura was child’s play.

King Kamsa grew restless after Krishna killed Arishtasura, the bull demon that Kamsa had sent to kill Krishna. Ever since it was prophesied that Krishna will be the reason for evil Kamsa’s death, the latter had tried to kill Krishna many times. The fear of death had brought Kamsa to a state where he did not hesitate to order the killing of his own nephew, Krishna.

Sage Narada, son of Lord Brahma, went to Kamsa after the death of Arishtasura and told him that the prophecy is indeed true. According to Narada, Krishna would soon kill Kamsa. Infuriated at this disclosure, Kamsa called the long-haired, demon – Keshi.

Keshi was an extremely powerful mystic demon. Kamsa ordered Keshi to leave for Vrindavan and kill Krishna – the boy who wore a peacock feather in his hair, at once. Keshi assumed the form of a giant mad horse and left for Vrindavan. He could move at the “speed of thought”. He galloped so fast that his hooves tore into the earth.

Meanwhile, unaware of Keshi’s intent, Krishna was busy playing with his fellow cowherds. One of his closest friends, Madhumangala, said to Krishna, “Dear Friend, everyone in Vrindavan loves you. They never forget to offer you laddus. Why don’t you share your peacock feather with me and your dress so that I can get some laddus from the villagers.” Krishna agreed to lend his dress for some time. Madhu was very happy and started walking towards the village.

Keshi, upon reaching Vrindavan, started looking for a boy with a peacock feather on his head. As soon as he saw Madhu, he started charging towards him. Madhu cried for help and before the wild beast could harm Madhu, Krishna reached the spot and challenged Keshi.

Keshi got infuriated and attacked Krishna instead and tried to trample the latter with his hooves. Krishna caught Keshi by his legs and tossed him in the air. Keshi fell down with a loud thud. He got up and raging with anger attacked Krishna once more. The duel between the two continued this way. Keshi would attack and each time, Krishna would repulse the attack, wounding the demon some more. Keshi refused to back down and after gathering some strength, would attack Krishna again.

Finally, tired and exhausted, Keshi tried to devour Krishna whole and attacked with his mouth wide open. Krishna thrust his arm into Keshi’s mouth and pushed it right till the animal’s belly. Then he expanded his arm till the demon could no longer breath. Keshi’s lifeless body then fell on the ground.

Who was demon Keshi?
As Keshi’s body fell down, his soul appeared in the form of a human. The soul bowed in front of Krishna and paid obeisance. He then said, “Mighty Lord Krishna, my name is Kumuda. I was the servant of Lord Indra and used to carry his chhatra (Parasol/Umbrella). To absolve himself of the sin of killing a brahman (sage) – Vritrasura, Lord Indra decided to perform Ashwamedha Yagna (Horse Sacrifice). The horse was magnificent and it ran at the speed of thought. I yearned to ride it and thus stole it and took it to Patal-loka (Nether World). I was caught by servants of Indra and produced before him. He cursed me to be a demon in a horse’s body. Today, Krishna, you have freed me from that curse. I respectfully offer you my obeisance”.

Saying this the soul embarked on the journey towards Vaikuntha (Heaven).

Krishna is said to have killed Keshi at the Keshi Ghat, a bank of river Yamuna to commemorate the slaying by the lord. Every story associated with Krishna has a life lesson and this is no different.

The Name Keshava: Lord Krishna earned the divine name “Keshava” after slaying the demon Keshi. The name is associated with His victory over Keshi, while “Keshighna” (केशिघ्न) specifically means “the slayer of Keshi.”

Mahabharata 115
No Entry for Wisdom
Alok Puranik
Krishna has arrived to persuade Duryodhana and prevent the Mahabharata war. But Duryodhana has already made it clear that he has no interest in any deal.

Krishna: I am not here for a deal or a bargain. I am here to find a solution.

Duryodhana: The solution is simple. The Pandavas should forget their share. In my kingdom, a solution is one where only the other side suffers a loss.

Krishna: I am not asking you to give them the entire kingdom. Just give them five villages.

Duryodhana: Not even five villages! A concession is something that should benefit only me.

Krishna: Think carefully. A war can cost you dearly. You could even lose this throne.

Duryodhana: I have an army, great warriors and Karna on my side. What do I have to fear? When you have a crowd behind you, why would you need advice?

Duryodhana was like a boss who makes up his mind before the meeting and asks for opinions afterwards, only to hear everyone say, "Yes, sir!"

Whether it was Bhishma, Vidura or Krishna, everyone tried to reason with him. But for Duryodhana, a good adviser was someone who could repeat his own opinions back to him and explain them as if they were great wisdom.

Tulsidas wrote in the Ramcharitmanas:

सुमति कुमति सब कें उर रहहीं।
नाथ पुरान निगम अस कहहीं॥
जहाँ सुमति तहँ संपति नाना।
जहाँ कुमति तहँ बिपति निदाना॥

Meaning: Every heart contains both wisdom and foolishness. Where wisdom prevails, prosperity follows. Where foolishness prevails, disaster is bound to arrive.

In Hastinapur, wisdom did knock on the door, but the guards of foolishness turned it away.

An arrogant person shuts the doors of his establishment to wisdom. What remains inside is not intelligence, but merely ego masquerading as wisdom. Fools often mistake their arrogance for intelligence.

There are plenty of people willing to offer advice, but very few willing to accept it. And those who refuse to listen are eventually taught a lesson by history on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

To be continued...

Voiceover by Aakash Sethi ji

text:
They asked Homi Bhabha for ₹5 lakh. He asked what the world's great radio telescopes had cost.

In 1961, four Indian radio astronomers working abroad wanted to return home together and build a research group. Their 1st phase proposal was for ₹5 lakh.

Bhabha responded with a telex, asking the 3 in America to meet him in Washington. T.K. Menon met him that November.

Bhabha asked about the cost of Jodrell Bank in England and Parkes in Australia. Afterwards, Menon wrote to his colleagues that Bhabha had discussed an outlay of ₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore.

"Unbelievable for us at present but he seemed perfectly sincere and credible."

That line survives in Govind Swarup's reminiscences. This was not an extra grant handed over at a meeting. It was Bhabha taking their ambition seriously at a scale they had not expected.

On 20 Jan 1962, he sent all four a telegram:

"we have decided to establish Radio Astronomy Group. Letter follows with offer".

Swarup returned to India. When he proposed a large telescope, Bhabha questioned him for 2 hours. First establish the experimental group at TIFR, he told him; approval for the big instrument would follow.

The group built its 1st telescope at Kalyan. In Aug 1965, Bhabha approved the ₹50-lakh Ooty project: a radio telescope 530 metres long, built along a hillside.

That December, he visited the site and then went to Madras to help secure government approval for the forest land it needed.

He died the following month. He never saw the completed instrument.

On 18 Feb 1970, Swarup's team made its 1st observations with the Ooty Radio Telescope. Swarup recalled detecting one predicted and two uncatalogued radio sources. They had not slept for 2 nights.

Remembering Homi Bhabha on his birth anniversary today, 30 October. This is one of the things he helped build beyond India's atomic programme, and did not live to see finished.

P.S. A radio telescope detects radio waves from space rather than making an optical image like an ordinary telescope.

Source: Govind Swarup, "Radio Astronomy at TIFR, some highlights and reminiscences", ASI Conference Series, 2014. The correspondence quoted is reproduced there from the NCRA archives.

Photo 1: Homi J. Bhabha, circa 1965. 

Photo 2: Bhabha's telegram to Govind Swarup at Stanford, 20 January 1962: 'We have decided to establish Radio astronomy Group. Letter follows with offer.' 

Photo 3: Bhabha's signed letter to Swarup, 3 April 1962. He writes that the project could lead to 'some very much bigger equipment and work in Radio Astronomy in India than we foresee at present.

Photo 4: The first step: the Kalyan Radio Telescope near Bombay. Swarup's group built its 32-dish array before the larger Ooty instrument. Photograph reproduced in Swarup's memoir, credited there to Swarup and colleagues, 1966.

Other Image Sources: TIFR Archives, via Google Arts & Culture.

text:
🚢 L&T + Exail: Plugging a 20-Year Gap in India's Mine Countermeasure Capability

📌 WHAT: L&T (India) and Exail (France) have partnered to offer an Unmanned Mine Counter-Measure (MCM) Suite for the Indian Navy's planned 12 Mine Counter Measure Vessels (MCMVs)
🏢 WHO: Larsen & Toubro, Exail, Indian Navy, Ministry of Defence
📅 WHEN: Partnership announced May 2026; DAC approved the ₹45,000 crore program in July 2025; formal RFP still pending

🎯 WHAT IS THIS?
MCMVs are specialist ships that detect, classify, and neutralise naval mines — and India has had zero dedicated minesweepers since INS Kozhikode (its last Soviet-era Natya-class vessel) was decommissioned in 2019. This isn't a new problem: the Navy first proposed 12 minesweepers in 2005; a later Goa Shipyard–Kangnam Corporation (South Korea) deal collapsed in 2018 just as construction was about to start. An internal Navy assessment reportedly calls for at least 24 MCMVs to cover India's coastline and 200+ ports — the current 12-vessel plan covers half that assessed need.

• L&T is prime contractor; Exail is the technology partner, offering this suite to ALL shipyards bidding on the program (not exclusive to one bidder)
• Exail's mine-warfare tech includes SeaScan/K-Ster C ROVs, T-18M towed synthetic aperture sonar, and A-9M/A-18M AUVs — already operational with other navies
• L&T brings its own underwater portfolio: Amogh, Maya, Adamya AUVs, and the SOV400 midget submarine
• RFI-stage unmanned requirements: 2 CASCADE ASVs, 4 Heavy Weight AUVs, 1 ship-launched multicopter, 20+ smaller ROVs per vessel
• Each MCMV: 87m long, 2,800 tonnes, armed with a 76mm gun, VSHORADS, and either directed-energy weapons or 30mm EOIRST-controlled mounts
• First ship delivery estimated at 7+ years after contract signing — the formal RFP hasn't even been released yet

🧠 OUR ANALYSIS
The slide's core warning tracks with the Defence Minister's own public remarks (National Defence Industries Conclave, 19 March 2026): "a significant number of critical [drone] components are currently imported from China" across most manufacturing nations, and self-reliance "must" extend to moulds, software, engines, and batteries — not just final assembly. That's a real, independently-confirmed statement, though made about drones broadly rather than MCMVs specifically. The slide's framing — that an unexportable, unscalable indigenous design "is not yet a strategic capability" — is a fair reading of India's 20-year MCMV saga: two prior deals collapsed, and even this program's most optimistic timeline is 7+ years post-contract, with no contract yet signed.

❓ WHAT WE DON'T KNOW
Exact RFP release date; whether L&T-Exail is the frontrunner or one of several competing technology offers; how much of the MCM suite itself (versus the hull/shipyard build) would be domestically produced.

📷 Credit: L&T

text:
@WhiteHouse
@BernieSanders

With my current assessment of where we're headed this needs to be implemented right away please consider

**Tariff-Funded Free Tech Education and AI Transition Pathway**

Use the revenue collected from tariffs to fund free education for Americans who choose to train for careers in technology and AI. Participants would remain in the program at no cost as long as they maintain above a C average and demonstrate they can do the work. Upon successful completion, the program would provide free placement support and transition training into AI companies or related roles, along with the specific knowledge and skills needed for the ongoing shift in the economy.

The transition we are in is not going to be easy. We are moving into a period of much higher productivity and automation—sometimes compared to a Star Trek-style future of abundance—and that requires people who are prepared and capable. For a long time, higher education has been treated primarily as a business. Making targeted technical education free, with clear performance requirements, would allow people to choose a path into the sectors that are growing and give society a broader base of people ready for the change.

### Fact-check of the core claims

**Tariff revenue is real and substantial, but not unlimited or permanent.**  
In fiscal year 2025, net U.S. customs duties were about $195 billion. In fiscal year 2026 they were roughly $173 billion after large refunds (much of the higher gross collections came from IEEPA tariffs later struck down by the Supreme Court). Net annual tariff revenue has been in the roughly $170–200 billion range recently.

**Education costs make large-scale free programs expensive.**  
Average total cost of attendance for a public in-state student is roughly $23,000–$34,000 per year (tuition, fees, room, board, etc.). Private colleges are substantially higher. Funding even one million people at public-college cost levels would run into the tens of billions of dollars per year. Existing federal student aid, state funding, and community-college systems already cover part of this landscape.

**AI and tech talent demand is strong; pure displacement is real but smaller than headlines often suggest.**  
Surveys show the large majority of U.S. employers expanding tech headcount, with AI, cybersecurity, systems architecture, and related skills among the hardest to fill. AI-related job postings have risen sharply. At the same time, McKinsey has estimated that roughly 11 million American workers (about 7% of the workforce) may need to change occupations by 2035 because of AI-related effects. AI-cited announced job cuts through September 2026 were about 120,000—still a small share of total U.S. layoffs. Entry-level roles in AI-exposed occupations have been more affected than overall employment.

**Guaranteed placement into private AI companies is not something government can unilaterally deliver.**  
Private employers decide whom to hire. Programs can subsidize training, offer apprenticeships, create tax incentives for hiring graduates, or partner with companies, but they cannot force firms to absorb unlimited numbers of new workers. A C average is also a relatively low academic bar for competitive AI and advanced technical roles; many employers look for higher performance or demonstrated skills beyond grades.

**The “Star Trek era” framing is aspirational, not a precise economic forecast.**  
Elon Musk and others have described possible long-term abundance driven by AI and robotics. Near-term data show both skill shortages and the need for occupational transitions, not an automatic end to work.

text:
There are 5 stages of market awareness you need to understand if you want to nail your marketing and positioning.

Every buyer sits at one of them.

This concept is so important, I recently filmed a loom video to my team explaining it to them in depth.

Here are the 5 stages of awareness:

1- Unaware

This is the broadest market.

They don't know they have a problem.

Life feels fine. They aren't looking for anything.

How to market to them: a story about someone like them getting a result they didn't know was possible.

Example headline: "How 19-year-olds are making $40k a month selling AI automations to local dentists"

Hint: Iman Ghadzi was running a headline like this one on his last launch. 

2- Problem aware

They know something's off.

Stuck in a job, income capped, watching other people get ahead.

They don't know what fixes it.

How to market to them: describe the pain better than they can, then I troubleshoot your solution.

Headline: "Why working harder at your 9-to-5 will never make you rich (and what the people quitting theirs are doing instead)"

3- Solution aware

They know they have a problem , and they know about the solutions available to them.

They're comparing different options, but have never heard of you.

How to market to them: show why your way beats the other ways.

Headline: "Why AI automation agencies are beating dropshipping and Amazon FBA for beginners in 2026"

4 - Product aware

They know your product. They've watched your videos. They're on the fence.

How to market to them: proof. Numbers, case studies, receipts.

Answer the objection keeping them on the fence.

Headline: "312 students landed their first $3k client within 30 days. Here's exactly how they did it, even with zero tech skills"

5 - Most aware

They want it. They're waiting for a reason to move.

How to market to them: make an irresistible offer

Headline: "Doors close Friday at midnight. Join today and get our automated client outreach system $997 value - now $99”

Understanding deeply where your market is on this spectrum allows you to tailor your message to speak directly to them.

You may realize that you’ve been with tier 5 messaging (most aware) only, while the majority of your market actually sits in tier 2 (problem aware).

text:
Wall Street could rebound on Friday. A wave of selling does not necessarily mean a market crash.
Thursday’s sharp decline in the Nasdaq index sparked concerns among investors—particularly those with exposure to the technology, artificial intelligence, and semiconductor sectors. The key question now is whether Friday might bring a recovery.

There are reasons to believe that a technical rebound is possible.

The recent selling pressure was driven by several factors: disappointing reactions to the financial results of major companies, concerns regarding massive spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, questions about future profitability, and renewed uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) interest rate policy.
However, there is an important distinction between a broad-based market sell-off and a deterioration in the fundamentals of individual companies.
Thursday’s market action offered an interesting signal: while the Nasdaq fell by approximately 1.38%, the Russell 2000 index rose by about 1%. This suggests that investors have not necessarily abandoned the stock market as a whole; rather, they have reallocated their capital, pulling back from certain technology stocks and high-growth companies.
What could trigger a recovery on Friday? Three factors deserve special attention:

1. Nasdaq futures: An overnight recovery could signal a easing of selling pressure.
2. Major tech stocks: A stabilization in shares of Amazon, Alphabet, and Intel could help restore confidence across the entire technology sector.
3. Government bond yields: A decline in bond yields could provide additional support for growth stocks and companies with higher valuations.

text:
10 Last Minute Halloween Marketing Ideas

Halloween is almost here, but there’s still time to make your marketing feel relevant to the season.

You don’t always need weeks of preparation, a big budget, or an elaborate campaign to get people interested. Sometimes, a timely offer, a creative social media post, or a small seasonal twist on your existing content is enough to catch someone’s attention.

The key is to choose ideas that fit your brand and are realistic to execute before Halloween arrives. Focus on what you can launch quickly, make the message clear, and give your audience a reason to engage.

Here are 10 last-minute #Halloween marketing ideas to help your business make the most of the spooky season without starting from scratch.

10 Last-Minute Halloween Marketing Ideas

01. Launch a 24-Hour Halloween Discount

Create a limited-time offer that gives customers a reason to purchase before Halloween. Promote it through your website banner, email list, and social media channels.

02. Create a Halloween-Themed Social Media Post

Give your regular content a spooky twist using Halloween colors, themed visuals, or a playful caption that fits your brand.

03. Offer a Spooky Bundle Deal

Combine a few relevant products or services into one Halloween-themed package. Bundles can help customers discover more of your offerings while making the promotion feel seasonal.

04. Run a Halloween Giveaway

Offer a product, gift card, or small prize in exchange for simple actions such as commenting or sharing a post. Keep the entry requirements easy so you can launch quickly.

05. Send a Last-Minute Halloween Email

Send subscribers a short, themed email featuring a special offer, seasonal recommendations, or products they can still purchase before Halloween.

06. Share a Halloween Countdown

Post a countdown on your social channels with daily tips, product highlights, or special offers leading up to Halloween.

07. Create a Spooky Behind-the-Scenes Post

Show your team, workspace, products, or packaging with a Halloween-inspired touch. This is a quick way to make your brand feel more relatable and timely.

08. Offer a Flash Sale on Seasonal Products

Highlight Halloween-related products or services with a short promotion. Make the deadline clear and ensure customers know whether delivery or collection is possible in time.

09. Launch a Halloween Poll or Quiz

Ask followers to choose between Halloween favorites, vote on themed products, or answer a fun seasonal question. Use the responses to encourage interaction and learn more about your audience.

10. Refresh Your Website with Halloween Creatives

Update your homepage banner, promotional graphics, or featured product section with a Halloween theme. A few targeted visual changes can make your existing marketing feel current without requiring a full redesign.

text:
Troy Aikman's 25-year career calling NFL games could be nearing its end, with the Hall of Fame quarterback saying there's only a 50-50 chance he'll return to television in 2027.

• Aikman's contract with ESPN expires after this season's Super Bowl, and the network has not offered him an extension. His longtime broadcasting partner Joe Buck recently secured a new six-year deal, raising additional questions about the future of their Monday Night Football partnership.

• Aikman's options elsewhere appear limited. CBS recently committed to J.J. Watt alongside Jim Nantz, Fox has Tom Brady under a 10-year, $375 million contract, and Amazon extended Kirk Herbstreit's deal. A move to another network remains possible, but no agreement has been reported.

• The three-time Super Bowl champion has also expressed interest in returning to the Dallas Cowboys in a front-office capacity. Aikman said he would seriously consider a conversation with Jerry Jones if the organization believed he could help improve the team.

Aikman has been a fixture in NFL broadcasting since 2001, including more than two decades alongside Buck. With his ESPN future unresolved, February's Super Bowl could mark the end of one of football's longest-running broadcasting partnerships.

text:
DATA BREACH ALERT: Panera Bread kiosks are leaking previous customers’ email addresses.

At the Carlisle, PA location, the Panera Bread self-service kiosk’s “Sign in with your email” field immediately offered prior users’ addresses in the predictive text bar—including a business email tied to our firm. Anyone standing at the machine can recover someone else’s email with a few keystrokes. From there it’s trivial to start account recovery, phishing, or worse.

Because of this exposure we have already retired that specific email address. We are treating it as compromised and have moved away from it. We strongly encourage anyone who has used a Panera kiosk (or has a MyPanera / Sip Club account) to do the same: change the email on the account if you can, enable two-factor authentication, and monitor for suspicious recovery attempts.

This is a basic shared-device failure: session data and form auto-complete were never cleared between customers. Proper kiosk configuration (ephemeral profiles, full session wipe on timeout/logout, auto-complete disabled on login fields) prevents exactly this. It is not complicated. It is the minimum standard when a public terminal touches customer accounts.

Companies that outsource their digital systems and support overseas routinely ship customer data to jurisdictions with weaker controls and higher fraud rates. That data ends up in the hands of scammers who already specialize in targeting Americans. When the same organizations also fail to lock down basic kiosk isolation, the exposure compounds.

My Company Berks Technology Solutions is U.S.-based (Pennsylvania and Florida). We do not outsource operations overseas. We do not sell or share client data. We configure shared systems, kiosks, and public-facing terminals so prior-user information does not survive to the next person. If your business runs any public terminal that collects emails, accounts, or payment data, this is the exact class of gap we close before it becomes a customer complaint or a headline.

Records obtained by KARE 11 show that CoreCivic offered to sell the Appleton prison to Minnesota in May 2025 for $75 million, including upgrades needed to reopen it.

“$75 Million vs. $495 Million: Who Is Being Held Accountable?”

There is a Somali proverb that says, “Miskiin ayaa misko la fuulo leh,” meaning, “It is always the poor and powerless who get trampled on.”

This proverb comes to mind when considering President Trump’s repeated attacks on Minnesota’s Somali community and the latest KARE 11 investigation.

According to KARE 11, a private prison in Appleton, Minnesota, was offered to the state for $75 million in 2025. Yet, just one year later, the Trump administration agreed to pay $495.6 million for the same facility—a difference of more than $420 million.

While this price difference alone does not establish fraud, it raises serious questions about government spending, oversight, and accountability.

Meanwhile, an entire Somali community faces public suspicion and collective blame over fraud cases involving particular individuals.

Fraud is fraud, regardless of who commits it. Those responsible should be held accountable, but no entire ethnic community should be condemned for the actions of a few.

The Somali proverb captures the injustice of selective scrutiny: the powerless often become easy targets, while those holding political and financial power face different levels of public attention.

Accountability should never depend on someone’s ethnicity, wealth, or political influence. The same standards must apply to everyone.

text:
Why EU volume beats the UAE label for IBRX uptake

The UAE approval is the broadest on paper — bladder plus metastatic lung cancer. But a broad label doesn’t move U.S. community urologists. Patient volume does. The EU has more than 150,000 new bladder cancer diagnoses a year across 27-plus countries, sold through Accord Healthcare’s 85-person sales force with a Dublin supply-chain subsidiary. That’s real-world experience at scale, from multiple countries at once — the kind community doctors can actually see and copy.

Community urologists are also the ones who got burned hardest by the BCG shortage. They watched shelves sit empty while patients waited, with no alternative to offer. That frustration is a motivator. When a drug arrives that doesn’t depend on TICE supply, these are the doctors most eager to try it. They’ve lived the problem.

Dr. Karim Chamie, the UCLA doctor who led the main ANKTIVA trial, put it simply: “What makes this really remarkable is its ability to spare patients from invasive procedures like a cystectomy, significantly enhancing quality of life.” Removing the bladder is major surgery with lifelong consequences. ANKTIVA’s 84% cystectomy-free rate at 3 years means most patients keep theirs.

Insurance is the other gatekeeper. Payers and pharmacy benefit managers are watching those cystectomy costs — $50,000 to $100,000 or more per patient, plus lifelong urinary diversion. An independent analysis by Valeris of over 267 million covered lives found ANKTIVA already leads coverage with 158 million lives for the CIS indication, ahead of Adstiladrin at 115 million and Keytruda at 113 million. The insurance side is already there, not hypothetical.

The Jan 6 PDUFA for the papillary sBLA is the domestic planning date. The Q4 BCG-naïve sBLA is the bigger swing — if that filing lands clean, ANKTIVA stops being a RESCUE DRUG and becomes a FRONT-LINE OPTION, which resets the entire uptake math. Dr. Angelo de Claro at the FDA said this approach “may also help guide the development of future treatments.” And on October 21, when the BCG-naïve database locked, Soon-Shiong posted: “Chemo free and save our lymphocytes is the 21st century mantra.”

In the Philippines, Halloween lands on the eve of Undas, so costume parties in Poblacion and across the Philippines and cemetery visits share the same long weekend. But where did the celebration come from, and how did it blend with the Filipino way of remembering the dead?

IT ALL BEGAN WITH SAMHAIN

Halloween traces back more than 2,000 years to Samhain, a festival of the Celtic peoples of Ireland, Britain and northern France. The World Book Encyclopedia says the name means "summer's end." Held around November 1, it closed the harvest and opened the dark winter season. Historian Nicholas Rogers told Live Science there is "no hard evidence" that it centered on the dead.

HOW THE CHURCH CALENDAR GAVE IT A NAME

The name itself is Christian. Encyclopaedia Britannica traces All Saints' Day on November 1 to Pope Gregory III (731–741); in 837, Pope Gregory IV extended it to the whole church.

In medieval England the feast was called All Hallows, so October 31 became All Hallows' Eve, which World Book notes was eventually shortened to Halloween.

WHERE THE CUSTOMS CAME FROM

According to History, trick-or-treating grew from two medieval British customs: "souling," when the poor went door to door for soul cakes and offered prayers for the dead in return, and "guising," when costumed children sang or recited poems for treats.

Lesley Bannatyne's Halloween: An American Holiday, an American History adds that some Celts wore disguises so roaming spirits would take them for fellow spirits. Jack-o'-lanterns began as carved turnips in Ireland and the immigrants to America switched to pumpkins.

THE FILIPINO WAY OF HONORING THE DEAD

Western-style Halloween only became common here under American colonial rule, but Filipinos already had customs of their own, and many survive today.

"Pangangaluluwa" is the original Filipino trick-or-treat. The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) describes groups going house to house at night before Undas, dressed as souls from purgatory and asking for alms. The UP Center for Ethnomusicology says the singers carol for money or rice, often to Spanish-era tunes like the habanera and the waltz, blending pre-colonial belief in ancestral spirits with Catholic practice.

Ilocano families offer "atang", an indigenous ritual of food for the dead, during All Saints' and All Souls' Days. For Ilocanos, November 1 becomes a family picnic among the graves.

At a wake or "lamay", relatives and friends stay up with the body until burial, often playing games to keep the grieving company.

And finally, Undas itself. According to SCJ Phiolippines, the name comes from the Spanish "honras", or "honors". On the eve, families clean graves; then they bring flowers, light candles, pray and keep vigil into the night, turning the cemetery into a reunion. Some parishes also hold a "Parade of Saints," with kids dressed as saints instead of ghouls.

Halloween may have reached us from Celtic Europe by way of America, but here it opens the door to something older, and entirely our own.

text:
One year ago, against this same team, he went down with a torn ACL and his season was over.

Tonight he caught the first touchdown of the game, and Green Bay won it.

Tucker Kraft is a tight end for the Green Bay Packers, and he is from Timber Lake, South Dakota.

Timber Lake has 513 people in it. It sits on the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe Reservation, and in 2024 they made him an honorary member of the tribe.

He lost his father Doug in 2013. He was 12 years old. He has two brothers, Cody and Tanner. His mother was seriously ill with an autoimmune disease around the same stretch.

Here is how he puts it.

He says he came from adversity, and that he figured out early he was going to have to make his own way.

At Timber Lake High School he played running back, middle linebacker and punter, because that is what you do at a school that size. As a senior he ran for 1,405 yards and 24 touchdowns and made first team All-State.

Then he went to South Dakota State, redshirted, and turned into a consensus All-American. He caught 65 passes for 780 yards there as a redshirt sophomore and made first team all conference twice. In 2022 that team won the national championship.

Power Four schools came after him with six figure offers to transfer out. He stayed in Brookings.

Green Bay took him in the third round, 78th overall, in 2023. About 100 people from Timber Lake watched that draft with him back home.

He played all 17 games as a rookie and scored his first NFL touchdown against Detroit. The next year he caught 50 passes for 707 yards and seven touchdowns, and tore a pectoral muscle in the spring on top of it.

Now here is the stretch that makes tonight land.

In Week 8 of last season he went for 143 yards and two touchdowns against Pittsburgh. That was the best game he had ever played.

Week 9 was Carolina. He came down wrong, the MRI said torn ACL, and that was his year.

In September the Packers gave him four years and 75 million dollars with 26 and a half million guaranteed up front. He got married in 2024. His daughter Charlotte was born a few months before the knee.

Be straight about it. A 12 yard touchdown is not a season. He is 25 and he has already torn a pectoral muscle and an ACL in three years, and tight ends who get hurt like that tend to keep getting hurt.

But think about the schedule for a second.

The last time he saw Carolina, he got carried off and did not play again.

He saw them again tonight and put the first points of the night on the board.

text:
Grocery prices keep climbing. But what if local grocers could cut their costs, and pass the savings on to you?  

Supporting grocers requires several things at once: addressing retail theft, cutting red tape, and lowering costs.   

Today with FAACTS SF we’re launching the District 5 Grocery Affordability Pilot, a new public-private partnership to tackle the costs piece.  

How it works: local grocers pool their orders with larger nonprofit food providers to get bulk pricing. In return, they offer up to 25% off a basket of everyday goods.  Grocers get better margins. You keep more money in your wallet.  

This model, called a Group Purchasing Organization (GPO), has already worked in Paris and Philadelphia. The pilot costs just $200K to launch and will support at least 5 stores. After that, it pays for itself with no further donations needed. Thanks to an initial check from @saikatc, we’re starting today.  

Thank you to FAACTS, @FarmingHope, Booker T. Washington, and all our partners who made this possible.

The American Dream has Slowly Disappeared -          On Purpose

BY DARRELL PITTS

The American middle-class dream rested on three forms of private property: a job, a car, and a house.

For generations, an ordinary American man could build an independent life on these foundations. 
A production job supplied the income to support a family. 
A reliable vehicle expanded the places he could work and the opportunities he could reach. 
A house gave his family lasting security and something he could eventually leave to his children.

His labor earned the property. 
His vehicle multiplied his choices. 
His home anchored his stability. 
Together, they gave him the practical freedom to refuse unacceptable conditions and pursue a better path.

It was all held together by free-market competition.

Under that system, employers competed for workers, automakers and dealers competed for buyers, and builders and sellers competed for homebuyers. 

The resulting pressure kept wages higher, vehicles more affordable, and housing more accessible than a system of concentrated ownership or directed outcomes would allow.

That foundation has been weakened by Socialist policy decisions in Washington, Socialist priorities set in corporate boardrooms, and the growing influence of Socialist large financial institutions.

These are shares managed for clients, yet the associated votes and private engagement give the managers leverage through director elections, shareholder proposals, and meetings with management; Alinsky j-jit-su.

On workforce policy, the record shows concrete pressure. 

BlackRock’s 2021 guidelines called for disclosure of workforce demographics—including race, ethnicity, and gender—and steps to advance diversity, equity, and inclusion, stating that shortcomings could lead it to vote against relevant directors. 

State Street’s earlier policies included potential votes against compensation committee chairs at S&P 500 companies that did not disclose their EEO-1 report, along with board-diversity expectations. 

Vanguard’s earlier guidelines included expectations on gender, racial, and ethnic diversity on boards. 

A major shareholder communicating expectations, with potential voting consequences for directors, gives management an incentive to obey. 

During 2025–2026 the Big Three weakened or removed several explicit diversity expectations due to President Trump's Orders. 

BlackRock’s February 2025 internal memo cited “significant changes to the U.S. legal and policy environment” when ending workforce representation goals and requirements for diverse interview slates, following the Trump administration’s January 2025 order directing enforcement against illegal discrimination and preferences associated with DEI. 

The record shows that a small number of asset managers possess influence across businesses that supply employment. 

Their documented use of voting leverage on workforce and board policies makes that concentration a legitimate cause for alarm. 

The practical effect on the American male's independence is clear: when production jobs disappear and concentrated owners can shape corporate priorities away from white American males, an ordinary working man has fewer routes to the income that once bought a car and a house.

The car  -

When transportation becomes unaffordable, working families lose more than purchasing power. 

They lose choices about where to live, where to work, and how to build a future. 

That is why overlapping investments by BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street across the automobile industry deserve scrutiny.

Competition on the sign does not necessarily mean separate financial interests behind the business. 

A study published in the Journal of Industrial Economics documented overlapping holdings by the three managers across major automakers, including Ford, GM, Toyota, Honda, BMW, Volkswagen, and Stellantis. 

The researchers explained how such common ownership can weaken incentives to compete. 

The connections continue downstream. 
AutoNation’s 2026 proxy reported BlackRock holding 6.7% and Vanguard 10.4%. 

Asbury Automotive reported 15.2% and 12%, respectively. Carvana and Cars. com further reach into auctions and valuations that affect how dealers obtain inventory and set prices. 

They establish a serious common-ownership question: whether shareholders with interests across competing businesses use their influence in ways that soften independent competition.

The middle-class affordability problem is measurable. 

In September 2026, overall used-car inventory rose 3.3% from a year earlier, yet inventory priced below $15,000 fell 16.2%. More cars were available, but fewer sat in the affordable range. 

For a dealer trying to sell dependable vehicles under $5,000, acquisition costs, auction fees, transportation, repairs, and overhead quickly erase the margin. 

Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis estimated that increased car prices  contributed between 34.7% and 61.7% of new-vehicle consumer inflation during 2019–2022. 

In the early 2020s the big 3’ stewardship guidelines explicitly linked votes against directors to insufficient progress on climate disclosures, transition plans, and workforce demographic metrics. 

Larry Fink stated that BlackRock would be increasingly disposed to vote against management on sustainability shortfalls. 

Parallel climate initiatives reinforced the signal. 
The same period saw regulatory and subsidy pressure favoring electric vehicles and higher-content trucks over conventional gasoline models. 

Post-COVID chip shortages amplified the price spike, yet the product-mix shift and governance pressure moved in the same direction: fewer low-cost, simple vehicles and higher average transaction prices. 

Overlapping Big 3 ownership of virtually all the companies producing the cars and all the companies buying the cars creates the common-ownership incentive researchers have examined as creating  softer competition.

An energy lawsuit from 11 states on behalf of coal companies against Black Rock, State Street and Van Guard makes shareholder influence more than abstract. 

States sued BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street, alleging they used holdings in competing coal producers to pressure lower production and raise energy prices. 

A federal court found the allegations—including circumstantial evidence—sufficient for antitrust claims to proceed. 

The lawsuit showed why overlapping ownership plus public commitments on non-financial criteria warrant investigation.

Fink’s 2020 statement that BlackRock would vote against directors for insufficient sustainability progress made corporate influence an expressly stated strategy. 

If that pressure discourages affordable production across competing companies, consumers can face higher costs even without any single firm owning the entire market. 

The practical stakes are clear: expensive vehicles narrow employment choices, longer loans consume money that could become savings or a down payment, and an economy that preserves margins while pricing ordinary families out of ownership fails a basic test of opportunity.

The Home -

Housing completes the picture. 

The same Big 3 investment managers hold positions across homebuilders, listing platforms, brokerages, mortgage companies, and large rental operators, while Blackstone-managed vehicles have acquired substantial portfolios of single-family homes.

Invitation Homes’ 2026 proxy lists Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street positions totaling approximately one-third of its shares. 

Blackstone-backed Tricon and Home Partners of America portfolios encompassed roughly 63,000 single-family homes in June 2026 disclosures, with ownership distributed among funds and joint ventures. 

BlackRock and Blackstone both illustrate the distance between an individual household seeking a home and the financial institutions investing across the housing economy.

The ownership map extends further. 

June 2026 filings show substantial Big Three positions in CoStar (Homes. com, Apartments. com), Zillow Group (Zillow, Trulia, Street Easy), and Rocket Companies. 

The Big 3 also hold stakes in major builders such as D.R. Horton and Lennar, and BlackRock has reported a position in Opendoor. 

The pattern of overlapping investment across competing or adjacent businesses in the housing chain is obvious.

When an institutional buyer purchases a house and builds the house for rental or sale, the property price becomes dependent on the political choice  of the Big 3. 

In a supply-constrained market, the same purchase places an aspiring homeowner in competition with professionally financed capital that can spread risk across thousands of units. 

GAO examination of six metropolitan areas found institutional investors owned between 4% and 22% of single-family rental homes. 

The public-policy question is whether families retain a realistic opportunity to acquire the asset themselves rather than continually rent access to it.

This concentration raises legitimate questions about competition: whether institutional purchasing tightens starter-home inventory locally, whether landlords gain pricing power in concentrated neighborhoods, whether consolidation raises transaction costs, and whether shareholder pressure favors rents and returns over greater supply. 

Establishing coordinated price control would require evidence of conduct beyond the ownership map. 

The map itself, however, shows institutional capital present at multiple points in the chain that once ran more directly from builder or seller to individual buyer.

None of this abolished private title. Americans can still own houses. 

The practical concern is whether ownership remains attainable through ordinary work when supply is constrained and professionally financed buyers compete for the same limited stock. 

A family can retain the legal right to buy while losing the income or facing the competition that makes purchase realistic. 

Private property protects independence only when ordinary people have a workable path to acquire it.

US Vice President JD Vance has offered to meet Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei personally to discuss a negotiated settlement to the war, The Washington Post reported Thursday, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations. Vance sent Rezaei a letter last week focused on the national interests of both countries in negotiations, according to the report. The official said Vance stressed that Washington’s central interest was ensuring Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon.

The vice president described Iran’s interests as rebuilding its war- and sanctions-hit economy and preserving its national sovereignty, while also conveying that Tehran needed to provide representatives empowered to discuss nuclear issues. 

The Trump administration views Rezaei, a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as the essential point of contact in Tehran and the only person who could build a consensus behind an agreement to halt Iran’s nuclear program, the Post reported.

A Colorado mother says her family was denied $12,000 in taxpayer-funded preschool benefits because she chose Catholic school for her children — and the case is now headed to the Supreme Court.

Erika Nagle, whose kids attend St. Mary Catholic School in Littleton, says the state's so-called "universal" preschool program excludes Catholic families by imposing participation requirements that burden their religious admissions practices. The program offers roughly $6,000 per child, and families can use it at the school of their choice — unless that school is Catholic.

Nagle says two preschools in the archdiocese have already shut down as families face pressure to leave faith-based education. The Supreme Court takes up the case Tuesday.

text:
Randy Smith
·
I feel it is my duty to explain to Americans why gas is so expensive today.
Politicians and evening news broadcasts love to tell you that the war in Iran is the sole reason gas prices are sky-high. This is a massive misconception that completely ignores history. ( the only thing we learn from history??….)
The truth is, the United States doesn't even buy oil from Iran. The war only caused a crisis because past government policies had already pushed our fuel system to the absolute edge.
Let me explain and ask you to consider
When a barrel of crude oil costs $103 today, you pay about $4.35 a gallon at the pump [Fortune]. But 15 years ago, when a barrel of oil cost that exact same $105, gas was only $3.51 a gallon.
So WHY is gas so much more expensive now for the exact same barrel of oil?
The United States is actually the largest oil producer in the entire world, pumping out record-breaking amounts of raw crude oil. But raw oil straight out of the ground is useless—you can't dump it into your car's gas tank. It has to go to a refinery to be cooked and cleaned into gasoline and diesel.
The PROBLEM is that past government administrations fundamentally broke the refining industry.
Over the last 30 years, Washington politicians passed massive, expensive environmental rules. They didn't directly order refineries to close, but they made running them so expensive that smaller, independent factories couldn't afford to stay open and went out of business.
On top of that, the government started offering huge tax-credit bribes to big oil companies if they stopped making regular fuel and switched to green biofuels instead.
ARE YOU FOLLOWING?
Because past governments squeezed the industry from both sides, America lost dozens of processing plants. The current remaining refineries are completely redlined, running at 98% capacity with absolutely zero backup plan!!
We have all the raw oil we could ever need, but because past government policies choked off our ability to refine it, those few remaining factories can charge a massive scarcity premium just to turn that cheap oil into gas.
Here’s who to be upset with:
📷 Bill Clinton (1993–2001)
• The Rule: He passed strict new anti-smog rules that forced factories to make special, complicated fuel mixes for big cities.

1. NY Daily News: Catalina Corona, 62, a longtime personal assistant to former Salomon Brothers banker Richard Schmeelk and his wife Priscilla, was sentenced to four years in federal prison and ordered to repay $9.6 million after pleading guilty to wire fraud. Prosecutors said she forged checks and exploited access to the couple’s accounts to steal millions between 2017 and 2024, spending heavily on luxury goods and electronics. The scheme continued after Schmeelk’s death in 2022 and was uncovered when a bank fraud alert prompted a direct call to his wife in early 2024.

2. Wall Street Journal: Weil, Gotshal & Manges plans to dissolve after losing many of its highest-earning partners and failing to secure a merger, leaders told employees Wednesday. The collapse of a profitable, prestigious firm with roughly 1,200 lawyers worldwide highlights the risks of intensifying competition for legal talent, as rivals offer compensation packages exceeding $20 million and departures of major rainmakers threaten firms’ stability.

3. The Times of Israel: With all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 Knesset seats, Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc 48 and the Arab parties a record 19, leaving neither main bloc with the 61 seats needed for a majority. Arab-party support could give the opposition a majority, but most of its leaders have ruled out such cooperation, creating a political stalemate. Turnout reached 77.9%, with more than 5.7 million ballots cast. President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders after receiving the certified results Wednesday, while election officials say the investigation into alleged irregularities will not affect the outcome.

4. NBC News: Alphabet shares suffered their worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, while Intel plunged 23% after hours Thursday after forecasting quarterly revenue below expectations and warning of negative cash flow this year. Intel faces weak PC demand, manufacturing bottlenecks, heavy expansion spending and a factory explosion expected to cost $600 million in revenue over two quarters. The declines underscore growing investor anxiety about how quickly massive AI investments will generate returns.

5. Financial Times: Mercedes-Benz pledged to remain in China despite a 34% decline in revenue there and a 21% drop in sales of its most profitable top-end models, contributing to a 51% fall in adjusted passenger-car operating profit to €560 million. The company cut its 2026 margin forecast to 2–3% and plans to reduce costs through local sourcing while improving driving-assistance technology. Meanwhile, Stellantis shares rose 6% after its quarterly operating loss narrowed to €331 million from €5.7 billion, while Aston Martin halved its adjusted operating loss to £24.9 million but reported rising net debt of £1.6 billion.

6. CMT News: Canada’s six largest banks raised their prime lending rates by a quarter percentage point to 4.70%, effective October 29, following the Bank of Canada’s increase in its policy rate to 2.50%. The changes will increase borrowing costs for variable-rate mortgages, home-equity lines of credit and other prime-linked loans; borrowers with fixed-payment variable mortgages will generally see more of each payment go toward interest.

7. Bloomberg News: Oil prices fell as renewed US-Iran diplomatic efforts eased concerns about a possible resumption of American strikes, with West Texas Intermediate slipping toward $102 a barrel and Brent near $115. President Trump confirmed negotiations through mediators but expressed uncertainty about their success. Despite the decline, Brent remained up 11% for October as continued conflict risks kept prices elevated, adding pressure on consumers and complicating efforts to control inflation.

8. 24/7 Wall Street News: Sam Altman warned that increasingly capable AI could uncover security vulnerabilities faster than organizations can fix them, requiring a shift toward AI-powered defenses. The article links this threat to a cybersecurity stock rally, with CrowdStrike up about 120% and Okta 146% this year. However, it cautions that much of the expected growth may already be reflected in share prices, noting CrowdStrike’s valuation of roughly 232 times earnings.

9. CHICAGO (AP): An alleged mass-shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, has shaken Chicago’s South Asian community, which prompted heightened security and calls for a hate-crime investigation. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, faces charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a firearm. Community leaders warn that rising anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hostility is threatening worshippers’ safety, while emphasizing their determination to continue religious celebrations and community life despite the fear.

10. Financial Times: Christine Lagarde will step down as European Central Bank president in February, nine months before her term ends in October 2027, triggering a major leadership reshuffle as inflationary pressures return. Her tenure spanned the pandemic, Russia’s war in Ukraine, soaring inflation and a US trade war. Lagarde has been in talks to chair the World Economic Forum, while potential successors include former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Bank for International Settlements chief Pablo Hernández de Cos. Her departure coincides with Isabel Schnabel’s early exit from the ECB board and the approaching end of chief economist Philip Lane’s term.

11. AgWeb News: Corn futures rebounded Wednesday, with December contracts closing above $4.50 a bushel, but analyst Mark Schultz cautioned that ongoing harvest pressure makes it too early to declare a bottom. Wheat continued falling amid weak exports and prospects for increased Black Sea supplies, while soybeans declined despite Chinese buying, weighed down by investment funds selling positions, stronger yields and a weaker Brazilian currency. A strong US dollar remains a challenge for grain exports. Livestock markets also weakened, with cattle retreating and hog futures hitting six-year lows amid sluggish demand.

12. Axios: House progressives plan to push for votes in 2027 on Medicare for All, abolishing or defunding ICE, restricting offensive weapons transfers to Israel, and tighter AI regulations. Their affordability agenda includes a living wage, universal childcare, expanded public housing and lifting the payroll tax cap to strengthen Social Security. According to Axios, the strategy aims to shape the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and a potential Democratic administration’s agenda in 2029, even if it forces divisive votes within the party.

13. KeNews: Rwanda’s milk bars, which specialize in milk rather than alcohol, are attracting tourists eager to experience a distinctive part of the country’s food culture. Serving fresh milk and other milk-based drinks, the bars also provide gathering places for locals, reflecting dairy’s role in everyday life. Al Jazeera’s Marah Rayan explores how this simple tradition has become a visitor attraction and a window into Rwandan culture.

14.  Yahoo Finance: DoorDash announced a $17 billion deal to acquire grocery-delivery rival Instacart, expanding beyond its core restaurant-delivery business. The offer values Instacart at $65 per share, a 26% premium to its October 22 closing price, with 75% of the transaction paid in cash. Instacart’s board unanimously approved the acquisition, which aims to combine its grocery expertise with DoorDash’s delivery network. DoorDash shares rose more than 5% in premarket trading, while Instacart shares edged lower.

AI × Global Tech Markets | October 30, 2026 · Morning Brief
AWS revenue surged 39%, yet Amazon shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading. The more concerning number wasn't cloud revenue growth—it was Amazon's trailing 12-month free cash flow: negative $42.4 billion.

Core thesis: AI cloud computing has demonstrated strong demand. But investors are now demanding a second scorecard: Can revenue growth translate into sustainable cash returns?

This could increasingly favor AI infrastructure suppliers that generate positive cash flow over cloud platforms still making enormous upfront investments.

1. Amazon: AWS accelerates, but free cash flow deteriorates

On October 29, Amazon reported its Q3 2026 results.

AWS revenue reached $46 billion, up 39.3% year over year, its fastest growth in nearly five years.

AWS operating income reached $17.8 billion, implying an operating margin of approximately 38.7%.
Trailing 12-month operating cash flow increased 29% to $168.3 billion.
However, trailing 12-month free cash flow fell from positive $14.8 billion to negative $42.4 billion.
Amazon maintained its 2026 cash capital expenditure outlook of approximately $220 billion.
CEO Andy Jassy projected AWS revenue growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028.
Why it matters: AWS is growing faster, but Amazon is consuming more cash.

That doesn't necessarily mean its AI investments are unprofitable. Data centers require substantial upfront spending before generating revenue.

However, strong demand and signed contracts alone cannot establish that returns on invested capital will be attractive.

Who is affected? GPU manufacturers, server suppliers, networking companies, and power and cooling providers benefit from infrastructure expansion. Amazon shareholders face greater capital recovery risk.

What to watch: Whether free cash flow recovers as AWS growth materializes.

Source: Amazon Investor Relations

2. AWS Agents: Token usage grows 17-fold

Amazon also disclosed significant growth in enterprise AI adoption.

Bedrock token processing volume increased nearly 17-fold year over year.

Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock increased nearly sevenfold.
AgentCore attracted tens of thousands of customers.
Agent deployments during Q3 exceeded the combined total of the preceding three quarters.
AWS introduced a public preview of Bedrock Managed Agents powered by OpenAI models.
Why it matters: Enterprise AI competition is expanding beyond model quality into agent deployment, security, orchestration, and operational infrastructure.

But 17-fold token growth does not imply 17-fold revenue growth, much less profit growth.

Potential beneficiaries: Agent infrastructure, inference platforms, security, and observability providers.

Key risk: Falling inference prices could offset increasing usage.

Source: AWS News

3. Intel: Data center revenue jumps 78%, but Foundry remains deeply unprofitable

On October 29, Intel reported Q3 2026 results.

Total revenue reached $16.5 billion, up 21%.

Data Center and AI revenue increased 78% to $7.3 billion.
Intel Foundry revenue increased 58% to $6.7 billion.
However, Foundry still recorded an operating loss of $1.85 billion.
Q4 revenue guidance was $15 billion–$16 billion, below Q3 revenue.
An important distinction: Intel Foundry revenue includes substantial internal transactions. It should not be interpreted entirely as external customer demand.

My interpretation: Intel's data center CPU business is showing meaningful improvement, but a sustainable Foundry turnaround remains unproven.

AI infrastructure expansion benefits more than GPU suppliers. However, Intel Foundry still needs to demonstrate external customer traction, competitive manufacturing yields, and a sustainable reduction in losses.

Source: Intel Investor Relations

4. Linde: AI semiconductor expansion is translating into cash flow

On October 29, Linde reported:

Q3 revenue of $9.4 billion, up 9%.

Adjusted EPS of $4.59, up 9%.
Operating cash flow of $3.17 billion.
Free cash flow of $1.78 billion.
Project backlog of $11 billion.
Electronics was an important contributor to volume growth, while Asia-Pacific organic growth reached 8%, supported by electronics and chemicals-related demand.

Why it matters: Unlike cloud operators investing heavily ahead of future demand, some industrial gas suppliers are already generating positive cash flow from semiconductor capacity expansion.

Linde is not a pure-play AI company, however, and its results also reflect broader industrial demand.

Source: Linde Investor Relations

5. Air Liquide: AI infrastructure spending extends into semiconductor materials

On October 29, Air Liquide disclosed:

Comparable Q3 Electronics revenue growth of 12%.

Electronics investment during the first nine months of 2026 approaching twice the full-year 2025 level.
An investment backlog of €6.2 billion.
More than €170 million of new investment in Japan supporting semiconductor manufacturing.
More than $170 million of investment in Indiana to supply ultra-high-purity gases to SK hynix's new facility.
The company also reaffirmed its margin improvement objectives for 2026 and 2027.

Why it matters: HBM and advanced semiconductor expansion creates demand not only for manufacturing equipment but also for specialty gases, materials, and fabrication infrastructure.

However, announced investments are not the same as realized revenue. Factory commissioning and production ramp-ups remain important.

Source: Air Liquide Investors

Three expectations to test

AWS: Can Amazon deliver its projected 40%+ AWS growth in 2027–2028 while restoring free cash flow?

Intel: Can rapid data center growth translate into smaller Foundry losses and more external manufacturing contracts?
Semiconductor materials: Can Linde and Air Liquide convert their investment pipelines into higher earnings without materially reducing returns on capital?
The investment debate

Which part of the AI infrastructure value chain offers the better risk-adjusted opportunity?

A. Cloud platforms: Faster revenue growth, but substantial capital requirements and longer cash recovery periods.

B. Industrial gases and semiconductor materials: Potentially slower growth, but some companies already demonstrate positive free cash flow.

The real question is no longer whether AI demand exists. It's who will retain the most cash profit after the next infrastructure expansion cycle.

text:
Pace Handicapping Thought of the Day

  The Science of Energy Distribution

           !!!Paragons & Energizers!!!

Understanding the Architecture of Energy Distribution

“The fastest horse does not necessarily possess the most effective energy distribution. The advantage belongs to the horse whose expenditure of energy allows it to meet the demands of the competition.”

Beyond the Traditional Measurement of Speed

One of the fundamental lessons of the Sartin Methodology is that speed, by itself, tells us surprisingly little about how a horse will perform against a particular group of competitors. Two horses can finish a race in nearly identical times while getting there in completely different ways. One may establish its advantage through superior early velocity, forcing the competition to expend additional energy simply to remain within striking distance. Another may surrender ground during the opening stages but preserve enough energy to become considerably more effective as the race progresses. Both horses have demonstrated ability, but that ability is expressed through different patterns of energy distribution. Understanding those differences is essential because a horse's effectiveness is determined not simply by how fast it can run, but by how its particular abilities interact with the demands imposed by the competition.

The ENERGY program was developed to examine these relationships beyond the limitations of conventional speed figures and final-time comparisons. Among its analytical components are Paragon A, Paragon B, and the Energizer, three measurements that provide additional perspectives on how horses distribute their available energy. These were never intended to function as independent guarantees of success. Their usefulness comes from examining them alongside the Dream Race, matchup deficiencies, supporting velocity measurements, and projected variegates. Each contributes another piece of information to a much larger picture, and understanding how those pieces fit together is where the real education begins.

Understanding Paragon A

Paragon A provides a perspective on early competitive ability within the ENERGY program. Its rankings help identify horses whose energy characteristics may give them an advantage during the opening stages of the matchup. However, there is an important distinction between possessing an early advantage and possessing the ability to maintain that advantage throughout the race. A horse capable of establishing position through superior initial velocity may perform exceptionally well when its opponents offer little resistance. Put that same horse against competitors capable of matching its early expenditure, and the situation can change dramatically. What previously appeared to be a comfortable advantage may suddenly become an expensive proposition.

This is why Paragon A cannot be interpreted without considering the competition. An early advantage is meaningful only when we understand what the horse must do to establish it and what that expenditure may cost later in the race. The original ENERGY workbook provides an excellent illustration through a six-furlong race at Golden Gate Fields. A horse identified as TEMP ranked first in Paragon A and Early EXDC despite having raw total energy below the field average. Its early matchup deficiency was zero, indicating that its early competitive characteristics remained significant even though its overall energy measurement was not among the strongest in the field.

That example reinforces a lesson frequently overlooked in conventional handicapping. A horse does not necessarily need the highest total energy to possess a meaningful competitive advantage. Sometimes the distribution of that energy is more important than the amount being measured. TEMP demonstrated that a favorable relationship within one component of the matchup could exist even when another measurement appeared comparatively ordinary.

Understanding Paragon B

Paragon B examines the competitive relationship from another perspective. While Paragon A emphasizes the early component of the matchup, Paragon B provides a contrasting evaluation that should be considered alongside sustained ability and the supporting energy measurements. The distinction matters because early superiority and overall effectiveness are not always the same thing. A horse may possess enough initial velocity to establish command but lack the distribution necessary to preserve that advantage when the competition becomes more demanding. Another contender may not demonstrate the same early strength yet possess characteristics that allow it to maintain velocity more effectively as the race develops.

Rather than forcing these different abilities into one universal ranking, ENERGY presents the Paragons separately. That separation encourages the handicapper to examine the underlying relationships instead of assuming that the horse ranked first in one category must also be superior in every other respect. When Paragon A and Paragon B identify different contenders, the disagreement should not automatically be viewed as a problem. It may be telling us something important about the competitive makeup of the field.

Consider a matchup in which one horse demonstrates superior early characteristics while another possesses a more favorable relationship among the remaining energy measurements. Neither advantage exists in isolation. Their significance depends upon the type of competition expected to develop and whether the horse can express its particular strengths under those circumstances. The objective is not to declare one Paragon universally superior to the other, but to understand what each contributes to the evaluation.

The Role of the Energizer

The Energizer introduces another analytical dimension by identifying a contender whose energy characteristics deserve attention within the projected matchup. It appears alongside the Paragons and variegate information in the ENERGY summary, giving the handicapper another reference point for evaluating the competitive relationships among the horses.

To appreciate its importance, we must remember that ENERGY does not examine horses as though they are running individual time trials. Every horse contributes something to the competitive environment. A strong early contender may influence how much energy its opponents must expend during the opening stages, while a horse possessing greater sustained characteristics may become increasingly effective as those early expenditures begin to take their toll. These relationships are central to the methodology because the competitive environment can change the effectiveness of an otherwise impressive performance.

The Energizer should not be mistaken for another conventional speed figure or a simple ranking of total energy. Its purpose is to provide an additional perspective within the program's broader evaluation. The original Kansas City ENERGY workbook illustrates this through the same Golden Gate Fields example discussed earlier. TEMP occupied the leading Paragon A position, while another contender, M00-3, appeared as the leading Paragon B selection and Energizer.

That distinction is worth examining because the program identified different horses through its separate analytical components. Rather than producing one answer and repeating it across every category, ENERGY revealed that different contenders possessed different competitive characteristics. This is precisely why its output should be studied as a collection of related measurements rather than reduced to a single ranking.

Supporting Energy Measurements

The Paragons and Energizer become considerably more informative when examined alongside the measurements introduced throughout this series. Early Pace evaluates velocity during the initial stages of the race, while Sustained Pace considers the relationship between early performance and finishing ability. Factor X examines the relationship between the first and third fractions, providing another perspective on how a horse distributes velocity across different portions of the race. Hidden Energy and Late Pace contribute additional information about the ability to maintain effective velocity as the race progresses.

The matchup deficiencies are equally important. EMUV represents the early matchup deficiency, while SMUV examines the sustained component. UXR combines those deficiencies into a broader measurement of how closely a contender approaches the theoretical requirements established by the Dream Race. These measurements were not designed to tell us exactly the same thing. Each examines a different aspect of the competitive relationship, and their value comes from understanding what happens when those measurements are considered together.

A horse may rank favorably in one of the Paragons while displaying substantial deficiencies elsewhere. Another may lack a particularly impressive individual ranking but demonstrate greater consistency across several measurements. Those differences deserve investigation because they reveal something that a simple speed comparison cannot. The important question is not merely which horse occupies the highest position on the screen, but whether the various measurements support a coherent picture of competitive effectiveness.

Energy Distribution and the Variegates

This brings us back to the variegates discussed in Chapter Five. Early, Presser, and Sustained describe different patterns of energy distribution and the competitive requirements associated with them. Their significance becomes clearer when we examine how the Paragons, Energizer, and supporting measurements relate to the projected matchup.

A favorable early measurement may become particularly meaningful when the competitive environment allows a horse to establish position without excessive expenditure. However, when the competition demands greater early effort, the ability to preserve velocity becomes increasingly important. Under those circumstances, sustained characteristics may deserve greater consideration because the horse that appears strongest during the opening stages is not necessarily the one best equipped to remain effective through the finish.

The original ENERGY documentation also emphasizes the importance of the information supplied to the program. Inconsistent contender selection or performances that do not accurately represent a horse's competitive characteristics can distort the relationships among the measurements. A computer can perform its calculations with remarkable consistency, but it cannot determine whether the information entered provides a meaningful representation of the race. That responsibility remains with the handicapper.

The Science Behind the Numbers

Perhaps the greatest contribution of the Paragons and Energizer is that they reinforce one of the most important principles underlying the Sartin Methodology: thoroughbred performance cannot be adequately explained through a single measurement. Speed figures, fractional velocities, total energy, and individual rankings all provide useful information, but none can independently describe the full complexity of a competitive matchup.

Paragon A, Paragon B, and the Energizer expand that perspective by examining different dimensions of energy distribution. Their purpose is not to eliminate uncertainty or provide an automatic selection, but to help explain why horses possessing similar apparent ability may perform very differently when confronted with the same competition. When the measurements agree, they may strengthen the interpretation of a contender's competitive characteristics. When they disagree, the differences can be equally educational because they encourage us to investigate what each measurement is revealing.

The real advancement comes when we stop treating every ranking as a separate contest to identify the best horse and begin understanding how the measurements describe the relationship between the competitors. A horse may possess exceptional early velocity but encounter a matchup that makes expressing that advantage difficult. Another may appear less impressive through conventional measurements yet possess an energy distribution better suited to the demands of the race.

Ultimately, ENERGY asks us to move beyond the familiar question of which horse is fastest and consider something considerably more revealing: how is that speed produced, how is it distributed, and how effectively can it be sustained against today's competition?

That is the central lesson of the Paragons and Energizer. Energy distribution must be understood as a competitive relationship, not an isolated statistic. The horse possessing the greatest apparent ability is not necessarily the horse best equipped to express that ability when the demands of the race begin to unfold.

This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.
