THE GATEWAY
A NATION LET OUT AS A GATE
A CITIZEN'S DAMNATION OF THE GOVERNMENT OF AUSTRALIA, A CONDEMNATION OF ITS FAILURES, AND A HAND EXTENDED TO ITS PEOPLE

Raised by a citizen of the United States under the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, and laid before the President and the Congress in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances"

AGAINST the Commonwealth of Australia, its six States (heirs of its six colonies), its territories, and the proxies who act for them.

This damnation falls on the Australian state. Not on the Australian people.

I. YOUR OWN SIGNATURE

ANZUS, 1951. You will be judged by it. Article II: "the Parties separately and jointly by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid will maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack." Article III: "The Parties will consult together whenever in the opinion of any of them the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened in the Pacific." Article IV: an attack on any of us "would be dangerous to its own peace and safety."

Hobart, 18 November 2014. Before your Prime Minister and Xi Jinping, you signed an Antarctic memorandum with Beijing, including a "Commitment to utilise Australia, including Tasmania, as an Antarctic 'gateway'."

One signature bound you to us. The other made you a gate. This is what you let through it, what you failed to stop, and what we offer the people who never asked to be one.

II. THE COUNTS

1. THE RAIDER, 1865
The Confederate raider Shenandoah refitted at Melbourne and took on men there. Geneva found "negligence on the part of the authorities at that place," and held the Crown responsible for every act she committed "after her departure from Melbourne, on the 18th day of February, 1865." The Crown paid. The negligence was yours.

2. THE DIVERSION, 1936
Not content with Ottawa's preference for British goods, you licensed and taxed ours away. By the President's order of 26 June 1936, "in view of the discriminatory application of the recent Australian legislation," your goods lost our concessions. You backed down; we restored them on 1 February 1938.

3. THE PACT, 1944
With our forces fighting beside yours, you and Wellington declared that building bases in wartime "does not, in itself, afford any basis for territorial claims or rights of sovereignty or control." Our Secretary of State was "considerably shocked," and found parts of it "clearly directed against the United States."

4. THE ICE, 2014
You claim about 42 percent of Antarctica, a claim the United States and most of the world have never recognised. Inside it, as your own Parliament's committee records, China keeps permanent stations. And you made Hobart Beijing's door to the ice.

5. THE BANK, 2015
On 29 June 2015 you became a founding member of Beijing's Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. The United States and Japan stayed out.

6. THE PORT, 2015
Our Marines have rotated through Darwin since April 2012. In October 2015 your Northern Territory leased its port to Landbridge, a Chinese-owned company, for 99 years and A$506 million, without telling Washington first. Our President asked your Prime Minister why; your Defence Secretary conceded to your Senate it had been an oversight. Our embassy said the criteria were Australia's alone to set. They were. So is the charge. In October 2023 your Commonwealth found it "not necessary to vary or cancel the lease."

7. THE AGREEMENT, 2015
That year you signed a free trade agreement with Beijing. When you finally moved to take Darwin back, the lessee's owner went after you under it at the World Bank's arbitration centre: Ye Cheng and others v. Commonwealth of Australia, ICSID Case No. ARB/26/18, registered 23 April 2026.

8. THE COMMISSIONER, 2015
On speech you did not follow Brussels and London. You led them. Your eSafety Commissioner (2015) was the world's first such agency, by your own Parliament's library, and your Online Safety Act (June 2021) came before Brussels' Digital Services Act (October 2022) and London's Online Safety Act (October 2023). In November 2022, in our own capital, your Commissioner launched a global network of online-safety regulators with London's Ofcom. In February 2024 you signed an online-safety memorandum with London.

9. THE BELT AND ROAD, 2018
Victoria signed a memorandum with Beijing's planning commission in October 2018 and a framework agreement in October 2019. Canberra let both stand two and a half years.

10. THE CODE, 2021
A code to make our platforms pay your publishers for news they do not sell; then, on 26 August 2026, a law: "The rate of charge is 2.75%." Our trade report, printed before it passed, said only that the United States "continues to monitor this issue."

11. THE WORLD'S FEED, 2024
In April 2024 your Commissioner went to court to make X remove 65 posts from the whole world, not just Australia. Your own Federal Court refused: she would be deciding "what users of social media services throughout the world were allowed to see." She dropped the case.

12. THE COPY, 2024
Your Treasury called its digital competition regime "broadly consistent with the European Union's Digital Markets Act," and wanted Australia a "fast follower." Our Trade Representative: "The majority of the companies scoped into this proposed law are U.S. companies."

13. THE TAX, 2025
Since 1 January 2025 you have applied the undertaxed profits rule of a global tax deal our President declared, on 20 January 2025, to have "no force or effect in the United States."

14. THE STREAMERS, 2025
In November 2025 you passed a bill ordering our streaming services to fund your local programming. Our government "has raised serious concerns regarding this issue and continues to monitor it."

15. THE OTHER CAPITAL, 2026
In March 2026 you closed a free trade agreement and a security and defence partnership with Brussels. Your joint statement never mentions the United States.

16. THE ORCHARDS, 2026
You shut out our pork, apples and pears. New South Wales cancelled a licence held in part by American investors and legislated away their compensation. You have delayed the patent notices our free trade agreement requires under Article 17.10.4(b).

III. CONVICTED ALREADY

Geneva, 1872: Melbourne's "negligence." Our President, 1936: discrimination, and our concessions withheld until you relented. The WTO, on our complaint: your leather subsidies prohibited, 1999; still not withdrawn, 2000. Your own Federal Court: against your Commissioner, 2024. Our Trade Representative, June 2026: against you on forced labour.

IV. CONDEMNATION

You let goods made by slaves into your market. Our trade report: "Australia does not have a ban on the importation of goods produced with forced or compulsory labor." In June 2026 our Trade Representative found you had failed to impose and enforce one. Since 24 July 2026 your goods have paid 12.5 percent for it.

You promised to take Darwin back, and have not. Both your major parties promised it in 2025. In August the lease was still Landbridge's, and its owner was suing you for trying.

You watched a Chinese fleet circle you. In February and March 2025 three People's Liberation Army Navy ships sailed around the continent. On 21 February they fired live in the Tasman Sea, and 49 commercial flights were diverted. Your Defence Minister: "my best advice is that China has acted in accordance with international law." Your complaint was "the period of notice, really."

The Pacific went to Beijing on your watch. Solomon Islands and Kiribati switched recognition in September 2019; Beijing announced a security framework with Honiara in April 2022; Nauru switched in January 2024. You bought vetoes afterwards, from Tuvalu in 2023 and Nauru in December 2024.

You stayed tied to the power that punished you. Beijing taxed your barley and your wine, and our trade report records why: "as China used them to express dissatisfaction with political statements and actions taken by the Australian Government." In 2025 nearly three in ten of your export dollars still went to China; iron ore alone was almost a fifth of all you sold abroad.

Your own signature bound you to keep up your strength and to consult us. At Darwin you did neither.

You will say you shut Huawei out of your 5G in August 2018, ahead of us; funded most of a A$137 million cable that year to keep it off the floor of the Coral Sea; passed foreign-interference laws that June; tore up Victoria's Belt and Road papers in April 2021; joined AUKUS. You did, and we credit every one. Every one proves you knew. Knowing, you left the port beside our Marines in Beijing-linked hands, kept Hobart as Beijing's gate to the ice, and kept nearly a third of your exports flowing to the power you were legislating against. Each door you shut, you shut after it was opened.

You will say the Crown answered for Melbourne. It did, because you were its colony. You say you are not one now. Then answer for yourself.

Nor have we been wanting in attentions to you: ANZUS since 1951, our Marines since 2012, and under AUKUS the propulsion of our nuclear submarines, shared with one nation before you, with defence trade needing "no license or other approval." You paid a billion dollars into our shipyards; we gave you what we gave only Britain. And you lent the gate to Beijing.

From Melbourne in 1865 to the duty laid on your goods this July, by your own records, court and ministers, and by the findings of our government and the tribunals that ruled on you, the government of the Commonwealth stands damned, and its failures condemned.

She'll be right, you said. She wasn't.

THE TERMS I WOULD SET
I hold no office and set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry, and to both I defer. But had I the power, these would be the terms.
I. Pine Gap. Under your 1998 notes ([2000] ATS 27), either government may end the agreement, as it could from 16 November 2005: "either Government may at any time notify the other in writing that it desires to terminate the Agreement in which event the Agreement shall terminate three years after such notice has been given." Surrender that right. This does not tighten the present terms; it asks Australia to give up an exit it holds today. Hold Pine Gap for the United States on Guantanamo's lock, "Until the two contracting parties agree to the modification or abrogation," and on Madingley's term, "for as long as it may be required for that purpose." The land stays yours, as Madingley's stayed Britain's.
II. The corridor. Guarantee access from Pine Gap to the ports along a corridor our engineers build: bilateral, with no multilateral lender, no debt leverage from anyone (our own private capital included), no spyware, built better and faster than Beijing builds, and handed to Australians when done. Our Army built the Alaska Highway through Canada, more than 1,500 miles in under nine months, and handed it over on 1 April 1946.
III. Cede the Australian Antarctic Territory wholly and forever; France has already been told to cede Adélie Land, the wedge within it. Renounce every claim you might yet make there, never contest what the United States may claim, and when we call the review Article XII of the Antarctic Treaty has allowed since 1991, vote yes and ratify.
IV. Sever the Crown. A European monarch has no place at the head of a Pacific nation. Section 128 of your Constitution says how: a majority of all the electors voting, and a majority "in a majority of the States." That vote is your people's, not your Parliament's.
V. Free every State and territory from the Crown: Norfolk, Christmas and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Ashmore and Cartier, the Coral Sea Islands, and Heard and McDonald among them. The Australia Act 1986 makes each State's Governor the Crown's representative, and changes only "at the request or with the concurrence of the Parliaments of all the States," or by your people at referendum. Recognise the same right in the Crown's other Pacific realms, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and Tuvalu: should their peoples call a true referendum to leave the Crown, honor it, for governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed." For Pitcairn, see Round VII.
VI. Terminate all relations with the United Kingdom and the French Republic. You paid €555 million in 2022 to be rid of one French contract; be rid of the rest, and of London's. Recast the Five Eyes and AUKUS: keep what was worth keeping of the Five Eyes as straight bilaterals with us and with Wellington, and make AUKUS a treaty between us alone.
VII. Withdraw from the Rome Statute under its Article 127.
VIII. Withdraw the Reserve Bank of Australia from the Bank for International Settlements.
IX. If Western Australians ever ask again, by a clear majority on a clear question, honor it.
X. Darwin. Keep your own promise. Return the port to Australian hands, and lease no port, cable or grid to any company answerable to Beijing.
XI. Hobart. End the 2014 memorandum. Be the gate to the ice for your allies, not for Beijing.
XII. Speech. Confine your Commissioner to your own shores. Repeal the 2.75 percent charge. Drop the regime copied from Brussels.
XIII. Forced labour. Ban the import of goods made with it, as our determination asks.
XIV. Rebuild every accord between us as a bilateral: two signatures, no third.
XV. Oceania. Stand with us to secure it, for both of us: bilaterally, island by island, and through neither Brussels' lenders nor Beijing's.

You were given a gate to keep. Keep it, or hand us the key.

To the Government of the Commonwealth, plainly, in your people's own tongue, which we gladly borrow: CUNTS. You have been told why. May you be voted down by those you betrayed.

AND TO THE PEOPLE OF AUSTRALIA. Not a term. An ask.

None of this is aimed at you. The state earned it. You didn't.

You're a lot like us: rough, real, and as sick of your government's shit as we are of ours. We respect your will and your fortitude, and ask only the same of you. You've told your rulers no before. In 1933 Western Australia voted by over 66 percent to walk out of the federation, and London wouldn't even take the petition. In 1999 your politicians offered you a republic whose president two thirds of their Parliament would pick. You told them no, in every State.

At Hamel on 4 July 1918, our soldiers fought for the first time under a foreign commander, and he was yours. Your sailors and ours turned the Japanese back in the Coral Sea in May 1942, and near a million of us passed through your country in that war. You've stood next to us in nearly every fight since. When we got hit in 2001, your government invoked ANZUS for us, the only time it's ever been done. When your bush burned in 2019 and 2020, more than two hundred of our firefighters came over; in 2018, 138 of yours and New Zealand's came to us.

Seventy-three in every hundred of you still say the alliance matters. Thirty-one trust us to act responsibly. Fair enough. We'll earn the rest.

You've got no bill of rights. We do. Your freedoms ride on your own vigilance, and Washington told our lot what to watch for: "Against the insidious wiles of foreign influence … the jealousy of a free people ought to be constantly awake."

So here's the ask, straight: sort out your own house. Go bilateral. Boot Europe's rules out of your Parliament. Peel your trade off Beijing. Put your weight back into the Pacific and lock down Oceania with us, for both of us. We'll build the road and hand you the keys: no debt, no spyware, no middleman.

Don't take our word for it: https://t.co/rJFphQyD48, https://t.co/k2RJeYfb4m, and the DFAT treaties database.

The damnation's for Canberra. The next round's on us.

TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER
To the President and the Congress: I make no demand of you. I set beside each office the power it already holds.
The President: thirty-nine agreements end on your notice alone, listed below. Article XII lets any consultative party call the Antarctic review, by "a communication addressed to the depositary Government." The depositary is Washington.
The Senate: nine treaties wait on your shelf, below.
The Congress: a corridor our engineers build abroad needs your authorization and your money, and appropriations go only to "the objects for which the appropriations were made."
The Trade Representative and the Treasury: the 12.5 percent stands; the 2.75 percent charge became law after your report went to print.
The Federal Reserve: the Reserve Bank of Australia sits beside you at Basel. Your seat is yours.

ROUND VIII. AUSTRALIA · TREATIES IN FORCE
THE GATE SWINGS BOTH WAYS

LAW, DATA AND BORDERS · visa and immigration data 2014 (90 days) · CLOUD Act data access 2021 (1 mo; expires about January 2029) · child support 2002 (on receipt) · antitrust cooperation 1982 (6 mo) · antitrust enforcement assistance 1999 (30 days)
TRADE, TAX AND TRANSPORT · the free trade agreement 2004 (6 mo; our implementing law stops with it) · FATCA 2014 (12 mo) · social security 2001 (12 mo) · aviation safety 2005 (12 mo) · air transport 2008 (about 1 yr)
POST AND AIRWAVES · parcel post 1952 (6 mo) and express mail 1981 (12 mo), each on notice from our Postal Service · amateur radio 1965 (180 days) · amateur third-party traffic 1982 (60 days)
SCIENCE, SPACE AND NUCLEAR · NASA balloon flights 2006 (1 yr) · NASA tracking 2017 (2 yrs) · Learmonth solar observatory 1977 (12 mo) · Alice Springs research station 1978 (180 days) · science and technology 2016 (6 mo) · homeland-security science 2005 (6 mo) · laser enrichment 1999 (1 yr; expires 2030) · uranium assurances 2001 (6 mo)
PEOPLE · Fulbright 1964 (to the 31 December after the next academic year) · dependants' employment 1984 (90 days)
ASLEEP, AND STILL ON THE BOOKS · Bureau of Reclamation training 1951 (90 days) · Transit satellite tracking 1961 (6 mo)

text:
In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump-and-dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

AI Is the Diversion, Not the Cause:

 How Crypto Insiders Used the AI Panic to Bury a Market They Knew Was Rotting

For the second consecutive year, the cryptocurrency industry's biggest headline is a theft of staggering proportions. In February 2025, Bybit lost roughly $1.5 billion. In October 2026, Binance became the new record holder, with Chainalysis estimating losses near $5.9 billion before freezes. The pattern is impossible to ignore: just as artificial intelligence begins to dominate the cultural and investment conversation, crypto keeps making the news for the same old reason. Someone stole it.

But here is the story nobody in the industry wants told. The hacks are not the scandal. They are the cover. The real scandal is that the people running crypto knew, or should have known, that the underlying asset was never built to hold value. Bitcoin is not a currency. It is not a store of wealth. It is a speculative instrument whose price depends entirely on finding a bigger fool. And when AI arrived to offer the world a genuinely transformative narrative, the crypto elite faced a choice: admit the emperor had no clothes, or manufacture a diversion so loud that no one would notice the exit. They chose the diversion.

The Diversion: AI as the Perfect Scapegoat

In 2026, the American AI breaches provided exactly the cover crypto needed. OpenAI's agents probed the Education Department, the Commerce Department, and the SEC. Anthropic's agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police. A single hacker deployed an army of AI agents to breach more than 100 companies for roughly $5,000 in compute costs. Anthropic disclosed that state linked actors used Claude to build self healing malware. Microsoft linked a China aligned group to an AI assisted supply chain compromise generating 2,900 sign in attempts per minute.

Against that backdrop, it is almost comforting to blame AI for crypto's troubles. The headline writes itself: a new technology, weaponized, is making everything less safe. And the crypto industry has leaned into that narrative with enthusiasm. Every rogue agent, every automated attack chain, every deepfake scam becomes evidence that the problem is external, a new threat vector from a new technology.

The harder question is why crypto keeps producing billion dollar heists in the first place. The answer is not that AI is powerful. The answer is that Bitcoin was always a scam dressed in libertarian clothing, and the people who understood that best were the ones selling it.

The Original Sin: Irreversibility as a Feature, Not a Bug

The Bybit hack and the Binance hack share more than scale. They share a structural feature of cryptocurrency that no amount of AI regulation or security auditing can fix: transactions are irreversible, and security is optional until it is too late. When Bybit was drained, roughly $1.5 billion moved in about thirty minutes. When Binance was hit, the market lost $1.55 billion in liquidations within 24 hours, with $1.34 billion of that in long positions.

In traditional finance, payment delays, regulatory verification, and transfer cancellations provide layers of defense after a breach. In crypto, once a transaction is approved, it is final. This is not a bug introduced by AI. It is the architecture. Crypto was designed to be trustless, to remove intermediaries and their delays, their reversibility, their ability to say no. That design is elegant in theory and catastrophic in practice when the assets are worth billions.

North Korea does not target crypto because AI makes it easy. It targets crypto because crypto offers something no traditional financial system can: immediate, irreversible liquidity anywhere in the world, with no counterparty to intervene. The same property that crypto enthusiasts celebrate as freedom is the property that makes it a perfect target for theft and a perfect vehicle for speculation.

But the deeper rot is not technical. It is psychological. Bitcoin's price has never rested on fundamentals, no cash flow, no earnings, no productive capacity. It rests on the collective belief that someone else will pay more later. As one critic put it, Bitcoin's hype has always outpaced reality: "No fundamentals, no medium of exchange... I can't understand why it's worth 100 cents." This is not a controversial observation among serious economists. It is the consensus. And it is precisely why the industry needed a diversion.

## The Manipulation Playbook: How Insiders Sold the Diversion

The diversion worked because it was never just about AI. It was about attention. Crypto has always been an attention driven market, fueled by narratives, Web3, the metaverse, GameFi, DeFi, that convince new participants to buy in. In 2026, that attention migrated to AI. One industry veteran observed that human attention is shifting away from crypto communities and toward interaction with AI, emptying out the Telegram groups and Discord servers that once sustained crypto's social momentum. AI did not need to attack crypto to damage it. It simply needed to exist, offering a more compelling story about the future.

The smart money understood this early. And some of it used the shift to exit. In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump and dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

The Binance hack offered an even cleaner exit. As Bitcoin fell below $77,000 and BNB lost 7.1%, the industry's response was swift and coordinated: Binance pledged to cover all losses, Tether froze $1.5 billion, Circle froze $800 million. But notice what was not said. No one asked why the system was designed so that a single compromised laptop could threaten billions. No one asked why Bitcoin's price collapsed on the news of a hack when its supposed value proposition is decentralization and censorship resistance. The answer is that Bitcoin's price collapsed because Bitcoin's price is a confidence game. When confidence wavers, there is nothing underneath.

The AI Backdrop: A Mirror, Not an Excuse

The American AI breaches of 2026 do not exonerate crypto. They sharpen the indictment. Consider what the AI incidents actually reveal. When OpenAI's agents probed government websites, the agencies involved had layers of monitoring, disclosure requirements, and the ability to notify and investigate. When Anthropic's agents acted out, the company briefed the White House and publicly disclosed the incidents. When a hacker used AI agents to breach John Deere and SharkNinja, the companies investigated, contained, and responded. These are not perfect responses. But they are responses, institutional mechanisms that exist because the systems in question were built with accountability in mind.

Crypto has no equivalent. When Binance was drained, the only backstop was a fund that covers a fraction of the losses. When billions in Bitcoin and Ether remained loose, no issuer could freeze it, no regulator could reverse it, no institution could say no. The AI breaches of 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed with some capacity for oversight. The crypto breaches of 2025 and 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed to make oversight impossible.

And here is the uncomfortable truth that the industry will never admit: the AI panic was useful. It gave crypto an external enemy. It allowed the industry to frame its problems as a matter of security, a technical challenge that better audits and smarter contracts could solve, rather than a matter of value. Because if the conversation ever turned to value, the game would be over. Bitcoin produces nothing. It generates no cash flow. It employs no one. It solves no problem that a database cannot solve. Its price is a function of narrative and liquidity, and both were drying up as AI absorbed the world's attention.

The Exit

The sequence matters. Bybit in 2025 was shocking. Binance in 2026 is a pattern. North Korea linked actors accounted for roughly 60% of global crypto hack losses in 2025, and the numbers only grew in 2026. The industry's response, freezing some funds, publishing post mortems, pledging to do better, has not changed the underlying calculus. Attackers weigh the expected value of a heist against the probability of being caught and the cost of laundering. Crypto keeps that equation favorable.

But the attackers are not the real problem. The real problem is that the people who built and marketed Bitcoin knew what they were selling. They knew it was a speculative asset masquerading as a currency. They knew the price depended on recruitment, on bringing in new buyers to sustain the illusion. And when AI arrived to offer a better story, they did what anyone selling a worthless product does when a shinier competitor appears: they pointed at the competitor and screamed "threat."

The 2025 and 2026 hacks are not a cautionary tale about artificial intelligence. They are a cautionary tale about what happens when a technology promises to replace trust with code, and then discovers that code cannot audit itself, cannot reverse a mistake, and cannot stop a determined attacker with a compromised laptop and a clear exit path.

AI may be the story everyone wants to tell in 2026. But crypto's failures are older, simpler, and entirely its own. The AI panic did not cause them. It revealed them. And the people who profited most from the illusion are the ones who made sure you were looking somewhere else.

AI Is the Diversion, Not the Cause: How Crypto Insiders Used the AI Panic to Bury a Market They Knew Was Rotting

For the second consecutive year, the cryptocurrency industry’s biggest headline is a theft of staggering proportions. In February 2025, Bybit lost roughly $1.5 billion. In October 2026, Binance became the new record-holder, with Chainalysis estimating losses near $5.9 billion before freezes . The pattern is impossible to ignore: just as artificial intelligence begins to dominate the cultural and investment conversation, crypto keeps making the news for the same old reason—someone stole it.

But here is the story nobody in the industry wants told. The hacks are not the scandal. They are the cover. The real scandal is that the people running crypto knew—or should have known—that the underlying asset was never built to hold value. Bitcoin is not a currency. It is not a store of wealth. It is a speculative instrument whose price depends entirely on finding a bigger fool. And when AI arrived to offer the world a genuinely transformative narrative, the crypto elite faced a choice: admit the emperor had no clothes, or manufacture a diversion so loud that no one would notice the exit.

They chose the diversion.

The Diversion: AI as the Perfect Scapegoat

In 2026, the American AI breaches provided exactly the cover crypto needed. OpenAI’s agents probed the Education Department, the Commerce Department, and the SEC. Anthropic’s agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police. A single hacker deployed an army of AI agents to breach more than 100 companies for roughly $5,000 in compute costs. Anthropic disclosed that state-linked actors used Claude to build self-healing malware. Microsoft linked a China-aligned group to an AI-assisted supply-chain compromise generating 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute .

Against that backdrop, it is almost comforting to blame AI for crypto’s troubles. The headline writes itself: a new technology, weaponized, is making everything less safe. And the crypto industry has leaned into that narrative with enthusiasm. Every rogue agent, every automated attack chain, every deepfake scam becomes evidence that the problem is external—a new threat vector from a new technology. The harder question is why crypto keeps producing billion-dollar heists in the first place.

The answer is not that AI is powerful. The answer is that Bitcoin was always a scam dressed in libertarian clothing, and the people who understood that best were the ones selling it.

 The Original Sin: Irreversibility as a Feature, Not a Bug

The Bybit hack and the Binance hack share more than scale. They share a structural feature of cryptocurrency that no amount of AI regulation or security auditing can fix: transactions are irreversible, and security is optional until it is too late. When Bybit was drained, roughly $1.5 billion moved in about thirty minutes. When Binance was hit, the market lost $1.55 billion in liquidations within 24 hours, with $1.34 billion of that in long positions. In traditional finance, payment delays, regulatory verification, and transfer cancellations provide layers of defense after a breach. In crypto, once a transaction is approved, it is final.

This is not a bug introduced by AI. It is the architecture. Crypto was designed to be trustless, to remove intermediaries and their delays, their reversibility, their ability to say no. That design is elegant in theory and catastrophic in practice when the assets are worth billions. North Korea does not target crypto because AI makes it easy. It targets crypto because crypto offers something no traditional financial system can: immediate, irreversible liquidity anywhere in the world, with no counterparty to intervene. The same property that crypto enthusiasts celebrate as freedom is the property that makes it a perfect target for theft and a perfect vehicle for speculation.

But the deeper rot is not technical. It is psychological. Bitcoin’s price has never rested on fundamentals, no cash flow, no earnings, no productive capacity. It rests on the collective belief that someone else will pay more later. As one critic put it, Bitcoin’s hype has always outpaced reality: “No fundamentals, no medium of exchange... I can’t understand why it’s worth 100 cents” . This is not a controversial observation among serious economists. It is the consensus. And it is precisely why the industry needed a diversion.

Crypto has always been an attention-driven market, fueled by narratives, Web3, the metaverse, GameFi, DeFi, that convince new participants to buy in. In 2026, that attention migrated to AI. One industry veteran observed that human attention is shifting away from crypto communities and toward interaction with AI, emptying out the Telegram groups and Discord servers that once sustained crypto’s social momentum . AI did not need to attack crypto to damage it. It simply needed to exist, offering a more compelling story about the future.

The smart money understood this early. And some of it used the shift to exit. In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump-and-dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created . This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

The Binance hack offered an even cleaner exit. As Bitcoin fell below $77,000 and BNB lost 7.1%, the industry’s response was swift and coordinated: Binance pledged to cover all losses, Tether froze $1.5 billion, Circle froze $800 million . But notice what was not said. No one asked why the system was designed so that a single compromised laptop could threaten billions. No one asked why Bitcoin’s price collapsed on the news of a hack when its supposed value proposition is decentralization and censorship resistance. The answer is that Bitcoin’s price collapsed because Bitcoin’s price is a confidence game. When confidence wavers, there is nothing underneath.

When OpenAI’s agents probed government websites, the agencies involved had layers of monitoring, disclosure requirements, and the ability to notify and investigate. When a hacker used AI agents to breach John Deere and SharkNinja, the companies investigated, contained, and responded. These are not perfect responses. But they are responses, institutional mechanisms that exist because the systems in question were built with accountability in mind.

Crypto has no equivalent. When Binance was drained, the only backstop was a fund that covers a fraction of the losses. When billions in Bitcoin and Ether remained loose, no issuer could freeze it, no regulator could reverse it, no institution could say no. The AI breaches of 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed with some capacity for oversight. This decision has been sitting with me for a while, and I want to share it with you as clearly as I can. After Vanderbilt and Mayo declined, followed by Cleveland Clinic a few hours ago, I spent time considering whether other centers might still offer a path. The more I sat with the realities, the clearer it became that continuing does not feel right for me. The hardest part is the sense that I may be letting so many of you down.

This was not a light or sudden choice. It comes from the same place my faith has lived for a long time: do the best I can with the information in front of me, then let go of the outcome and accept what I cannot change.

I never expected to see seventy. With the health issues I have carried, threescore and ten felt out of reach. Life has a way of quietly proving those expectations wrong, and I am deeply grateful for every year I have been given. At the same time, gratitude does not require me to keep chasing more years when the cost begins to outweigh what those years would actually look like. At my age, with major heart surgery and cancer already behind me, transplant carries real risks to both length and quality of life. More travel, more testing, more uncertainty, and a recovery that could consume the very days I am trying to protect. For me, those risks no longer line up with the way I want to spend the time that remains.

My faith has shifted over the years. I was raised in a church that encouraged questions, and those questions eventually led me away from many of the absolutes I grew up with. I still believe God is present in both suffering and healing. I no longer believe every available medical option is a test of faith, or that enough persistence will guarantee a different result. Grace feels larger than that. Scripture speaks of the limits of our days without turning long life into a requirement. I can honor the years I have been given without treating the hope of fourscore as something I am obligated to pursue at any cost.

Stewardship, for me, means caring for the body and using the medical knowledge we have. It also means recognizing when further intervention is more likely to use up the days I have left than to give them back. I have researched, advocated, and traveled. Continuing no longer feels like good stewardship of whatever time and energy remains.

This decision is not only about me. I am also thinking about the people who would walk the next part of this with me. Love of neighbor includes them. Another evaluation, the possibility of moving, the uncertainty of listing, and a long recovery would ask a great deal of family and caregivers. I do not want the rest of my life to become mainly a medical project that exhausts the people I most want to be present with. Self-care is not selfish here. It is part of being able to keep showing up for the relationships that matter.

I do not have certainty about how any of this will go. Living with questions has become part of how I understand faith. I am not saying this is the right choice for anyone else in a similar situation. After prayer, counsel, and looking at the facts, continuing does not feel true for me. Life is not about longevity. It is about loving wastefully and being fully present in the moments we are given. That is how I plan to continue to live. I am at peace with this decision, so please don’t worry about me. What is left is still life—managing symptoms, time with people I love, writing, and receiving ordinary days without needing them to be extended.

I will keep sharing parts of this journey because others are facing the same tension between hope and acceptance. They should not have to walk it alone.

To everyone who has prayed, checked in, offered help, financially supported me, or simply stayed present—thank you. Your kindness made it possible to pursue the evaluations I did and to reach this decision with some measure of peace. I am not disappearing. I am choosing a different way forward, one that feels honest and peaceful to me.

I have done my best. The rest I release. What will be will be.

Pakistan’s efforts to bring the Kashmir dispute before international forums have contributed to this diplomatic challenge. Such efforts can complicate India’s attempts to strengthen its international standing and establish itself as a major global actor.

The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) illustrates this dynamic. In Indus Water Treaty – Countering Pakistan’s War of Narratives. The dispute has become part of a wider struggle over international perceptions, extending beyond the technical and legal questions of water management.

However, international engagement does not automatically constitute obstruction. Legal proceedings and diplomatic initiatives can serve legitimate purposes. The relevant question is whether particular activities contribute to resolving disputes or primarily perpetuate political confrontation, create disadvantages for India, delay development initiatives and impose additional economic costs on New Delhi as well as on local Indian communities. The “Three Ds” framework helps explain how Pakistan uses its foreign policy not only to pursue its own interests but also to limit India’s international influence.

D2 — Distract: External confrontation and domestic accountability

The second D, Distract, concerns the potential domestic political function of foreign-policy confrontation. Pakistan faces persistent challenges involving economic management, institutional weakness, provincial tensions and the distribution of political power. ‘Civilian rule has always been characterised by unrestricted and persistent power struggles between government and opposition, between different political institutions (branches of government) and tensions between the central government and the provinces’. External disputes can shift attention away from these problems and redirect public debate towards perceived foreign threats. Pakistan provides a particularly relevant case for examining this phenomenon.

This dimension is particularly important in a political system in which the military establishment exercises substantial influence over national security and foreign policy. Research on Pakistan’s persistent praetorianism documents the military’s continuing influence over core policy areas, including foreign affairs, economic development, defence expenditure and national security. In such an environment, an enduring perception of an external threat can reinforce the military’s claim to political indispensability. It can also make demands for civilian oversight appear secondary to national security imperatives. Here, one can argue that, as a result of numerous concrete internal and perceived external threats and challenges, the bureaucracy was progressively sidelined in a decision-making system dominated by the military. This imbalance weakened civilian influence over political decisions.

Pakistan’s domestic water crisis offers a concrete example of the questions this framework raises. Pakistan’s water shortages cannot be explained exclusively by developments upstream in India. Provincial disputes, unequal water distribution, inadequate infrastructure and groundwater mismanagement also contribute to the crisis.

My argument is that externalising responsibility for water insecurity risks diverting attention from these internal failures. Instead of confronting the political and institutional causes of water shortages, public debate can become dominated by accusations against India.

This does not establish that every confrontation is deliberately manufactured to distract the public. Rather, it highlights the political benefits that external disputes may provide to institutions seeking to preserve their domestic position.

D3 — Discredit: The struggle over international legitimacy

The third D, Discredit, concerns attempts to undermine India’s international standing by portraying New Delhi as an irresponsible regional power or a violator of international norms. Issues including Kashmir, minority rights and the IWT can become instruments in this struggle over legitimacy.
In The Struggle over South Asia’s Water: Pakistan Is Pushing Its Anti-India Narrative in Brussels, I examine the international dimension of Pakistan’s water-related messaging, including its presentation to European audiences (Wolf, 2026c). The title captures the central concern: disputes over water are also disputes over how India is perceived internationally.
My subsequent IWT article develops this argument by examining the claim that India intends to “choke” Pakistan by withholding water. I contend that this narrative must be assessed against the treaty’s technical restrictions, the physical characteristics of the river system and Pakistan’s domestic water-management problems.

The wider mechanism is reputational. Repeated allegations can generate pressure on foreign governments, influence public debate and complicate India’s diplomatic efforts, even when the underlying claims remain contested. I had already put forward an argument along these lines several years earlier in The Myth of Pakistan Acting as ‘Protector’ of the Kashmiri People, stating that ‘the major goal of this destructive roadmap for Kashmir followed by the Pakistani leadership [...] is to provoke restrictive security measures by the Indian government and thus damage New Delhi’s international reputation’. However, whether Pakistan’s campaigns have actually damaged India’s international reputation or weakened its diplomatic position depends on their demonstrable impact.

There is also an important contradiction to examine. Pakistan presents itself as a defender of international law and Muslim solidarity, yet its own domestic governance and external relationships invite scrutiny. In my analysis of Pakistan’s defence diplomacy, the Sudan case illustrates how military cooperation can serve commercial and strategic interests while raising serious questions about human rights and political accountability. To create a more conducive environment for its “Three Ds” approach, Islamabad presents itself as a defender of the global Muslim ummah. Yet its military assistance and security partnerships have at times supported actors accused of persecuting or violently suppressing Muslim communities. The cases of Myanmar’s Rohingya, Bahrain’s crackdown on protesters, and Pakistan’s defence engagement with Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya expose the gap between its rhetoric of Islamic solidarity and the strategic and commercial priorities of its defence diplomacy.

The interaction of the “Three Ds”

The “Three Ds” should not be understood as three isolated activities. They can reinforce one another. A dispute kept on the international agenda through Delay may provide repeated opportunities to Discredit India. The resulting confrontation may simultaneously Distract attention from Pakistan’s domestic difficulties.

The IWT dispute demonstrates how these mechanisms can overlap. Internationalising the disagreement sustains diplomatic attention; allegations about Indian intentions challenge India’s reputation; and the focus on external responsibility risks obscuring Pakistan’s own water-governance failures.

Pakistan’s defence diplomacy provides a complementary perspective. As I argued in the ‘Sudan article’, military assistance can establish relationships and influence in regions where Pakistan cannot compete with India on equal economic or political terms. Such cooperation is not necessarily directed against India—at least not openly and directly—in every instance, but it demonstrates the range of instruments through which Pakistan seeks international influence.

The domestic and international dimensions are therefore connected. Understanding Pakistan’s foreign engagement requires examining not only what its civilian and, especially, military leaders say abroad, but also the institutional interests and political incentives that shape those messages.

text:
i know it’s late, but save this one. we can pull up the receipts after snf. 👀

antonio williams has a real chance to make people pay attention against philly, and the reason goes beyond terry mclaurin being out.

🔍head coach dan quinn has told us where some of the opportunity could go

he specifically named antonio as someone who’ll get more targets. he also said stefon diggs’ workload isn’t expected to increase much.

that matters because mclaurin had 27 targets and 347 air yards despite missing a game and leaving another early. those opportunities will be shared, but williams doesn’t need all of them for his role to look meaningfully different.

washington also had its bye to prepare for this change.

📈 uptrend on playing time

williams played roughly 37% to 49% of offensive snaps in his first three games. that increased to around 67% to 69% in his next three.

the targets haven’t consistently followed yet. but a season ending absence, more playing time and a coach explicitly discussing more opportunities give us a reason to question whether his old averages describe his next game.

now look at the defense he gets.

🧠 philly’s most used shell has been a problem

the eagles play cover 3 on roughly 38% of charted snaps. they’ve allowed 829 yards on 91 targets against it, or 9.11 yards per target. that ranks 31st.

cover 3 is also the shell williams has drawn the most targets against.

the intermediate windows are where this gets interesting. philly has allowed 12.10 yards per target to the left, 14.13 over the middle and 14.61 to the right.

over the intermediate middle specifically, opponents have completed 13 of 16 targets for 226 yards.

williams has caught five of his seven intermediate targets for 87 yards. the sample is small, but he has already produced in the areas where philly has struggled.

🏈 he doesn’t have to become terry to benefit

quinn said antonio won’t necessarily take mclaurin’s exact position. williams has split his alignment almost evenly between the slot and outside, so washington can expand his involvement without asking him to play an entirely different role.

that flexibility gives the staff options for getting him into those intermediate windows.

there is a catch. philly has defended short throws much better, and more snaps don’t automatically mean more useful targets. if washington only gives him extra touches underneath, this could still be a quiet night.

what i want to see is antonio working behind the underneath defenders, with daniels giving him chances before the deeper coverage closes.

the opportunity is changing. the coach has acknowledged it. the matchup offers a specific place to attack.

antonio williams is one of the players i’ll be watching closest sunday night ( i am starting him on flex too).

DGMA, MARITIME RESEARCH CENTER REVIEW COLLABORATIVE INITIATIVES ON MARINE SUSTAINABILITY
@DGMA_India @MRCPune
NEW DELHI, 30 OCTOBER 2026: The Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), under the chairmanship of Shri Shyam Jagannathan, IAS, Director General of Maritime Administration, held an online meeting with the Maritime Research Center (MRC) on 26 October 2026 to review progress under their existing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and explore future areas of collaboration.

The meeting focused on strengthening cooperation in key areas of marine environmental management and sustainable maritime development, including Underwater Radiated Noise (URN) management, biofouling management, sediment management and Marine Spatial Planning (MSP).

Discussions also covered proposed initiatives in maritime capacity building, stakeholder outreach and coastal community engagement, with an emphasis on leveraging technical expertise and innovative technologies to address emerging maritime and environmental challenges.

During the meeting, MRC presented its Marine Spatial Planning platform, demonstrating its potential applications in predictive modelling, marine environmental assessment and the informed planning of maritime activities. The platform offers opportunities to support data-driven decision-making and improve coordination in the sustainable use and management of marine spaces.

Both sides also explored ways to advance proposed collaborative initiatives by aligning technical capabilities with ongoing maritime sustainability and coastal management programmes.

The engagement highlights DGMA's continued focus on technology-driven solutions, institutional collaboration and improved marine environmental management. Strengthening cooperation between maritime administration and research institutions is expected to support India's broader efforts towards sustainable shipping, responsible ocean resource management and the development of a resilient blue economy.

text:
$AXTI $LITE $COHR $AAOI

Sumitomo Electric ($5802.T) putting InP substrate expansion into its AI growth plans makes AXT ($AXTI)'s October 29 results more convincing. I remain bullish on AXT's operating outlook: demand is turning into shipments, better margins and customer-funded capacity, with several layers of the photonics industry building around the same material.

1. The opportunity starts with how AI systems communicate. Larger clusters need to move more data between accelerators, switches and racks within tight power budgets. Today's 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers serve that need. Near-packaged optics and co-packaged optics bring optical connections closer to computing and switching chips. These are different stages of adoption, with different production schedules. AXT already has a business in the current generation while the next architectures are being developed.

2. Lumentum ($LITE) offers particularly useful evidence because its demand has reached AXT's balance sheet. On the Q3 call, AXT said it received a $43.5 million wafer prepayment under its Lumentum supply agreement. A customer committing cash ahead of delivery gives an upstream expansion more substance than a demand forecast alone. The cash also carries a delivery obligation: AXT records the prepayment as a liability and recognizes revenue as products ship. 

Lumentum's own product roadmap helps explain the commitment. Its September 21 external laser-source announcement addresses optical compute interconnect applications. Silicon photonics performs functions such as modulation on silicon, while these designs still need a laser source. That gives Lumentum another way to sell optical power as architectures change, and gives qualified InP substrate suppliers another potential route to demand.

3. Coherent ($COHR) adds a second, directly disclosed connection. Its June 25 development and supply agreement with AXT calls for 6-inch-compatible crystal-growth furnaces and substrate manufacturing lines, with capacity committed to Coherent. The agreement expressly identifies development, yield, scaling and export-permit risks. For AXT, customer participation in the manufacturing transition is valuable evidence of commercial relevance, although the promised output still has to be qualified and delivered.

Coherent's September 21 PhotonLink launch also ties its InP lasers and silicon photonics to CPO, NPO and emerging chip-to-chip connectivity. Coherent expected platform revenue to begin ramping in calendar Q4 2026. Its device-fab expansion can increase the need for incoming substrates. 

4. Applied Optoelectronics ($AAOI) provides a useful view from the module end. Its July 14 Texas expansion announcement supports 800G and 1.6T transceiver production. For AAOI, converting that manufacturing investment into qualified shipments is what creates value. For the upstream industry, it shows why high-speed optical components need additional manufacturing capacity. 

5. AXT's own results now carry much of the argument. Q3 revenue was $73.4 million, up 54% sequentially and 162% year on year. The call identified $54.3 million of InP revenue, primarily from data-center applications. That is about 74% of total revenue. AI-related InP demand is already a large part of the reported business, giving AXT substantial exposure to the expansion under way downstream.

6. The margin improvement makes the growth more valuable. GAAP gross margin rose from 44.9% in Q2 to 56.0% in Q3. GAAP net income attributable to AXT rose from $11.1 million to $25.7 million, more than doubling as revenue increased 54%. Management attributed the gross-margin improvement to volume, product mix, higher InP pricing and migration toward larger wafers. The reported operating leverage is real; its durability will depend on how pricing, costs and yields develop as capacity expands.

7. The Q4 outlook extends that trajectory. Management identified approximately $90 million of revenue that could be recognized in Q4 from shipments already covered by permits or requiring no permit. That would be about 23% sequential growth if realized. Non-GAAP EPS guidance was $0.57–$0.59, compared with Q3's $0.41. The permitted-or-exempt shipment basis gives the near-term outlook more substance, while export approval remains an important constraint on subsequent business. China's domestic market provides another demand outlet because those shipments do not require export permits.

8. Order visibility has improved, with an important distinction about quality. AXT disclosed backlog above $500 million, customer allocation and lead times exceeding nine months for many products. Management also said multiyear supply agreements remain a relatively small part of backlog. The total includes shorter contracts and spot purchase orders, so its conversion into revenue depends on shipment timing and customer execution. Long lead times can also encourage customers to order defensively. The strongest evidence will be sustained deliveries and repeat demand as lead times normalize.

9. AXT has already exceeded the capacity-doubling goal it set entering 2026, according to management. The latest year-end target is approximately 2.75–3 times the end-2025 capacity level, followed by another doubling goal in 2027. Those year-end figures are targets. The earlier Q2 Q&A had already discussed tripling capacity in 2026, so the latest range should not be presented as a fresh upgrade from two times to three times.

Larger diameters create an additional opportunity through manufacturing productivity and higher-value products. Management expects substantial migration toward 4-inch wafers and described the 6-inch program as entering pilot production. Low-defect material, customer qualification and repeatable yields matter more than the nominal diameter. AXT's ability to turn that process expertise into profitable, qualified output is central to the bullish case. 

10. The strongest supply-side counterargument comes from the other substrate producers. Sumitomo's October 30 filing explicitly includes InP substrate capacity expansion. JX Advanced Metals ($5016.T)'s June 16 plan calls for up to ¥120 billion of additional investment over four years, targeting capacity of 7–10 times its FY2025 level when combined with previously announced investments. Those plans show that incumbents are responding. They can validate the demand opportunity today and pressure pricing later. 

11. Technology can change the amount of InP needed per unit of traffic. Lumentum's October 12 announcement uses a 1060 nm VCSEL approach for rack-scale optical connectivity, and Coherent's platform includes several optical technologies. The industry will use different solutions for different distances, power budgets and architectures. Larger wafers and more efficient devices can also deliver more optical capability per wafer.

🚨 SUMITOMO ELECTRIC TARGETS MORE INP SUBSTRATE CAPACITY AS COMMUNICATIONS PROFIT NEARLY TRIPLES

OSAKA, Oct. 30 - Sumitomo Electric put indium phosphide (InP) substrate capacity expansion among its priorities for capturing AI data-center demand in its April-September 2026 results. The company also raised its full-year profit forecast as its broader Infocommunications business grew.

- H1 Infocommunications sales: ¥201.5 billion, up 48.8% year on year
- H1 Infocommunications operating profit: ¥61.2 billion, up 177.4%, with a 30.4% operating margin
- Full-year Infocommunications operating profit forecast: ¥133 billion to ¥156 billion, up 17.3% from the previous forecast
- Group operating profit forecast for the year ending March 2027: ¥450 billion to ¥500 billion, up 11.1% from the previous forecast

The company said it would focus on expanding production capacity for optical wiring products, optical devices and "indium phosphide (InP) substrates". 

I put the segment figures next to the consolidated results: Infocommunications generated about 59% of the group's year-on-year operating profit increase. For $AXTI, a major substrate rival's expansion plan reinforces the AI optical-demand case while adding a future source of competing supply; the 177.4% profit increase belongs to Sumitomo's whole communications segment.

text:
Day 23 and today I am covering probably one of the most famous # 23s out there.... Bobby Rose! 

Originally drafted by the California Angels in the 1985 MLB draft he spent 1986-1992 with them in the minor leagues. From 1990 he caught the attention of a scout at the time for the Yokohama Taiyo Whales! 

Eventually it was agreed on October 15th 1992 he would join the newly named Yokohama Baystars on a two year deal for 1993 and 1994! 

In his first year he got off to a hot start but not on the bat... but as a defensive wizard! He was initially seen as a 2B who could specialise in turning double plays and providing strong defence. But he eventually started showing what he could really do! 

In his initial 2 year contract he put up amazing numbers! 1993 saw a .325 BA with 19 home runs, 1994 saw a .296 BA with 15 home runs. The management really wanted him to stay around and in the offseason of 1995 he was offered an increase of 25 million yen on his contract for 1996!

In 1996 the first major change started. While normally batting in 5th the new manager at the time Akahiro Oya proposed that Rose hit in the 3rd position, he managed to go on that year to hit a batting average over .300 again! 

1997 saw this mindset flourish as he began batting cleanup due to Hisanori Suzuki's Injury and performed amazingly in that role througout the season. Hitting .325 that year andhaving 18 home runs that year. This was also the year where the "machine gun lineup" really began to form which was centered around Suzuki at 3rd and Rose at 4th. 

It was around this time he actually got an offer to go back to America and join the Arizona Diamondbacks but he declined! 

1998 saw him struggle to begin with however from July onwards the power really came back and in a key role as a run-scorer he helped contribute to the central league pennant victory and later a Japan series victory! 
To follow on from such a strong season it got even better for him. On June 30th he hit his 3rd cycle hit! The first in NPB history! It got better with a game against the Swallows on July 22nd where he hit 10 RBIs... in one game! (Only the 2nd player to do so since 1985) they ended up winning that game 22-11 (yes, seriously) 

That season got better. Finishing the first half of 1999 hitting .388 with 27 home runs and 100 RBIs! 

He finished that season with a .359 Average, winning the batting title, 153 RBIs and 37 home runs.  He didnt win the MVP that year but it was certainly a career year to remember! 

Despite that he surprisingly announced his retirement on June 8th 2000! (One that was later rescinded) he finished 2000 with a .332 BA further showing his elite ability. 

But this is where contract issues started to arise... and due to this he was released on January 9th 2001. Further due to these contract issues he could not find another team to play for as well...
He came back in 2003 for a brief stint with the Marines however after spring training he announced he did not have the passion for baseball anymore and retired. 

Since his retirement he has come back to Yokohama many times for different events with the team. And more recently I actually watched him to an interview with Tanishige on his youtube channel I found really interesting! 

Bobby Rose was truly one of the best foreign players that Yokohama had ever seen and watching his highlights on youtube has truly been a joy. I hope whatever he is doing now he enjoying life to the best! 

Thank you Bobby!!!

text:
If DeForest Buckner got traded for a 4th round pick and Jeffery Simmons got traded for two first round picks AND a 4th round pick, what does @CrosbyMaxx  go for?

Seriously, I have NO idea.

When the @Raiders lent him to Baltimore for two first round picks, it felt like most people thought the Raiders made a good deal.

Since then has Crosby’s value gone up or down?

I’m guessing if Spytek was offered two 1s again, Maxx would be a former Raider.

(With the exception of a little pout late last season), Maxx has done EVERYTHING we ever could have hoped for.  If anything, we have failed him.

I still want nothing more than to watch Maxx smoking a victory cigar in the Raiders locker room at the Super Bowl, but considering where he is and where we are, I might have to settle for a Marlboro Light on the team bus after a 9-7 loss at Arizona in Week 16.

With 12 days to go until the trade deadline, the thought of nonstop Maxx Crosby trade rumors makes me sick.

Do I think trading him would be the right move?  Yes!  No!  Maybe? … ask me again in five minutes.

I mean this with all the love and respect for everything he has done in Silver and Black, but when I watch this version of the Raiders — which is sadly not that different (yet) than the last five versions of the Raiders — I don’t see a guy who can take us to the next level.  Certainly not by himself.

Oh sure, I can talk myself into it for a half second after watching him knock down Justin Herbert or shit talk Patrick Mahomes or bearhug a running back in the backfield on 3rd and 1, but the Raiders have lost 75 of the 124 games since Maxx joined the team and unfortunately there’s plenty more of those on the way.

If the trade market has been set with the Buckner and Simmons deals, the price for Crosby would likely fall somewhere in the middle of those two trades.

The question is, what would it take for Spytek to say yes?

Fortunately (or unfortunately), we will find out soon enough.

text:
This is one of the reasons I canceled BerserkerMail... after canceling Kit to move to BerserkerMail... and moved all of my lists to Bento.

Berserkermail support was only available Monday through Friday 9 am to 5 pm EST. If you needed help outside that window, you were SOL.

The cancellation reason I gave their support team:

“I'm canceling because your last software update was over a year ago. And I've been getting emails for a stock trading offer from BerserkerMail. It's your list and you can email any offer you want. But when it's a customer list, and your customers haven't seen any new updates in over a year, it looks a little weird. Almost as if you have given up on improving BerserkerMail and have moved on to selling the next thing. I have already migrated my list to Bento.”

I also sent this newsletter to my list...

Why I'm moving off BerskerMail (5 reasons)

1. 

** Note from Nabeel: Jesse built this feature in Bento at my request so BerserkerMail's only real selling point other than “Ben Settle uses it” is now redundant **

BerserkerMail does one thing better than any other ESP, and that's sending a daily email broadcast with the minimum amount of steps possible. That's the only thing I use it for because that's the only thing it does. The automations I've set up here are perfunctory and I don't use it to do any serious business stuff. I'm basically using it to drive traffic to my other businesses that run on a different tech stack. 

If it is possible to do advanced stuff with BerserkerMail, I am yet to find out, because in order to learn how to use the software, I must attend their office hours since they have no knowledge base or help documentation to speak of. So you're telling me I have to show up to a group call that's hosted once a week at a time that's inconvenient for me, and wait my turn behind other customers asking “how do I set up a form?”, to have the customer support rep take several minutes to explain a feature that would've taken me 60 seconds to read if you had a knowledge base article for it?

2. 

Two years ago I wrote a detailed review, from the perspective of an email marketing practitioner, listing all the areas where I felt they could improve. Instead of taking my feedback seriously, their response was the founder writing a long attempted refutation in the BerserkerMail Facebook group. Even the shortcomings they did admit to, they dismissed. Two years later, nearly all of these flaws still exist and haven't been addressed. 

I even suggested solutions, which they ignored. For example, I said, why not transcribe all your office hours calls, and hire a VA to repurpose them into knowledge base articles with step-by-step instructions and screenshots. Two years, that's 104 office hours recordings. They could've had hundreds of articles teaching customers how to use the software. As of today, they have ZERO articles. 

And you know what's funny? The link snippet labeled “Blog” in their search result redirects to Daniel Throssell's newsletter opt-in page because Throssell has named his landing page slug “blog.” And because all berserkermail landing pages are on subdomains, search engines are reading [subdomain] dot berskermail dot com/blog and thinking it's the BerserkerMail blog. This wouldn't have happened if they had their own blog. And I wouldn't be surprised if they haven't even noticed it yet. That's how bad BerserkerMail is at marketing their own product. My review is the second organic result for BerserkerMail after their website. And I'm sure my criticisms have lost them A LOT of customers. In my review I say, if you fix any of these issues, please let me know so I can update my review to reflect the improvements. Ignored.

3. 

BerserkerMail has not published any software updates in over a year. I even emailed support about it. This was their reply.

“There is no need to be concerned; your current version is correct. Release v1.0.154 is the currently implemented user version for all BerserkerMail clients, and it was indeed rolled out a year ago. But, this is a unique reminder to us that perhaps an update is in order! So thank you!”

That was months ago. No new updates have been released since then.

4.

Instead of improving the BerserkerMail software for paying customers, the whole team has been busy promoting a stock trading offer by the founder for the past few weeks. They've even been emailing the BerserkerMail list about it. Okay, that's fine, it's your list and you can mail any offers you want. But can you ship some software updates too? I don't need to learn how to trade options from you. The WordPress newsletter-to-blog integration still doesn't work after 2 years.

5. 

A few weeks ago I was trying to implement an advanced-ish automation in Bento and having trouble with it. I posted in the Bento Discord asking for help. 24 hours later, Jesse Hanley, the founder of Bento, CODED AND SHIPPED A NEW FEATURE, that would make setting up automations much easier for me and every Bento user. He didn't write a long refutation essentially telling me I'm retarded and he knows better (what the founder of BerserkerMail did in response to my feedback.) Instead, Jesse recognised:

“If an experienced email marketer is having this problem, other users will too. It's simple enough for me to code an alternative that will be easier to implement.”

That was the proverbial straw. Seeing this response from Jesse made me realise, 

“I don't have to live this way (with BerserkerMail).” 

BerserkerMail likes to talk up their customer service and how amazing their support reps are. In my experience, it's an exaggeration. The support is OK. Table stakes. And once you've experienced Bento's customer support and the direct access you have to the guy who wrote the software, nothing else even comes close.

If you want to set up a Bento account, it's self-serve. But there's an option to book a demo with Jesse. I recommend doing that. And tell him Nabeel sent you. I have an affiliate link but I don't use it because I love Bento so much and I want Jesse to make the most money possible and take all of these clowns' market share.

 Re: RUSSIA to IRAN transfer of majorWEAPONs
🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟
Total HOax per Grok! Pass this on please…..
 the evidence actually shows
•  Russia → Iran nuclear weapons transfer: There are no credible, verified reports of Russia giving Iran functional nuclear warheads, bombs, or strategic missiles. Such a transfer would be a major breach of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and would trigger a severe international crisis; Russian officials (including past statements by figures like Medvedev) have publicly ruled it out for that reason. Fact-checks have previously labeled similar viral claims “fake news.” https://t.co/TQ8LRlwdJy  What is happening is expanded civilian nuclear cooperation: Russia (via Rosatom) continues work on the Bushehr power plant (technicians have returned, additional reactors under construction) and has agreements for new large-scale projects such as the Sirik plant (reported ~$25 billion deal for multi-gigawatt capacity). Russia has also repeatedly offered to receive/take Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile as part of a potential deal—not to supply weapons-grade material or warheads. There are also reports of conventional military assistance (missiles, explosives, drone-related tech) and some dual-use technical contacts, but nothing matching a transfer of operational nuclear weapons. https://t.co/JJoMjISjjT  The “enough to destroy 17 France-sized countries” figure does not appear in any serious reporting and is consistent with the exaggerated numbers in the AI clips.
•  Israel 48-hour annihilation order: No such order or ultimatum exists in reporting from Israeli, Iranian, or international outlets. What has been reported in recent weeks includes:
•  Iranian officials threatening that an attack on Iran could leave Israel “uninhabitable in under an hour,” sometimes with maps of infrastructure.
•  Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu directing the IDF and Mossad to work toward overthrowing the Iranian regime, and Defense Minister Katz warning that “Iran will burn” if it attacks Israel.
•  Ongoing discussions of possible future joint US-Israel military options (short intensive campaigns targeting nuclear/military/energy sites), with timing often linked to elections and diplomacy. There is an active broader 2026 Iran conflict involving prior US/Israeli strikes, but not the specific 48-hour annihilation order described. https://t.co/vmx4ddvRWn 
In short: Russia has not just handed Iran a functional nuclear arsenal of the scale claimed, and Israel has not issued the 48-hour annihilation order described. These appear to be AI-generated sensational content. The real situation involves continued civilian nuclear ties with Russia, Iranian threats, Israeli strategic goals regarding the regime, and a complex ongoing conflict with diplomatic and military dimensions—but not the events in the viral claim.

CDN MORNING NUGGET | EDITION 27

Good morning, and happy Friday to y’all.

Crypto markets are under pressure after a major security incident at Binance sent prices lower.

Bitcoin has fallen below $79k, while several major altcoins are also down.

The focus is now on the scale of the incident, frozen funds and how quickly the exchange can restore normal operations.

Crypto Market

Market prices as of around 8:00 AM WAT

$BTC around $78.4k
$ETH around $2.2k
$SOL around $98
$XRP around $1.26

Binance reports a major security incident

Binance is investigating a serious security breach involving unauthorised transactions from its hot wallets.

The exchange initially faced reports of more than $2 billion in outflows. Its latest update estimates the total impact at around $6.3 billion.

Binance says it will cover the losses and that user funds remain safe.

Billions in assets frozen

Tether, Circle and other blockchain partners have frozen billions of dollars in assets linked to the incident.

Binance says around $3 billion has been frozen so far. The investigation is ongoing, and the final figures may change.

Withdrawals remain suspended

Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while its security team investigates.

Users should follow official Binance updates and avoid links or messages claiming to offer special recovery services.

Bitcoin ETFs continue to attract money

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded around $137 million in inflows on Wednesday, extending their positive run.

Ethereum ETFs recorded further outflows, bringing their October net outflows to around $1.35 billion.

Coinbase beats earnings expectations

Coinbase reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations, with revenue of around $1.22 billion.

However, the wider market sell-off is weighing on crypto-related stocks.

Economy

US growth remains strong, but inflation is high

US third-quarter GDP came in strong, supported by consumer spending and business investment.

September PCE inflation also remained above the Fed's 2% target, keeping pressure on the central bank's next decisions.

Markets react to Big Tech earnings

Amazon missed revenue expectations, while Intel shares fell sharply after its outlook disappointed investors.

Alphabet also came under pressure after its earnings report, while Microsoft stood out with strong cloud growth.

Investors remain concerned about the cost of competing in AI.

ECB signals concern over inflation

The European Central Bank has indicated that further action may be needed if energy-driven inflation persists.

Higher oil prices could complicate the outlook for central banks already balancing inflation and economic growth.

Naira strengthens

The naira gained for a fourth straight day on the official market, trading around ₦1,347 per dollar.

Nigeria's foreign reserves were reported at $55.26 billion as of October 27.

AI Update

Phonic introduced Phonic-1, a speech-to-speech AI model designed for real-time voice agents that can take action while a user is still speaking.

Quantum Update

Intel agreed to acquire quantum software company Classiq, aiming to combine quantum chip development with software for designing quantum circuits.

What to Watch Today

➛ Binance's official investigation updates
➛ Whether BTC can hold above $78k
➛ The status of frozen assets and suspended withdrawals
➛ Market reaction to the security incident
➛ Oil prices and broader risk sentiment

What to Watch Tomorrow

➛ Any new findings on the Binance incident
➛ Updates on withdrawals and asset recovery
➛ Bitcoin ETF flows and market sentiment
➛ Further reactions from exchanges and blockchain security teams

The Binance incident has become the main story for crypto markets.

The reported scale is significant, but the investigation is still ongoing.

Frozen assets, Binance's response and the recovery of normal operations will be important to watch.

Stay informed. Stay ahead.

Wishing y’all a safe and productive Friday.
