text:
Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
Europe’s political crisis may bring new leaders, but Russia has little reason to assume they will choose peace over confrontation
Published 29 Oct, 2026
https://t.co/0v65C4NsX5
By Timofey Bordachev, Program Director of the Valdai Club
-------
For Russia, developments in the rest of Europe matter primarily insofar as they affect our national interests. Above all, this concerns security given that, for centuries, Russia has faced its greatest challenges from the West, and there’s little reason to assume that this historical pattern has disappeared.
Western Europe’s leading countries now stand at a crossroads, yet the choice confronting them isn’t simply between competing models of domestic development, it’s between war and peace with their neighbors, foremost among them Russia, whose size and historical role have repeatedly made it the principal obstacle to Western European expansion.
The unrest sweeping several European countries this autumn marks a new phase in the continent’s systemic crisis as it reflects the convergence of two long-term problems that much of Europe’s political establishment has proved incapable of resolving.
The first is the exhaustion of the socioeconomic model that sustained Western European prosperity throughout the Cold War and its aftermath. That model depended on Europe’s privileged position in the global economy and the absence of serious competitors beyond the Western world, but China’s rise, combined with increasingly limited resources, has undermined those advantages.
Closer economic integration with Russia, and access to its enormous natural wealth, might have offered Western Europe a final opportunity to preserve its exceptional position, but instead regional leaders allowed their own arrogance to prevent an accommodation with Moscow because they couldn’t accept that Russia wished to live peacefully with its neighbors, but on terms consistent with its own interests.
The second problem is Western Europe’s longstanding absence of genuine sovereignty.
Integration into the American-led NATO system has deprived even major powers such as Germany, France, and Britain of the freedom to pursue fundamental political change and one of the alliance’s practical functions has been to preserve the existing political order within its member states.
Any serious attempt to transform that order would require a reassessment of relations with Washington and such independence is something these European governments have long been unwilling, or unable, to contemplate.
Together, these structural weaknesses have left Western Europe’s political and economic establishments effectively paralyzed.
For nearly two decades, governments have substituted the appearance of activity for meaningful reform. Successive emergencies, involving migration, the pandemic, hostility towards Russia, and preparations for military confrontation, have allowed leaders to avoid addressing deeper problem and this helps explain the temptation to interpret today’s unrest as another exercise in political manipulation. Emmanuel Macron, for example, has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to survive the consequences of disastrous decisions through tactical maneuvering.

text:
SA ready for AGOA eligibility decision | @SAgovnews 

Friday, October 30, 2026

South Africa is ready for the outcome of the United States’ (US) annual review of its eligibility for African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) benefits, with Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau saying the economy will remain stable and exporters will continue trading regardless of the decision.

The US is expected to announce its decision on South Africa’s eligibility for AGOA benefits for 2027 on 2 November 2026.

AGOA provides eligible sub-Saharan African countries with duty-free access to the US market for more than 1 800 products, in addition to the more than 5 000 products eligible for duty-free access under the Generalised System of Preferences programme.

Tau said government stands ready to support the economy, particularly South African businesses and their employees, who form the backbone of communities.

He said government is confident that the US will respond favourably to the offers South Africa has made during negotiations over the past year.

 “This is what is in the best interest of our two nations – the US and SA -as well as of partners in the African continent. We remain committed to engagement and our doors remain open for dialogue. Government has engaged constructively on all concerns raised by the United States,” Tau said.

In September, Tau met US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer in Washington, DC, to discuss bilateral trade relations and the future of AGOA.

“Our meeting was preceded by two rounds of discussions at senior officials’ level, where substantial progress on addressing the issues was made. Recently, two rounds of senior officials' talks were held,” the Minister said.

Tau reaffirmed that the US remains a valued partner, with bilateral trade reaching $28.8 billion in 2025.

“More than 600 American companies operate here, supporting around 134 600 jobs. In the last year alone, more than $5 Billion investment commitments have been made by US companies, demonstrating increased investor confidence in SA as an investment destination,” the Minister said.

He said South Africa supplies 12 of the 50 minerals the US considers critical and is ready to partner with the US to beneficiate them at source.

“We have tabled practical proposals through the proper channels. It would not be appropriate to set out their detail in public while that engagement continues.

“What I can say is that every proposal respects due process, preserves our constitutional values and imperatives, is aligned with our obligations under World Trade Organization rules and reinforces our duty to protect animal health, local producers and SA consumers,” the Minister said.

Tau reiterated that South Africa remains open to practical arrangements to grow trade and investment between the two countries.

“These matters are best resolved through diplomatic and trade channels, and that is where we will continue to pursue them. If the United States concerns remain, South Africa will have 60 days to address them before any suspension, full or partial, could take effect,” Tau said.

He said South Africa will continue engaging the US to stabilise trade and investment relations while pursuing opportunities in other markets.

“Companies on both sides need a normalised trade environment because of existing value chains in key sectors. We are ready, whatever the decision. 

“We are prepared and are implementing our Cabinet-approved Industrial Development Strategy, and through the Butterfly Strategy, we are opening markets across the African Continental Free Trade Area, India, Southern African Development Community (SADC), the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), MERCOSUR [Mercado Común del Sur] and China.

“We have concluded negotiations with the EU on cumulation to protect hybrid and electric vehicle exports and secured an interim arrangement for steel. New markets have opened for our citrus, avocados, grapes and apples,” Tau said.

Exodus 12:5 says the Passover lamb had to be without blemish. Leviticus 1:3 and Leviticus 22:19-25 say the same for the burnt offerings and other sacrifices. The animal had to be perfect. No defect. No flaw. That is what spotless means under the law. It could not be lame, blind, or damaged in any way. God would not accept a defective offering.

Those animals were only a picture. Hebrews 10:1-4 says the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins. They had to be offered over and over because they never really dealt with the problem. They pointed forward to the real sacrifice.

Jesus is that sacrifice. First Peter 1:19 calls Him a lamb without blemish and without spot. Hebrews 9:14 says He offered Himself without spot to God. He was born under the law (Galatians 4:4). He kept it perfectly. He never sinned (2 Corinthians 5:21, Hebrews 4:15, 1 Peter 2:22). That is what spotless means for Him. Not just physical perfection. Moral perfection. He lived without sin so He could be the offering the law required.

Then He offered Himself once for all (Hebrews 9:12, 10:10-12). The old system repeated the picture. Jesus was the reality. One perfect life. One perfect sacrifice. That satisfied the demand of the law and opened the way for mercy.
The law required a spotless offering. Jesus was that offering.

text:
There is nothing resembling slavery in modern voluntary employment contracts, especially in capitalist countries where freedom of contract exists and workers can choose among different employers.

You are free to accept or reject a job offer, negotiate your wages, leave your employer, or seek better opportunities elsewhere. That is the fundamental difference between voluntary employment and slavery.

Where genuine restrictions on labor freedom exist is in systems where the state is effectively the only employer.

In Cuba, people do not enjoy genuine freedom in the labor market. In North Korea, they do not have that freedom either. Under communist rule in the Soviet Union, workers lacked the freedom to participate in a genuinely competitive labor market.

The difference is simple: capitalism allows workers to choose whom they work for, while communist systems concentrate economic power in the hands of the state.

Having to work to earn a living is not slavery. Being denied the freedom to choose your employer or negotiate the terms of your employment is a restriction on economic liberty.

text:
HT - HYBRID TECHNOCRACY

The Quiet Shift Beyond Left and Right

The politics of the future will not be defined solely by the old struggle between left and right. It will increasingly be defined by a more practical question: can we govern a complex society intelligently, effectively, and without surrendering democratic freedom?

Hybrid technocracy is a proposed answer.

It combines three sources of power: democratic authority, specialist knowledge, and artificial intelligence. Each has a distinct role. The public determines the direction of society. Elected leaders establish priorities and remain accountable for their decisions. Qualified specialists apply their knowledge, while AI and advanced computing help analyze information, test proposals, anticipate consequences, and identify failures.

The aim is neither government by an unelected elite nor government driven by popular opinion alone. It is a system in which democratic legitimacy and technical competence reinforce one another.

People decide what matters. Expertise establishes what is possible. AI helps determine what is likely to work.

Beyond the Old Political Divide

For generations, political debate has been organized around competing ideologies. The left and right disagree over taxation, public spending, markets, regulation, equality, and the proper role of government. These disagreements reflect real differences in values, and hybrid technocracy does not make them disappear.

It changes the way governments approach the problems beneath them.

Instead of treating ideological loyalty as a substitute for results, hybrid technocracy asks whether policies achieve their stated objectives, what they cost, what consequences they produce, and how they can be improved.

A left-leaning government could use it to deliver better healthcare, coordinate infrastructure, and reduce waste in public services. A right-leaning government could use the same methods to simplify administration, improve productivity, and eliminate ineffective expenditure.

Neither side needs to abandon its values. Both should be expected to examine the evidence.

The question is not whether a policy sounds progressive or conservative, but whether it works, whom it benefits, what it costs, and whether a better alternative exists.

Ideology may establish the destination. It should not exempt the journey from scrutiny.

Intelligence Applied to Government

Modern societies operate through systems of extraordinary complexity. Energy networks, healthcare, transportation, food distribution, financial infrastructure, and global supply chains generate more information than traditional administrative methods can effectively process.

Political institutions were not designed to evaluate every variable in real time. Legislatures cannot debate every operational detail, and ministers cannot possess specialist knowledge of every field for which they are responsible.

AI can help close that gap.

It can process vast quantities of data, identify emerging patterns, simulate policy outcomes, detect inefficiencies, and warn of developing problems. It can help governments compare alternatives before committing public money, rather than discovering the consequences after the damage has been done.

Specialists provide the domain knowledge needed to interpret those findings, challenge faulty assumptions, and understand practical constraints. Elected officials determine priorities, weigh competing interests, and make decisions for which they can be held accountable.

The potential benefits are considerable: infrastructure that is better maintained, shortages identified earlier, public services that respond more effectively to demand, and public money used with greater care.

These outcomes are not automatic. Bad data, poor incentives, incompetent management, and flawed models can produce expensive failures. But a government capable of continuously testing its decisions and correcting its mistakes has an advantage over one that treats established policy as an article of faith.

Government should be a process of informed action and continuous correction, not a permanent contest between political certainties.

The Limits of Expertise

Technocracy has an obvious attraction: competent specialists may understand a problem better than politicians who must divide their attention among dozens of competing demands.

But technical competence does not confer unlimited political authority.

An engineer can calculate the most efficient way to build a railway. That calculation cannot, by itself, decide which communities should bear the disruption, whether the environmental cost is acceptable, or how the benefits should be distributed.

A computer can compare healthcare policies against specified targets. It cannot legitimately determine society's entire moral hierarchy simply because someone has translated certain priorities into numbers.

Efficiency is a means, not an ultimate purpose. A system can be efficient at pursuing the wrong objective.

This is where democratic authority remains indispensable. Citizens and their representatives must retain the power to determine priorities, establish limits, protect rights, and challenge decisions that impose unacceptable costs.

Hybrid technocracy must therefore distinguish between questions that can be substantially informed by technical analysis and questions that require political judgment, ethical reasoning, and public consent.

The distinction will not always be neat. That is precisely why accountability matters.

The Danger of Rule by Algorithm

AI is not neutral simply because it operates through mathematics.

Its conclusions depend on the data it receives, the objectives it is instructed to pursue, the assumptions built into its models, and the people who control its deployment. A system designed to maximize efficiency may neglect fairness. One designed to minimize costs may sacrifice resilience. One trained on biased historical data may reproduce existing inequalities while presenting them as objective findings.

Nor are experts immune to self-interest, professional conformity, institutional pressure, or error.

The greatest danger is not necessarily that machines will take power by themselves. It is that human institutions will use machines to make their own power harder to challenge.

A controversial decision can be presented as a technical necessity. A political preference can be hidden inside an algorithm. Responsibility can be dispersed among officials, contractors, specialists, and software until no one appears accountable.

That is not hybrid technocracy. It is elite control with a technological disguise.

Any legitimate system must make its decisions open to scrutiny, explain their reasoning in accessible language, provide independent review, and preserve meaningful ways to appeal or reverse them. High-impact decisions must not become immune to challenge merely because they involve sophisticated technology.

A Different Architecture of Power

Hybrid technocracy depends on a clear division of responsibility.

AI analyzes. It processes information, models alternatives, identifies patterns, and proposes possible courses of action.

Experts evaluate. They interpret the evidence, test the assumptions, explain the trade-offs, and identify the limits of the analysis.

Elected leaders decide. They set priorities, make political judgments, and accept responsibility for the consequences.

Citizens retain the final democratic authority. They question decisions, defend their rights, influence public priorities, vote leaders out of office, and insist that the system remains accountable.

These are guiding principles, not rigid compartments. Experts can contribute to policy goals, citizens can possess specialist knowledge, and elected governments can delegate routine operational decisions. But delegation must never become a means of permanently surrendering accountability.

Where speed, consistency, and precision are essential, carefully supervised automation can improve administration. Where decisions affect fundamental rights, personal liberty, or the distribution of social burdens, there must be meaningful human responsibility and legitimate avenues of challenge.

The objective is not to automate politics. It is to use technology to make government more capable without making citizens less powerful.

The Future Is Not Inevitable

Elements of hybrid technocracy already exist wherever governments combine data analysis, specialist advice, automation, and democratic oversight. The next step would be to integrate these elements into a coherent philosophy of governance.

As societies become more interconnected and technologically complex, the pressure to do so will grow. Governments will need to respond faster, anticipate problems earlier, and make better use of limited resources.

But the spread of AI will not automatically produce better government. The same technology can support competent public administration or enable intrusive surveillance, concentrated power, and decisions that ordinary people cannot meaningfully contest.

The outcome will depend on the institutions we build around it.

Hybrid technocracy must be judged not merely by how much it can accomplish, but by how it distributes power, corrects mistakes, protects individual freedom, and responds when the public disagrees with those in charge.

Its promise is a government less dependent on political theatre, less tolerant of demonstrable failure, and better equipped to manage the complexity of modern life.

Its condition is that technical competence must never become an excuse for political unaccountability.

The old left-right divide will not vanish. But it need not remain the only framework through which we imagine government. A new dimension is emerging: not simply what a government believes, but how intelligently it acts, how honestly it evaluates its results, and how effectively it corrects its failures.

Hybrid technocracy offers a way to bring democratic choice, human expertise, and machine intelligence into a single governing framework.

Not government by machines. Not government by experts alone. Not government by political instinct.

Government that combines the intelligence to act, the humility to correct itself, and the democratic restraint to remember whom it serves.

That is the quiet shift beyond left and right.

And it may be one of the defining political questions of the coming age.

The Sumerian Classification of 8 Human Bloodline Types — And What Each One Was Bred For

The theory presented in the video posits that ancient Mesopotamian texts describe eight distinct, engineered human bloodlines, each with a specific biological design, intended role, and set of constraints.

They are all summarized according to the 'ancient astronaut' framework presented in the video:

1.  The Adamu represents the foundational human bloodline—the original genetic template from which humanity was derived.

Here is a detailed breakdown of this bloodline:

Origin and Design Purpose

Definition:  The term Adamu (or Adama) is interpreted here not just as 'man,' but as a specific, purpose-built hybrid organism.

Genetic Creation:  The Adamu resulted from combining pre-existing hominin genetic material with Anunnaki genetic code.

Primary Function:  They were engineered specifically for labor (the Lulu Amalu or 'primitive worker'). Their purpose was to bear the work of the Igigi—performing tasks such as digging canals, working in mines, and maintaining the agricultural infrastructure necessary for Anunnaki operations on Earth.

Biological and Cognitive Specifications

Motor and Cognitive Limits:  While the Adamu were granted motor functions significantly better than their hominin predecessors, their cognitive capacity was strictly limited to following complex instructions and learning specific, repetitive task sequences.

Reproduction:  The original Adamu template lacked the capacity for independent reproduction; this was a feature added later by Enki through a secondary genetic intervention.

Constraint Mechanisms:  The Adamu were explicitly denied access to the ME—the 'tablets of civilization' containing advanced knowledge.

They were not taught language beyond basic communication, lacked the ability to write or record information, and had no access to the astronomical or technical data used by the Anunnaki.

Lifespan:  To ensure their role as a controlled labor force, they were designed with a shortened lifespan compared to the Anunnaki.

Summary of the Adamu Experience

Within this theory, the Adamu type represents the baseline of the human population. They were the most widely distributed, used across all ancient Sumerian settlements, and they embody the deepest 'suppression of potential'.

Their design was a deliberate attempt to create a workforce that was useful enough to maintain an empire, but restricted enough—via biological and cultural 'ceilings'—to never threaten the authority or hierarchy of their creators.

__
2.  The Adapa is classified as the second human bloodline type, serving as an administrative upgrade to the baseline Adamu template":

Design and Purpose

Administrative Interface:  While the Adamu were built for manual labor, the Adapa were engineered to serve as the critical interface layer between the Anunnaki hierarchy and the general labor population.

Technical Designation:  The Adapa classification, often treated in mainstream academia as a singular legendary figure, is viewed by researchers as a specific genetic type given enhanced administrative and cognitive capabilities by Enki.

Key Capability (Namzu):  They were endowed with Namzu—translated as 'deep knowing' or 'wisdom of the deep.' This refers to technical knowledge required for complex planning, astronomical calculations, precise language, and the ability to interpret 'signs' or operational directives from the Anunnaki.

Roles and Limitations

Institutional Function:  They operated as temple functionaries, record-keepers, and scribes. They were housed near ziggurats—identified not just as religious sites, but as administrative and communication hubs for the Anunnaki.

Restricted Potential:  The Adapa bloodline includes the story of a deliberate 'ceiling.' In the Adapa myth, the character is called before the god Anu and offered the 'bread and water of life'—symbolizing full Anunnaki inheritance, immortality, and total cognitive unlock.

Enki famously instructs Adapa to refuse these, which researchers interpret as a protective measure: allowing them to reach full status would have threatened the social and labor hierarchy of the Anunnaki operation.

Summary of the Adapa Legacy

Suppression vs. Utility:  The Adapa were designed to be highly useful for maintaining the system but were strictly constrained by their biological design. They represent the delicate balance between enabling high-level administration and preventing the created class from ascending to the status of their creators.

__
3.  The Abcalu are not merely mythological sages, but are classified as a third, highly specialized human bloodline type. They represent a genetic specification designed to be significantly closer to the Anunnaki baseline than the Adamu worker type.

Design and Purpose

Living Libraries:  The Abcalu were engineered as "living libraries". Rather than relying on external records that could be destroyed, they carried foundational knowledge—such as mathematics, astronomy, agriculture, metallurgy, medicine, law, and language—directly within their biological design.

Genetic Origin:  Researchers argue their creation involved a sophisticated two-donor genetic procedure, contributing more Anunnaki material to their makeup than standard humans.

Their association with fish-suit iconography in ancient art is interpreted as a connection to the Abzu (Enki's laboratory domain beneath the earth), suggesting this was his deepest and most protected experiment.

Role and Legacy

Advisors and Anchors:  The seven pre-flood Abcalu were assigned to early cities to act as advisors and "genetic anchors" for royal lineages, helping to preserve elevated inheritance ratios across generations.

Post-Flood Shift:  After the Great Flood, the Abcalu lineage was reconstituted with reduced specifications as part of a negotiated settlement between divine factions.

Underground Continuation:  While the formal Abcalu designation disappeared from official records after the Anunnaki withdrawal, proponents argue their knowledge-preservation function persisted through history in various mystery schools, esoteric lineages, and gnostic traditions that claim access to "pre-flood" wisdom.

Ultimately, the Abcalu serve as the template for high-level knowledge transmission, designed specifically to ensure that the foundational data of civilization would survive catastrophe, fire, and the deliberate destruction of archives.

__
4.  The Lugal (Sumerian for "big man" or "great man") is classified as a distinct genetic bloodline engineered for political administration and high-level leadership.

Design and Purpose

Divine Interface:  The Lugal type was designed to serve as the direct link between the Anunnaki administration and the broader human population.

Genetic Endowment:  Researchers interpret the Nam Lugal-ship (the essence of kingship) not as a metaphor for divine right, but as a specific genetic endowment.

This includes:

Enhanced Cognition:  Superior pattern recognition for managing social instability and coordinating diverse, multi-typed populations.

Bioelectric Presence:  The Melamu—described as a "terrifying radiance" or divine luminosity—is theorized to be a biological feature, possibly a bioelectric field, designed to command natural authority and force compliance from others.

Role and Succession

Pre-Flood Longevity:  The extraordinary reign lengths of pre-flood kings (such as Alulim and Alalgar) are interpreted as evidence of a higher concentration of Anunnaki DNA, allowing for near-divine cellular repair and vastly extended lifespans.

Bloodline Maintenance:  Succession was not arbitrary; it relied on strict maternal lineage protocols documented in royal archives. This attention to genealogy ensured the stability of the Anunnaki inheritance ratio across generations.

Post-Flood Trajectory

Dilution:  Following the Great Flood, the Lugal specification underwent intentional dilution. The rapid decline in reign lengths recorded in the Sumerian King List represents the gradual mixing of this specialized bloodline with the general population, reflecting a shift in policy where a less autonomous, more manageable leadership was desired.

Ultimately, the Lugal served as the primary political operator of the ancient world. While their biological inheritance waned over time, their archetype persisted in historical figures who claimed divine favor or possessed the same commanding presence and administrative ambition.

__
5.  The Aaron (Sumerian for "troops," "soldiers," or "military forces") is identified as a distinct human bloodline engineered specifically for military function, physical performance, and loyalty.

Design and Purpose

Engineered Traits: Unlike the Adamu laborer type, the Aaron were bred for enhanced physical parameters, including a higher pain threshold, greater muscle density, and faster reflexes.

Loyalty Mechanism:  Perhaps their most critical feature was a neurological bonding mechanism—referred to in the tablets as the Nam-Aaron oath.

Researchers argue this was not merely a ritual, but a biological state: a neurochemical response that created intense, near-instinctual loyalty to a specific Anunnaki patron or institution.

Strategic Constraints:  While built for combat, the Aaron were explicitly denied access to high-level ME (knowledge packages) related to long-range planning, mathematics, and astronomy. They were designed for tactical execution on the battlefield rather than autonomous strategic command.

Operational History and Legacy

Conflict Proxies:  The Aaron served as the ground-level force during factional conflicts between the Anunnaki (e.g., the Anzu myth), effectively acting as human proxies in divine disputes.

The Post-Withdrawal Trajectory:  Following the Anunnaki departure, the Aaron specification faced a crisis of function. Because their loyalty-bonding capacity was designed to anchor to a specific, divine administrative framework, that capacity now often bonds to whichever political or institutional structure manages to trigger the protocol.

In the ancient astronaut view, the Aaron type explains the historical tendency for military populations to endure extraordinary hardship and display extreme loyalty to political regimes that may not serve their interests—a legacy of an engineered bonding mechanism operating without its original, intended anchor.

__
6.  The Sangum (also referred to as the sanangum or sanu) is the sixth bloodline type, distinct from the other classifications due to its specialized role as a biological interface for advanced Anunnaki technology.

Design and Purpose

Beyond Priesthood:  While mainstream scholarship often labels them as high priests or temple administrators, the video argues that the Sangum were specifically engineered to operate the temple apparatus, which served as a functional power station or communication hub between human and Anunnaki domains, rather than merely a place of worship.

Sensory Enhancements:  The Sangum were granted neurological capabilities exceeding all other human types. They were described as having the ability to see and hear frequencies outside the normal human baseline and could "know the heart of a place," identifying technological or energetic signatures.

Role and Biological Maintenance

Interface Safety:  The inner sanctum of early temples (Bit Akitu) housed high-energy Anunnaki technology. The Sangum biological modifications were essential to interact with this machinery without suffering physical harm—a critical safety protocol often mistaken by historians as religious boundary-setting.

Selection Protocols:  Candidates were not chosen by human institutional training but were identified by Anunnaki overseers through what the video describes as "divine attention"—a biological scan to detect the Sangum genetic marker in the population.

Rigid Lifestyle:  To protect their sensitive neurological and biological profile, Sangum individuals were subjected to strict celibacy, dietary, and behavioral codes, effectively acting as high-maintenance biological components for the temple machinery.

Legacy and Post-Withdrawal Trajectory

After the Anunnaki withdrew, the Sangum specification faced a crisis of function. Without the original technology to operate, these enhanced sensory capabilities persisted but became "capacities in search of a function."

Proponents of this framework argue that the Sangum lineage manifests today in various shamanic, prophetic, and mystical traditions, where individuals report consistent access to perceptual domains that the rest of the population cannot reach.

__
7.  The Mushkenu represents the seventh bloodline classification and is identified as perhaps the most deliberately obscured type within historical and academic records.

While mainstream scholarship characterizes the Mushkenu as a lower-status free person or commoner, the ancient astronaut perspective argues this designation was fundamentally a biological and functional specification.

Design and Purpose

Social Architecture:  The Mushkenu were optimized for tasks that the Adamu (laborer) type could not perform effectively. They served as the crucial population layer between the directed labor force and the administrative class, acting as artisans, small traders, and village coordinators.

Cognitive Profile:  They required enough cognitive capacity to manage complex social exchanges, mediate local disputes, and handle community-level cooperation without requiring constant top-down supervision from the Anunnaki or Lugal.

The 'Commoner Ceiling':  Researchers identify a 'commoner ceiling' in ancient civilizations—a high level of competency in local, immediate social environments, but a specific, designed resistance to abstract political thinking or challenging the structures above them.

Role and Biological Function

Reproductive Equilibrium:  The Mushkenu acted as the primary vehicle for bloodline mixing within the general population. When higher types (like Lugal or Apkallu) mixed with the Adamu baseline, the Mushkenu represented the 'stable equilibrium point' of these various inheritance ratios, creating a sustainable and functional population.

Social Intelligence:  In the modern context, researchers describe the Mushkenu specification as producing the 'social intelligence specialist'—individuals gifted at holding community fabrics together through interpersonal care and negotiation, even while potentially disengaged from macro-political systems.

Legacy

Because the Mushkenu were built to be the binding agent of the human social fabric, their function remains arguably the most consistent of all eight types. Their role—maintaining local coherence and community ritual—is a constant requirement of human society, which is why this type has remained the most numerous and stable element across history.

__
8.  The Wardom (often associated with the Akkadian word for slave, though researchers argue this is a later legal distortion) is identified as the eighth and most distinct bloodline type.

Unlike the other classifications that suggest a high degree of Anunnaki genetic inheritance, the Wardom is interpreted as the type furthest from the Anunnaki spectrum.

Design and Purpose

Hominin Baseline:  Researchers propose that the Wardom specification represents the most complete expression of the original hominin genetic baseline that existed on Earth prior to any divine genetic intervention.

The 'Outside' Category:  Because they carry the lowest Anunnaki inheritance, they are often described as the "outside" category. They were not integrated into the primary ME (knowledge package) distribution system designed for the higher functional types.

Role and Administrative Valuation

Administrative Utility:  Within the Enlil framework, which evaluated human types by strict administrative utility, the Wardom were the least valued. This led to their historical classification as a servile, legal category—a social status that researchers argue obscures their true biological origin.

The Enki Counterweight:  Despite the administrative dismissal of this type, the Enki framework insisted on their inclusion in the divine household narrative, asserting that every created human type possessed inherent value, even if that value was not "legible" to the administrative system.

Legacy and Trajectory

Post-Withdrawal Suffering:  The Wardom type experienced the most painful post-withdrawal trajectory. Without the Enki framework—which provided a dignifying purpose for all types—this population became the most vulnerable to forced labor, dispossession, and systematic denial of access to knowledge.

Global Pattern:  Ancient astronaut researchers argue that the historical patterns of oppression seen across various cultures are not mere coincidences of social history, but are systemic outcomes of the Enlil administrative hierarchy continuing to operate in the absence of the Enki counterweight.

__
The ME (plural Me) are far more than traditional "divine laws" or "civilizational arts." They are described as encoded knowledge packages or transferable functional programs. When transferred to a human, the ME acted as an installation that activated specific biological and cognitive capacities.

The Nature and Purpose of the ME

Functional Packages:  The ME represent a set of technological and administrative instructions required to operate civilization. When Inana takes the ME to the city of Uruk, it is described as a physical event that fundamentally changes the city's operational capabilities.

Biological Keying:  A critical aspect of the system is that these packages were keyed to the recipient's genetic specification. A human could only activate the ME they were biologically engineered to handle; the installation was not just conceptual, but physical.

__
ME Distribution by Bloodline Type

Access to the ME was strictly tiered by bloodline classification to ensure each type performed only its designated function:

Adamu:  Received the ME for basic labor coordination, agricultural cycles, and resource management.

Adapa:  Received the ME for administrative functions, language precision, recordkeeping, and astronomical observation.

Akalu:  Granted the deepest ME packages, which encoded the seven foundational civilizational domains.

Lugal:  Received the ME of Kingship (Nam-Lugal), military administration, and the Melamu (a marker of divine radiance).

Aaron:  Received the ME for military function, tactical coordination, and loyalty bonding.

Sangum:  Received the ME for temple technology operation and sensory extensions to interface with Anunnaki apparatuses.

Mushkenu:  Received the ME for social coordination, local exchange, and community ritual maintenance.

Wartom:  Received only the minimum ME set necessary for basic participation in the human social structure.

The video maintains that while mainstream archaeology interprets these records through the lens of social history and mythology, the 'ancient astronaut' framework views them as an operational history of a divine administration that left behind a legacy embedded within the human genome itself.

text:
I'm shopping for a home battery to go with my solar system, and the decision is coming down to Tesla Powerwall or Enphase. 🔋☀️

I already have Enphase solar and drive a Tesla, so both make sense. Enphase offers tighter integration with my existing solar equipment, while Tesla has attractive battery capacity, software, and pricing.

Both have options for participating in Xcel Energy's battery incentive program here in Colorado. But there's more to this decision than price and battery capacity.

Do I want backup power when the grid goes down, or do I want to lower my electric bill by storing solar energy for nighttime use? Both are possible, but those goals can compete for the same stored electricity. And there's something else I've started thinking about.

As we get older, technology should make our lives easier, not more complicated. I don't want another app, another account, or another system to babysit. I want everything working together, preferably without me having to think about it.

Sometimes the best technology isn't the one with the most features. It's the one that quietly does its job.

If you've installed a home battery, what do you wish you'd known before buying it?

text:
October 10 Saint Francis Borgia: General of the Jesuits.
(1510-1572)
Patronage:
against earthquakes
Portugal
Rota, Marianas
.
Saint Francis Borgia, named for Francis of Assisi at his birth in 1510, was placed under the tutelage of his uncle, Archbishop of Saragossa, after the death of his mother when he was ten years old. Soon he had to go to the court of Spain, as he was destined to be one of the great lords of that nation. There he remained Christian, modest and virtuous. His noble and beautiful appearance soon brought upon him snares which he succeeded in escaping, setting for himself regimes of prayer and study to escape from the dangers. He wore a hair shirt, and never would enter into any of those games of chance which cause the loss not only of money but of time, the spirit of devotion, and peace of soul. The Empress arranged for him to marry Eleanor de Castro of Portugal, who like himself was very pious. They were blessed with eight children, five sons and three daughters, who continued to practice the virtue of their parents.
.
Having become the Duke of Gandia after his father's death, he became one of the richest and most honored nobles in Spain. In 1539, there was laid upon him the sad duty of escorting the mortal remains of his once beautiful sovereign, the Empress Isabella, who had died still young, to the royal burial ground at Granada. The coffin had to be opened for him, that he might verify the body before it was placed in the tomb; and so unrecognizable, so astonishing a sight met his eyes that he vowed never again to serve any earthly sovereign, subject to so drastic and terrible a change.
.
It was many years before he could follow the call of his Lord; the emperor named him Captain-General of Catalonia, and sent him to bring to justice a group of bandits who had ravaged the countryside. The poor found in him strong protection against oppression. Vices were banished by his ordinances; he endowed poor girls and assisted families ruined by misery and reversals; he delivered debtors from prisons by paying what they owed. He was in effect the very Christian Viceroy of the Emperor. Saint Francis was relieved of this duty when he asked the Emperor, after the death of his father, to return and govern his subjects at Gandia. In Gandia he again did much public good; he built monasteries, founded hospitals, helped the poor in every possible way. But suddenly, his wife was taken from him. He was told by God that this loss was for both his and her own advantage, and amid his tears he offered his own life and that of his children, if that would please the Eternal Master.
.
After making a retreat according to the Exercises of Saint Ignatius, under Blessed Peter Favre, he made the vows of a Jesuit privately until he could see to the establishment of his children. When he went to Rome with one of them, it was rumored he would be made a cardinal like two of his brothers. But he wished to avoid all dignities, and succeeded in doing so by leaving Rome as soon as possible. Saint Ignatius made him his Vicar General for Spain, Portugal, and the East Indies, and there was scarcely a city of Spain and Portugal where he did not establish colleges or houses of the Company of Jesus. At the death of Saint Ignatius two years later, the Order chose him to be its General. Then his journeys became countless; to narrate them all would be an impossibility.
.
The Turks were threatening Christendom, and Pope Saint Pius V commissioned two cardinal-legates to go and assemble the European Christian princes into a league for its defense. The holy Pope chose Francis to accompany one of the Cardinals and, worn out as he was, the Saint obeyed at once. The fatigues of the embassy exhausted what little life was left to him. Saint Francis died in the same year as Saint Pius V, happy to do so in the service of God and the Church, when he returned to Rome in October, 1572.
.
Reflection: Francis Borgia learned the value of earthly grandeurs at the funeral of Queen Isabella. Do the deaths of friends teach us anything about what awaits us also?
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor St. Francis Borgia, and I give Thee thanks for all the graces Thou hast bestowed upon him. I ask Thee to please increase grace in my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to him by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, St. Francis Borgia might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

Scotland as a nation state in 1707 was annexed by England, and defunct as a state and autonomouse people. Yes, individual Scots participated in England's colonial settlements after that time. Yet, prior to 1707 they were banned from trading with any of England's foreign settlements.

Colonization is a co-opting and cooperative venture, and so it was Scotland's colonization, post-1707.  But Scotland as a nation had neither colony nor slave, either before England colonised it or after. Slavery, note, remained. pre- and post-union,  a crime under Scots law.

Colonization is about extraction, exploitation. How were the Anglo-British colonies in East Africa - Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania colonized and maintained? With 10,000 white elite – yes, among them Scots and Irish individuals, inducted into and offered opportunities in England's colonial expansion – but crucially with 300,000 individuals from the Indian sub-continent; administrators, tradesmen, military. 

England's African colonization was well underway in the 17th Century; Ghana from the 1630s,  notorious for being the seat of England's slave trade; Gambia, the Barbary Coast including Tangier, and the Cape of Good Hope. Where were those African slaves taken? England's colonies in N. America – Virginia (from 1607), Massachusetts (1620) and New  York (1664), and of course England's Caribbean colonies  - among other  lesser islands, St Kitts (1623), Barbados (1627) and Jamaica in 1655. English dictator, Oliver Cromwell, who annexed Scotland in 1650, send 'indentured' (i.e. enslaved) Scots to these islands to work their colonies, where they died in their thousands from the disease that was rife there, a fate which the English plantation owners wished to avoid. Many of those Scots were educated and  skilled. They stayed and ran English slave  owners' plantations. But look at those English parish names in Jamaica. 

The Chinese at one time were a maritime trading nation, travelling the oceans, notably to Africa. But while the English sent gunboats to make war, Chinese vessels came to trade. Scotland, pre-1707, did exactly the same.  It had numerous highly regarded and successful trading 'colonies' all around the European mainland, North Sea and the Baltic. These became the earliest 'trade embassies'.  That is what it tried to replicate in Panama and with the Darien Company, also known as "Company of Scotland Trading to Africa and the Indies". These Scots maritime ventures were diplomatic and commercial in nature. Like the Chinese, the Company's stated purpose was trade and settlement, not conquest the subjugation of existing populations or slave plantation.

Returning to your glib statement, it is the charge frequently levelled by the English at Scots as an attempt to undermine Scotland's righful and historically unassailable claim that England annnexed and colonised it in 1707, in no "voluntary partnership" but rather in a militarily maintained bogus treaty. No-one was ever fooled by England's story outside of the British Isles. And Scots won't stand any longer for the English colonial gaslighting you repeat here.

text:
Are you getting serious about church planting? You should consider the Carey Center at Grimke Seminary  It offers both a church planting residency and church planting courses. I serve on the faculty as a lecturer.

Here is the opening to one of my lectures I've prepped for next week (they aren't recorded): 

There are so many ways we could consider this wonderful book. But since we only have an hour, and this is a course on church planting, I want to give you a simple grid that I think will help you better grasp the context God has called you to minister in.

There are just three Ps: people, place, and past.

These three Ps will tie into our later discussion on localism, so I want to introduce them now.

I want to tell you a little bit about my personal history with this book because it ties directly into what we're doing here this week.

I had been planning to plant a church on the east side of Cincinnati since about 1999. After graduating from a small pastor's college, we almost moved back home to the Cincinnati area. But I felt like I needed more time to grow as a leader, and we surprised everyone when I took a call as an associate pastor down in South Carolina.

That required me to go back to seminary, which I hadn't wanted to do, but it ended up being really good for me. So we moved to Spartanburg, South Carolina, intending for it to be a temporary stay before returning home to plant a church.

We had a really difficult time in South Carolina, but it was also one of the most important times of my life. I grew by leaps and bounds in all sorts of ways.

It was while I was there that I began to realize just how much I loved the Midwest.

South Carolina doesn't have much by way of corn or wheat. The soil just isn't good for it. And I had grown up surrounded by cornfields my entire life. Sometimes, when I was studying Hebrew or doing sermon prep, I would pull up an eight-hour HD recording of a cornfield that I had found on YouTube, put it on our big-screen TV, and just let it play in the background.

I recognized all the birds and the sound of the wind going through the cornstalks.

I loved the people I was serving, but I was longing for home.

And then, in either 2016 or 2017, I read two books back-to-back that helped me really zero in on my call. The first was Hillbilly Elegy by J.D. Vance, now our vice president. The second was The Man Who Moved a Mountain by Richard Davis.

These books pair well together.

In Hillbilly Elegy, Vance talks about growing up in a dysfunctional family as a poor, white, working-class Midwestern American. He describes the Hillbilly Highway, the great migration of Scots-Irish and Appalachian Americans who moved north looking for industrial jobs, particularly in the automobile industry, about a hundred years ago.

Many of these families settled along the way, including Vance's grandparents, who moved from Kentucky to Middletown, Ohio, only about an hour from where I live.

These were the same kinds of people Bob Childress ministered to in the mountains of Virginia.

So when I read Vance's story, I heard my story.

I grew up white trash in the '80s and '90s, and I could relate to so much of what Vance described and what Childress encountered in his ministry.

Their people were my people. Their problems were our problems.

I understood the thick honor culture, where you do not involve the authorities. You don't do it. Snitches get stitches. That deep suspicion of authority. The drug abuse, the laziness, the pride, the violence. All of it was familiar to me.

But what struck me about these two books was that, while both dealt with Appalachia and its very real problems, neither had that sniveling, judgmental, condescending attitude you so often get from Hollywood and Democratic politicians who see that whole world as flyover country.

Instead, there was a deep love for these people.

And so, as I was down in South Carolina, suffering through endless conversations about Clemson football, being served sweet tea that you could rightly call diabetes juice, and missing cornfields, I began to understand why I had such a strong call to the Midwest.

Ironically, it was while living somewhere else that I came to better understand the place God was calling me to.

And that brings me back to you.

You're here because you're either planting a church or you want to plant a church. And I'm telling you, to do that well, you must love the place God has called you to and the unique people who reside there.

And you need to know their past. Because their history will help you understand their sins, their strengths, their potential, and the battles that lie ahead of you as a pastor planting a church.

I love Clermont County, Ohio, and the Ohio Valley. It owns my heart.

And Bob Childress loved the people of the Buffalo Mountain region. They owned his heart.

Who has God laid on your heart? What is the unique mission field He has called you to?

Let's dive into it...

text:
Marking an end to the woke era in Fine Gael should mean clearly separating what stays and what goes. I can't speak for everyone who supports the center-right motion, but you won't find many FG members nowadays who don't agree it was right to pass:
✅ The gay marriage referendum
✅ Repeal the 8th

There is also progress that FG members see in the right direction: 
✅ Asylum numbers and accommodation costs falling
✅ Full employment
✅ Growing capital spending
✅ Income Tax bands moving higher
✅ Personal Investment Accounts

The "centre" in "centre-right" means a party still open to ideas that reach the centre of Irish politics from either side. Raising the minimum wage is a traditionally left idea, but we have done it countless times. It becomes even more essential in an era of inflation, so the lowest paid workers aren't left behind.

The "progressive centre" era has too many hallmarks I want left behind. Again, I can't claim all supporters of the motion agree, but I offer them as my own:
❌ Growing real current spending at unsustainable rates
❌ Family and Care referendums
❌ Hate speech bill
❌ Non-EU workers now accounting for the majority of job additions
❌ Gender quotas in all areas of life
❌ Transgender rights to the detriment of biological sex
❌ Siding with Gaza flotillas ("act of courage") and the Ulm 5
❌ The 3-day wait, safe access zones and surrogacy
❌ Don't hug your granny and the "tradwives" campaign to come in 2027

The centre-right motion is about where the party goes from here. It's about seeing more fruitful and sensible ideas from the right of politics, with its focus on preserving institutions and ideas that have stood the test of time.

A revival of Christian Democratic thinking should mean FG reviving its core principles:
👩‍👩‍👧‍👦 The family and communities as a core unit of society
💪 Personal responsibility
⤵️ Subsidiarity - Placing a renewed focus on political decisions taking place as local as is possible and practical. A credible plan for a United Ireland must consider decentralisation.
 💼 Enterprise as the engine of all shared wealth. This is something Fine Gael already does well but must not be overlooked either. Gay Mitchell, former MEP for Dublin, said it best in my earliest days of canvassing for the party. He believed in "rights, responsibilities, social justice and enterprise".

A strong centre-right is needed to push back far-right movements that are gaining pace elsewhere in Europe. It's about an injection of common sense into how the party formulates policy going forward.

𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗚𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗥𝗨𝗡 𝗢𝗨𝗧 𝗢𝗙 𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗘𝗬… 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗬 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗬𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗚𝗢𝗟𝗗.

Gold representing wealth and financial security
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Every financial crisis eventually becomes a political one.
At first, the problem appears technical — deficits, borrowing, monetary policy, temporary instability. Governments reassure the public that reforms are coming. Committees are formed. Experts debate solutions.
But when the treasury finally empties and the options narrow, the problem becomes brutally simple.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆.

At that moment, the definition of wealth quietly changes.

What citizens once called private property becomes, in the eyes of the state, available resources.

History shows how this story ends. Not with polite defaults or careful restructuring. But with the sudden realization — often arriving at the end of a dusty road — that the state has decided it knows exactly where the wealth is.

The Roman Republic learned this lesson many times.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗔 𝗥𝗢𝗠𝗔𝗡 𝗦𝗘𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗢𝗥 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗔𝗘𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗔𝗡 𝗚𝗨𝗔𝗥𝗗
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
A Roman senator sits on the shaded portico of his villa in Campania. The afternoon air is warm. A Greek slave reads Homer — the fall of Troy, a city that believed its walls eternal. The senator listens half-heartedly. His thoughts drift to accounts and estates: grain from Sicily, rents from vineyards in Gaul, and the gold he accumulated during his years as governor of Upper Gaul.

Then he sees it.

A cloud of dust rising on the distant road.

Hoofbeats follow.
Praetorian cavalry.
He does not need to ask why they have come.
The emperor — perhaps Tiberius, perhaps another — has declared him an enemy of the state. The charges will be vague: corruption, disloyalty, treason against Rome.
But the senator knows the real reason.

The treasury is empty. They are not coming for his slave. They are not coming for his harvest. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗴𝗼𝗹𝗱. What will follow will be described as justice. As necessity. As fairness in service of the Republic.

But it is confiscation. Pure and simple.

And it has happened before.

And it will happen again.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗟𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡 𝗜𝗡 𝗣𝗢𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗦
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
When states run out of money, they follow a path as old as civilization itself.

The sequence rarely changes:

𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘀 → 𝗖𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗗𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 → 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹𝘀 → 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

It does not matter whether the system is a monarchy, a democracy, or a revolutionary regime. The motive is the same everywhere. Power must be preserved.

Politicians who spend win elections. Rulers who distribute wealth secure loyalty. Debt postpones consequences. Eventually, the bill arrives, and the state begins searching for assets. By now the pattern should be obvious.

History shows where it looks first.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗢𝗡𝗘 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗧𝗘 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗠𝗣𝗧𝗬 𝗧𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗦𝗨𝗥𝗬
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Empires rarely collapse because of invasion first. They collapse because of promises they cannot afford.

Athens offered one of the earliest warnings. In the 5th century BC, Pericles moved the treasury of the Delian League from Delos to Athens. Funds meant for collective defence quietly became funding for monuments — the Parthenon, temples, and civic works glorifying the city. The money belonged to the alliance. But Athens spent it anyway.

Rome repeated the pattern centuries later. Civil wars drained the treasury. Armies demanded pay. Politicians promised land and rewards to veterans. When money ran out, Rome found another solution. Proscriptions.
In 82 BC, Sulla published lists of wealthy citizens in the Forum. Anyone named could be killed without trial. Their property was confiscated by the state. Heads of the condemned were sometimes displayed in the Forum — a grim reminder that the lists were not theoretical. Gold flowed into the treasury.
A generation later, the Second Triumvirate — Mark Antony, Octavian, and Lepidus — revived the practice. Thousands died. Estates were seized. Even Cicero Rome’s greatest orator, was hunted down and executed.
Armies were paid. Power was secured.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗧𝗪𝗢 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗢𝗜𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
When confiscation cannot keep pace with spending, rulers turn to the currency itself. Rome provides the textbook case.
In the early empire, the silver denarius contained nearly pure silver. By the third century AD, emperors desperate to fund armies and bureaucracies began diluting it. Silver content collapsed. The coin looked the same. Its value did not.

Prices surged. Trade faltered. Confidence vanished. Diocletian imposed price controls. Constantine introduced new coinage. But the underlying problem remained. The state was spending far more than it could fund.

Modern governments rarely debase coins with copper. They achieve the same effect through monetary expansion, inflation, and debt monetization.

Savings lose value. Capital begins searching for refuge. And throughout history, that refuge has often been gold.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗥𝗘𝗘 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗢𝗖𝗞𝗘𝗗 𝗩𝗔𝗨𝗟𝗧
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
When capital begins fleeing a failing monetary system, governments respond predictably. They close the exits. China provides early examples.

The reformer Wang Mang attempted sweeping nationalizations of land and wealth during the first century AD. Centuries later, the Qing emperor Yongzheng confiscated fortunes of officials accused of corruption.

Modern history offers equally stark examples.
In 1968, India passed the Gold Control Act, restricting private ownership of bullion and forcing citizens to convert holdings into jewelry or surrender them to the financial system.
In 2013, Cyprus delivered a shock. Depositors woke to discover their bank accounts frozen. Withdrawals were restricted. A portion of deposits was simply seized to recapitalize failing banks.
The message was unmistakable: 𝗪𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗙𝗢𝗨𝗥 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗟 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗠
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Eventually the state turns toward the asset citizens believed would protect them from monetary collapse. Gold.
History offers relentless examples.

During the French Revolution, the government seized church lands and precious metals to support the collapsing assignat currency.

In 1933, the United States ordered citizens to surrender their gold. Private ownership was banned; citizens were forced to sell at $20.67 per ounce. Shortly afterward, the government raised the price to $35. The difference went to the state.

In India, gold ownership was restricted for decades.

In Cyprus, deposits became the target.

The pattern is clear: gold is treated as insurance by citizens, but when a monetary system fails, the state notices who owns the insurance — and claims it.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗟 𝗧𝗥𝗨𝗧𝗛
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝘁 — 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁.
Of course, modern governments insist such measures would never be necessary today. History suggests otherwise.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗠𝗢𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗕𝗘𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
The sequence is simple: political survival.
Deficit spending buys votes.
Redistribution secures loyalty.
Inflation hides the cost.

Democracies and tyrannies differ in form, not incentive. When power is threatened, wealth becomes the easiest target.

Fairness, Equality, Emergency, Necessity. These are just the words used to justify it. The reality remains unchanged.

Today, the pressures are quietly returning. Government deficits across the developed world have reached levels once seen only during world wars. Public debt climbs relentlessly. Political movements frame wealth as injustice. In New York, politicians such as Zohran Mamdani openly advocate redistribution models once considered fringe.

Modern wealth rarely sits in chests buried beneath villas. It sits in brokerage accounts, ETFs, and digital ledgers — far easier for governments to identify.
None of this should surprise anyone who studies history. What is surprising is how often investors convince themselves that this time will be different.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗡𝗟𝗬 𝗦𝗘𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗖𝗟𝗨𝗦𝗜𝗢𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗚𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁. 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲.
And insurance only works if it is available when the house is on fire.
No homeowner would accept a policy that pays only after permission from the same institution that is burning the house down.
Yet millions hold gold in exactly that way: through ETFs, pooled vault accounts, or banks.

These are not gold. They are claims on gold.

History has shown what happens to claims during crises: they can be frozen, redefined, or disappear overnight.

𝗜𝗳 𝗴𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀, 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗹𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗴𝗼𝗹𝗱.

But ownership alone is not enough. Location matters. Assets that are visible, centralized, and easy to reach become the first targets.

Modern investors often assume institutions will protect them. They protect themselves first. Nations abandon treaties when interests shift. Governments change rules when crises appear.
Which leads to three principles every holder of gold should understand:
𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁: If you do not control it, you do not own it.
𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱: If it sits entirely in the financial system, it is accessible to the system.
𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗱: If it sits entirely in one jurisdiction, it is subject to that jurisdiction’s laws — especially when those laws change overnight.
Rome confiscated wealth.
Revolutionary France seized precious metals.
America confiscated gold.
India restricted it.
Cyprus seized deposits.
The method changes. The logic does not.

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗲𝘁.

Because when the dust rises, the riders may no longer be the Praetorian Guard.

They may be the IRS.

Or HMRC.

And they will not be asking politely.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗟 𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Gold protects you from failing money. But history leaves one final warning:

When governments run out of money, they remember who has it — and they come to collect.
𝗚𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. 𝗣𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗠𝗘𝗥

text:
Italy's Shelves Went Bare in Days. The Pantry Was the Missing Piece.

Around October 20, truck drivers in southern Italy parked their rigs over the price of diesel. Within days, reports described partly empty supermarket shelves in Sicily, Calabria and Puglia, with fresh pasta, packaged cheese and produce short, and pumps empty in Naples. By October 26 an emergency decree had eased it, and police were clearing roadblocks so stores could restock.

Most people don't notice how short the chain is until something interrupts it. Via @yanasatv, the delivery system gets described as a 72-hour one, which is their number, but the Italian shelves offered a fair illustration. Diesel there is reported roughly a third above its pre-war level after a tax discount lapsed.

A food system built to the hour, and a fuel protest was enough to find the edge of it.

A few days later and an ocean away, an explosion and fire hit the Quaker Oats plant in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, on October 24. It is the largest oat-milling facility in the world, processing over two million pounds a day by the company's own account. Nobody was hurt, the cause is under investigation, and no shortage has been reported. Still, it made the concentration visible.

It's worth noticing where these stories end. Italy's shelves were restocked by decree and police. What nobody counts is how many days of food a household was already holding when the trucks stopped. Reports mention shoppers stockpiling as a cause of the shortage, as though the pantry were the problem rather than the buffer.

For this community, late October is the other side of that story. Squash is curing. Onions and garlic hang drying, a process the fall homestead guides put at two to four weeks. Potatoes and beets go into the cool dark, and the freezer fills. With gas at $4.23 a gallon, about 39 percent over last year, and ground beef at $6.79 a pound, a stocked shelf is also money not spent at the register.

There are people who treat a cellar as a hobby, and people who treat it as insurance. Every once in a while, a headline from somewhere else shows which one it was.

It is interesting what a decree can put back on a shelf, and what only a household can.

text:
High Inflation Haunts Trump and Republicans on Eve of Election

Listen · 8:42 min
30OCT2026
By Tony Romm
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/wtw03b6bfM
Reporting from Washington

A backlash over high prices helped Republicans capture a majority in 2024. Now, it may be the source of the party’s own undoing.

On the final Tuesday before the midterm election, President Trump found himself in Corpus Christi, Texas, musing aloud about the political forces that had propelled his return to office two years earlier.

“I got elected because of high prices,” he told rallygoers in a state that has become the site of an unexpectedly close Senate race. Then the president turned his ire toward Democrats: “I didn’t have the high prices. They had the high prices.”

For Mr. Trump, that previous source of political strength now threatens to topple Republicans in 2026. The fate of the party’s control of Congress may well hinge on the depth of voters’ fury with the rising cost of living — and the president’s unmet promises to do something about it.

The concern among Republicans has been evident as Mr. Trump crisscrosses the country in an 11th-hour campaign sprint. He has tried to present the economy as strong, growing and rife with new investment, while downplaying the fact that inflation has clearly worsened under his party’s stewardship.

Offering a final snapshot on the state of the economy before Election Day, a set of government reports on Thursday confirmed some of Mr. Trump’s claims and undercut others. The data showed that the economy was indeed expanding at a faster clip, with a key measure of its total output increasing at a 3.4 percent annual rate this summer. But prices also accelerated, rising more rapidly in September compared with a year earlier, and continuing to outpace wage gains.

As a result, Mr. Trump’s message contrasted with the experience of voters, who see the harsh realities of a high-cost economy every day — when they fill up their gas tanks, shop for groceries, pay their health insurance premiums, receive their credit card bills and confront the difficulties of homeownership.

Having weathered almost two years of high tariffs, geopolitical discord and other economic shocks, voters seem inclined to exact another round of political vengeance at the ballot box, or so the latest polls suggest. Depending on the extent of that rebuke, it could strip Republicans of their congressional majority and curtail Mr. Trump’s economic ambitions for the rest of his presidency.

Tomas J. Philipson, an economist at the University of Chicago who advised Mr. Trump during his first term, attributed some of the price increases to what he described as laudable goals, including the attempt to disarm Iran. He added that the economy showed plenty of signs of strength despite the sour national mood.

But, he added, “people don’t keep track of aggregate statistics.”

“They go to the grocery store every week, and they go to the gas station maybe every other week, and they are upset about that,” Mr. Philipson said. “People are still upset at those price increases.”

More than any other economic issue, it was soaring costs under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. that helped sweep Republicans into power in 2024. On the day of his inauguration, Mr. Trump committed to “marshal” the whole of government to “rapidly bring down costs.”

By that point, inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index had fallen to about 3 percent, and many experts believed it would continue to decline from the heights of the pandemic. Instead, prices began to increase as Mr. Trump’s agenda catalyzed a series of costly economic shocks.

In a bid to boost domestic manufacturing, the president imposed withering tariffs on imports. Frequently challenged in court and recalibrated, the ever-changing duties raised revenue yet made foreign goods more expensive for U.S. purchasers.

Hoping to spur more investment, the president also sought to unwind a bevy of regulations, and he clinched a package of tax cuts that offered substantial savings for businesses. But the law also worsened the federal debt, which topped $40 trillion under Republicans’ watch. That helped to make government borrowing — and, with it, consumer borrowing — more expensive.

That same law set in motion cuts to federal food and health benefits for low-income families. While it helped to lower tax bills for some Americans, the effect may have been less noticeable, as the war with Iran sent energy prices higher. The conflict, now in its ninth month, has ricocheted across the global economy, raising the costs of airfares, farming, heating, shipping and transportation.

As a result, many staples of American life — gasoline, groceries, health insurance, mortgages and more — have become more expensive this year. Overall, the price increases have also outpaced workers’ hourly wages, according to the government, compounding the financial toll.

To be sure, the economy on the whole has its bright spots. Hiring has been sluggish but stable, markets are riding high and consumers are continuing to spend. That spending, a major driver of overall growth, rose at a 3.8 percent annual clip in the third quarter, according to the data released on Thursday.

That suggests Americans still have some amount of confidence that their financial footing is sound. Yet voters have also signaled — in political polls and in economists’ surveys — that their mood remains grim with the election just days away.

The data “points to an economy that is running pretty strong,” said Satyam Panday, the chief U.S. economist for S&P Global Ratings. “The only sore spot in the economy is inflation, and I think despite the strong consumption and growth, you’ve got this pessimism.”

Alex Jacquez, a former aide to Mr. Biden now serving as senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research at Groundwork Action, a liberal group, said the “conundrum” facing Mr. Trump this November bore some resemblance to the forces that swept Democrats out of power last time. Both parties sought to convince voters that the economy was on better footing because of their policies — only to incur their wrath, despite the gains, because of unchecked costs.

“When you make a promise to get elected to bring down prices, and fail to do so, I really think that’s going to be the only number that matters,” Mr. Jacquez said.

In the waning moments of the 2026 race, Mr. Trump and his aides have responded to the backlash with a mixture of optimism and dismissal. They have promised anew that they can bring down costs quickly, while denying at times that there is a problem at all.

On Fox Business on Thursday, Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said that “really huge” growth figures from last quarter reflected a strong economy under Mr. Trump. He said the uptick in output was also putting “downward pressure on prices.”

“You can pick and choose specific prices and say, ‘Oh, I’m very frustrated about that,’ and it’s a legitimate concern, a legitimate feeling, but as an economist, you’ve got to look at things in the aggregate,” Mr. Hassett said.

Only days earlier, though, Mr. Hassett described the concerns around an affordability crisis as a “myth.” That echoed Mr. Trump’s oft-stated belief during the 2026 campaign that the affordability issue was a “hoax.”

But in a sign of Republicans’ vulnerability, the president has ramped up his appearances in the final stretch of the election, even appearing in states like South Carolina and Texas, which were once seen as safer political terrain for Republicans. Having previously described the economy as a “public relations” problem, the president mounted a heightened effort to recast its strength.

“You know, we got inflation down,” he claimed at a rally in Michigan on Sunday, while greatly understating the nation’s inflation rate.

Two days later, in Lubbock, Texas, Mr. Trump insisted that gas prices had fallen, even though they were more than $1 per gallon higher than they were on the day he took office, according to AAA. By Thursday, he was in Rock Hill, S.C., hailing what he described as better-than-expected growth numbers and an economy that was “booming.”

Among the crowd, as he spoke, a smattering of signs nevertheless read: “LOWER PRICES.”

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.
