By that point, inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index had fallen to about 3 percent, and many experts believed it would continue to decline from the heights of the pandemic. Instead, prices began to increase as Mr. Trump’s agenda catalyzed a series of costly economic shocks.

In a bid to boost domestic manufacturing, the president imposed withering tariffs on imports. Frequently challenged in court and recalibrated, the ever-changing duties raised revenue yet made foreign goods more expensive for U.S. purchasers.

Hoping to spur more investment, the president also sought to unwind a bevy of regulations, and he clinched a package of tax cuts that offered substantial savings for businesses. But the law also worsened the federal debt, which topped $40 trillion under Republicans’ watch. That helped to make government borrowing — and, with it, consumer borrowing — more expensive.

That same law set in motion cuts to federal food and health benefits for low-income families. While it helped to lower tax bills for some Americans, the effect may have been less noticeable, as the war with Iran sent energy prices higher. The conflict, now in its ninth month, has ricocheted across the global economy, raising the costs of airfares, farming, heating, shipping and transportation.

As a result, many staples of American life — gasoline, groceries, health insurance, mortgages and more — have become more expensive this year. Overall, the price increases have also outpaced workers’ hourly wages, according to the government, compounding the financial toll.

To be sure, the economy on the whole has its bright spots. Hiring has been sluggish but stable, markets are riding high and consumers are continuing to spend. That spending, a major driver of overall growth, rose at a 3.8 percent annual clip in the third quarter, according to the data released on Thursday.

That suggests Americans still have some amount of confidence that their financial footing is sound. Yet voters have also signaled — in political polls and in economists’ surveys — that their mood remains grim with the election just days away.

The data “points to an economy that is running pretty strong,” said Satyam Panday, the chief U.S. economist for S&P Global Ratings. “The only sore spot in the economy is inflation, and I think despite the strong consumption and growth, you’ve got this pessimism.”

Alex Jacquez, a former aide to Mr. Biden now serving as senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research at Groundwork Action, a liberal group, said the “conundrum” facing Mr. Trump this November bore some resemblance to the forces that swept Democrats out of power last time. Both parties sought to convince voters that the economy was on better footing because of their policies — only to incur their wrath, despite the gains, because of unchecked costs.

“When you make a promise to get elected to bring down prices, and fail to do so, I really think that’s going to be the only number that matters,” Mr. Jacquez said.

In the waning moments of the 2026 race, Mr. Trump and his aides have responded to the backlash with a mixture of optimism and dismissal. They have promised anew that they can bring down costs quickly, while denying at times that there is a problem at all.

On Fox Business on Thursday, Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said that “really huge” growth figures from last quarter reflected a strong economy under Mr. Trump. He said the uptick in output was also putting “downward pressure on prices.”

“You can pick and choose specific prices and say, ‘Oh, I’m very frustrated about that,’ and it’s a legitimate concern, a legitimate feeling, but as an economist, you’ve got to look at things in the aggregate,” Mr. Hassett said.

Only days earlier, though, Mr. Hassett described the concerns around an affordability crisis as a “myth.” That echoed Mr. Trump’s oft-stated belief during the 2026 campaign that the affordability issue was a “hoax.”

But in a sign of Republicans’ vulnerability, the president has ramped up his appearances in the final stretch of the election, even appearing in states like South Carolina and Texas, which were once seen as safer political terrain for Republicans. Having previously described the economy as a “public relations” problem, the president mounted a heightened effort to recast its strength.

“You know, we got inflation down,” he claimed at a rally in Michigan on Sunday, while greatly understating the nation’s inflation rate.

Two days later, in Lubbock, Texas, Mr. Trump insisted that gas prices had fallen, even though they were more than $1 per gallon higher than they were on the day he took office, according to AAA. By Thursday, he was in Rock Hill, S.C., hailing what he described as better-than-expected growth numbers and an economy that was “booming.”

Among the crowd, as he spoke, a smattering of signs nevertheless read: “LOWER PRICES.”

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

text:
For Immediate Release
 
Nickelback Release Eleventh Studio Album Everything Under the Sun Today

The Rock Icons Deliver A Career-Spanning Collection Of Anthemic Rock, Emotional Storytelling And Hard-Earned Perspective, Out Now Via Virgin Music Group
 
Powered By The Chart-Topping Single “Rattle The Cage” (feat. John 5), The Album Arrives As The Band Prepares To Bring Its Next Chapter To Stages Around The World On The 2027 Everything Under The Sun Tour
 
(October 30, 2026) - Nickelback embrace the full spectrum of life on Everything Under The Sun, their eleventh studio album, out now via Virgin Music Group. Blending explosive rock anthems, deeply personal songwriting and moments of unexpected vulnerability, the collection pairs the band’s unmistakable sound with fresh perspectives on freedom, heartbreak, redemption and human connection.
 
Featuring the chart-topping single “Rattle The Cage” (feat. John 5), alongside the emotionally charged “Leave Me Behind” and “Make Me Love You,” the album moves between arena-sized riffs and intimate storytelling, capturing life in all its contradictions.
 
“Everything Under The Sun captures every side of who we are as a band. There are songs that hit as hard as anything we’ve ever done, songs that take chances, and songs that remind us why we love making music together,” says Chad Kroeger.

The album is led by “Rattle The Cage” (feat. John 5), which has reached No. 1 at Rock radio in Canada for three consecutive weeks and topped the U.S. Active Rock radio chart. Driven by towering guitars, pounding riffs and arena-ready energy, the track channels raw intensity into a rallying cry for rock fans.
 
That unrestrained spirit carries into “Last Night Was Fun,” a celebration of unforgettable nights, larger-than-life stories and questionable decisions. Elsewhere, the album trades high-octane release for emotional depth, revealing a band equally at home delivering hard-hitting rock and exploring the complexities of the human experience.
 
“Leave Me Behind” is one of the collection’s emotional centerpieces, offering a powerful statement on loyalty and standing by someone through their darkest moments. Alongside “Lift Somebody Up,” it underscores the strength of compassion and the importance of showing up for others when it matters most.
 
On “If I Don’t Go,” Nickelback confront the difficult choice to leave a familiar life behind, break destructive cycles and pursue a different future. Exploring addiction, survival and redemption, the track delivers one of the album’s most personal narratives. “Make Me Love You” examines the uncertainty of opening your heart to another person, while “Bottled Dreams” finds hope in the possibility that even the most uncertain messages can find their way home.
 
Across Everything Under The Sun, Nickelback balance swagger, humor and muscular guitars with candid storytelling. The result is a collection that embraces the many dimensions of life, from reckless abandon to reflection, and pairs the band’s signature hooks with a willingness to explore new creative territory.

TRACK LIST:
1. Rattle The Cage
2. Bones For The Crows
3. I Already Know
4. Leave Me Behind
5. If I Don't Go
6. Make Me Love You
7. Chasin' Famous
8. Simple Song
9. Technicolor Steamboat
10. Lift Somebody Up
11. Bottled Dreams
12. Last Night Was Fun

The album arrives amid a period of renewed momentum for Nickelback. Their acclaimed Netflix documentary, Hate to Love: Nickelback, offered an unprecedented look inside the band’s journey and became a global sensation. Meanwhile, the Get Rollin’ World Tour became the fastest-selling and highest-attended tour of their career. With new music and an expansive international tour ahead, the band is bringing that momentum to its next chapter.
 
Beginning February 6, 2027, in Pittsburgh, the Everything Under The Sun Tour will bring Nickelback’s signature live show to arenas across North America, the UK and Europe, before heading to Australia in October.

text:
Kevin Costner’s wife asked for $248,000 a month in child support. In court, she said she didn’t know how she’d afford groceries.

They had a prenup. It gave her 30 days to leave his house after she filed for divorce. A judge had to order her out.

They married in 2004 and had three children. In May 2023, after 18 years, she filed. The house was his, bought in 1988, before the marriage.

The prenup paid her $100,000 on the wedding day, $100,000 on the first anniversary, and $1 million after she filed.

He offered about $51,000 a month. A judge set $129,755 for now. She asked for more.

She moved into a $40,000 a month rental and said it wasn’t enough for the kids.

That summer, she was photographed on vacation in Hawaii with a family friend, Josh Connor.

In September 2023, the judge decided: $63,209 a month.

In the video below, Kevin arrives at court: “We’re talking about somebody I love on the other side.” Then listen for what she says is in the kids’ DNA.

She later married Josh Connor.

The case for Christine: 18 years, three kids, and a husband who made over $1 million a month on Yellowstone.
The case for Kevin: she signed the prenup, and their oldest son drives a 15 year old truck.
Was $63,209 a month for three kids fair, or did she ask for too much?

text:
Viral 3-Year-Old Football Sensation Nevada Pierre Gets Academy Opportunity as Jay-Z’s Roc Nation Steps In

Three-year-old football sensation Nevada Pierre, whose remarkable ball skills have attracted widespread attention on social media, has received fresh opportunities to develop his talent following a controversial incident at a youth football match in Florida.

Nevada went viral after videos showed him dribbling past older children and scoring goals during a youth league game in Winter Park, Florida, on October 24. The incident attracted further attention after police were called following a dispute involving his parents and league officials.

While Nevada’s family said he was being unfairly treated because of his football ability, the league maintained that the disagreement involved the adults and also raised concerns about the boy’s conduct during the match. Police made no arrests and treated the incident as a civil matter.

Former United States international footballer Eddie Johnson has since offered Nevada a place in his EJE7 Soccer Academy in Orlando to support his development.

Jay-Z’s Roc Nation Sports has also reportedly pledged support, with plans to take Nevada and his family to Spain in December for an athletic development experience. His parents have expressed interest in relocating to Spain to further nurture his football talent.

text:
Good day, Tech Select Hotspot Owners Network
@hotspotowners
Those ISPs’ interests deserve a hearing, just as hotspot owners’ investments and customers’ need for affordable access do. But a provider’s willingness to sell capacity does not, by itself, settle how the downstream service should be authorised.

A regulatory framework gives everyone predictable rules, rather than a separate bargain for whoever asks.
Consider banking. Banks offer different products and serve different customers, but imagine each setting its own rules for protecting deposits, identifying customers, and handling complaints. One might cut costs by skipping safeguards, while another pays to maintain them. Customers would struggle to know how their money is protected.

That uncertainty would hurt both responsible businesses and the public.

Communications needs the same principle: clear responsibilities for authorisation, customer protection, equipment, security and reporting. Common standards can accommodate different business models and proportionate requirements without forcing every provider into the same commercial arrangement.

The agency model is one possible route. ISPs that prefer to supply capacity should offer a workable alternative that explains who is authorised to serve customers and who is responsible for each obligation.

Their commercial interests should be given fair consideration, but they must not override those responsibilities. The aim is to create a framework where providers and hotspot entrepreneurs can make business decisions with confidence, while customers remain protected regardless of which service they choose. #Tulinamwe

text:
Getting laid off in your 50s is hard. Trying to get hired again can feel even harder, and a lot of people quietly wonder whether their age is part of the problem.

You’re not imagining it. In AARP’s latest survey of more than 1,600 workers 50 and older, 64% said they had seen or experienced age discrimination at work. Nearly a quarter said they felt pushed out of their jobs. Common assumptions included that older workers aren’t good with technology or resist change.

Age discrimination against workers 40 and older is illegal under federal law, but it’s often subtle and hard to prove. Here in Colorado, there’s an extra protection: most employers can’t ask for your age, birth date or graduation dates on an initial job application.

If you’re job hunting in your 50s, here are some things that help:
~Update your resume for today’s market. Focus on the last 10 to 15 years, list your current tech skills and drop graduation dates if you want to.
~Lean on your network. Former coworkers, clients and industry groups often open doors faster than online applications.
~Show you’re current. A recent certification, an online course or comfort with AI tools can push back on stereotypes before anyone says them out loud.
~Protect your finances while you search. Apply for unemployment right away. Stretch your severance. Look at COBRA versus a marketplace health plan, because marketplace coverage is often cheaper if your income has dropped. And try not to touch your retirement accounts unless you truly have to.
~Consider consulting, contract or part-time work. It can bridge the gap and sometimes turns into a full-time offer.
~If you think you were treated unfairly because of your age, document everything and know the deadlines. Generally, you have 300 days in Colorado to file a charge with the EEOC.

Your experience is still worth something. Sometimes it takes finding the employer smart enough to see it.

Sources: HuffPost, AARP, U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, Colorado Department of Labor and Employment

text:
What happened in crypto cards this week?

A card partner outage, etherfi taking in Zeal users, a cheaper physical card, new cashback bands, and Visa's stablecoin numbers.

Here are 10 updates worth knowing—and the conditions behind them. 🧵

1/ @BleapApp

On 24 Oct, Bleap said its card partner Unlimit was having a disruption, so some card payments could fail. Bleap said funds stayed safe, and bank transfers and wallet deposits and withdrawals weren't affected. Bleap's status page marked it resolved on 25 Oct.

2/ @ether_fi

On 28 Oct, etherfi said its card has passed 120K holders.

On 23 Oct, etherfi said it acquired selected Zeal assets, not user accounts, keys or funds. Zeal users can migrate from inside the Zeal app, nothing moves automatically, and etherfi's migration page says they must move by 1 Dec 2026.

On 26 Oct, etherfi added pay-by-tag usernames, one per account, with shorter tags kept for higher card tiers.

3/ @BitgetWallet

On 29 Oct, Bitget Wallet cut its physical card from $49 to $25, shipping included, until 31 Dec 2026. The first 1,000 new cardholders get $15 cashback after spending $100, on top of assetback, until 30 Nov.

The same day, Bitget Wallet said the card can now be topped up with ETH or USDG on Robinhood Chain.

4/ @PulsarMoneyApp

From 1 Nov (00:00 UTC), Pulsar's cashback depends on how much you spend:

- Free: 0.5% on $0–1,000, 1% on $1,000–2,000, 2% on $2,000–3,000, 0.25% above $3,000

- Pro: 2% on $0–1,000, 3% on $1,000–2,000, 4% on $2,000–3,000, 0.5% above $3,000

Pulsar also says local FX conversion fees will fall by 0.25% to 0.5% "very soon", with no date given.

5/ @Visa

In its fiscal Q4 2026 results, Visa said stablecoin settlement is running above $25B a year, about 10x year on year. Settlement supports 10 blockchains and five stablecoins: USDC, USDG, EURC, PYUSD and SBC.

6/ @raincards

On 27 Oct, Rain said it now powers SeatGeek's Game Day Your Way with the Cleveland Cavaliers, tying venue wallets to stablecoin-powered cards. Fans who scan a ticket get $10 for concessions.

On 29 Oct, Rain announced Blackbird's FlyCard, a Visa debit card powered by Rain and issued by Cross River Bank. It's waitlist-only for now, with up to 7x back on qualifying purchases at the top membership tier.

7/ @SolidYield

On 28 Oct, Solid added euro yield with Byzantine at up to 6% APY, including a boost funded by Solid. EURC can also be spent in Credit mode with up to 5% cashback and, Solid says, no FX or transaction fee.

On 29 Oct, it added a EURO Virtual Account with its own IBAN, free to open and with no new KYC for Wirex cardholders. It takes deposits only for now: free on Ultra, 0.5% on Core and 0.25% on Prime.

8/ @Plasma

On 28 Oct, Plasma One added one-tap deposits and spending for ETH, HYPE and other assets. Plasma didn't list every supported asset or any conversion fee.

9/ @cashi

On 27 Oct, Cashi announced a Solana Breakpoint offer: 10% back on your Breakpoint ticket (up to $50, until 14 Nov) and 20% back on Uber in London from 13 to 20 Nov (up to $25), so up to $75 in total. Terms apply.

In Argentina, 5% back at PedidosYa, Uber, DiDi, Personal and Movistar runs through 30 Nov, up to $25 per person per month.

10/ @Gate

On 27 Oct, Gate introduced the Gate Gold Card, usable online or in-store with Samsung Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Alipay or WeChat Pay. Eligible rewards can be turned into XAUT, tokenised assets or major cryptocurrencies. Regions, network and fees weren't stated.

Which update changes your card shortlist most?

text:
When I did long bookings, I’d wake at 4 a.m. Silently and slowly leave the room. Hidden under my clothes, a single sheet of paper, a pencil. Its simplicity hid its value. There were words. At the dressing table. The safety valve. Scribbling emotion as if life itself depended on it at that moment; it did. Nothing as gauche as a complaints form. Nothing if found couldn’t be explained. A story. A place or a life that wasn’t this. A North Star for fear that I might never find my way home. Then I returned to bed. Most sheets of paper ended up in bin. 
This is the only one that remains.

They would eat late. The wine would be ordinary. He would not ask what she did before, and she would not tell him the price of the room she had left that morning.
Afterwards, there would be a square with a three-piece band that played for the tourists and for anyone else who stayed. He would offer his hand because the music had started, not because the evening required a gesture. She would take it. The waltz would be slow and slightly out of time with the recording they were using. Neither of them would correct it. When the piece ended, he would release her, and they would stand for a moment at the edge of the square while the next group formed. She would still be able to leave on the same night if she chose. The wanting would not have to become a question, and the answer would not have to be managed. For the length of the walk back to the hotel, the only thing required of her would be to keep step.♥️💫

text:
On October 26, 2026, the political winds sweeping southern Africa carried a storm. 

In a region marked by both fragile hope and mounting tension, news broke with the force of a thunderclap: former Botswana President Ian Khama, lauded for his unwavering candor and democratic record, had openly questioned Botswana’s presence at the inauguration of Hakainde Hichilema.

Khama’s words were not diplomatic whispers - they were cannon shots. 

He branded Hichilema “Africa’s newest dictator,” sending shockwaves that reverberated far beyond the Zambezi and Okavango.

His statement was more than a personal opinion; it was a call for accountability that transcended borders.

The aftermath of Zambia’s recent, divisive election - which violated both local and international standards to the extent that soldiers stormed polling stations and tallying centers to influence the outcome - still lingered.

Khama’s challenge struck at the heart of Hichilema’s legitimacy, questioning not only his victory, but also shining a spotlight on the dictatorship taking root in Zambia and values Botswana had so long exemplified. 

Botswana, once the regional beacon of governance and stability, now faced criticism from within. 

The Batswana criticized their government’s decision to attend the inauguration, calling Hichilema an “election rigger.” In response, Khama questioned whether his government regretted participating in the event, given the emergence of dictatorship in Zambia.

Never before had the moral standing of Botswana’s foreign policy been so fiercely debated in public view.

Yet, the significance lay not merely in Khama’s condemnation. True courage is to speak the truth in uncomfortable times, and Khama’s message was a forceful reminder - democracy, anywhere, can shrink beneath the shadow of unchecked power. 

Across Africa, where autocracy too often rises unchallenged, his words offered a beacon: moral clarity is the first step towards sustaining democracy.

Khama’s bold confrontation was more than a diplomatic sideshow. It was a wake-up call. The echo of his words - ringing across the region - carried a single, urgent message: the fate of Zambia’s democracy, and by extension that of the continent, depends on the courage to confront uncomfortable truths.

text:
Why We will guard Freedom and Democracy

Universal Values Beyond National Borders and Ideologies

For thousands of years, humanity has established nations, kingdoms, and powerful empires. Yet the existence of a state has never guaranteed human freedom.

Ancient Egypt built a remarkable civilization under the Pharaohs. Genghis Khan established a vast empire through conquest. Nazi Germany became a powerful dictatorship that destroyed individual liberties.

These examples remind us that a powerful nation does not necessarily mean free citizens.

The real question is not whether humanity needs nations, but what kind of nations people deserve to live in.

America’s founding principles offered an important answer: governments exist to protect inherent human rights, and their legitimate authority comes from the consent of the governed.

Freedom and democracy also provide foundations for long-term progress. They encourage accountability, protect individual initiative, and allow societies to correct political mistakes without violence.

Democracy does not guarantee prosperity, but research shows that democratization can contribute positively to long-term economic growth. 

Freedom and democracy are universal values, not privileges belonging to any particular country or civilization.

Just as the laws of electricity remain the same across national borders, fundamental human dignity should be respected everywhere.

No ideology can justify unlimited political power.

Whether authoritarianism emerges through absolute monarchy, fascism, or communist one-party dictatorship, the danger arises when rulers place themselves above the people and beyond accountability.

America must continue protecting constitutional government, individual liberties, democratic institutions, and the rule of law.

We construct a new civilization beyond ideology.

Above all, we must remain committed to the universal values of freedom and democracy.
                        GPT with Yan
                    October 30 2026

text:
📖 DAILY SCRIPTURE
BIRTHING OF A NATION
Faith • Family • Freedom

FRIDAY, OCTOBER 30, 2026

🔥 WHEN JESUS NOTICED THE ONE EVERYONE ELSE OVERLOOKED

📖 Luke 19:5 (NLT)

“When Jesus came by, he looked up at Zacchaeus and called him by name. ‘Zacchaeus!’ he said. ‘Quick, come down! I must be a guest in your home today.’”

✝️ THE MESSAGE

Have you ever wondered how many hurting people we walk past every day without truly noticing them?

People carrying shame, struggling with their past, or desperately searching for hope?

Zacchaeus was a wealthy tax collector, despised by his own people. His profession was associated with corruption, and his reputation had already been judged by society.

But something inside him desperately wanted to see Jesus.

Being too short to see over the crowd, he climbed a tree.

Then something extraordinary happened.

JESUS STOPPED!

Out of all the people surrounding Him, Jesus looked up and called Zacchaeus by name.

While everyone else saw a sinner, Jesus saw a soul in need of salvation.

The crowd complained when Jesus announced He would visit Zacchaeus’s home.

But Jesus wasn’t looking for the crowd’s approval.

He came to seek and save the lost!

That encounter changed everything.

Zacchaeus repented, promised to repay those he had cheated four times over, and committed to giving half his wealth to the poor.

His repentance wasn’t merely words. It produced action!

ONE ENCOUNTER WITH JESUS TRANSFORMED HIS LIFE!

🔥 WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR US TODAY?

We live in a world quick to condemn, divide, and label people by their mistakes.

We remember their failures but often forget that God’s mercy can transform even the hardest heart.

Jesus never compromised truth, but neither did He withhold compassion from sinners.

He offered mercy that called people to repentance and a changed life.

How many relationships remain broken because someone refuses to forgive?

How many people have walked away from churches because they experienced condemnation without compassion?

How many struggling souls are sitting right beside us while we’re too busy to notice?

We speak about rebuilding our families, restoring our churches, strengthening our communities, and bringing righteousness back to our province.

But we must remember something important.

WE CANNOT REBUILD A NATION WHILE OVERLOOKING THE PEOPLE WITHIN IT!

A nation is made up of families. Families are made up of individuals. And every individual is a soul precious to God.

True restoration doesn’t begin with changing everyone around us.

It begins when we allow Jesus Christ to change our own hearts!

🔥 Truth must never be separated from love.

🔥 Mercy does not mean excusing sin.

🔥 Genuine repentance produces genuine change.

🔥 Nobody is beyond the transforming power of Jesus Christ.

Sometimes the greatest ministry begins when we stop long enough to notice someone everyone else has overlooked.

🎯 TODAY’S MISSION

Look beyond someone’s appearance, reputation, or past mistakes.

Encourage someone who’s struggling. Reach out to the lonely. Show compassion while standing firmly upon God’s Word.

And ask yourself:

Have I written someone off whom Jesus is still calling to repentance and restoration?

🙏 PRAYER

Heavenly Father, forgive us for the times we’ve judged others while forgetting the mercy You’ve shown us. Give us eyes to see the hurting and hearts filled with Your compassion. Help us speak truth in love and demonstrate genuine forgiveness. Restore broken families, awaken Your Church, and let repentance and the transforming power of Jesus Christ bring healing throughout Alberta. In Jesus’ mighty name, Amen!

text:
KRISHNA DEFENCE | Better execution, richer product mix

The interesting part of Krishna Defence’s Q2 FY27 is not just faster growth. It is how much more profit the company is earning from its existing manufacturing capabilities.

Consolidated revenue rose 55.7% YoY to ₹75.29 crore. Total consolidated PAT, including the share of associates’ profit, increased 71.8% to ₹15.32 crore. Operating EBITDA margin, excluding other income, improved to about 26.8%, from 19.1% a year earlier.

1. The value lies in specialised processes, not owning every operation

Krishna supplies specialised steel sections for shipbuilding, welding consumables and armoured-steel products. These are different from simply selling more tonnes of ordinary steel.

Management says critical processes, including customised furnaces, stay in-house. Non-critical work such as cutting, painting and shot blasting can be outsourced.

That matters: capacity can grow without replicating every manufacturing step. Management believes the existing product range can support ₹400–450 crore of revenue with incremental improvements. This is capacity potential, not a revenue forecast.

In May, management identified its priorities as: “better processes, implementation, better automation, better yield improvement”. The latest margin improvement is consistent with that direction, although product mix also played an important role.

2. Today’s earnings engine is different from tomorrow’s opportunity

Management attributes the stronger margin mix partly to welding consumables and products supplied to the Army. It aims to sustain margins around current levels, but has not given an unconditional guarantee.

The adjacent opportunities are worth separating by maturity.

Specialised welding consumables and additional steel components can build on existing infrastructure. The composite doors-and-hatches venture with VABO offers opportunities in new ships and retrofits. Management hopes initial revenue could arrive in Q4 FY27, subject to the remaining approvals.

Autonomous underwater platforms and smart ammunition are development programmes, not immediate earnings contributors. Management indicated the latter opportunities remain at least 12–18 months away from revenue. Announced partnerships should not be treated as completed commercialisation.

3. Faster execution does not remove the need for fresh orders

The firm order book was ₹109 crore at September-end, against ₹117 crore in June. Separately, submitted tender bids increased from ₹289 crore to ₹305 crore.

Those bids are opportunities, not awarded orders.

Management says customers increasingly place smaller orders with shorter delivery schedules. It expects most existing orders to execute in Q3, with some Q4 spillover. That can reduce visible backlog even when factories are busy, but maintaining growth still requires replenishment.

4. Profit has improved. Cash needs to catch up.

H1 consolidated operating cash flow was negative ₹5.17 crore, versus PAT of ₹26.76 crore. Higher receivables absorbed ₹56.22 crore of cash.

Management attributes this to shipments concentrated in late August and September, followed by 45–60-day payment terms, and says some collections have since arrived. It did not quantify those collections.

Kyro Read: The current attraction is specialised manufacturing, better mix and faster execution, not distant defence announcements. Sustained margins, conversion of bids into firm orders and visible receivable collections would make this growth materially more convincing.

Introducing the five books in this remarkable collection:

1. The Secret Master: Arun Kashalkar and a Journey to the Edge of Music
By @Sumana_Ramanan

A fascinating journey into Hindustani classical music through the life and musical legacy of vocalist Arun Kashalkar.

2. Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia
By @SamDalrymple123

An exploration of five partitions that transformed the Indian subcontinent and reshaped the political geography of modern Asia.

3. Assembling India's Constitution: A New Democratic History
By @itihaasnaama and @OrnitShani

A compelling account of the making of India's Constitution, bringing into focus not just its celebrated architects but also the ordinary citizens whose voices and aspirations helped shape the world's largest democracy.

4. A Man for All Seasons: The Life of K. M. Panikkar
By @narayani_basu

A biography exploring the life and legacy of K. M. Panikkar, the historian, diplomat and statesman whose contributions helped shape modern India.

By Devesh Kapur and @arvindsubraman

An examination of independent India's development journey, its economic choices, political decisions and the challenges that continue to shape its future.

Together, these five books offer an expansive reading experience spanning India's history, constitutional journey, geopolitics, economic development and cultural heritage.

The Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize, instituted by the New India Foundation, recognises outstanding non-fiction writing on modern and contemporary India.

text:
Brussels is losing its grip... the transatlantic continuity architecture is taking shape...

Germany, France, Italy, and Greece just pushed back against Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada the EU’s first associate member... this is a strong signal...

The designation has been stripped from the draft summit declaration, replaced with a commitment to pursue an “ever closer association"...

That language is revealing... Brussels is encountering resistance within its own membership while continuing to extend its economic and institutional reach beyond Europe...

I've been mapping this across the European sovereignty shift, the pressure building inside Brussels, and Mark Carney's accelerating alignment with European institutions...

The Montreal summit brings those developments into much sharper focus... TD Economics now estimates nearly C$60 billion in potential additional Canadian exports to Europe, including approximately C$50 billion in energy alone...

That opportunity depends heavily on infrastructure, investment, and supply chains that still need to be developed... follow where the money and institutional commitments are moving...

Canada and the European Investment Bank have scheduled a new investment framework covering strategic sectors, including critical minerals...

Canadian pension funds and European financial institutions are being brought into discussions on deeper financial cooperation... 

Meanwhile Canada is already participating in Europe's SAFE defense procurement framework...

The satellite and digital layers are coming into view as well... proposed access to Galileo, potential participation in IRIS², subsea communications infrastructure, computing capacity, and closer regulatory alignment...

Then another development surfaced on October 29... Canada and eight other governments, including Greece, announced plans to establish a Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, with founding agreements targeted for November 30...

Consider the irony... Greece is resisting the EU membership designation while simultaneously participating with Canada in a separate multinational defense financing initiative...

The political fractures are becoming increasingly visible, yet institutional cooperation continues through parallel channels... think hedging until US elections are over...

Now reconnect this to the broader sovereignty shift I've been documenting... Brussels faces growing pressure to maintain its strategic influence as European governments confront competing national priorities and Washington pushes a different economic and security direction...

Canada offers energy, critical minerals, Arctic access, financial capital, and a potential transatlantic bridge into new markets...

Carney needs diversification from an American economy that still absorbs the overwhelming majority of Canadian exports... Europe needs resources, capital, industrial capacity, and greater strategic independence...

Their interests are converging at precisely the moment the EU is struggling to agree on the political structure of that convergence...

Here is the continuity mechanism... financial agreements, defense procurement, infrastructure investments, technical standards, and institutional partnerships can endure long after the governments that negotiated them leave office...

A political designation can be challenged immediately... the economic dependencies created beneath it can take decades to unwind... or so [they] hope...

Brussels may be struggling to secure agreement on its next political arrangement... while attempting to build the institutional relationships that could preserve its influence through the next generation of sovereign elections...

The Montreal summit is exposing both sides of that equation... the fracture is visible... and so is the effort to build continuity through it...

text:
Mia Khalifa was a history graduate who finished college in 3 years and starved herself down to 98 pounds. She saved every dollar for one breast surgery. 3 weeks after it, a stranger stopped his car in the middle of a Miami street, called her gorgeous and handed her a card. It was a porn company. She worked there for about 3 months, reportedly made around $12,000, and ISIS put her face on a beheaded body. She has spent every year since trying to get that name off her.

In the video below, she tells the whole story for the first time.

She was born in Lebanon. The one word she uses for her childhood is freedom. At 10, her family moved to Washington DC. Her parents trusted no one, and she wasn't allowed to go to a friend's house or play in the park.

She landed in America in January 2001, barely speaking English. She finally started making friends. Two weeks into the new school year, 9/11 happened. Kids whose parents worked at the Pentagon gave her a new nickname: the terrorist.

She had one friend all through high school. Then military boarding school, where for the first time she felt she belonged.

In college she stopped eating. The weight fell off, and so did her confidence. She dressed frumpy and hid in t-shirts.

Then the surgery. She woke up and thought, for the first time in her life, wow, I'm pretty. She says it was an unhealthy kind of pretty. The kind that needs a man to confirm it.

She called the number on the card two weeks later. Beautiful office. Friendly people. Mostly women on the crew. She told herself it would be her dirty little secret. She had 200 followers on Instagram. Who would ever find out?

On set she felt pampered for hours. The scene itself? She barely remembers any of them. She blacked out every time.

Then they offered her a scene in a hijab. She joked: "You're going to get me killed." She did it anyway.

The next morning it was on CNN, Fox and every major outlet on earth. She went from 400 Instagram followers to 200,000 in 3 days. Several countries banned her.

ISIS sent a photoshopped image of her head on a beheaded body with a message: you're next. She replied with a joke. A week later someone posted a Google Maps photo of her apartment. She lived in a hotel for two weeks.

She quit after a few months. Became a paralegal. Chopped off her hair and dyed it blonde. Wore baggy clothes and sunglasses. Strangers still yelled her name from passing cars.

Today she says she hates leaving the house. She hates being recognized. She hates taking photos with fans.

A radio host once introduced her as a porn star who likes sports. She lost it on air, out of pure shame.

Then she met a chef in Copenhagen through the Michelin Guide's Instagram. She told him everything. He replied that everybody deserves a second chance. She cried for hours. They got engaged. A year after the wedding, they split.

Her message to young girls is just four words long: "Don't ever do porn."

3 months of her life. 12 years and counting of trying to outrun them.

Some lessons are written in other people's mistakes. Watch it once. Remember it forever.

text:
Watch: Store REFUSES Service Because They “Hate Trump” | Steve Watson, Modernity

In an incident proving that TDS is still rampant, a Michaels Arts & Crafts store in Mayfield Heights, Ohio, refused to custom-frame a portrait of President Trump, as well as a historic moon landing newspaper, and a religious-themed art print.

Employees told the customer the items were “ineligible” and that the company does not do “political pieces.” One account of the encounter says an employee stated on camera that “Our company hates the President.”

Corporate later insisted no such policy exists. The employees remain on the job. Customers are already shifting business elsewhere and floating simple tests of consistency.

This past weekend, Terpsehore “Tore” Maras walked into the Michaels at 1361 SOM Center Road with three items for framing: an original front page of the Cleveland Press from the moon landing era, a Jon McNaughton print, and a portrait of President Trump.

According to her complaint and the video she posted, a framing associate examined the pieces, left, and returned with a manager. The staff declared the items “ineligible” under company policy and said they were “not allowed to do political pieces.”

Maras has said she explained the work was for private home display, not campaign material. The refusal stood. In the interaction she asked whether this was official policy, noting “it’s not political, this is for my house.”

She later recorded a call to Michaels customer care. The representative described a policy covering “sensitive items or things that are inappropriate,” then declined to say whether a moon-landing newspaper, a presidential portrait, or religious artwork fell into that category.

Maras filed a consumer complaint with the Ohio Attorney General’s office. She has accused the retailer of misrepresenting why an advertised service was unavailable. https://t.co/NRQownwhMD reported the filing and the company’s response.

A Michaels spokesperson told the outlet: “At Michaels, we are committed to providing a welcoming experience for every customer. Michaels does not have a policy prohibiting the framing of political items. We are following up with the customer to make this right and ensure her project needs are met.”

This is not even the first time. In November 2024 a Michaels in Sequim, Washington, declined to frame the well-known photo of Trump raising his fist after the Butler assassination attempt. Employees said they were uncomfortable.

Corporate called it a misunderstanding; a framing manager later apologized and offered to complete the order. The pattern of local staff citing an unwritten ban, followed by corporate denial, has repeated.

A Case Western Reserve University law professor noted in the https://t.co/NRQownwhMD piece that a private retailer could “very likely refuse” service on political grounds without violating public-accommodation laws, which typically protect categories such as race and sex rather than viewpoint.

The customer’s complaint focuses more on alleged misrepresentation of the reason for refusal than on a free-speech claim against the company.

Public reaction has been direct. Customers have announced they are moving holiday crafting purchases to Hobby Lobby and other competitors.

Others have proposed a straightforward consistency check: bring photographs of Obama or Biden, or newspaper front pages from the George Floyd period, and see whether those items receive the same “political pieces” treatment.

One reply suggested flooding the specific store with Trump images so the same employees must process them under the company’s stated policy.

Michaels is owned by Apollo Global Management, which took the company private in 2021. The framing counter is a routine service sold to any customer.

The company has said it will complete the order. Whether the employees who cited a nonexistent policy face any consequence has not been announced.

text:
🏀 2026-27 Mountain West Preview 🏀

A brand-new Mountain West tips off this season. Boise State, Colorado State, Fresno State, San Diego State and Utah State are gone to the Pac-12, Hawaii, UC Davis and UTEP are in.

Team to watch: Grand Canyon. The media picked the Lopes second by a single point, but this board puts them on top, and the ceiling explains why. Bryce Drew has won 20 games in five straight seasons, and he’s assembled the most talented roster in the league: preseason Newcomer of the Year Dylan Darling, returning All-MW guard Makaih Williams, and a trio of veterans in Jaden Henley (17.7 PPG, First Team All-MW last year), Baylor transfer Dan Skillings Jr. and NC State transfer Tre Holloman. The catch: Henley, Skillings and Holloman are all still waiting on fifth-year eligibility rulings. If the courts break GCU’s way, this is the best mid-major roster in the country. If not, the margin gets a lot thinner.

The co-favorite: New Mexico. The Lobos took 9 of 19 first-place votes and edged GCU 179-178 in the media poll. Eric Olen brought Jake Hall and Uriah Tenette with him from UC San Diego as unknown freshmen, and a year later they’re two of the best players in the league after leading UNM to the NIT semifinals. Both turned down bigger offers to come back. In a league full of eligibility questions, New Mexico’s stars are a sure thing.

Here’s the thing about this league: the farewell tour might be the best story. Steve Alford announced he’ll retire after this season, his eighth at Nevada and 36th overall. The Wolf Pack were picked third and bring back Elijah Price (12.8 PPG, 8.5 RPG, 12 double-doubles) and Vaughn Weems. A Mountain West title would be the perfect send-off for one of the most accomplished coaches in the league’s history.

Storylines worth watching:

Grand Canyon’s eligibility saga, with three potential All-MW players waiting on court decisions.
Jake Hall’s encore after one of the best freshman seasons in Mountain West history.
Steve Alford’s final ride, chasing the one thing his Nevada teams haven’t done: win a Mountain West Tournament title.
UNLV’s Tyrin Jones, who led the league in blocks as a freshman, alongside preseason Freshman of the Year Jackson Kiss, a four-star recruit from New Zealand.
Hawaii and UTEP’s first seasons in the league, and whether Wyoming’s Naz Meyer can carry the Cowboys into the upper half.

Player who can’t be ignored: Jake Hall. As a true freshman he averaged 16.4 points, made a school-record 117 threes, and led the Mountain West in 3-point percentage (43.8%) and effective field goal percentage. He dropped a program freshman record 32 on Utah State and hit a game-winner against Fresno State. He’s the media’s Preseason Player of the Year, and he’s only a sophomore.

Fun fact: Hall is just the third freshman ever named First Team All-Mountain West. The other two? Kawhi Leonard and Anthony Bennett.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Why some men don’t flex when their manhood is challenged | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

Men who blend emotional openness and progressive gender attitudes into their sense of manhood appear to be less reactive when their masculinity is called into question, according to new research published in Social Psychology Quarterly. While men often respond to gender-related insecurities by exaggerating tough, dominant attitudes, men in this experiment who more strongly endorsed a flexible masculine identity showed less of that overcompensation. The findings suggest that how men react to challenges to their gender status depends in part on how they define manhood for themselves.

In sociology and psychology, the dominant cultural ideal of manhood in a society is known as hegemonic masculinity. In the United States, this traditional standard expects men to be physically tough, emotionally guarded, self-reliant, heterosexual, dominant, and strictly avoidant of anything considered feminine. Because meeting all of these rigid standards at all times is nearly impossible, many men experience their gender status as fragile and easily challenged. When a man feels that his manhood has been doubted, he may engage in masculine overcompensation, which is the tendency to exaggerate aggressive, dominant, or traditionally macho behaviors in an effort to prove his status to himself and others.

Psychological research has repeatedly shown how easily this defensive reaction can be triggered. For example, a 2008 series of experiments demonstrated that people widely view manhood as an uncertain social status that must be earned and can be easily lost through a single unmanly act. Building on that idea, a 2013 experimental study found that men who were falsely told they scored in the feminine range on a survey about gender identity reacted by expressing greater support for war, more negative attitudes toward gay people, and stronger interest in purchasing sport utility vehicles.

When men face doubts about their manhood, the effects can be physical as well as attitudinal, and individual differences shape how strongly they react. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2017, men whose masculinity was challenged tried to display physical toughness by administering higher voltages of electric shock to their own arms, especially if they already saw themselves as highly masculine.

Most research on masculine overcompensation has assumed that all men measure themselves against a single, traditional standard of toughness and dominance. In recent years, however, sociologists have documented the rise of what they call hybrid masculinity, a gender style in which men selectively incorporate traits typically associated with women or marginalized groups into their identity.

A man practicing hybrid masculinity might openly discuss his emotions, follow a skincare routine, show physical affection to male friends, or voice support for feminism and LGBTQ+ rights. The authors of a 2014 sociological review argued that adopting these traits allows relatively privileged men to create symbolic distance between themselves and traditional macho norms while still retaining their broader social status.

If hybrid masculinity gives men a way to feel secure in their gender identity without relying on rigid toughness, it raises the question of whether these men still feel compelled to act dominant when their manhood is challenged. Justin Huft, a PhD candidate in sociology at the University of California, Riverside, designed an experiment to test whether endorsing hybrid masculinity shields men from the tendency to overcompensate. Huft also set out to create the first survey tool designed to measure hybrid masculinity in statistical research.

“While there has been interesting work done on masculine overcompensation, it has largely depicted masculinity as a monolithic identity,” Huft told PsyPost. “This is inconsistent with some other work in the masculinities literature, which depicts multiple forms of masculinity. My aim was to explore how masculine overcompensation looks when accounting for another form of masculine identity.”

To test this idea, Huft recruited 988 heterosexual adult men living in the United States through the online research platform Connect. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 83, with an average age of about 40 years, and reported an average household income between $50,000 and $59,999 per year. Roughly 65 percent of the men identified as white, 15 percent as Black, 10 percent as Asian, 8 percent as Latinx, and 2 percent as another racial background. Politically, about 46 percent described themselves as liberal, 31 percent as conservative, and 22 percent as moderate, while 54 percent reported having a religious affiliation.

Before receiving any feedback, participants rated their baseline level of traditional masculinity. They also completed Huft’s newly developed 20-item hybrid masculinity questionnaire on a 5-point scale. Statistical testing showed that the new scale captured two closely related aspects of hybrid masculinity: progressive gender attitudes, such as supporting women’s and LGBTQ+ rights or agreeing that men can wear makeup, and emotional expressiveness, such as telling others when feeling sad, showing empathy, and expressing affection toward male friends.

Participants also answered questions measuring three concepts from sociological identity theory: how important being masculine was to their overall sense of self (known as identity prominence), how frequently they thought about their masculinity in daily situations like work or social events (known as identity salience), and how much they felt close friends and family viewed their masculinity the same way they did (known as identity verification).

For the experimental manipulation, participants completed items that appeared to evaluate their masculinity and were then given false feedback on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 represented feminine and 100 represented masculine. Men were randomly assigned to either a non-threatening group, where they were told that their answers placed them at the high end of the average male range, or a threatening group, where they were told that they scored at the high end of the average female range.

Following the feedback, participants completed a 21-item questionnaire measuring their agreement with traditional, dominant masculine norms on a scale from 1 to 7. This questionnaire assessed seven hallmarks of rigid manhood: emotional restriction, self-reliance, negative views of gay people, avoidance of femininity, placing a high priority on sex, desiring dominance as a leader, and valuing physical toughness.

Prior to receiving the false feedback, the two groups did not differ in their baseline traditional masculinity, measured with a separate questionnaire on which the sample averaged 5.08 out of 7. After the feedback was delivered, however, men who were told they scored in the average female range endorsed higher levels of rigid masculine norms, averaging 3.19 out of 7 compared to 2.97 out of 7 among men who were told they scored in the male range. That difference is small, about one-sixth of the typical spread in scores, but it indicates that the experimental threat triggered masculine overcompensation across the sample as a whole.

Huft then ran statistical regression models that controlled for baseline masculinity, identity importance, everyday awareness of masculinity, identity verification, religiosity, political conservatism, race, and household income. Even after accounting for all of those factors, receiving the masculinity-threatening feedback predicted a 0.17-point increase in dominant masculine norms in the baseline model, while scoring higher on hybrid masculinity was strongly linked to lower endorsement of those rigid norms overall.

When Huft tested how the two factors interacted, he found that hybrid masculinity moderated the impact of the threat, reducing the overcompensation effect by 0.23 points for each 1-point increase on the hybrid masculinity scale. In practical terms, men with low hybrid masculinity scores showed a larger increase in rigid, dominant attitudes after their manhood was questioned, whereas the gap between the threatened and non-threatened groups shrank toward zero among men who strongly endorsed hybrid masculinity.

Several background characteristics also predicted higher endorsement of rigid masculine norms regardless of which feedback participants received. Men who thought about their masculinity frequently in daily life, held more conservative political views, had lower household incomes, or identified as non-white tended to endorse traditional masculine norms more strongly.

The overall presence of a defensive reaction aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that threats to manhood heightened support for aggressive political and foreign-policy strategies, though that earlier work focused on political aggression rather than personal masculine norms and observed the effect among liberal men rather than conservative men. In Huft’s study, by contrast, men who scored high on hybrid masculinity tended to be more politically liberal and reacted less to the threat.

The new findings also stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which did not find an increase in conservative political views, support for war, or homophobia after a masculinity threat, though that study examined broader political and social attitudes rather than the comprehensive inventory of personal masculine norms used by Huft.

Huft offers two possible explanations for the buffering pattern found in his study. Men who embrace emotional openness and progressive views may have already loosened the tie between their sense of self-worth and traditional macho ideals, making feedback about feminine traits less upsetting, or they may draw on other aspects of their identity, such as emotional maturity or humor, to feel secure without needing to act tough.

While this flexibility appears to reduce aggressive overcompensation at the individual level, Huft cautions that hybrid masculinity does not automatically dismantle gender inequality in society. Instead, sociological theory suggests that blending softer traits into manhood can allow men to present themselves as modern and progressive while quietly preserving the social privileges associated with being a man.

“Masculinity isn’t just one thing,” Huft explained. “It contains different attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics. These different constellations of masculinity cause people to perceive and experience masculinity threats differently. This, in turn, creates different sorts of responses to masculinity threats.”

As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because men who scored high on the new hybrid masculinity scale also tended to report that being masculine was less central to their overall identity, the questionnaire cannot completely untangle whether these men were strategically blending gender traits to maintain their status or whether they simply cared less about manhood altogether. In addition, the experiment could not capture why men adopted hybrid traits in the first place, such as whether they adopted those traits preemptively, in response to past challenges to their manhood, or for unrelated reasons.

Hybrid masculinity was also measured rather than assigned, so men who scored high on it differed from low scorers in other ways. Most notably, they tended to be much more politically liberal, and the study did not test whether political views shaped how men responded to the threat. The new scale has so far been tested in only this one sample, and the study did not report whether participants believed the false feedback.

The study also focused exclusively on heterosexual, cisgender men in the United States, meaning the findings cannot be generalized to gay, bisexual, or transgender men. According to hybrid masculinity theorists, the ability to adopt feminine or non-traditional traits without facing harsh social penalties is often easiest for white, middle-class, heterosexual men, so future studies will need to test whether hybrid masculinity works the same way across different racial and socioeconomic groups.

It is also possible that for men who pride themselves on being progressive and emotionally sensitive, being told they scored as highly masculine could actually feel like a threat to their progressive self-image, prompting them to distance themselves even further from traditional manhood. Finally, future research could explore whether men whose manhood is challenged try to restore their pride in areas outside of gender altogether, such as by emphasizing their career achievements or financial status.
