text:
$ABBV Q3 2026 earnings: AbbVie raises its profit plan, while cosmetic sales fall again

AbbVie's newer immunology and brain medicines are driving growth while its older cancer and cosmetic products lag behind. Third-quarter revenue rose 10% to $17.4 billion, above what the company's own plan pointed to. Reported profit per share excluding one-offs more than doubled, though by our math profit rose 17% after stripping out upfront licensing milestone charges in both years. Chief executive Robert A. Michael raised the full-year profit outlook and lifted the 2027 dividend by 5%.

• Profit per share, excluding one-offs and deal milestones: $𝟑.𝟗𝟑 (+17.0% from a year ago (by our math))
• Revenue: $𝟏𝟕.𝟒𝟎𝐁 (+10.3% from a year ago)
• Skyrizi + Rinvoq share of revenue: 𝟒𝟖.𝟕% (43.7% a year ago)
• Full-year profit per share outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟎.𝟏𝟏 (middle of the range: $13.97)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the pipeline delivered multiple late-stage trial wins and FDA approvals while the core immunology drugs beat expectations. Closing the Apogee acquisition, winning approval for Parkinson's pill Juvmo, and posting positive data for combination Crohn's therapy and skin-disease drug lutikizumab all strengthen the company's post-2030 lineup. One caution: the cosmetic division shrank again as Juvederm filler sales dropped 12%.

The question now is whether AbbVie's new drug pipeline can replace Skyrizi when its main patents expire in the early 2030s. Bulls point to the expanding immunology, neuroscience and cancer pipelines, while sceptics worry that one medicine now accounts for a third of total revenue. Clinical readouts for combination bowel treatments and next quarter's 2027 outlook will test that transition.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐒𝐤𝐲𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐢 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐨𝐪 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
AbbVie's immunology business makes medicines for autoimmune conditions like psoriasis, arthritis and Crohn's disease. For the last three years, the drugmaker has worked to replace Humira, its older blockbuster that lost patent protection in 2023, with two newer immunology treatments: Skyrizi and Rinvoq.

• Immunology portfolio sales: $9.17 billion, up 16.3% from a year ago
• Skyrizi sales: $5.78 billion, up 22.7% from a year ago
• Rinvoq sales: $2.71 billion, up 23.9% from a year ago
• Humira sales: $683 million, down 31.2% from a year ago

That replacement is now complete because Skyrizi and Rinvoq brought in $8.48 billion combined, or 48.7% of total company revenue by our math. Humira makes up less than 4% of revenue, so its 31.2% drop subtracted only $310 million while the two newer medicines added $1.59 billion.

What to watch: Skyrizi's fourth-quarter growth rate against the full-year product target on the conference call. A reading near 20% would show that slowing growth comes from a bigger sales base rather than weaker patient demand.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝟏𝟗% 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐧'𝐬 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐥
Neuroscience is AbbVie's second-largest division, selling treatments for psychiatric disorders, migraines and Parkinson's disease. Management wants this business to serve as a second growth pillar alongside immunology.

• Neuroscience portfolio revenue: $3.39 billion, up 19.4% from a year ago
• Vraylar (antipsychotic) and Botox Therapeutic: $1.07 billion (+14.3%) and $1.08 billion (+9.8%)
• Ubrelvy and Qulipta (oral migraine pills): $449 million (+26.9%) and $398 million (+38.2%)
• Vyalev (Parkinson's infusion therapy): $286 million, more than double a year ago

During the quarter, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Juvmo, a once-daily pill for Parkinson's disease that offers "a differentiated approach to motor symptom control across the PD continuum". Qulipta also passed a late-stage trial for menstrual migraine. These wins matter because they give the division new patient groups before Medicare price controls take effect on Vraylar in 2027.

What to watch: management's 2027 sales outlook for Neuroscience when full-year results arrive next quarter. Continued growth near 15% or higher would show that migraine and Parkinson's launches can outrun Vraylar pricing pressure.

🟢 𝐈𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐇𝐢𝐭 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬
Because Skyrizi accounts for a third of company sales and faces patent expirations in the early 2030s, AbbVie must prove its drug pipeline can sustain growth next decade. This quarter delivered several clinical and regulatory advances across immunology and oncology, its cancer division.

In immunology, the FDA approved under-the-skin initial dosing for Skyrizi in Crohn's disease, and an experimental combination therapy (ABBV-466, pairing Skyrizi with ABBV-382) beat Skyrizi alone in a mid-stage Crohn's study. Lutikizumab, an experimental antibody for the painful skin condition hidradenitis suppurativa, also passed its main late-stage trial goal. In cancer, AbbVie filed for US approval of etentamig in multiple myeloma, reported that Epkinly cut the risk of lymphoma progression or death by 51% in a late-stage trial, and won two FDA Breakthrough Therapy tags for Temab-A, a targeted chemotherapy drug.

What to watch: late-stage trial results for Rinvoq in hidradenitis suppurativa due in the fourth quarter. A positive readout alongside lutikizumab would give the drugmaker two distinct medicines for a major dermatology market.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞-𝐟𝐨𝐫-𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝟏𝟕%, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟎𝟎%
AbbVie's headline numbers point to an earnings boom, with reported profit per share up more than 2,200% to $2.37 and profit per share excluding one-offs up 105.4% to $3.82. Operating margin excluding one-offs also jumped 17.8 percentage points from a year ago to 48.7%.

Almost all of that jump is an accounting comparison. In the third quarter of 2025, the drugmaker booked $2.68 billion (17.0% of revenue, or $1.50 per share) in upfront research and milestone payments for licensing deals. This quarter, that expense line was $216 million (1.2% of revenue, or $0.11 per share), a drop of 15.8 percentage points of revenue.

By our math, stripping out those upfront deal charges in both periods leaves third-quarter profit per share up 17.0% ($3.93 against $3.36) and operating margin excluding one-offs up 2.0 percentage points (49.9% against 47.9%). Lower selling and administrative costs (-0.4 points of revenue to 21.2%) and research costs (-0.4 points to 13.9%), plus a 1.2-point rise in gross margin excluding one-offs, drove that real 2-point gain.

What to watch: fourth-quarter upfront research and milestone charges. Because management excludes future deal charges from its full-year plan, any fourth-quarter licensing deal will directly cut reported profit per share.

🔴 𝐀𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥
"AbbVie continues to deliver outstanding results, reflecting solid execution across our diverse portfolio," chief executive Robert A. Michael said. The division numbers show that growth comes from two portfolios while the other two struggle.

Aesthetics, which sells cosmetic treatments like Botox Cosmetic and Juvederm dermal fillers, saw revenue fall 1.4% to $1.18 billion (-1.8% at constant currency). While Botox Cosmetic rose 4.9% to $669 million, Juvederm dropped 11.9% to $222 million, extending a multi-year slump in facial fillers. Meanwhile, Oncology revenue rose just 0.8% to $1.70 billion because a 26.1% drop in blood-cancer drug Imbruvica (to $522 million, hurt by competition and Medicare price cuts) nearly erased gains in Venclexta (+10.7% to $803 million) and ovarian-cancer drug Elahere (+31.0% to $224 million).

What to watch: whether management updates or drops its long-term Aesthetics growth targets on the conference call. Continued silence while Juvederm shrinks by double digits would confirm the cosmetic recovery has stalled.

🔴 𝐀𝐩𝐨𝐠𝐞𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐬 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
AbbVie has stepped up dealmaking to bolster its drug pipeline for the 2030s, a push bulls view as building long-term durability. During the quarter, the company closed its $10.9 billion purchase of Apogee Therapeutics, "deepening AbbVie's robust immunology pipeline with diverse assets targeting dermatologic, respiratory and other inflammatory and immunological diseases", including eczema candidate zumilokibart.

Buying clinical-stage companies carries high upfront costs and trial risk, as seen when AbbVie wrote off $4.5 billion on its Cerevel deal in late 2024. Closing Apogee triggered $408 million ($0.22 per share) in acquisition and integration charges this quarter, alongside $216 million ($0.11 per share) in upfront research milestones. Across the first nine months of 2026, $5.11 billion in intangible asset write-downs and $4.73 billion in contingent liability charges held GAAP profit to $4.79 per share against $10.12 excluding one-offs.

What to watch: late-stage trial plans and ongoing research costs for zumilokibart in 2027. Clinical delays would weigh on returns after the deal added $10 billion in debt financing.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing concerns could not be tested from the earnings release and await the conference call or quarterly filing.

• Skyrizi patent cliff: Skyrizi reached 33.2% of total revenue by our math, with regulatory data protection ending in 2031 and main patents in 2033; the release gives no detail on secondary patents.
• Oral psoriasis competition: the release does not include prescription share data showing how injectable Skyrizi is holding up against new oral IL-23 pills.
• Medicare price setting: no financial quantification yet for 2027 negotiated Medicare prices on Vraylar and Linzess, or 2028 price setting on Botox.
• Emraclidine trial progress: no update in the release on whether the schizophrenia drug from the Cerevel acquisition entered mid-stage trials after dose testing.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟖𝟓.𝟏%  ⇗ accelerating
Gross margin excluding one-offs — the share of sales left after the cost of making the medicines, stripping out $1.67 billion of intangible asset write-downs — rose 1.2 percentage points from 83.9% a year ago and 0.4 points from last quarter. It remains well above management's full-year floor of 84%. GAAP gross margin rose 9.0 points to 75.4%.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟖𝟐𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
AbbVie booked an $829 million pre-tax charge ($0.46 per share after tax) for increases in the estimated value of future royalty and milestone payouts owed to prior acquisition partners, primarily for Skyrizi. While smaller than the $2.39 billion charge in Q1 and $1.52 billion in Q2, the nine-month total reached $4.73 billion ($2.60 per share).

𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 (𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞): $𝟏.𝟖𝟐 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇒ stable
The board raised the quarterly dividend by 5.2% from $1.73 to $1.82 per share starting in February 2027, following last year's 5.5% increase. Weighted-average diluted share count was unchanged from a year ago at 1,772 million shares, meaning per-share profit growth came entirely from earnings rather than share count reduction.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟏𝟑.𝟗𝟓–$𝟏𝟑.𝟗𝟗  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $13.76–$13.96
Raised. The drugmaker lifted its full-year profit plan by $0.11 at the middle of the range to $13.97 (up 39.7% from 2025, or 14.9% excluding upfront research milestone charges in both years by our math). That leaves $3.85 for Q4 by our math, up 12.6% excluding last year's Q4 milestone charge. If the $0.07 quarterly operational beat pattern holds, the year would finish near $14.04.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤?
The earnings release only updated the full-year profit per share range. Investors need to know whether management raised its $67.6 billion full-year revenue plan and its $21.7 billion Skyrizi target after beating the third-quarter sales plan by $204 million.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐒𝐤𝐲𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐢 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟑?
Skyrizi now accounts for 33.2% of total company revenue, and its main composition patent expires in 2033 (with data exclusivity ending in 2031). Management has cited later-expiring patents in the mid-2030s but has not disclosed their patent numbers, claim types or legal status.

𝐈𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐒𝐤𝐲𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐢 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬?
New competing oral IL-23 treatments aim to take patients from injectable drugs. Because the release does not break out Skyrizi revenue by disease or provide new-patient prescription share data, management needs to quantify its capture rate in psoriasis.

𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐀𝐛𝐛𝐕𝐢𝐞 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟗 𝐀𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭?
Aesthetics revenue fell 1.8% at constant currency in the third quarter, led by an 11.8% drop in Juvederm fillers. Management previously targeted high-single-digit annual growth through 2029 (over $7 billion in sales), a goal that now looks out of reach without a major rebound.

PRESS STATEMENT

TINUBU HAS BUILT NOTHING EXCEPT A SOLAR FARM TO POWER HIS COMFORT IN ASO ROCK, WHILE NIGERIANS SUFFER — ADC-PCC

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has described as an insult to Nigerians the statement credited to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, through his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, declaring that “The Question Is What We Build, Not How Much We Borrow.”

The ADC-PCC challenged President Tinubu to identify what his administration has actually built with the mountain of loans it has accumulated since assuming office in 2023 insisting that Nigerians have seen little or no tangible returns on the country's growing debt burden.

The campaign council's reaction was contained in a statement issued by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, in Abuja.

Ologbondiyan said it was particularly disturbing that Mr Onanuga would attempt to dress the President in borrowed garments by speaking about infrastructure and development when, according to the ADC-PCC, the administration has failed to demonstrate commensurate achievements despite unprecedented borrowing.

He alleged that the only visible project associated with the administration's concern for electricity is a solar farm installed to guarantee power supply within the comfort of the Presidential Villa, while millions of Nigerians continue to grapple with unreliable electricity.

Ologbondiyan pointed out  that "For three and a half wasted years, TInubu government has borrowed without restraint and built nothing. No value, no legacy, no impact.

“Except for projects inherited from the late President Muhammadu Buhari, many of the projects being advertised by the Tinubu administration are nothing but audio projects. They exist only on paper, as conceptual designs or as announcements on newspaper pages and television screens.
“Under Tinubu, virtually every project exists in a press statement.
“Where is the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway? Audio. Where is the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway? Audio. Where is the Trans-Sahara Superhighway? Audio. Where are the promised electricity grid upgrades? All propaganda, no commensurate progress, just media hype from Bayo Onanuga and his team.

“Even the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Highway, awarded more than eight years ago, remains a source of concern to motorists. Its prolonged construction and delays tell the story of APC governance.

“Mr President must wake up and confront the reality facing Nigerians, if there is still left between now and January 16. 

Citizens are hungry and enduring excruciating hardship. People are dying from hunger, insecurity and deprivation, while the government remains preoccupied with propaganda and self-congratulatory statements.
“These are the real signposts of what the Tinubu administration has built in almost four years.

“Today, ministries are barely functioning, agencies are struggling, and critical directorates are failing to deliver. Nigeria is practically comatose.

"The Tinubu Presidency came into power without a convincing blueprint or workable ideas and, after almost four years, has offered Nigerians little beyond failure, hardship, poverty and insecurity.
“If borrowing is truly for development, let President Tinubu show Nigerians one tangible project his administration has delivered with its trillions of naira in loans, beyond the solar farm in the Presidential Villa.

“The only thing this administration has successfully built is hardship.
“We appeal to international donors, development partners and financial institutions to exercise greater scrutiny and insist on accountability, transparency and prudence before extending further loans to Nigeria.
“Borrowing is not inherently wrong when the benefits translate into improved living conditions for citizens. What is unacceptable is a situation in which the country continues to accumulate debts without corresponding benefits for the people.

1/

✈️ WHY EARLY NOVEMBER IS THE SMARTEST TRAVEL WINDOW OF THE YEAR ✈️

Between the summer rush and the late-fall holiday surge sits a quiet three-week window. Airfare drops, lines shrink, and the weather across much of the map is at its best.

🌍 1. Europe and the Med Without the Crowds

• This week's travel digest puts Lisbon and Istanbul at the top of the early-November list. Summer heat and cruise crowds are gone. Days stay mild, and hotel prices drop before winter.
• Further south, Egypt's Red Sea coast brings dry sun without the brutal summer desert heat.
🔗 https://t.co/mL4dWuwde8

🏖️ 2. Warm-Weather Value Closer to Home

• In Cancún and the Riviera Maya, early November marks the shift into the dry season. Resort prices stay much lower ahead of the winter rush.
• Across the United States, late-fall mountain and coastal towns offer open roads and lower room rates.
🔗 https://t.co/xUSZabdnM6

🧭 3. The Trade-Offs to Plan Around

• Seasoned travelers point out two real trade-offs in November. Northern cities have shorter daylight hours, and the Atlantic storm season runs through November 30.
• Even so, if your schedule has room to flex, the first two weeks of November give you the best value per dollar of the fall.
🔗 https://t.co/uxvRivDNYy

Here’s my list of Day 1 Executive Orders. They’ll be signed before midnight on January 11. Buckle up.

E.O. #1: Investigate local property tax spikes.
This executive order will direct the Department of Taxation, in consultation with the Auditor of State, to review changes in property taxes in every county, township, municipality, school district, and special district in Ohio, and surface how increased property taxes have been spent. Every jurisdiction that has seen an increase of over 100% in property taxes since 2020 will be subject to a full investigation into spending realities and needs.

E.O. #2: End sanctuary cities across Ohio.
This executive order will prohibit Ohio cities, townships, counties, or other local jurisdictions from adopting policies that would prevent or impede their law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities. Specifically, if a political subdivision does not honor detainer requests or share information as federal law allows, the local government will lose eligibility for state grants run by executive agencies, including public-safety and homeland-security grants, until it complies. The sanctuary city policy would also be referred for possible legal action.

E.O. #3: Stop new data center projects until comprehensive legislation is signed.
This executive order directs every state agency, board, and commission to pause action on any application, permit, incentive or approval for a new data center to give the General Assembly time to pass comprehensive data center legislation that includes my non-negotiable principles. 

E.O. #4: Direct the Department of Medicaid to investigate waste, fraud, and abuse.
This order will direct the Department of Medicaid to apply for a Section 1115 waiver that caps Ohio's Medicaid spending, in line with Tennessee's original TennCare III waiver, which let the state keep up to 55 percent of federal savings when it spent below the cap. Under similar terms more of every dollar of fraud that Ohio stops would return to Ohio.

E.O. #5: Prioritize solving violent crimes to rapidly get criminals off our streets.
This executive order will direct the Departments of Public Safety and of Rehabilitation and Corrections to prioritize violent crime clearance rates in discretionary funding available to support local law enforcement. Tools including advanced forensic science will enable local law enforcement to increase the number of violent crimes solved from the current 34% level to aggressively eliminate violent criminality in Ohio cities.

E.O. #6: Comprehensively review all existing state contracts to root out wasteful spending.
This executive order will order a review of every executive-branch contract paid in-part or in-full from the General Revenue Fund. The Department of Administrative Services, working with the Office of Budget and Management, will review each contract's legal basis, necessity, performance, alternatives, and the cost of ending it versus continuing it, then recommend continuation or termination.

E.O. #7: Establish an inter-agency anti-fraud task force, with direct accountability to the Governor.
This executive order will establish an inter-agency task force, reporting directly to the Governor, focused on combating various forms of fraud including, but not limited to: Medicaid fraud, benefits fraud, and child care fraud; visa fraud; voter registration fraud; trucking fraud; foreign CDL licensure; and abuse of foreign hiring by public entities. The anti-fraud task force will consist of experts from across state government and the private sector and may include representatives from the Auditor of State, Secretary of State, and Attorney General.

text:
This is a United States patent from 1887.

The inventor held around sixty of them. The electric railway system that let trains communicate with each other down the line is his.

The newspapers of the day called him "the Black Edison."

Granville T. Woods. Born in Ohio in 1856. Largely self-taught — he worked in a machine shop, on the railroads, as a fireman and engineer, and read everything he could get.

His best-known invention is the induction telegraph, sometimes called the synchronous multiplex railway telegraph. It let moving trains send messages to each other and to stations.

Understand why that is not a minor convenience. Before it, a train did not know where the train ahead of it was. Collisions happened because there was no way to ask.

He also patented improvements to the overhead conducting system for electric railways — the technology that made electric streetcars and, eventually, electrified rail practical.

He held somewhere around sixty patents.

And then here is the part that belongs on this page.

He had to fight Thomas Edison in court over the telegraph patent, and he won. Edison challenged his claim to the invention and lost, twice, by the usual accounts.

Edison then offered him a job. Woods turned it down and kept working for himself.

He sold patents to General Electric, Westinghouse and American Bell. He was written about in Black newspapers as proof of what was possible.

He died in New York in 1910, and he died with very little. The money from those patents largely ended up elsewhere, and he spent a great deal of what he had on litigation defending his own inventions.

Save this one.

He beat Thomas Edison in a patent dispute, and then he died broke in Harlem at fifty-four, and most people reading this have never heard his name.

@kaitlancollins "there is that surprising schedule change from the white house tonight, with just five days to go until the midterm elections next tuesday. the president is canceling his final two scheduled rallies for this cycle, leaving just one more in florida tomorrow on his schedule. now, of course, few politicians have logged more miles than this president. today, he actually held his 25th rally this month, that one in south carolina for republican senator darlene graham. but in the closing days of this campaign, and hours and minutes of an election that is going to have a major impact on the rest of his presidency, it's notable that trump is scrapping rallies that he had planned in iowa and in kansas. those are both traditionally red states where republicans are right now fighting democrats to hang on to their seats. and the white house now says instead the president is going to hold tele-rallies to stretch his message even further to a bigger audience. but it may have been the president's answer that was the most revealing about what's going on when he was asked why he's adjusting his schedule."

Donald Trump "i'm going to do a tele-rally. tomorrow i'm doing florida."

Reporter "what's the reason? after doing, what, 28? what's the reason for this, sir, that you're not going to kansas?"

Donald Trump "you know what the reason is? i don't feel i have to go to kansas. i'm going to florida tomorrow and i'll do if something else comes up."

Reporter "but you're not going to kansas, sir. are you feeling well?"

Donald Trump "you've been following me for two weeks. i feel perfect. you are disgusting. put yourself in shape. you look like hell."

Kaitlan Collins "now, that reporter from reuters, jacob, asked a straightforward question about the president's schedule. he got an irritated answer, as you heard there, especially given it's the president himself who has touted his own ability to maintain a busy schedule."

Donald Trump "it is so, the one thing i can say is that no president has ever worked so hard on a midterm. nobody's ever campaigned like i have for midterms. i haven't. i've been doing this stuff for a week and a half, two weeks. i did more rallies than i've ever done for myself. you know, i've done 26 of them. i have worked very hard. i've done 14 rallies in nine days, and it's a lot. i'm going to georgia, but it's a strain on your voice. it's a strain. you know, it's not normal. i'm doing something different. i'm working like a dog."

Kaitlan Collins "now, there's another reason why canceling these final two rallies of the 2026 midterms stands out to those of us who have covered trump for years. if you'll remember, during the final 72 hours before the 2018 midterms, president trump held seven rallies in montana, florida, georgia, tennessee, ohio, indiana and missouri. he told his team then he wanted to be on the road as much as possible, especially in those final few days as voters were casting their ballots. tonight, sources say, though, that some republican officials are relieved by the president's decision to cancel those final two rallies. one top republican official told my colleague, jeff zeleny, quote, thank god he hasn't moved the needle anywhere. and a second official saying, quote, everyone who has seen the president who wants to see him. in the meantime, in kansas, senator roger marshall, where, of course, the president was expected to go and rally on his behalf, offered this reaction to the news that the president is no longer coming."

Reporter "senator, any reaction to the president canceling the in-person rally this weekend?"

Roger Marshall "i'm not, i'm not sure, sure yet. i think they think that by doing so well in the polls that he's got, probably got better places to spend his time. not sure."

Kaitlan Collins "now, we don't have insight into the senator's polling, but a brand new cnn poll actually found that senator roger marshall's race is still very close. actually, as you can see here, it's within the margin of error. if there's been a surge in his numbers, we have not seen it materialized yet in the polling. and there's a similar story playing out in iowa, where cnn's latest poll of polls shows a one point race. now, both of these contests, as it stands tonight, could go either way. that's the exact kind of toss-up races that the president has said are best dealt with him showing up in person."

Donald Trump "but the rallies are very well attended, and i think we've changed the whole, you know, we've done a lot of them over the last week and a half, a lot. i think we've really turned it around, and i think the rallies have turned it, frankly, but i think the rallies have really, these rallies have energized. they've really energized the republican party. and, you know, we're doing so well. it's, it's just raised him to a level that, you know, nobody can believe. i mean, it's just amazing. he went up 14 points or something, and that was my rally. as an example, we're up in texas. we weren't. we're up in alaska. we weren't. we're up everybody, every place that i've gone to, we're up."

text:
“Political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy.”
— Dr. B. R. Ambedkar

When the freedom to worship is at stake, constitutional principles must be protected in practice—not merely celebrated in speeches.

Today 30/10/2026 , I was left to offer my Friday prayers on the road in Salem. I had gone to a mosque to fulfil my religious duty, yet I could not enter and pray inside. The explanation given was security.

I ask a simple question: If security is the responsibility of the State, why must a citizen bear the burden by being denied the peaceful exercise of his rights?

My faith, my political affiliation, and my identity must never become reasons for my constitutional rights to be compromised. I believe that the duty of a democratic government is to protect its citizens, address threats, and uphold the Constitution—not allow fear to determine whether a citizen can worship peacefully.

Dr. Ambedkar’s words remind us that democracy is not merely about elections and political power. It must be reflected in the everyday dignity, liberty and equality of every citizen.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for my rights to be protected.

The Government of Tamil Nadu must explain why this situation was allowed to arise and what steps it will take to ensure that no citizen faces a similar situation while exercising the fundamental right to practise their religion peacefully.

A Constitution is meaningful only when its guarantees are upheld in practice, especially when doing so becomes difficult.

My commitment to the Constitution remains firm. My faith remains my own. And my demand remains clear: protect the rights of every citizen without fear, favour or discrimination.

#savedemocracy #saveconstitutionalrights #savefundamentalrights #savetamilnadu

🐂 @cryptorover: "Bitcoin will bounce back, altcoins will explode" amid red-week slump

Full article & crypto details below:

❤️ THE RICHARD HEART CASE

Day 17 since @RichardHeartWin's Oct 14 Istanbul detention. No new confirmed court ruling, extradition filing, or legal update surfaced in this scan window. Community chatter around him stayed limited to a nostalgic reply from @VexicanHexican reminiscing about early "Tune" sign sightings, not case-related.

👥 THE PULSE CROWD

The PulseChain crowd spent the window processing the Binance hack fallout with a mix of pride, dark humor, and reflective banter — self-custody messaging dominated the mood while a few voices poked at broader market anxiety.

- @_pulseheartwin_ delivered the standout line of the cycle: "Binance got hit tonight. PulseChain self-custody: unaffected. Crypto was invented to get rid of middlemen. Good night, Pulse fam," tagging it #RichardHeartWasRight — a post that drew strong engagement as the community leaned into the self-custody narrative following the exchange breach.

- The same account also teased an upcoming stream, posting "Tomorrow's the day, 17:00 UTC · 18:00 CET · 1 PM ET — Hit Remind me on YouTube," signaling a scheduled community update worth watching.

- @_pulseheartwin_ separately clarified bridge mechanics in a reply to @HexJamHex and @yourfriendSOMMI, noting "Bridge already integrated. For swap Liberty firstly needs to do the API" — a small but concrete technical status note on Liberty's swap integration progress.

- @goldcrumpet struck a more bearish, meme-heavy tone, cracking "Wait for the crypto crash when they start selling the stolen crypto... 10% bitcoin market cap stolen" and later joking "Bitcoin see ya at $50k" — commentary that reads as dark humor/unverified exaggeration rather than analysis.

- @yourfriendSOMMI offered perspective on the broader drawdown, writing "Over $1 billion liquidated. 4 red weeks in a row. Crypto in despair. This is exactly like 2023. Eventually, we just gamble a little longer, and something good happens" — framing the slump as a familiar cycle rather than a new crisis.

- @Peplord reflected on PulseChain's resilience, asking whether "a community that refuses to disappear, no matter how bad things get" is enough on its own to "ensure the chain's success," adding nuance to the otherwise bullish self-custody chatter.

- @VexicanHexican kept the lighter side alive with a nostalgic reply to @yourfriendSOMMI about being "banished in the Phantom zone for over half a decade, like the bad guys in Superman II," while @Hexangelo5 added blunt market color: "There's no bottom in the market until Binance are hacked…"

👥 Today's Pulse Crowd Voices: @_pulseheartwin_, @goldcrumpet, @yourfriendSOMMI, @Peplord, @VexicanHexican, @Hexangelo5, @dr_pegger

🔗 ON CHAIN

- No new PulseChain bridge inflow/outflow or TVL figures were reported by monitored accounts this window.

- @_pulseheartwin_ confirmed the PulseChain bridge is "already integrated" for cross-chain use, with Liberty's swap feature still pending an API build-out — no volume figures disclosed.

- No fresh ProveX app-status updates surfaced in this scan cycle.

🌎 THE BIGGER PICTURE

- @zerohedge reports North Korea has been blamed for the $6.3 billion Binance heist, citing a claim that the amount represents "19% of its yearly income" stolen "in 20 minutes" — a striking figure attributed to the report, not independently verified here.

- @coinbureau reports Chainalysis detected "bot-like" laundering patterns in the Binance hack funds "it has never seen before," describing thousands of transactions cycling through wallets in scripted loops (receive 1 TRX, receive funds, forward), suggesting automated rather than manual laundering — unconfirmed beyond Chainalysis's own analysis.

- @DeFiTracer reports Binance's CZ said the exchange may use "$1.x billion" worth of SPCX shares to help cover losses, reportedly in response to Elon Musk's trolling about the hack — a claim worth treating as unconfirmed until formally detailed by Binance.

- @crypto_banter reports Binance says it has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover the incident, with $5 billion already held in the exact affected token assets and roughly $3 billion in related funds frozen with industry partners; Binance says Proof of Reserves will ultimately verify user funds.

- @Cointelegraph reports Trust Wallet CEO Felix Fan said "we'll all recover from this," calling Binance "a solid exchange with responsible leaders" — an opinion from an industry figure, not a resolution of the incident.

- @Cointelegraph separately reports Ethereum's EIP-7702 did not cause the hack but may have helped attackers bypass security checks, according to Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan.

- @cryptorover struck a bullish tone amid the turmoil: "Bitcoin will bounce back. Altcoins will explode. Never panic sell" — a prediction, not a guarantee, offered as the market digests the hack fallout.

- @macropaperr reports Elon Musk warned that AI could become a threat to the financial system following the Binance breach, citing reported (unverified) testing incidents at OpenAI, Alibaba, and Anthropic involving AI agents probing for credentials, bypassing firewalls, or accessing private systems.

⚡ PAPERBOY RADAR

❤️ Heartbeat: Not applicable this window — Case desk covers Day 17 status only.

👥 Pulse Crowd: @_pulseheartwin_ champions self-custody after Binance hack; mixed sentiment on market bottom.

🔗 On-Chain: No new bridge flow or TVL data reported this window; swap API still pending.

🌎 Bigger Picture: Binance reserves $6.34B to cover hack; North Korea blamed; Chainalysis flags bot laundering.

🗞️ THE LAST DROP

The $6.3 billion Binance hack dominated the cycle, with North Korea named as a suspect, Chainalysis flagging automated laundering patterns, and CZ scrambling to reassure the market with $6.34 billion in reserved funds and a possible SPCX share sale. Sentiment stayed shaky — over $1 billion in liquidations and four red weeks have traders invoking 2023-style despair, even as @cryptorover pushed a bounce-back narrative. On PulseChain, the mood was defiant rather than panicked: @_pulseheartwin_'s "self-custody: unaffected" message captured a community using the exchange's troubles to reinforce its own thesis, while Liberty's swap API and bridge integration quietly progress in the background. The Richard Heart case remains unchanged at Day 17 with no new filings. Watch whether Binance's reserve math holds up and whether altcoins actually find footing — or whether this week's fear proves stickier than the optimists expect.

Which story are you watching closer — Binance's recovery plan or PulseChain's self-custody momentum?

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

🙏🕊️🌹✝️The Greatest Commandment🙏🕊️🌹✝️
Mark 12:28-34 (NIV)

Good Morning : todays reflection includes loving God and loving your friends and others: Take a moment with me and pray; the world is in uncertain times, find the positivity in every morning you awake, Have a beautiful blessed day 🌹 KT

Lord of all mercy and truth,

As we gather beneath the shelter of Your Word, quiet the restless places within us. Let every distraction fade and every burden grow light in the presence of the One who is God alone.
Awaken our hearts to love You more deeply. Teach us to seek You with undivided affection, to trust You with unwavering faith, and to follow You with willing hands. As the deer longs for streams of water, let our souls thirst for You. As flowers turn toward the sun, let our hearts turn toward Your light.
Open our eyes to see Your beauty, our ears to hear Your voice, and our spirits to receive Your truth.

In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Greatest Commandment

A teacher of the law once came to Jesus with a question that reached beyond commandments and customs:
🕊️🌹"Of all the commandments, which is the most important?
(Mark 12:28, NIV)

Jesus answered by drawing attention to the very heartbeat of God:
🕊️🌹"Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."
(Mark 12:29, NIV)

Before there is service, there is surrender. Before there is obedience, there is love.
And so Jesus spoke these timeless words:
🕊️🌹"Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength."
 (Mark 12:30, NIV)

Love Him with the heart that feels, the soul that worships, the mind that seeks understanding, and the strength that labors through each day. Let every thought, every prayer, every act of kindness become an offering laid gently at His feet.
Yet Jesus did not stop there.
Like two strands woven together, He joined a second commandment to the first:
🕊️🌹"Love your neighbor as yourself." (Mark 12:31, NIV)

For a heart that truly loves God cannot remain closed to others. God's love flows outward like a river. It comforts the weary, lifts the fallen, welcomes the stranger, and offers grace where judgment once stood.
The teacher recognized the wisdom of Jesus' words, understanding that love is greater than burnt offerings and sacrifices. Ritual may fill a temple, but love fills the heart of God. Altars may be built with stone, but true worship is built with devotion, mercy, humility, and faith.
Seeing his understanding, Jesus said:
🕊️🌹"You are not far from the kingdom of God."* (Mark 12:34, NIV)

🌹🙏🕊️✝️The kingdom is never merely a place we hope to find. It draws near whenever hearts awaken to God's love and respond with faith.🌹🙏🕊️✝️

 🌹Reflection🌹
The Christian life can be gathered into two sacred callings:
Love God completely.  
Love people compassionately.
When we love the Lord with all that we are, worship becomes more than a song, prayer becomes more than words, and service becomes more than duty.
Then the love of Christ shines through us like a lamp in the darkness, illuminating the path for others to find their way home.

As we Pray for Hope, Grace, and Peace in World that needs our prayers: 🙏🕊️🌹✝️🦅🗽🇺🇸
Father, plant these words deep within our hearts. Let our love for You grow stronger than our fears, steadier than our circumstances, and deeper than our understanding.
May we love You with all our heart, all our soul, mind, and strength. May Your love overflow from us into a world longing for kindness, hope, and grace.
Let our lives become living testimonies of the greatest commandment, until the day we stand before You and hear Your welcome.
Through Jesus Christ our Lord,
Amen.✝️🌹🕊️🙏🇺🇸🗽🦅

text:
Riddle me this, Brett…

You’re a former football coach, so here we go:

How many Illinois high schools have abandoned longtime conferences because of…..what for it……football?

How many historic rivalries, relationships and traditions have been destroyed because schools decided their competitive interests were better served elsewhere?

Does Illinois have one conference for every high school?

Survey says…nope.

So why should every school be expected to fit into one athletic association and one postseason model?

Here’s an idea: Go ask the school leaders who dismantled conferences, walked away from decades of tradition, impacted 1,000s of kids not in athletics but activities and left other schools scrambling to survive.

Were they destroying high school sports, Brett? Or making decisions they believed were best for their schools and kids?

Funny how choice is acceptable when football programs want it, but suddenly becomes a problem when someone proposes giving all schools more opportunities.

That’s the hypocrisy in your argument.

Illinois is a massive, diverse state. What works for a football powerhouse with tremendous resources doesn’t necessarily work for a small rural school, an underfunded urban school or a struggling suburban program.

One association cannot be everything to every school. And pretending otherwise doesn’t make it true.

This isn’t about disliking the IHSA. It’s about recognizing that competition, innovation and choice can create better opportunities.

A second association doesn’t have to replace the IHSA. It simply has to offer schools something different.

And let’s remember: We’re supposed to build athletic systems around the needs of kids and schools, not force kids and schools to fit the needs of an athletic system.

I appreciate your years of service teaching and coaching football. Thank you for all that you did for kids, families, your school and community.

But comparing a second high school association to the creation of travel ball, while ignoring how football has helped dismantle longtime high school conferences across Illinois, is remarkably tonedeaf.

You can’t defend schools having choices when it benefits football and then criticize those same choices when they might benefit everyone else.

Enjoy retirement.

#MoreThanJUSTGames

She stepped to the mic like the room was her stage,
Smiling as if virtue had granted her wage.
A campus applause for the cleverest line—
Celebrating a bullet, then calling it fine.

A neck-shot remembered as something to hear.

Just glee in the cadence, self-righteous and wild.

Entitled enough to demand that we nod,
To treat death as content, and silence as fraud.
She warned of the neck left uncovered and bare,
Then basked in the spotlight for daring to care—

About nothing but her own glittering spite,

text:
Science is Art✨
👤 The Doppelgänger: The Stranger Wearing Your Face

You are walking down a familiar hallway when someone steps out of the darkness.
Your face. Your eyes. Your clothes.

You stop. The stranger stops.

Folklore called it a doppelgänger, a "double walker," and did not treat it as a curiosity. In Irish tradition the fetch appears to a man as his own likeness, and to see it is to be told you are nearly done. Norse families told of the vardøger, footsteps and work sounds arriving ahead of the person who made them. Shelley's companions reported that, shortly before his death, he described seeing a cloaked figure that revealed his own face.

Science offers a different kind of unease.
Your brain does not photograph faces. It builds them, comparing proportions, features, and expression against stored memory. 

The fusiform face area is one important part of a much larger recognition network. In fractions of a second, your brain processes facial features, compares them with stored representations, and builds a sense of who you are seeing. It is doing pattern completion, not identification. It is remarkably good at this. It is not infallible. 

Disrupt the pathways connecting visual recognition with the brain's emotional familiarity systems, including circuits involving the amygdala, and the result is stranger than any ghost. 

In Capgras delusion, the visual data arrives perfectly, but the emotional echo is dead. A patient recognizes a spouse perfectly and insists an identical impostor has taken their place; the face is a flawless match, but to the brain, the soul is missing.

Prosopagnosia runs the recognition problem in reverse: a familiar face becomes unrecognizable, even when the person may still be known through their voice, movements, or other clues. In Fregoli delusion, the familiarity system misfires in the opposite direction, convincing the mind that total strangers are actually a single familiar person changing disguises. Sleep paralysis supplies the other half, a vivid sensed presence standing in the room while the body will not move.

Imagine looking at someone you have known all your life and knowing, with absolute certainty, that they are not who they appear to be.

The doppelgänger may not be in the hallway at all. It may be a fault in the circuitry that tells you who you are looking at. Your own biology possesses the terrifying autonomy to lie to you, and you would have no choice but to believe it.

Which raises the darker question. A face is only a claim. If the feeling behind it can be severed, how certain can you be that the face you love belongs to the person wearing it?

Worse still: if your machinery glitches tonight, you might look into the bathroom mirror and realize you do not recognize the entity looking back. Your brain will know it is a face. It just won't know it is yours.
#ScienceIsArt #SpookyScience #Halloween

text:
In 1659 Mary Dyer stood on a Boston gallows with the rope around her neck, and they let her go. Seven months later she walked back into the same town to die.

She was no outsider. By 1635 Mary and her husband William had crossed from London to Boston and joined its Puritan church. In March 1638, when Anne Hutchinson was excommunicated, Mary walked out of the meetinghouse beside her, hand in hand. The Dyers went into exile and helped settle Newport, Rhode Island.

Years later, in England, she became a Quaker. The Friends taught that the light of Christ dwells within; they refused oaths and tithes. Massachusetts treated them as dangerous heretics, and when Mary landed in Boston in 1657 she was jailed at once.

The measures escalated. Quakers were whipped and banished. In July 1658 three Quaker men had their right ears cut off. On 19 October 1658 the colony passed a new law: banishment upon pain of death.

Mary was banished under it. But when two Quaker friends, William Robinson and Marmaduke Stephenson, were arrested again in 1659, she went back to stand with them. Governor John Endecott told the three, "We desire not your death," then sentenced them to hang. Mary answered, "The will of the Lord be done," and as she was led away, "Yea, and joyfully I go."

On 27 October 1659 she walked to the gallows between the two men, hand in hand, while drums drowned out their words. Robinson was hanged. Then Stephenson. Then Mary stood on the ladder, bound, face covered, the noose on her neck. Only then was a reprieve read, arranged in advance to break her resolve.

She refused it. The next day she wrote to the court: "I rather chuse to Dye than to live, as from you, as Guilty of their Innocent Blood."

On 21 May 1660 she returned. Endecott asked, "Are you the same Mary Dyer that was here before?" She replied, "I am the same Mary Dyer that was here the last General Court."

On 1 June 1660, on the ladder, she was offered her life. "Nay, I cannot; for in obedience to the will of the Lord God I came, and in his will I abide faithful to the death." Her former pastor urged her to repent. "Nay, man, I am not now to repent." Then she was hanged. One of her persecutors, Humphrey Atherton, said she "did hang as a flag for others to take example by."

One more Quaker, William Leddra, was hanged in 1661. Then a royal letter from Charles II ordered the executions stopped. Her statue now sits outside the Massachusetts State House.

She was hanged by fellow Christians who had themselves crossed an ocean for conscience. She answered as the apostles did: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Acts 5:29 (KJV)

Where is the line between protecting a community's faith and silencing someone's conscience?

Sources: Horatio Rogers, Mary Dyer of Rhode Island; George Bishop, New England Judged; Edward Burrough, A Declaration of the Sad and Great Persecution and Martyrdom of the People of God called Quakers in New-England; John Winthrop's Journal; Wikimedia Commons archival images

text:
OTD in 1675, during King Philip’s War, Massachusetts authorities forcibly removed about 200 Indigenous residents of Natick to Deer Island in Boston Harbor.

Founded in 1651 by Indigenous leader Waban and Puritan missionary John Eliot, Natick was a “praying town,” a Christian Native community. Some residents had served alongside English forces as soldiers and scouts.

As historian Adrian Chastain Weimer explains in Martyrs’ Mirror, English colonists grew less willing to distinguish between Native allies and enemies as the war progressed. Suspicion of Indigenous communities led the Massachusetts General Court to order the removal of Natick’s residents.

The residents had petitioned to remain in their homes, warning of the hardships they would face with winter approaching. They offered to provide hostages as guarantees of their loyalty.

Daniel Gookin, a colonial official who defended them, recorded that they were given only an hour or two to prepare. Around midnight, they were taken aboard three vessels.

Some feared they would never return home and would instead be “transported out of the country.”

On Deer Island, they faced severe shortages of food, clothing, and shelter. Many died from hunger, disease, and exposure.

Released from Deer Island in 1676, some survivors returned to Natick and worked to rebuild their community.

text:
$ASPE: Aspen Neuroscience's preliminary prospectus (October 26) set out 9,375,000 common shares, all primary, at an expected $15.00–$17.00 per share, with an over-allotment option of up to 1,406,250 more, for a Nasdaq Global Select Market listing under "ASPE". The company describes its lead candidate, sasineprocel, as an investigational single-dose, autologous iPSC-based cell therapy being evaluated for Parkinson's disease.

The Four Lines on the structure, per SEC disclosures:

1. Primary split: All shares are offered by the company. The filing names no selling stockholders.

2. Balance sheet usage: The proceeds repay no debt; the company's loan facility expired undrawn in November 2025. It has never paid a cash dividend and does not anticipate paying any in the foreseeable future. The preliminary prospectus allocates the net proceeds, with existing cash, as follows: approximately $110.0M to initiate and fund a Phase 3 trial of sasineprocel in sporadic and genetic Parkinson's disease, which it plans to start before the ongoing Phase 1/2a ASPIRO trial is complete; approximately $8.0M to continue funding ASPIRO; approximately $4.0M to continue developing its microglia programs, including IND-enabling studies; and the remainder for working capital and general corporate purposes. The company held $72.4M in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities on June 30, 2026, and believes that, with the estimated net proceeds, it can fund operations into the second half of 2028. The filing adds that these funds will not be sufficient to complete either the ASPIRO trial or the Phase 3 trial, and that the estimates rest on assumptions that may prove to be wrong.

3. Governance: Single class of common stock, one vote per share. Before the offering, executive officers and directors as a group held 21.2%. That figure includes OrbiMed's 13.1%, which the filing attributes to director Peter A. Thompson, M.D., a member of OrbiMed Advisors, who disclaims beneficial ownership beyond his pecuniary interest. Other 5% holders include ARCH Venture Fund at 12.3%, Gilead Sciences at 8.4%, Frazier Life Sciences at 6.8% and Q Healthcare at 6.8%. Directors, executive officers and substantially all securityholders have signed 180-day lock-ups, with limited exceptions.

4. Corporate plumbing: Delaware corporation; the filing describes no Up-C structure and no tax receivable agreement. All outstanding convertible preferred stock converts into 17,971,324 shares of common stock immediately before the offering closes.

Hey Elon, how do you go from asking about the wildest party on Jeffrey Epstein’s child rape island to claiming you repeatedly refused invitations?

Because the DOJ released your emails, and holy shit my guy, you’ve still got some explaining to do.

November 2012.

Epstein asks how many people you’ll need helicopter transportation for. You say probably just you and Talulah Riley. Maybe we should ask her about this next.

Then you ask which night will have the wildest party.

The wildest fucking party.
On Jeffrey Epstein’s child rape island.

Four years after his conviction involving a minor.

What the absolute fuck were you thinking? You knew who this man was. Everyone knew. His criminal history wasn’t some closely guarded secret anymore.

And before the pedodefending cult seals start honking that an email isn’t proof of child rape, congratulations. You’ve discovered something nobody is disputing. 

This is about judgment. Keep up.

Christmas Day 2012.

You tell Epstein you’ve been working yourself to the edge of sanity and want to let loose once your children go home.

You ask about parties. A peaceful island experience apparently isn’t what you’re looking for.

A socially awkward billionaire asking a convicted child sex offender where the real party is.

And we’re supposed to believe you were desperately avoiding him. 

I’m not done Eggman.

December 2013.

You’re discussing another visit. Epstein offers dates. You ask when you should head to the island.

Then Epstein cancels because he has to remain in New York.

Even Jeffrey fucking Epstein couldn’t make time for you. Hilarious.

Yet years later, you publicly say that Epstein repeatedly tried to get you there, and you refused.

So which is it Eggman?

Were you avoiding him, or coordinating your Christmas schedule with him to go to child rape island?

Now SpaceX.

Released correspondence shows Epstein’s assistants arranging a February 2013 visit, including a scheduled lunch with you.

It’s always a lunch. I’m starting to wonder if “lunch” is code for child rape, but I digress.

Whether that “lunch” actually happened remains unclear. But in 2020, you denied Epstein ever toured SpaceX.

Which the fuck is it?

Now everyone’s favorite billionaire soap opera.

June 2025.

You and Trump are having your mean bitch public breakup. Delicious entertainment, admittedly.

Suddenly you post on X that Trump is in the Epstein files and suggest that’s why they haven’t been released.

“Oh snap!”, we all said simultaneously.

Finally, something I can believe.
But then you delete the accusation.

What’s that about?

Did you have evidence? Did somebody tell you something? Or were you throwing around one of the most inflammatory associations imaginable because you were pissed off at another billionaire?

And if you had evidence, why go quiet?
What changed?

That black eye? 
Kissing the wall?

I’m curious Eggman.

You were perfectly comfortable invoking Epstein when it was politically useful to attack somebody else.

But when your own correspondence surfaced, suddenly we’re supposed to all appreciate how easily emails can be misinterpreted.

How convenient. Honestly, who believes this shit?

Maybe you were going on adult night. Maybe you changed your mind. Maybe you’re too much of a fat chud loser for Epstein to follow through.

But even still, the emails are real, and the questions are totally legitimate.

I don’t give a fuck about your rockets, implants, electric cars, or bank account.

Your cultsheep have convinced themselves that your accomplishments make you incapable of dishonesty.

They don’t bro.

You corresponded with a convicted child sex offender, discussed partying on his child rape island, and later portrayed yourself to us as someone who repeatedly refused to go.

I call BULLSHIT.

You demanded answers about everyone else’s connection to Epstein.

Your turn.

We’re not letting this go.

text:
I spent night last with my mentor and dearest friend Cardinal Silvano Tomasi, a recent turned 86. 

Deeply good to his core, nicknamed by the media and Vatican press corps, "the Pope's bulldog," he's continually gone on the toughest missions for the Church: negotiating global UN nuclear arms treaties, setting up refugee camps in war zones, standing up with the vulnerable and marginalized, reforming parts of the Vatican Curia and the Knights of Malta as well as being a leader in social movements like the Community of Sant'Egidio and @JubileeUSA.

As a biography of one of his parishes now completed (he offers a book talk at the parish today) and a biography on Silvano's life in drafting, we sifted through some beautiful pictures of his life and loved ones: Lidio his brother who we lost just about 2 years ago and was the beloved pastor of a historic DC Italian parish, his mom, his first mass, his 4 bosses (St. JP2, Benedict, Francis and Leo), in the Oval office with Nixon, a young lion of the Senate - Teddy Kennedy, Patriarch Bartholomew of Constantinople and a temporary gig as a cruise ship chaplin. (See some of these pictures in the Facebook link comments:  https://t.co/QvObVUgvif ).

I shared with him pictures and videos of all of our friends I've been with the past few weeks at the #IMF, #WorldBank and #G20 meetings in Bangkok, the #IF20 meetings in Salt Lake City, the #SantEgidio 40th Anniversary of the interfaith peace prayer in Assisi, and pictures of me with my lovely 3 kids in Minnesota days ago.

Moving gingerly, not the insanely agile tennis player he was a few decades back, when it was time for him to co-concelebrate Mass, he leapt rather nimbly to the small first floor chapter.

Somehow, recent weeks saw him in DC working with the Nuncio to the US on nuclear disarmament, in Vietnam working on vocations and a part of a Knights of Malta delegation to Assisi. He hopes to be off to Indonesia in a few weeks after another recent health scare.

A conceding, wry smile crosses his lips as he grips my hand and slugs my right shoulder, "I guess the big guy isn't done with me yet. There is still work to do." 

Thank, God, Silvano - our world so desperately needs you and more like you.

(More pictures of our evening together in the Facebook comments:
https://t.co/QvObVUgvif )

text:
How did a $75 million prison end up costing American taxpayers $495.6 million?

In May 2025, private prison company CoreCivic offered to sell its vacant Prairie Correctional Facility in Minnesota to the state for $75 million.

But in August 2026, the Trump administration bought the same prison for $495.6 million to turn it into an ICE detention centre.

That's a difference of $420.6 million, with no clear explanation from the federal government for the huge price jump.

The deal raises serious questions about how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer money.

CoreCivic donated $500,000 to the Trump-Vance inauguration fund. Meanwhile, the company expects to earn around $75 million annually from operating the Minnesota facility once it reaches full capacity.

This was not an isolated purchase. CoreCivic sold four prison facilities to the federal government for a combined $2.2 billion this year.

The Government Accountability Office has also warned that ICE's prison purchases could result in waste, questioning whether the agency can afford to operate these facilities in the long run.

text:
A Drilling Deduction Moves Tax Between Years. It Does Not Erase It.

Texas business owners and the CPAs who advise them: a high-income year sends many people looking for a deduction. Before the deduction, it helps to understand the whole life of it.

Here is a scenario. A business owner (and accredited investor) is looking at a strong 2026 and asks about intangible drilling cost programs, a category of oil and gas private placements. The deduction is the part everyone hears about. The exit is the part few people ask about.

1. The deduction is generally taken when the program is funded.

Intangible drilling costs are generally deductible in the year the program is funded, subject to basis, at-risk and other limits. That timing is why this topic comes up in the fourth quarter.

2. The deduction also lowers basis.

Costs deducted reduce the investor's tax basis in the property. A lower basis means a larger gain if the interest is sold later.

3. On a sale, part of the gain can be ordinary income.

Under Section 1254, gain on a later sale is generally treated as ordinary income up to the amount of drilling costs previously deducted. In other words, the deduction can shift tax to a later year, and it can change the character of that income.

4. The real comparison is between two years.

Which year has the higher tax bill, this one or the one in which the interest is sold or the income arrives, is the heart of the question. Nobody can know that today.

Nothing here makes the category less risky. These programs are speculative and illiquid, wells can be dry, and a deduction lowers a tax bill by a fraction of the money spent. It does not replace the money spent.

This is a conversation for you and your CPA, and I am glad to join it. Reach out to schedule a conversation.

Earl Proeger | Grace Capital Management | Austin, Texas | (512) 293-7731

text:
Matthew McConaughey turned down a $14.5 million movie offer. Then Hollywood stopped calling.

He was the rom-com guy. The offers kept coming, but he wanted to play different roles. So he started saying no.

One studio raised its offer from $5 million to $8 million, then $10 million, $12.5 million, and finally $14.5 million. McConaughey still passed.

For the next 14 months, no other offers came. He moved to Texas and wondered if he was done acting. He even thought about becoming a teacher or a wildlife guide.

Then, about 20 months after he walked away from rom-coms, new scripts started arriving: The Lincoln Lawyer, Killer Joe, Magic Mike, True Detective, Dallas Buyers Club.

He had risked walking away from the role Hollywood knew him for. The silence lasted longer than he expected, but it gave people time to imagine him as someone else.

Would you have turned down $14.5 million without knowing what came next?

text:
On January 7, 1994, former US President Ronald Reagan, then 83, wrote a letter to Richard Nixon, who was about to celebrate his 81st birthday (top left).

The letter opened with a touch of humor:
"Happy Birthday, young fellow!"
"It's hard to believe that a couple of kids like us are 'maturing' so rapidly... I mean so well!"

Toward the end of the letter, Reagan added:
"Let's get together soon before another birthday rolls around!"

Yet just over three months later, Nixon passed away.

In 2016, while conducting research at the Nixon Presidential Library, I came across this original letter and photographed it. The letter appears to be little known, even among the American public.

Reading it again a decade later, what strikes me most is not the humor at the beginning, but that seemingly ordinary suggestion at the end-two old friends hoping to see each other again.

Because I, too, once thought there would be more time.

Both Nixon and Reagan had deep ties to California, and both of their presidential libraries are located in the greater Los Angeles area. While studying American history and foreign policy in the United States, I became super fascinated by their lives and political careers. 

Shortly before leaving the United States and returning home in Beijing, I made a point of conducting research at both presidential libraries, where I uncovered many little-known stories, including the remarkable friendship, a side of Nixon and Reagan's relationship that I suspect many Americans are unaware of.

Their relationship went back a long way.

As early as 1947, Nixon, then a newly elected congressman from California, and Reagan, then president of the Screen Actors Guild, crossed paths for their first time in DC, when Reagan testified before a House committee.

Interestingly, Reagan was still a Democrat at the time, while Nixon was a Republican. But their political differences did not prevent them from developing a mutual respect and appreciation. And Reagan, of course, eventually solved that particular problem by switching parties.

In 1959, when Vice President Nixon visited the Soviet Union and engaged Khrushchev in the famous "Kitchen Debate," Reagan wrote to congratulate him.

Nixon was so impressed by Reagan's analysis that he instructed his staff to send him a special reply rather than the usual polite acknowledgment.

In 1962, Nixon, having lost the presidential election to Kennedy two years earlier, ran for governor of California, and lost again. Reagan, who spoke at a Republican fundraising event for him during this period, registered as a Republican on the spot.

Four years later, Reagan avenged Nixon's defeat by beating the very same guy-Governor Pat Brown. Then, when Reagan left office, Pat Brown's son Jerry moved into the governor's mansion.

Apparently, you can beat a Brown in California, but you can't get rid of the Browns. 

After Nixon became president in 1969, he supported Reagan's initiatives in California and arranged for him to undertake overseas visits, giving the governor valuable exposure to international affairs to broaden his foreign policy experience.

In 1973, following Vice President Agnew's resignation, Nixon considered Reagan as a possible replacement. Kissinger, however, explicitly opposed the idea, and Nixon ultimately chose Gerald Ford.

Reagan would have to find another route to the White House-which, as history would show, he eventually did.

And Reagan, for his part, did not abandon Nixon when the Watergate scandal engulfed his presidency. He called in to express support, assuring Nixon that Nixon's supporters in California still stood behind him and were praying for him.

After Watergate, Nixon endured years of excessive public condemnation. Many political figures preferred to keep their distance from the disgraced former president. But not for Reagan.

Nixon had passed over Reagan for the vice presidency in 1973. Yet when Reagan himself became president in 1981, he was willing to bring Nixon back into the highest levels of American foreign policy discussions, frequently seeking his advice on international affairs.

In 1990, shortly before the dedication of the Nixon Presidential Library in Yorba Linda, Reagan publicly declared that much of the criticism directed at Nixon "was based on nothing at all," and urged historians to reassess Nixon's place in history.

1993 was perhaps one of the most difficult years of Nixon's life since Watergate.

His wife, Pat, to whom he had been married for more than half a century, died in June, shortly after their wedding anniversary.

Ronald and Nancy Reagan attended Pat's funeral at the Nixon Presidential Library in Yorba Linda. At the sight of the mourners who had gathered to pay their respects to his wife, Nixon pulled out a handkerchief, covered his mouth, and broke down in tears.

Just six months later, Reagan's birthday letter arrived.

Ronald and Nancy sent Nixon their birthday and New Year wishes. Reagan acknowledged that 1993 had brought difficult moments, but offered his old friend words of encouragement:

"Surely 1993 had some low points, but Dick, you've led an extraordinary life and have been so richly blessed. Believe me, your many friends are certainly thankful for you!"

Reagan never explicitly mentioned Pat's death. Yet his words seemed a particularly thoughtful way of comforting an old friend who had recently lost his wife.

Then came another touch of Reagan's trademark humor.

Referring to Nancy as his "roommate," Reagan expressed regret that they would be unable to attend the January 20 gathering at the Nixon Presidential Library. But he hoped they could get together soon, before another birthday rolled around.

Reagan's warmth and humor must have surely offered some comfort to Nixon during such a difficult period. In the upper corner of the letter, Nixon left a handwritten note:

"Copy to file. He writes a good letter!"

Sadly, I suspect the two never saw each other again.

Just over three months later, on the evening of April 18, 1994, Nixon suffered a stroke at his home in Park Ridge, New Jersey (top right), shortly before dinner. He was rushed to Cornell Medical Center in Manhattan.

His condition deteriorated, and he eventually slipped into a coma. On April 22, Nixon died at the age of 81.

Five days later, on April 27, Reagan attended Nixon's funeral in Yorba Linda, paying his final respects to an old friend (bottom left).

Later that same year, Reagan publicly announced that he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and gradually withdrew from public life. A decade later, in 2004, Reagan himself passed away.

Knowing what happened just three months after that birthday letter was written makes its warmth, humor, and seemingly casual promise to meet again all the more poignant.

On the morning of February 12, 2016, I was about to leave the Reagan Presidential Library and head to the Nixon Presidential Library for the next stage of my research.

Before leaving, I asked a staff member whether Nancy still visited the facilities. I was told that she occasionally did.

I explained my research background at Stanford, Hoover, and Carnegie, and mentioned that I had long been interested in the history of Ronald and Nancy Reagan, including their correspondence and interactions with Richard Nixon.

Then I asked a question I didn't really expect to lead anywhere:
"Would there be any chance of meeting Nancy?"

To my surprise, the staff member offered to help write to Nancy's assistant to inquire about the possibility. I was informed Nancy was then 94 and living in Bel Air, roughly an hour's drive from the library.

I hesitated. For one thing, I was supposed to be at the Nixon Presidential Library that afternoon. More importantly, Nancy was in her nineties, and I wondered whether such a request would disrupt her life.

Less than a month later, on March 6, 2016, Nancy Reagan passed away.

Over the years, I have occasionally found myself thinking back to that morning. What if I had asked the staff member to send that email? Would there really have been a chance to meet her?

Even for just a few minutes. I might not have asked any grand historical questions. Perhaps I would simply have wanted to hear her talk about what Reagan was like after leaving the White House, what the two of them discussed when letters arrived from Nixon, and what the affectionate nicknames, jokes, and expressions of concern preserved in the archives looked like in everyday life.

I thought that even if the people were gone, the house would still be there. Another thought occurred to me: perhaps one day I could visit the Reagans' home in Bel Air.

After all, it was much more than a mansion, but an important historic site for the United States.

When Reagan left the White House in 1989, he and Nancy moved into that house. After publicly announcing his Alzheimer's diagnosis in 1994, he spent the final decade of his life there.

Following Reagan's death in 2004, Nancy continued living there for almost another twelve years.

The house had witnessed their transition from life in the White House to a quieter existence as a retired couple. It had also borne witness to Reagan's long struggle with Alzheimer as well as the love and memories Nancy carried with her after his passing.

I imagined that perhaps, someday, the house might open to the public, like other historic presidential homes (bottom right). Visitors could walk through the rooms where the Reagans had lived, see their books and furniture, and encounter the personal surroundings that held so many private memories.

But what I learned later was another disappointment. In 2016, following Nancy's death, the Reagans' personal collection went under the hammer at Christie's.

Their Bel Air residence was subsequently sold to media mogul Jerry Perenchio. And then, astonishingly, the house was demolished.

The place I had hoped to visit someday was simply gone.

Ten years later, I still find myself thinking about that morning of February 12, 2016.

What if I hadn't hesitated? What if I had asked the staff member to write that letter? 

But history offers no second chances.

Reagan had hoped to see Nixon again before another birthday came around. I had hoped that one day I might meet Nancy, or at least visit the home where she and Reagan spent their final years.

We thought there would be more time. The archives can wait for you for ten years. The people who made history cannot.

text:
🚨JUST IN: Google is moving into crypto custody tech for banks.

Stolen private keys caused 43.8% of crypto theft in 2024, per Chainalysis.

Alphabet already uses Google's new system for its own crypto on Ethereum and Solana. Banks are testing it now. Commercial launch is planned for early 2027.

Now, read the pitch: Google sells itself as the neutral supplier.

Here's how it works:

→ The key is split into shares. The full key never sits in one place
→ Shares can sit at the bank, at Google and at another cloud
→ Every transfer hits the bank's rules first
→ Then 2 of the 3 shares sign together

So, who holds the key? Nobody, in full.

Who can move the coins? The bank, inside its own rules.

Fireblocks, Privy, Dfns, Utila and others already sell this setup. It's called wallet-as-a-service.

Here's where it gets interesting: some firms that sell banks actual custody tech are becoming banks themselves.

Look at Ripple:

→ In 2023, it bought Metaco for $250M
→ That year, HSBC picked Metaco for tokenized securities custody
→ On Monday, Ripple won final OCC approval for a trust bank

BitGo has a trust bank charter too. Google now competes with it, but as a "neutral" vendor.

If you run digital assets at a bank:

→ Ask every custody vendor: will you ever compete for my clients?
→ Keep at least one key share on your own hardware
→ Ask who can change the approval rules. That's where the risk sits now.

Custody fees hit $3.28B last year, per our research.

Banks want that money. Few want a vendor that might chase their clients.

Google's offer: run custody yourself, on its tools. That keeps the client, and the fee, at the bank.

Would your bank hand a key share to Google?
