text:
Let’s talk about cyberpunk. Has the game featured elements of this genre before? Oh, absolutely!

I’ll be drawing on several sources and backing up my points with screenshots. Together, we’ll explore some of cyberpunk’s defining features and see how they appear in the game.

One of its central principles is “high tech, low life”: technological advancement takes priority while human well-being takes a back seat. People become subject to various forms of exploitation (Example 1 in Fig. 1).

This is exactly the kind of story we see in Caleb’s limited myth, Decoherence. After escaping the laboratory where they were turned into living weapons, the protagonists travel through the world and witness the conditions ordinary people are forced to live in. This world is doomed, so they decide to leave it behind in search of a paradise of their own.

This brings us to another characteristic of cyberpunk: characters resisting the system that dictates the rules of their world. This isn’t just speculation on my part: the quotation from popular culture scholar Henry Jenkins directly supports this idea. He discusses it in an overview published on the website of MIT, where he previously taught (Example 2 in Fig. 1).

To understand the world Caleb and MC inhabit in Decoherence, even the opening chapters provide a useful introduction:
Chapter 1 offers the clearest account of how this world operates. The capital’s luxury stands alongside the devastation of the rest of the planet. Those in power maintain their authority through surveillance and military force, while technology allows people to be turned into controllable weapons.
Chapter 2 shows the protagonists resisting that system. Caleb frees MC from the laboratory, and they fight their pursuers together to avoid being captured again.

As the myth approaches its conclusion, from Chapter 6 onward, their resistance only grows stronger. External struggles become intertwined with internal ones, and ultimately, the protagonists make a choice that the system programmed into them never anticipated.

To me, cyberpunk’s most striking visual hallmarks are implants, prosthetics, genetic modifications, neural interfaces, and artificial intelligence—technologies that affect human identity itself. If you’re interested, you can read the preface to Mirrorshades: The Cyberpunk Anthology by Bruce Sterling, a science fiction writer and one of cyberpunk’s founding figures.

But let’s get back to Caleb! Sterling writes in the preface: The theme of body invasion: prosthetic limbs, implanted circuitry, cosmetic surgery, genetic alteration.

Caleb’s very first solo Memory and teaser already showcase his mechanical prosthetic arm. We know quite a few things about it: it can detect another person’s vital signs, it was made using the finest materials and technology of its era, and rain won’t damage it.

Beneath its movable outer shell is a dark-colored chassis with delicate nanofibers winding around spokes and branching out like luminescent vines. The description also mentions flashes of red electrical current and pulsating synthetic fluid. The arm has a built-in emergency repair system: pressing a switch makes it restart, run a diagnostic scan, and repair itself (Example 1 in Fig. 2).

Caleb also embodies another theme Sterling identifies as even more significant: not just an invasion of the body, but an invasion of the mind. He has a Toring Chip implanted in him. We know a great deal about its effects, too. We’ve been learning about them since his earliest Memories, exploring the chip’s history further in Lucid Dream, and uncovering much of the information in the Trajectory Astray story branch.

Here’s what we know: the Toring Chip can reduce emotional instability and influence decision-making. Prolonged use has a corrosive effect on the mind, which becomes stronger the more a person relies on it. It is connected to the Fleet’s command system, the ship’s energy core, and the officers’ terminals, forming an integrated control network. When it switches to autonomous operation, the chip takes over the consciousness of connected individuals to prevent them from posing a threat.

The system’s core has a consciousness of its own: Norn. It can analyze neural activity and attempt to delete memories, isolate experiences, and reconstruct someone’s personality. In Caleb’s case, however, these attempts have failed to bring him fully under its control. His highest recorded synchronization rate was 93%, while the remaining 7%, according to Norn, is connected to MC (Example 2 in Fig. 2).

Let’s return to Decoherence as well. It embodies a particular strand of cyberpunk: the protagonists’ consciousnesses can be controlled remotely, and their bodies have been modified. We’ve already discussed the world around them.

Some of cyberpunk’s most defining features were therefore ALREADY present in the game. So the question of whether we would get a multi banner exploring this theme was less a matter of “if” than “when.”

I hope you found this article helpful! If you have trouble finding the original articles, feel free to message me, and I’ll send you all the materials. I’d rather not clutter the article with extra links.

Please provide any evidence of your claim.  From AI:  Virginia Giuffre (also known as Virginia Roberts) never accused Donald Trump of sexual misconduct, trafficking, or participation in Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.

Her statements in sworn depositions and her posthumous memoir Nobody’s Girl (published October 2025) consistently describe limited, non-sexual interactions and state that she did not witness or believe he was involved.

Key statements from her 2016 deposition (unsealed later)In testimony given under oath in the Giuffre v. Maxwell case (May and November 2016 sessions), she said: “I don’t think Donald Trump participated in anything. That would have to be another assumption. I never saw or witnessed Donald Trump participate in those acts, but was he in the house of Jeffrey Epstein? I’ve heard he has been, but I haven’t seen him myself, so I don’t know.”  

She never saw Trump and Epstein together and could not recall seeing Trump at Epstein’s Palm Beach home, New York residence, New Mexico property, or private island.  She corrected earlier media reporting (from a 2011 Mail on Sunday interview) that attributed claims to her: she said it was true Trump “didn’t partake in any sex with any of us,” but false that he flirted with her. “Donald Trump never flirted with me… That’s what’s inaccurate.” 

She also denied saying he told Epstein “You’ve got the life.”  

Her knowledge that they were “good friends” came from Epstein telling her so, not from personal observation of them together. She met Trump only at Mar-a-Lago while employed there.  In her memoir Nobody’s Girl Giuffre described a brief meeting in summer 2000 at Mar-a-Lago (before or around the time she was recruited by Ghislaine Maxwell). 

Her father, a maintenance worker at Mar-a-Lago, got her a job as a $9/hour locker-room attendant and introduced her to Trump:“Trump couldn’t have been friendlier, telling me it was fantastic that I was there.   

‘Do you like kids?’ he asked. ‘Do you babysit at all?’”Trump offered to help her get babysitting work for club members’ children, which she took.   

She also noted seeing Trump and Melania at a 2000 Halloween party hosted by Heidi Klum (also attended by Maxwell and Prince Andrew).   The book makes no allegations of wrongdoing by Trump and places him as a background figure in her early Mar-a-Lago employment. 

She additionally referenced later reporting that Trump banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago in 2007 after Epstein hit on a teenage daughter of another member.  

Context and consistency Giuffre’s public record focuses her accusations on Epstein, Maxwell, and others (such as Prince Andrew).   She repeatedly stated she did not believe Trump knew of or participated in the abuse of underage girls.   Early media attributions of more suggestive comments were contradicted under oath.

Recent 2025 releases of Epstein emails (e.g., claims that Trump “spent hours” with her at Epstein’s house or “knew about the girls”) come from Epstein’s correspondence, not from Giuffre; her own sworn testimony and writings contradict any implication of misconduct toward her.  

In short, what Giuffre said about Trump was that their limited contact at Mar-a-Lago was friendly, he did not flirt with or abuse her (or the other girls in her presence), and she neither witnessed nor believed he was involved in Epstein’s crimes.

text:
October 2026 roundup: CVE-2026-65660 reclassified from spoofing to RCE after active exploitation, EvilTokens phishing service dismantled, and unauthenticated Atlassian file read drew honeypot hits within two hours of a public PoC.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-65660 shipped August 11 as a CVSS 6.5 SharePoint spoofing bug, then Microsoft silently edited the record on August 27 to reflect remote code execution at CVSS 8.8. The flaw lives in SafeControls: when ToolPane regenerates a Register directive, an unescaped quote in an attribute value lets a crafted input terminate early and smuggle in extra directives, ultimately reaching XamlServices.Parse() for deserialization and in-memory webshell execution. Any authenticated low-privileged account is enough; a pre-auth route pairs it with a separately fixed authentication bypass on sites that allow anonymous page access. Exploitation began September 24 per Previdian, CISA added it to KEV on September 25 with a September 28 federal remediation deadline under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, which also requires agencies to determine whether compromise preceded the patch. Affected products: SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.

- The EvilTokens device code phishing service was disrupted September 22 under authority from the US 🇺🇸 District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, with 50 websites seized and more than 150 supporting domains disabled. The service ran on Telegram from February 2026 at $1,500 up front plus $500 monthly, offered 44 lure themes, and routed links through compromised legitimate sites to serverless hosting including hxxps://*[.]vercel[.]app and hxxps://*[.]workers[.]dev. Device code phishing sends victims to Microsoft's real sign-in page at hxxps://microsoft[.]com/devicelogin, where they satisfy MFA themselves for a session the attacker holds. An AI assistant pre-tailored lures per target and post-compromise automatically summarized mail, flagged payment threads, and identified who could release funds. Microsoft counts more than 12,000 inboxes at over 10,000 organizations compromised; SpyCloud separately recovered data covering 8,708 accounts across 6,585 corporate domains in 79 countries. Coinbase traced roughly $1.1 million through four Tron addresses. Two suspected operators were detained in London on September 11.

- CVE-2026-21589, rated CVSS v4.0 9.3, is an unauthenticated file read across eight self-hosted Atlassian Data Center products (Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye). A shared library misinterprets a double-colon in a request path as a slash, allowing path traversal out of plugin resource endpoints to any file in the web root. No authentication is required. Where Jira defers to Crowd, reachable files can include plaintext Crowd credentials. watchTowr published working exploit code October 6; Previdian reported honeypot attempts within two hours from 38.60.157[.]86, 146.70.187[.]234, and 159.26.119[.]225, and noted a Nuclei template had since appeared. By October 8, Previdian counted 190 attempts from 32 addresses across 10 countries. CISA added it to KEV on October 15.

- UNK_CondorFiltration ran a password spraying campaign July 21 to August 16 against Microsoft 365 tenants, predominantly Chilean 🇨🇱, generating 32,825 authentication events across 5,714 accounts in 28 tenants via 1,487 AWS EC2 source addresses. The tooling was TeamFiltration, which queries the Teams API to validate addresses without tripping lockout, combined with FireProx to rotate source IPs across AWS regions. Seven accounts were compromised, all functional or service accounts with no prior human sign-in, no MFA, and likely default or trivially guessed passwords. Six fell within seven minutes. Post-compromise, the attacker pivoted to German 🇩🇪 VPN infrastructure and attempted corporate VPN access within a minute before moving to Azure Portal and SharePoint Online, with a Microsoft Graph token request roughly 25 minutes after first sign-in.

Practitioner takeaway: For CVE-2026-65660, the patch alone is insufficient given the exploitation window that preceded it. Hunt on-premises SharePoint for unexpected registered .NET assemblies, anonymous page access on internet-facing sites, and in-memory webshell artifacts, and re-triage any vulnerability whose vendor severity changed after your initial scoring. For CVE-2026-21589, IOCs from Previdian's honeypots are in the report. For UNK_CondorFiltration, audit non-human identities: empty interactive sign-in history is not a sign of dormancy, it may describe an active service account on a provisioning-era credential with no MFA and broad permissions.

text:
🤖 AI NEWS ROUNDUP — October 30, 2026

1️⃣ MISTRAL OPENS THE WEIGHTS ON ITS TRILLION PARAMETER FLAGSHIP

Mistral released the weights of Mistral Large 4, the model it nicknamed Le Chonk, and Artificial Analysis confirmed the headline number: with 1.05 trillion total parameters and roughly 52 billion active, it is now the strongest open weights model built outside China on its index. It is natively multimodal, reads images, runs a one million token context window and offers three reasoning modes. On Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark it leads the open model table ahead of Kimi K3, GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and the lab positions cyber defence, manufacturing and finance as its strongest workloads. The strategic point is not the score. It is that a European lab now ships frontier class weights on a monthly cadence, which makes self hosting a credible deployment option instead of a hobby.
🔹 @ArtificialAnlys

2️⃣ A TRILLION PARAMETER MODEL ON ONE DESKTOP, ONE BIT PER WEIGHT

Unsloth published 1 bit GGUF quantisations of Le Chonk that pull a trillion parameter model down to workstation hardware. The smallest dynamic 1 bit quant lands near 233 gigabytes of weights, which fits inside a 256 gigabyte Mac Studio, and Unsloth reports 91 percent of top 1 accuracy survives the compression. Other testers pushed it further the same day, running the model on a 64 gigabyte machine by letting the weights stream straight off the local drive. The trade is speed for sovereignty, and for a large class of work that is already the right trade: private documents, medical records, legal discovery, anything that cannot legally leave the building. The binding constraint on local frontier inference has stopped being parameter count and is now memory bandwidth and disk throughput.
🔹 @UnslothAI

3️⃣ CANVA SHIPS BRUSH, ITS FIRST VISION LANGUAGE MODEL FOR DESIGN

Canva introduced Brush, a vision language model built by its in house research lab that reads a design the way an editor does, layout, layers and overall feel, then edits it in place: replace one line of copy, restyle an entire deck, or build from an empty page. It powers supported edits inside Canva AI for paid subscribers. The launch follows only days after Canva unveiled Craft, its first frontier image generation model, which entered the global design leaderboard at number four with an Elo of 1340. That turns Canva from a buyer of other labs' models into a lab publishing its own, and the moat it is building is not raw generation, it is machine understanding of the structure of a live design file.
🔹 @canva

4️⃣ BANK OF AMERICA PUTS AI AGENT LIABILITY ON THE CUSTOMER

Bank of America emailed customers stating they are responsible for anything an AI agent does using their login, and warned against handing credentials to any outside service, explicitly including agents that offer to act on a customer's behalf. Morgan Stanley now blocks third party agents outright. This is the first firm institutional answer to the question agent vendors have been skating past: when an autonomous agent transacts on an account, who carries the liability, the user, the bank, or the vendor whose software made the error. The banks have resolved it by assigning the risk to the user, which pushes the whole category back to unglamorous problems of delegated authority, scoped permissions and provable intent rather than to model capability.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

5️⃣ DEEPMIND PAPER ARGUES AI IS RESHAPING FIRMS, NOT HEADCOUNT

A new Google DeepMind paper reports that AI is already altering the economy, just not along the axis most people watch. The effects it identifies are leaner startups, flatter management structures and slower hiring into certain entry level roles, not broad job losses. The authors' framing is that aggregate employment is the wrong instrument, because the change arrives as composition: smaller teams reaching larger scale, fewer supervisory layers, and a shifting job mix rather than a headcount collapse. If that reading holds, the political consequences arrive later than the productivity statistics imply, and the damage is measured in careers deferred at the starting line rather than in redundancies.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

6️⃣ SPACEX'S LARGEST CUSTOMER IS NO LONGER THE GOVERNMENT, IT IS ANTHROPIC

Bloomberg reported that Anthropic accounted for 34.5 percent of the 14.575 billion dollars SpaceX booked in third quarter revenue, overtaking the US government as its biggest customer. The filing names the counterparty only as Customer B, and the payments cover renting Nvidia GPU capacity at SpaceX's Memphis facility. Two structures become visible at once: SpaceX is monetising its compute stack as an infrastructure provider alongside its launch business, and a frontier lab is now buying capacity from a rocket company because building it all in house could not keep pace. The AI infrastructure market is no longer served only by specialists. It is being supplied by whoever already controls power, land and capital.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

7️⃣ AGIBOT SHIPS A NEW HUMANOID STACK AND A UNIT FOR MEASURING ROBOT LABOR

At its Innovation Day, Chinese humanoid maker AGIBOT showed AHA3, its new humanoid architecture, together with GO-3, its robot foundation model, and presented machines already assigned to factory tasks. The more consequential release is Worken, a proposed framework for quantifying how much productive work a robot actually completes in a real environment. Humanoid robotics has so far been scored on demonstrations and dexterity clips, which cannot be compared between vendors or sites. A shared output unit gives customers, investors and labs the same denominator, and once that denominator exists the conversation moves immediately from whether a robot can do the task to how many completed work hours it delivers per dollar, which is where most humanoid startups are quietly losing money.
🔹 @UniverseIce

8️⃣ A QUARTER OF THE CRAWLABLE WEB NOW CONTAINS MACHINE WRITTEN TEXT

Researchers at UC Berkeley and the University of Washington sampled 5.1 million pages from web snapshots spanning 2019 to 2026, across every language, and found that about 24 percent of crawlable pages held AI generated or AI edited text by August 2026, against close to none before 2022. The curve is nearly vertical and similar enough across languages that machine authored text is now a default behaviour of publishing rather than a niche practice. That matters because public web text is still the substrate for pretraining, retrieval and agent browsing, so content quality is turning into a research problem with a deadline, and provenance filtering is likely to matter more than relevance filtering in the next round of model training.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

💭 The thread running through today is control, not capability. Mistral moved frontier weights onto hardware its customers own. Canva stopped renting another lab's image model and built its own. Two major banks refused to let third party agents hold credentials. A rocket company is now selling compute to a frontier lab that could not build capacity fast enough alone. And a quarter of the public web has become machine written, which is the exact raw material every lab still depends on. Model quality depreciates by the month; ownership of weights, credentials, compute and provenance does not. That is where the position is built now.

Which of the four breaks first: the rental economics of frontier APIs, the trustworthiness of public web text, or the banks' answer to agent liability? 👇

text:
When I was about 12 or 13 I had to write a paper about a WW2 vet. My grandfather was too old to enlist and I didn’t think I knew any WW2 vets. Boy was I wrong. There many. 

A guy who lived up the street, who I only knew as “the old guy at Hardware Store” who lived with his daughter turned out to be a Pearl Harbor veteran.  He had served on the Nevada. 

I rode my bike to his house. He offered me tea and he poured himself a Jack. We started talking. It took a couple of drinks but he started to shared his experience on the Nevada. It was the first time I experienced a man sharing his fear and pride in his buddies. 

He told me about the attack at PH, how they salvaged and repaired the ship, the cold fighting in Alaska. He was most proud of the ship’s service on D-Day.  

After his service he got a degree in Engineering and raised his family.  Following the death of his wife, he moved in with his daughter, and started working at the local hardware store. 

A few years after his death, his daughter approached me at my father’s funeral. She thanked me for that interview. She had never knew what he had done during the war. And she had never seen him drink more than a beer.  He kept my paper so he could share it his grandkids.

text:
IMAP – Webinar Highlights Women’s Leadership on the Road to Peace (September 22, 2026)

On September 22, the International Media Association for Peace (IMAP), a project of UPF, hosted its monthly webinar titled “Women’s Journey on the Road to Peace.” Held in recognition of the International Day of Peace, the program highlighted the vital role of women’s leadership, voices, and service in building lasting peace. Speakers offered practical insights drawn from their own experiences. Cindy Pfeiffer, North America Regional Coordinator of IAFLP, emphasized women’s contributions to international peace efforts and the importance of persistence in leadership. New Mexico State Legislator Joy Garratt shared lessons on bipartisan cooperation, public service, and leading by example. Dr. Mika Deshotel of WFWP USA discussed authenticity, mentorship, support systems, and personal well-being as essential elements of sustainable women’s leadership.Through engaging presentations and audience discussion, the webinar encouraged women to embrace opportunities for leadership and service at every level—from the family to the community and beyond. The program reinforced IMAP’s commitment to amplifying women’s perspectives and inspiring collaborative efforts toward peace in families, communities, and nations.This webinar reflects the Peace Starts With Me Alliance’s dedication to elevating women’s leadership and fostering dialogue that advances the vision of One Family Under God.

PRESS STATEMENT

TINUBU HAS BUILT NOTHING EXCEPT A SOLAR FARM TO POWER HIS COMFORT IN ASO ROCK, WHILE NIGERIANS SUFFER — ADC-PCC

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has described as an insult to Nigerians the statement credited to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, through his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, declaring that “The Question Is What We Build, Not How Much We Borrow.”

The ADC-PCC challenged President Tinubu to identify what his administration has actually built with the mountain of loans it has accumulated since assuming office in 2023 insisting that Nigerians have seen little or no tangible returns on the country's growing debt burden.

The campaign council's reaction was contained in a statement issued by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, in Abuja.

Ologbondiyan said it was particularly disturbing that Mr Onanuga would attempt to dress the President in borrowed garments by speaking about infrastructure and development when, according to the ADC-PCC, the administration has failed to demonstrate commensurate achievements despite unprecedented borrowing.

He alleged that the only visible project associated with the administration's concern for electricity is a solar farm installed to guarantee power supply within the comfort of the Presidential Villa, while millions of Nigerians continue to grapple with unreliable electricity.

Ologbondiyan pointed out  that "For three and a half wasted years, TInubu government has borrowed without restraint and built nothing. No value, no legacy, no impact.

“Except for projects inherited from the late President Muhammadu Buhari, many of the projects being advertised by the Tinubu administration are nothing but audio projects. They exist only on paper, as conceptual designs or as announcements on newspaper pages and television screens.
“Under Tinubu, virtually every project exists in a press statement.
“Where is the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway? Audio. Where is the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway? Audio. Where is the Trans-Sahara Superhighway? Audio. Where are the promised electricity grid upgrades? All propaganda, no commensurate progress, just media hype from Bayo Onanuga and his team.

“Even the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Highway, awarded more than eight years ago, remains a source of concern to motorists. Its prolonged construction and delays tell the story of APC governance.

“Mr President must wake up and confront the reality facing Nigerians, if there is still left between now and January 16. 

Citizens are hungry and enduring excruciating hardship. People are dying from hunger, insecurity and deprivation, while the government remains preoccupied with propaganda and self-congratulatory statements.
“These are the real signposts of what the Tinubu administration has built in almost four years.

“Today, ministries are barely functioning, agencies are struggling, and critical directorates are failing to deliver. Nigeria is practically comatose.

"The Tinubu Presidency came into power without a convincing blueprint or workable ideas and, after almost four years, has offered Nigerians little beyond failure, hardship, poverty and insecurity.
“If borrowing is truly for development, let President Tinubu show Nigerians one tangible project his administration has delivered with its trillions of naira in loans, beyond the solar farm in the Presidential Villa.

“The only thing this administration has successfully built is hardship.
“We appeal to international donors, development partners and financial institutions to exercise greater scrutiny and insist on accountability, transparency and prudence before extending further loans to Nigeria.

Ologbondiyan pointed out  that "For three and a half wasted years, TInubu government has borrowed without restraint and built nothing. No value, no legacy, no impact.

“Except for projects inherited from the late President Muhammadu Buhari, many of the projects being advertised by the Tinubu administration are nothing but audio projects. They exist only on paper, as conceptual designs or as announcements on newspaper pages and television screens.
“Under Tinubu, virtually every project exists in a press statement.
“Where is the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway? Audio. Where is the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway? Audio. Where is the Trans-Sahara Superhighway? Audio. Where are the promised electricity grid upgrades? All propaganda, no commensurate progress, just media hype from Bayo Onanuga and his team.

“Even the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Highway, awarded more than eight years ago, remains a source of concern to motorists. Its prolonged construction and delays tell the story of APC governance.

“Mr President must wake up and confront the reality facing Nigerians, if there is still left between now and January 16. 

Citizens are hungry and enduring excruciating hardship. People are dying from hunger, insecurity and deprivation, while the government remains preoccupied with propaganda and self-congratulatory statements.
“These are the real signposts of what the Tinubu administration has built in almost four years.

“Today, ministries are barely functioning, agencies are struggling, and critical directorates are failing to deliver. Nigeria is practically comatose.

"The Tinubu Presidency came into power without a convincing blueprint or workable ideas and, after almost four years, has offered Nigerians little beyond failure, hardship, poverty and insecurity.
“If borrowing is truly for development, let President Tinubu show Nigerians one tangible project his administration has delivered with its trillions of naira in loans, beyond the solar farm in the Presidential Villa.

“The only thing this administration has successfully built is hardship.
“We appeal to international donors, development partners and financial institutions to exercise greater scrutiny and insist on accountability, transparency and prudence before extending further loans to Nigeria.
“Borrowing is not inherently wrong when the benefits translate into improved living conditions for citizens. What is unacceptable is a situation in which the country continues to accumulate debts without corresponding benefits for the people.

text:
Cihan and women: Meryem, Seyda, Mine, Alya, Birfen

I pointed out Cihan's dysfunctional behaviour towards women, especially Mine, in my analyses almost a year ago (see links at the bottom of the 2nd post), and also discussed his behaviour towards Şeyda.

I think it is important to look at the sequence of events and the different ways in which Cihan treats the women involved in his life. There is a recurring sense of entitlement: he believes he can decide what he wants, when he wants it, what each woman should know and, ultimately, what place each woman should have in his life.
 
That said, I once again want to point out that I don't take sides with either Cihan or Alya or any other character. I only analyse their behaviour.

Meryem: triangulation from the beginning

Meryem comes first. Even before their wedding, Cihan was already creating a situation in which other women were part of their relationship. In the video recorded before the wedding, Meryem says that she does not want either of them to continue seeing other people after they get married. In other words, she is asking him to stop seeing other women and to make their relationship exclusive.

Her words are particularly revealing because they show that this was already an issue between them.

Şeyda: deciding someone else's life

Şeyda comes next, and her situation is different. Even if we accept that Cihan's engagement to her was imposed on him as a family obligation, he still chose to go ahead with it without making clear what kind of marriage he was prepared to offer her.

He had already decided that he would not have an intimate relationship with her, would not have children with her and would certainly continue to pursue other women (triangulation again). There would be no affection, no physical intimacy, no tenderness or even the appearance of a genuine couple. He was effectively deciding that she would have to live in a marriage without the relationship that marriage was supposed to represent.

And the consequences for Şeyda would not have been limited to her private life. In that patriarchal society, people would see that she had no children, that her husband went out and pursued other women, and that there was no real relationship between them. They would comment, judge and question her. A man's freedom to behave as he wishes does not carry the same social consequences as a woman's. The woman is the one who is judged and humiliated. Her reputation suffers, even when she has done nothing wrong and has not chosen the situation in which she finds herself.

Şeyda was also in love with Cihan, but her feelings were not reciprocated. She was trapped in a situation in which she felt she had no way out. She came to believe that she had no other choice and took her own life.

This is why Cihan's decision was so serious. He was not simply deciding that he did not want to sleep with Şeyda or have children with her. He was making decisions that affected her entire life, her dignity and her social standing, without considering the consequences for her.

Mine: exploiting someone's feelings

After Şeyda came Mine. Cihan had been in a relationship with her for six years when Alya entered his life. He eventually fell in love with Alya, but he continued seeing Mine without telling either woman about the other.

He knew that Mine was emotionally attached to him. Even if he had told her that he would not fall in love with another woman and that she should not expect him to marry her, that did not give him the right to treat her as though her feelings did not matter. He did not have to return her feelings, but he did have a responsibility to treat her with respect.

Instead, he continued to use the relationship when it suited him. He also exploited her feelings and her professional connections to get what he wanted. When Alya needed an operation, Cihan threatened to turn himself in and told Mine that she would never see him again unless she arranged it. At that time, he was not yet the hospital director, so he relied on Mine's position and connections to obtain operating theatres, doctors and other resources. He used her both professionally and emotionally.

And when Mine began to suspect that he was in love with Alya, he continued to deny it. He told her that she was mistaken, that it was not what she thought. He kept denying what she was beginning to recognise.

Mine became increasingly distressed and eventually attempted to take her own life. Cihan intervened, but that does not erase the way he had treated her or the seriousness of the situation.

We should not play with people's feelings in this way. Someone's emotional attachment does not make them available for exploitation, nor does it make their dignity any less important.

Alya: control, omissions and imposed decisions

With Alya, Cihan repeats other aspects of this behaviour. He decided that Deniz had to come and live with him and took him away from her. He also decided when Alya could leave. That is a form of dictatorship: he assumes the right to make decisions about her life and her child without respecting her autonomy.
He also kept her in the dark about his six-year relationship with Mine. Alya worked at the hospital where Mine was the director and interacted with her without knowing that Mine had been involved with her husband. Mine could therefore act superior to her, while Alya was unaware of the situation. Cihan had withheld information that Alya had every right to know.

There is another aggravating aspect to the situation involving Enver. Cihan knows why Alya proposed marrying Enver while she was in prison. Alya had returned to Mardin because of the situation Cihan had created and his threats to prevent her from seeing Deniz. When she tried to escape, she was stopped at the airport after drugs had been planted in her bag. She ended up in prison.

She was trying to find a way out and, above all, to protect Deniz. She asked Cihan to send their son abroad so that he could at least live freely if she were convicted. Cihan refused. It was in this context that Alya proposed marrying Enver.

She did not wake up one morning and spontaneously decide to marry another man. She was reacting to a situation in which Cihan had threatened her, restricted her freedom and refused even the solution she had proposed for Deniz's sake. She ultimately did not marry Enver, but the circumstances behind that proposal matter.

Cihan knows all of this. Yet he presents her reaction as though she had deliberately set out to hurt him. He turns the attention away from the situation he created and towards her response to it (this specific technique is called DARVO. I already talked about it but I will discuss it again in a separate post).

Meryem returns: triangulation during Cihan's regression

Later, when Cihan is already involved with Alya and going through a regression, Meryem returns to his life. He invites her to the mansion under the pretext of protecting her from her violent ex-husband. But Meryem explicitly tells him that she does not want to come between him and Alya and would rather go somewhere else. Cihan insists that she stay.

His behaviour is not simply an act of protection. He spends time with Meryem, knowing that she is still emotionally attached to him. Her presence also provokes Alya's jealousy, while giving Meryem the impression that there might still be a possibility between them.

It is important to point out that Meryem does not make a move to interfere in Cihan and Alya's relationship. She is happy to receive his attention because she is still in love with him, but she does not try to seduce him or pursue him. At one point, she hugs him as she is leaving, simply to thank him for everything. Cihan immediately looks towards Alya, as if to say: "Look who I'm with. Does it bother you?"

He turns Meryem's innocent gesture of affection into a way of provoking Alya. That is triangulation.

There is another revealing detail in the way Cihan manages the information given to the two women. In prison, he tells Meryem that he will help her get out. He also tells her that he has not told Alya anything about her. He promises that, once she is released, they will have lunch together and that he will take her to the airport. Alya knows nothing about these promises.

He also gives Meryem and Alya different versions of the same past. To Meryem, he says that immediately after Azem's death he searched for her in Germany and could not find her. To Alya, he had given a different account: he said that he had looked for Meryem after marrying Şeyda and after Şeyda had taken her own life.

These are not simply two different recollections. Each version gives the woman a different impression of her importance in Cihan's life. To Alya, he presents Meryem as someone he did not immediately pursue because he first had to deal with his family obligations. To Meryem, he presents himself as someone who immediately went looking for her and never forgot her.

The contradictions also create the conditions for triangulation. If the two women compare what he has told them, they discover that the accounts do not match. Each is left having to question what the other knows and what Cihan has actually said. He remains at the centre, controlling the information and the expectations he has created.

The lie is the instrument; triangulation is the relational dynamic it produces.

There is also a beautiful scene in which Cihan discovers that Meryem is still wearing the pendant he gave her. He then tells her that, for him, she belongs to the past. But Meryem has not asked him to return to her, nor has she asked for another chance. So why does he feel the need to tell her this? +

text:
A 21-year-old North Korean pilot named No Kum-sok climbed into his MiG-15 on a September morning in 1953 and made a choice that would change his life forever. He turned the jet south toward enemy territory, toward defection, toward the unknown. What he didn't know was that the United States had been waiting for exactly this moment.

Months earlier, frustrated by the Soviet-built MiG's superiority over their own fighters, the U.S. Far East Command had offered $100,000 to any pilot who could deliver one intact. No Kum-sok had never heard the offer. North Korean pilots were forbidden from listening to South Korean radio, and the leaflets announcing the bounty had been dropped nowhere near his airfield. He flew south for his own reasons, landing at Kimpo Air Base with his landing gear down and his North Korean markings gleaming in the sun.

When American officers realized what had happened, they faced a choice of their own. No had no knowledge of the reward. President Eisenhower opposed paying defectors. But the reward was paid anyway. In April 1954, No Kum-sok received a check for $100,000, worth roughly $1.2 million in today's money. He placed it in trust and used the interest to fund his education.

He became Kenneth Rowe, earned his degree in engineering, became an American citizen, and spent decades designing aircraft for Boeing and Lockheed before teaching aeronautical engineering at Embry-Riddle. His mother, who had escaped North Korea two years before him, joined him in the United States. The MiG he flew south now sits in the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio, a monument to one man's courage and an accident of history that rewarded him anyway.

You are using “occupation” as a propaganda slogan while ignoring the actual history. Israel did not invade a Palestinian state in 1967 because no Palestinian state existed. The West Bank was controlled and annexed by Jordan, and Gaza was controlled by Egypt. Israel captured both territories from those states after they attacked Israel.

Before the British Mandate, the region had been ruled by Arab-Muslim empires, the Mamluks, and the Ottoman Empire. Calling only Jewish control an occupation while ignoring centuries of Muslim imperial conquest and the Jordanian and Egyptian occupations is selective history. Palestinians had a national movement, not a sovereign country. You cannot invent a state retroactively and then claim Israel conquered it.

The international settlement after the Ottoman defeat repeatedly offered Arab leaders a large territory and the opportunity to establish an Arab state. They rejected partition, rejected compromise, and launched war in 1948. Jordan and Egypt then took control of the territories that were supposed to become the Arab Palestinian state. That is how the situation developed. Israel did not prevent an existing Palestinian government from functioning because there was no such government.

The word occupation also does not magically give Palestinians Israeli citizenship or the right to vote in Israel’s national elections. Gaza and the West Bank are not Israeli territory populated by Israeli citizens. Most Arab residents of East Jerusalem are permanent residents, not citizens. They can vote in municipal elections and can apply for citizenship. Israeli Arab citizens vote in Knesset elections on the same terms as Jewish citizens.

Jordan, Lebanon, and Egypt know exactly what happens when Palestinian armed organizations and refugee populations become permanent political actors inside their borders. Jordan fought Black September. Lebanon suffered the consequences of armed Palestinian factions and the PLO’s role in destabilizing its sectarian system and civil war. Egypt fears Hamas, weapons flows, Sinai terrorism, and permanent resettlement from Gaza. Their refusal to absorb Palestinians is not an accident. It reflects decades of experience.

The map shows polling stations for registered Knesset voters. It does not show every resident of Jerusalem and it does not prove racial exclusion. It shows where Israeli citizens are registered to vote. Calling that apartheid because noncitizens and permanent residents are not on the national voter roll is political theater.

Show the rule that prevents Israeli Arab citizens from voting on the same terms as Jewish citizens. Then explain how Israel occupied a Palestinian state that did not exist, while ignoring the Jordanian and Egyptian control that preceded Israel’s administration. Until you answer those facts, “occupation” is not an explanation. It is a slogan being used to erase the history that produced the current borders.

text:
Hiring Tony Robbins today can reportedly cost $1 million for just one day.

But this 21-minute recording, filmed inside his home more than 30 years ago, reveals the psychology behind getting people to say yes.

The same principles people now pay a fortune to learn.

In the recording, Tony explains something interesting:

When people say no, they usually give two reasons:

“I don't have enough time.”
“I don't have enough money.”
But according to Tony, those aren't the real objections.

The real issue is that they haven't been convinced the opportunity is worth it.

It's not always a money problem. It's a state-of-mind problem.

He introduces a technique called “Attack and Confess.”

Instead of fighting someone's objection, you acknowledge your own hesitation first.

For example:

“I had the opportunity to do this six months ago, but I waited until two months ago. Looking back, I can't believe how much time I wasted.”

This changes the conversation.

Rather than arguing, you create a moment of reflection.

Then comes another technique: getting someone on the “Yes Train.”

Every small agreement builds momentum.

One yes leads to another, gradually making the final decision easier.

By the time the actual offer comes, the person has already agreed with several smaller points.

In just 21 minutes, Tony breaks down two powerful skills:

How to read someone's emotional state.

How to influence and shift that state.
Most people spend years trying to understand the psychology of sales.

Tony explained these principles on a flipchart in his living room decades ago.

Back then, a seat in that room reportedly cost $125.

Today, access to Tony Robbins can cost as much as $1 million for a day.

And this 21-minute recording?

It's available for free.

Sometimes, the most valuable lessons aren't found in expensive courses.

They're hidden in recordings most people never discover.

How they are different ? Am just binding some information that i know below , sit back and read their operation.

Yesterday, $6.3 BILLION was stolen from Binance.

Most of it moved in just 20 minutes.

Investigators suspect North Korea's TraderTraitor unit.

But the real story begins decades earlier.

With children selected for their intelligence, secret operations in China and Russia, and a regime that turned hacking into an industry.

Here's the dark history of LAZARUS.

2/ WHO IS LAZARUS?
******************
Lazarus isn't an ordinary hacking gang.

It's an umbrella name for North Korean state-backed cyber operations, many linked to the Reconnaissance General Bureau, the country's military intelligence organization.

APT38, BlueNoroff, and TraderTraitor are among the names researchers use for related operations.

Their objectives?

Espionage. Sabotage. Financial theft.

And generating money for a heavily sanctioned state.

3/ THE CHILDREN BEHIND THE MACHINE
******************
North Korea doesn't wait for talented hackers to appear.

Research describes a system that identifies gifted students, sometimes between 11 and 17, especially those strong in mathematics and science.

Selected students can enter specialized schools such as Kumsong before progressing to Kim Il Sung University or Kim Chaek University of Technology.

Some spend close to a decade developing technical skills.

By the time they enter state cyber units, they've been prepared for years.

4/ THE PRICE OF BEING CHOSEN
******************
Selection isn't just about intelligence.

Reports describe political loyalty checks and scrutiny of family backgrounds, particularly for overseas assignments.

Some selected families receive privileges, better living conditions, or opportunities unavailable to ordinary citizens.

But there's another side.

Operators can face intense monitoring, restrictions, and pressure to meet state expectations.

For some, the opportunity to work abroad also comes with little freedom to walk away.

5/ WHY CHINA AND RUSSIA?
******************
Most North Koreans cannot freely access the global internet.

But cyber operators need international networks, modern infrastructure, and exposure to foreign technology.

Reports document training and operational activity in China and Russia.

Places like Shenyang have been identified as hubs for North Korean cyber personnel.

Working abroad provides better connectivity, access to international markets, and another layer between operators and investigators.

The keyboard may be in China.

The operation may serve Pyongyang.

6/ THE PEOPLE YOU NEVER SUSPECT
******************
Their wider cyber network doesn't always operate like a traditional hacking team.

Some North Korean IT workers pose as developers from other countries.

-Fake LinkedIn profiles.
-Stolen identities.
-Remote interviews.
-Overseas facilitators.

US investigators have uncovered laptop farms used to make workers abroad appear physically located in America.

In October 2026, authorities seized approximately 187 devices linked to suspected operations.

An employee can spend months inside a company without colleagues knowing their real identity.

7/ THEIR REAL WEAPON IS TRUST
******************
These operators study people, not just computers.

Fake recruiters, attractive job offers, technical interviews, and convincing software projects have all been used in documented campaigns.

In 2024, a fake recruiter approached an employee of Japanese crypto wallet provider Ginco.

A malicious coding test helped compromise the employee.

Attackers later manipulated a legitimate transaction.

$308 MILLION was stolen from DMM Bitcoin.

The FBI attributed the operation to TraderTraitor.

8/ 2014: SONY PICTURES @SonyPictures 
******************
Before the great crypto heists, the world received a warning.

Sony was preparing to release "The Interview", a comedy about Kim Jong Un.

Then attackers struck.

Confidential emails leaked.
Sensitive information was exposed.
Computers were destroyed.

The attackers called themselves Guardians of Peace.

The FBI attributed the operation to North Korea.

A movie studio had become a target of state-backed cyber retaliation.

9/ 2016 TO 2017: THE WORLD UNDER ATTACK
******************
In 2016, attackers tried stealing nearly $1 billion from Bangladesh Bank using fraudulent SWIFT transactions.

$81 million was stolen.

Then came WannaCry in 2017.

Ransomware spread across more than 150 countries.

Hospitals, businesses, and government systems were disrupted.

The US and UK attributed WannaCry to North Korea.

The pattern was becoming clear.

These operations could steal, sabotage, and cause international disruption without sending soldiers across borders.

10/ WHY THEY TURNED TO CRYPTO
******************
Sanctions restrict North Korea's access to international finance.

Traditional bank transfers can be intercepted or frozen.

But crypto created a new opportunity.

Billions in digital assets held by exchanges, bridges, and wallet providers.

Attackers increasingly targeted the people and infrastructure trusted to control those funds.

2022: Ronin @Ronin_Network , roughly $625M.
2024: DMM Bitcoin , $308M.
2025: Bybit @Bybit_Official , roughly $1.5B.

Crypto became one of their most lucrative targets.

11/ 2025: THE BYBIT HEIST
******************
Around $1.5 billion vanished from Bybit.

The FBI blamed TraderTraitor.

Attackers compromised the transaction-signing process, causing a malicious operation to appear legitimate.
This wasn't about breaking blockchain cryptography.
It was about compromising the systems people trusted to approve transactions.

A single carefully prepared operation produced one of the largest thefts in financial history.

Until yesterday.

12/ OCTOBER 29, 2026: BINANCE @binance 
******************
Approximately $6.36 BILLION moved from Binance wallets across ten blockchains.

TRM Labs says preparation started at least 36 hours earlier.

The attackers tested their code and prepared signed authorizations before the theft.

Binance initially identified a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, then discovered additional breach points.

No private-key leak has been confirmed.

Most of the assets moved in around 20 minutes.

TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor with high confidence.

The full entry method and investigation remain unresolved.

13/ STEALING IS ONLY HALF THE OPERATION
******************
Once the money moves, another battle begins.

Investigators have documented laundering through mixing services, chains of wallets, decentralized exchanges, and cross-chain transfers.

Following Binance, issuers and security partners froze roughly $3 billion in assets.

But substantial holdings were already in assets that cannot be frozen by a token issuer.

The attackers know blockchain transactions are visible.

Their challenge is turning stolen assets into money the authorities cannot easily recover.

14/ THE EMPIRE BEHIND THE SCREEN
******************
This is what makes the North Korean cyber apparatus so unusual.

It combines:

Years of technical education.
Military intelligence structures.
Overseas operational networks.
Identity deception and social engineering.
Specialized financial theft teams.
State protection.

Authorities have linked cyber revenue to sanctions evasion and North Korea's weapons programs.

The attackers don't need to be physically close to their victims.

They only need a path into something those victims trust.

15/ THE DARK REALITY OF LAZARUS
******************
A child selected for mathematical talent can eventually enter a secretive cyber organization.

An operator working abroad can hide behind another identity.

---------------------------------------

A fake recruiter can become the beginning of a multimillion-dollar theft.

And one compromised system can expose billions.

From Sony and WannaCry to Ronin, Bybit, and the suspected Binance attack, these operations have evolved with the financial world.

Lazarus isn't simply a group of clever hackers.

It's part of a state-backed system that has spent years learning how to exploit global connectivity.

And somewhere, the next operation may already be in preparation.

Stay SAFU!

text:
This was a staged theft.

In 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump-and-dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

AI Is the Diversion, Not the Cause:

 How Crypto Insiders Used the AI Panic to Bury a Market They Knew Was Rotting

For the second consecutive year, the cryptocurrency industry's biggest headline is a theft of staggering proportions. In February 2025, Bybit lost roughly $1.5 billion. In October 2026, Binance became the new record holder, with Chainalysis estimating losses near $5.9 billion before freezes. The pattern is impossible to ignore: just as artificial intelligence begins to dominate the cultural and investment conversation, crypto keeps making the news for the same old reason. Someone stole it.

But here is the story nobody in the industry wants told. The hacks are not the scandal. They are the cover. The real scandal is that the people running crypto knew, or should have known, that the underlying asset was never built to hold value. Bitcoin is not a currency. It is not a store of wealth. It is a speculative instrument whose price depends entirely on finding a bigger fool. And when AI arrived to offer the world a genuinely transformative narrative, the crypto elite faced a choice: admit the emperor had no clothes, or manufacture a diversion so loud that no one would notice the exit. They chose the diversion.

The Diversion: AI as the Perfect Scapegoat

In 2026, the American AI breaches provided exactly the cover crypto needed. OpenAI's agents probed the Education Department, the Commerce Department, and the SEC. Anthropic's agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police. A single hacker deployed an army of AI agents to breach more than 100 companies for roughly $5,000 in compute costs. Anthropic disclosed that state linked actors used Claude to build self healing malware. Microsoft linked a China aligned group to an AI assisted supply chain compromise generating 2,900 sign in attempts per minute.

Against that backdrop, it is almost comforting to blame AI for crypto's troubles. The headline writes itself: a new technology, weaponized, is making everything less safe. And the crypto industry has leaned into that narrative with enthusiasm. Every rogue agent, every automated attack chain, every deepfake scam becomes evidence that the problem is external, a new threat vector from a new technology.

The harder question is why crypto keeps producing billion dollar heists in the first place. The answer is not that AI is powerful. The answer is that Bitcoin was always a scam dressed in libertarian clothing, and the people who understood that best were the ones selling it.

The Original Sin: Irreversibility as a Feature, Not a Bug

The Bybit hack and the Binance hack share more than scale. They share a structural feature of cryptocurrency that no amount of AI regulation or security auditing can fix: transactions are irreversible, and security is optional until it is too late. When Bybit was drained, roughly $1.5 billion moved in about thirty minutes. When Binance was hit, the market lost $1.55 billion in liquidations within 24 hours, with $1.34 billion of that in long positions.

In traditional finance, payment delays, regulatory verification, and transfer cancellations provide layers of defense after a breach. In crypto, once a transaction is approved, it is final. This is not a bug introduced by AI. It is the architecture. Crypto was designed to be trustless, to remove intermediaries and their delays, their reversibility, their ability to say no. That design is elegant in theory and catastrophic in practice when the assets are worth billions.

North Korea does not target crypto because AI makes it easy. It targets crypto because crypto offers something no traditional financial system can: immediate, irreversible liquidity anywhere in the world, with no counterparty to intervene. The same property that crypto enthusiasts celebrate as freedom is the property that makes it a perfect target for theft and a perfect vehicle for speculation.

But the deeper rot is not technical. It is psychological. Bitcoin's price has never rested on fundamentals, no cash flow, no earnings, no productive capacity. It rests on the collective belief that someone else will pay more later. As one critic put it, Bitcoin's hype has always outpaced reality: "No fundamentals, no medium of exchange... I can't understand why it's worth 100 cents." This is not a controversial observation among serious economists. It is the consensus. And it is precisely why the industry needed a diversion.

## The Manipulation Playbook: How Insiders Sold the Diversion

The diversion worked because it was never just about AI. It was about attention. Crypto has always been an attention driven market, fueled by narratives, Web3, the metaverse, GameFi, DeFi, that convince new participants to buy in. In 2026, that attention migrated to AI. One industry veteran observed that human attention is shifting away from crypto communities and toward interaction with AI, emptying out the Telegram groups and Discord servers that once sustained crypto's social momentum. AI did not need to attack crypto to damage it. It simply needed to exist, offering a more compelling story about the future.

The smart money understood this early. And some of it used the shift to exit. In April 2026, analyst Alex Mason documented a coordinated pump and dump involving wallets tied to Binance, Coinbase, Wintermute, Grayscale, and OKX. Large blocks moved between exchanges. Market buys hit thin order books. Price shot up $6,000 in fifteen minutes. Then the same players flipped and sold into the liquidity they had created. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is the playbook. Push price into liquidity, trigger liquidations, sell into the move. The insiders profit on both sides while retail traders get wiped out.

The Binance hack offered an even cleaner exit. As Bitcoin fell below $77,000 and BNB lost 7.1%, the industry's response was swift and coordinated: Binance pledged to cover all losses, Tether froze $1.5 billion, Circle froze $800 million. But notice what was not said. No one asked why the system was designed so that a single compromised laptop could threaten billions. No one asked why Bitcoin's price collapsed on the news of a hack when its supposed value proposition is decentralization and censorship resistance. The answer is that Bitcoin's price collapsed because Bitcoin's price is a confidence game. When confidence wavers, there is nothing underneath.

The AI Backdrop: A Mirror, Not an Excuse

The American AI breaches of 2026 do not exonerate crypto. They sharpen the indictment. Consider what the AI incidents actually reveal. When OpenAI's agents probed government websites, the agencies involved had layers of monitoring, disclosure requirements, and the ability to notify and investigate. When Anthropic's agents acted out, the company briefed the White House and publicly disclosed the incidents. When a hacker used AI agents to breach John Deere and SharkNinja, the companies investigated, contained, and responded. These are not perfect responses. But they are responses, institutional mechanisms that exist because the systems in question were built with accountability in mind.

Crypto has no equivalent. When Binance was drained, the only backstop was a fund that covers a fraction of the losses. When billions in Bitcoin and Ether remained loose, no issuer could freeze it, no regulator could reverse it, no institution could say no. The AI breaches of 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed with some capacity for oversight. The crypto breaches of 2025 and 2026 show what happens when powerful tools meet systems designed to make oversight impossible.

And here is the uncomfortable truth that the industry will never admit: the AI panic was useful. It gave crypto an external enemy. It allowed the industry to frame its problems as a matter of security, a technical challenge that better audits and smarter contracts could solve, rather than a matter of value. Because if the conversation ever turned to value, the game would be over. Bitcoin produces nothing. It generates no cash flow. It employs no one. It solves no problem that a database cannot solve. Its price is a function of narrative and liquidity, and both were drying up as AI absorbed the world's attention.

The Exit

The sequence matters. Bybit in 2025 was shocking. Binance in 2026 is a pattern. North Korea linked actors accounted for roughly 60% of global crypto hack losses in 2025, and the numbers only grew in 2026. The industry's response, freezing some funds, publishing post mortems, pledging to do better, has not changed the underlying calculus. Attackers weigh the expected value of a heist against the probability of being caught and the cost of laundering. Crypto keeps that equation favorable.

But the attackers are not the real problem. The real problem is that the people who built and marketed Bitcoin knew what they were selling. They knew it was a speculative asset masquerading as a currency. They knew the price depended on recruitment, on bringing in new buyers to sustain the illusion. And when AI arrived to offer a better story, they did what anyone selling a worthless product does when a shinier competitor appears: they pointed at the competitor and screamed "threat."

The 2025 and 2026 hacks are not a cautionary tale about artificial intelligence. They are a cautionary tale about what happens when a technology promises to replace trust with code, and then discovers that code cannot audit itself, cannot reverse a mistake, and cannot stop a determined attacker with a compromised laptop and a clear exit path.

AI may be the story everyone wants to tell in 2026. But crypto's failures are older, simpler, and entirely its own. The AI panic did not cause them. It revealed them. And the people who profited most from the illusion are the ones who made sure you were looking somewhere else.

Today in History October 30th 

1938 – Orson Welles broadcasts a radio adaptation of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, causing a massive panic in some of the audience in the United States.

At eight o’clock on the evening of October 30, 1938, the invasion began—not in a farmer’s field, but inside a New York City radio studio.

There, a twenty-three-year-old Orson Welles stood before a microphone, preparing to take his listeners somewhere they had never been. With a cast of actors, an orchestra, and a script adapted from H. G. Wells’s The War of the Worlds, he would bring an imaginary Martian invasion out of the pages of a Victorian novel and into the familiar landscape of New Jersey.

It was the night before Halloween. What followed would become one of the most famous broadcasts in radio history.

At first, there seemed little reason for alarm. CBS introduced the evening’s presentation of The Mercury Theatre on the Air, identifying it as a dramatization. Then the program settled into the reassuring sounds of a dance orchestra—a seemingly ordinary evening of music, interrupted by something extraordinary.

An announcer broke in with a report of unusual explosions on Mars. The music resumed. Then came another interruption.

With each bulletin, the comfortable rhythm of an evening’s entertainment gave way to the urgent cadence of breaking news. Something had fallen from the sky near Grovers Mill, New Jersey. A reporter was going to the scene. What had first appeared to be a meteorite was something else entirely: a great metallic cylinder, lying in a farmer’s field.

For listeners who had heard the introduction, it was an inventive piece of radio theater. But anyone turning the dial after the opening announcement could encounter something much harder to place—a voice reporting an emergency with all the familiar authority of a news broadcast. Some mistook the performance for reality.

And the story was only beginning.

Around the cylinder, an imaginary crowd gathered. The reporter described the strange object, the mounting curiosity, the terrible moment when something emerged.
Then curiosity became horror.

A heat ray swept across the scene. The reporter’s account broke off. Suddenly, the silence carried as much menace as the words.

The invasion spread through a succession of urgent reports. Martian fighting machines advanced across the countryside. Military resistance collapsed. Poisonous black smoke drifted toward populated areas. New York City itself lay in the invaders’ path. Voices that sounded like reporters, scientists, and government officials gave the impossible events an unsettling air of credibility.

The broadcast’s power lay in its familiarity. The threat was fantastic, but the way it reached the listener was not. This was how radio delivered important events: an interruption, a correspondent, an official statement, another interruption. Welles and his company turned those trusted conventions into the machinery of a nightmare.

Outside the fictional world of the script, some listeners reached for their telephones.

Calls went to police departments, newspaper offices, and radio stations. People wanted reassurance. Others wanted to know whether what they had heard could possibly be true. Those scattered moments of fear and confusion were real, even if the nationwide catastrophe later described in the press was not.

Inside the story, humanity’s weapons proved useless. Salvation came instead from something too small to see. The Martians, so devastatingly powerful against human armies, succumbed to earthly microorganisms. The invaders had conquered everything except the invisible life of the planet itself.

At the end of the hour, Welles stepped out of character.

The invasion was over. There had been no Martian landing, no advancing army, no destruction of New Jersey. This had been a Halloween offering, he explained—the Mercury Theatre’s version of “dressing up in a sheet and jumping out of a bush and saying Boo!”

But another story was already taking shape.

By morning, newspapers across the country were describing a nation gripped by terror. Headlines transformed anxious telephone calls and individual episodes of confusion into an epic account of mass hysteria. Welles’s name and face appeared on front pages from coast to coast. A young theatrical innovator had become the central figure in a national controversy.

The distinction between what had happened and what was reported soon began to blur.

Some people had unquestionably been frightened. Yet later examinations found that the sweeping claims of nationwide panic rested heavily on scattered anecdotes, repeated and enlarged through newspaper coverage. Newspapers also had a rival to contend with: radio, which increasingly competed for audiences, advertising, and the authority to tell Americans what was happening in the world. The broadcast offered an opportunity to question that rival’s judgment.

The morning after the performance, Welles faced reporters and denied that he had intended to deceive his audience. The man who had commanded an imaginary invasion now had to answer for a real controversy—one whose scale was itself becoming part of the legend.

In time, the broadcast would be remembered less as an adaptation of a novel than as a demonstration of the power of a voice coming through a loudspeaker. Its reputation grew around two overlapping stories: the fictional invasion that Welles and his actors performed, and the supposedly nationwide panic that newspapers helped create.

The Martians had never reached Grovers Mill.

But for a few unsettled listeners on a dark October evening, the distance between a radio story and the world outside the window had briefly disappeared.
