text:
The post’s distinction between sportsbooks (the "house") and prediction markets (exchanges) regarding their incentive structures is logically sound—a point corroborated by Kalshi itself and various media outlets. A sportsbook’s revenue is derived from its customers' net losses; therefore, its optimal strategy is to attract "losers" while excluding "winners." In contrast, prediction markets generate revenue through transaction fees, remaining theoretically neutral as to who wins or loses—their growth hinges instead on liquidity and pricing accuracy. In practice, however, this distinction is not absolute: approximately 73% to 90% of the trading volume on prediction markets originates from sports-related contracts, and these platforms face lawsuits in multiple states alleging that they are "essentially gambling." This suggests that, in commercial reality, these two incentive structures are increasingly coming into conflict.

The Sportsbook Incentive: Profit Through Customer Loss

Traditional sportsbooks act as the "house," betting directly against their customers. The money lost by customers—minus any payouts—constitutes the sportsbook’s gross revenue. In a letter to members of Congress, Kalshi’s Chief Compliance Officer, Sudhir Jain, highlighted the implications of this model: "Those most likely to lose money are specifically targeted, often through predatory tactics—such as bonuses and promotions—designed to extract even more capital." Tarek Mansour, founder of Kalshi, described the logic of gambling operators even more bluntly in an interview with the Cato Institute: "I want to maximize my customers' losses, because their losses are my profits. It’s that simple. If someone is too clever, I ban them. Card counters get kicked out of casinos because they take money away from the house."

This structure dictates how gambling operators design their products. They favor bet types like "parlays"—which offer high potential payouts but carry very low actual odds of winning—because these products provide a larger "house edge." Furthermore, they monitor and restrict accounts that consistently turn a profit, as such winners directly erode their bottom line.

The Prediction Market Incentive: Fees and Liquidity

Prediction markets (such as Kalshi or Polymarket) operate under a different structure. Rather than acting as a bookmaker, these platforms facilitate matches between buyers and sellers, collecting a commission on every transaction. In a letter, Kalshi stated: "Our revenue is not equivalent to our customers' losses. Our brand relies on well-calibrated predictions, and well-calibrated markets depend on sophisticated trading—that is, seeking out knowledge about the world and trading on it in an open market."

Mansour uses the analogy of a stock exchange to explain this incentive structure: "We charge about 70 basis points—0.7%. So, we earn 70 cents, effectively collecting half from each side. It’s simply a transaction fee. It’s just like the New York Stock Exchange; exactly the same. We are indifferent to who wins or loses." Under this model, the platform’s objective is to maximize trading volume and liquidity, as revenue is tied to the total value of transactions. Higher volume translates to higher revenue for the platform, regardless of whether individual participants profit or incur losses. Consequently, the platform’s interest lies in attracting as many diverse participants as possible to enhance pricing efficiency, rather than filtering out "losers" or excluding "winners."

The Gray Area in Reality: Sports-Related Volume and Regulatory Controversy

However, the dichotomy presented in the post faces two significant counterarguments in the real world.

First, the composition of trading volume. Reuters Breakingviews, citing the *Financial Times*, reported that approximately 90% of trading volume on prediction markets is linked to sports; an independent analysis by Jonathan Becker estimates this figure at 73% for Kalshi. Breakdowns from NetEase/Wallstreetcn also indicate that, as of March 2026, sports-related transactions accounted for roughly 79%–80% of Kalshi’s volume. This suggests that while these platforms are structured as "exchanges," their commercial reality is heavily dependent on demand for sports betting. They attract users specifically looking to place sports wagers, while their status as an "exchange" allows them to bypass state-level gambling licenses and taxes (reports note that taxes on online sports betting operators can amount to approximately 33% of their revenue). This explains why several states and Native American tribes are suing Kalshi, alleging that it violates gambling regulations.

Second, the dispute over regulatory classification. In July 2026, the Czech Ministry of Finance added Polymarket to its list of unauthorized online gambling sites, while the Portuguese regulator, SRIJ, similarly classified it as an unauthorized gambling operation and ordered it to be blocked. The core logic behind these regulatory actions is that regardless of whether a platform labels itself a "prediction market" or an "exchange," if its offerings essentially amount to "wagering money on the outcomes of uncertain events," they should fall under the purview of gambling laws. Kalshi, by contrast, defends its position by citing its federal regulatory status under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), arguing that federal law takes precedence over state-level gambling statutes. This legal conflict underscores a key point: while differences in incentive structures are real, whether they are sufficient to legally distinguish prediction markets from gambling remains an open question.

Applying Munger’s Maxim

The applicability of the adage, "Show me the incentive, and I will show you the outcome," operates on multiple levels here. Structurally, the incentives for a bookmaker lead to the "extraction of value from losers," whereas the incentives for an exchange drive the "pursuit of liquidity and pricing efficiency"—a distinction that is both valid and well-documented. However, from a commercial perspective, when 73%–90% of a prediction market’s revenue is derived from sports-related contracts, the platform must confront a reality: its user base overlaps significantly with that of the sports betting market. While the platform itself may be indifferent to who wins or loses, its reliance on trading volume effectively positions it as another outlet for sports betting demand. The incentives do not alter the platform’s neutrality regarding the financial outcomes of individual trades, but they do fundamentally shift the platform’s relationship with the broader gambling ecosystem.

🚨 BREAKING: U.S. Department of Education’s Student Privacy Policy Office @usedgov just demanded that the Illinois State Board of Education (@ISBEnews) revise its guidance on mental health screenings for students as young as 3rd grade.

Starting in the 2027-28 school year under Public Act 104-0032, Illinois public schools must offer annual screenings on emotional well-being, depression, anxiety, trauma, suicidal thoughts, and more. ISBE’s current guidance relies on opt-out and makes including results in a student’s official education record optional—risking violations of the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA) and Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).

PPRA requires prior written parental consent for evaluations seeking sensitive mental/psychological information. Opt-out is not enough when school officials administer the tool. FERPA protects parents’ right to inspect and challenge education records; separating or hiding screening files can violate that right.

SPPO Director Frank Miller: “Students should not be pressured into disclosing intimate information… without their parents knowing and consenting. Parents… should be able to access critical information about their child’s wellbeing without schools hiding or separating such information.” ISBE has until Nov. 13 to revise.

This is exactly what @Awake_IL has warned about for years and prepared for. 

In September, Awake Illinois released “Opt-In Only: Guidance for Illinois Boards of Education”—a ready-to-use model policy that:

•  Meets the state requirement to offer free screenings (participation is not mandated)
•  Requires affirmative written parental consent (the federal gold standard under PPRA)
•  Protects parental rights and reduces district FERPA/PPRA liability
•  Treats schools as temporary custodians, not clinics or second parents

As founder @Shannon_A_IL put it: “Parents direct the upbringing, education, and medical care of their children. The gold standard is opt-in only.”

Illinois school boards: adopt (or adapt) the Awake IL model policy now to stay compliant with both state and federal law. Parents: demand it of your board. Full guidance and resources: https://t.co/kgqa0evOMq

text:
Here's WHAT to EXPECT from NYK @ PHI. ✍️

Philadelphia's defensive adjustments shut down New York's biggest actions in their first meeting.

1) Jaylen Brown's availability could significantly alter Philadelphia's perimeter rotation.

Brown is QUESTIONABLE with left knee soreness after playing all 5 games to open the season, averaging 20.6/6.6/4.2 across 36.3 MPG. His availability will be important against New York's physical wing rotation.

LeBron James and Joel Embiid are both absent from Philadelphia's early injury report, although this is the 1st of consecutive games for the Sixers. Jabari Walker, Dominick Barlow, Tacko Fall and Ariel Hukporti remain OUT, leaving their frontcourt depth thin. The 76ers did mention before the season that Lebron and Embiid won't play on both legs of back to backs to start the season and they would stagger their appearances, interesting to keep an eye out on their statuses.

New York, meanwhile, will be without Jose Alvarado. 

2) Nick Nurse's defensive adjustment was crucial in Philadelphia's opening victory.

Philadelphia's most interesting adjustment on October 20 came after halftime, when Nurse switched LeBron onto Karl Anthony Towns while moving Embiid onto Josh Hart.

Explaining the decision, Nurse said:

"It gives you some versatility to play some other coverages."

The switch allowed Philadelphia to approach Brunson and Towns' PnR differently rather than repeatedly involving Embiid in the same screening actions. Although Hart knocked down consecutive threes after the adjustment, Nurse felt it improved Philadelphia's defensive flexibility over the remainder of the game.

3) Karl Anthony Towns has a significant rebounding opportunity against Philadelphia.

New York has been one of the league's strongest rebounding teams through its opening 5 games, averaging 48.2 RPG and 14.6 OREB.

Towns has been central to that production, averaging 21.8 points and 13.8 rebounds. He recently erupted for 27/20 against Detroit, including 8 offensive boards, before adding 19 points and 13 rebounds against Chicago.

Philadelphia, meanwhile, has allowed opponents to collect 52.4 rebounds and 13.8 offensive boards per game through its first 5 appearances.

Nurse has acknowledged the team's difficulties controlling the defensive glass, particularly against opponents who send multiple players crashing.

4) Jalen Brunson has rediscovered his scoring rhythm ahead of a difficult defensive matchup.

Brunson entered the season slowly as New York dropped its first 3 games, but his recent performances suggest the early shooting struggles may be easing.

He scored 23 points against Detroit before producing 38 points and 7 assists against Chicago, shooting 13/25 FG and 6/10 from three. His 4th quarter scoring helped New York complete a comeback from a 19-point deficit.

Brunson is averaging 25.8 PPG through 5 games, but Philadelphia has already demonstrated how effectively it can disrupt his preferred actions with Towns.

5) Mike Brown's rotation changes have given New York's second unit a clearer offensive structure.

Brown experimented with lineups featuring neither Brunson nor Towns earlier in the season, but he wasn't satisfied with the results.

"I didn't like it," Brown explained when discussing those combinations.

He has since returned to staggering his two primary offensive players, ensuring that either Brunson or Towns remains available to initiate possessions through different stretches.

Alvarado's absence has also created an opportunity for Kolek, who delivered 9 points and 9 assists without a turnover against Chicago.

6) Anfernee Simons gives Philadelphia another scoring threat against New York's catch and shoot defence.

Simons has been adjusting to a different role since joining Philadelphia, particularly after missing training camp and preseason opportunities.

His recent performance against Indiana offered a reminder of his offensive value. Simons scored 20 points off the bench, hitting 6 threes as Philadelphia recovered from a 13-point deficit entering the 4th quarter.

Interestingly, Nurse still removed Simons during the final 3 minutes against Indiana despite his offensive production, explaining that Philadelphia needed "the defense and rebounding down the stretch."

7) Tyrese Maxey's late game scoring remains Philadelphia's most dependable offensive weapon.

Maxey has been central to Philadelphia's 4-1 start, averaging 28.4 PPG across his first 5 appearances.

He scored 28 points in the opening win over New York and followed with another important performance against Indiana, finishing with 27 points, including 17 in the 4th quarter.

Philadelphia scored 39 points in the final period against the Pacers after managing just 13 in the 3rd, with Maxey providing much of the decisive shot creation.

New York has generally defended the paint reasonably well, but Maxey's ability to change speeds, attack gaps and pull up before the rim protector commits presents a different challenge.

Conclusion:

New York's biggest advantages appear to be its rebounding, Towns' interior opportunities and the increased offensive flexibility created by Brown's rotation adjustments. Philadelphia, meanwhile, has already shown it can disrupt Brunson and Towns' preferred PnR actions while generating valuable transition possessions.

Brown's availability is the biggest uncertainty. If he sits, Philadelphia could rely more heavily on Maxey and Embiid for scoring, while also losing an important perimeter defender and downhill threat.

text:
Blessed Toirdhealbhach Albert O’Briain, also known as Terence Albert O’Brien, was an Irish Dominican priest, provincial, and bishop of Emly, and one of the Irish martyrs. He was born about 1600 or 1601 at Tuogh, or Tower Hill, in the parish of Cappamore in the diocese of Emly, County Limerick, the son of Murchadh O’Brien Aradh. Both parents belonged to the noble family of O’Brien Aradh, which claimed descent from Brian Boru; the family held a substantial estate that was later confiscated.

He entered the Dominican Order at Limerick in 1621, where his uncle Maurice O’Brien was then prior, and took the religious name Albert after Albertus Magnus. In 1622 he went to study at the Dominican house of San Pedro Mártir in Toledo, Spain. He was ordained priest there about 1627 or 1628 and returned to Ireland around 1630. He served twice as prior of Saint Saviour’s in Limerick and once at Lorrha, and in 1643 he was elected provincial of the Irish Dominicans. While attending a general chapter in Rome he sought support for the Catholic Confederation. He was a strong supporter of the papal nuncio Giovanni Battista Rinuccini. In March 1647 he was named coadjutor bishop of Emly with right of succession and was consecrated by Rinuccini in 1648. He adhered to the nuncio’s policy, signed the declaration against Inchiquin’s truce in 1648 and the declaration against Ormond in 1650, and, with other Catholic prelates, offered the protectorate of Ireland to the Duke of Lorraine in August 1650.

During the Cromwellian siege of Limerick in 1651 he exercised moral leadership in urging continued resistance. After the city surrendered on 29 October he was arrested, together with Major-General Purcell, in the plague house where he was tending the sick. He was tried immediately by court martial under Henry Ireton, excluded from the terms of quarter, and hanged at Gallows Green on 30 October 1651 in hatred of the Catholic faith. His body was afterwards subjected to further indignity by the soldiery. He was the third Catholic bishop executed in Ireland under the Puritan regime.

His cause was among those of the Irish martyrs examined from the late nineteenth century. He was declared Venerable on 6 July 1991 and beatified by Pope John Paul II on 27 September 1992 in Rome as one of the seventeen Irish martyrs. His feast is kept on 30 October, and he is also commemorated on 20 June with the other Irish martyrs.

text:
Editorial Disclaimer The views and personal accounts expressed by Tracy Shannon in this interview are her own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of the hosts, Cowtown Caller, or The Paradox Press.  In the interview, Tracy shares her experiences and perspectives regarding her former husband, his partner, and the impact on their family and children. These are her recollections and opinions, presented as her personal account. We invited responses from the other individuals discussed and welcome any response from them or anyone else named or referenced.   

Episode Summary In this installment of our pre-midterm interview series, we sit down with Tracy Shannon, a Texas activist and one of the most recognizable voices among women who call themselves “trans widows.” Tracy shares the story of her marriage, her family, and what happened when her husband began identifying as transgender. She discusses what she believes the public still misses about the human cost of the transgender movement.  This conversation is part of a series covering the issues most relevant to Americans ahead of the midterm elections next week.  

Who Is Tracy Shannon? Tracy Shannon is a Texas-based advocate and the former Texas director of MassResistance. She has testified before the Texas Legislature in support of Senate Bill 14, the 2023 law prohibiting gender-transition procedures and treatments for minors, and in support of related legislation. She is also a former wife whose marriage ended in divorce after her husband began identifying as transgender.  What Is a “Trans Widow”? Tracy uses the term “trans widow” to describe a spouse whose marriage and family are upended when a partner comes out as transgender. In her telling, the man she married no longer exists. She describes the loss as a kind of bereavement: she lost the husband she knew to his transgender identity, and the marriage ended in divorce. Not everyone accepts the term, and we invite listeners to hear her explain what it means to her in her own words.  

What We Discussed - The impact on her family. How the transition of a spouse and parent reshaped her household and her children’s lives. - The legal system. Her experiences navigating the courts during her divorce and custody proceedings. - The marriage itself. Her account of what happened inside the relationship. - A story that began before the national debate. Tracy’s experience took place in the 1990s and 2000s, long before transgenderism became a mainstream political and cultural topic, which meant she had little language, support, or public understanding to lean on. - The psychological world and her community. Her interactions with mental health professionals and with the people around her, and how she felt they responded.  

Why This Conversation Matters Right Now Our interview comes immediately after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office announced the opening of the nation’s first detransition clinic at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston on October 27, 2026. According to the Attorney General’s office, the clinic opened as a requirement of a landmark settlement Paxton secured with the hospital in May 2026. That settlement includes a $10 million payment to resolve claims brought under the Texas Health Care Program Fraud Prevention Act for billing Texas Medicaid for unallowable and illegal “gender-transition” interventions, including by using false diagnosis codes. Paxton’s office opened its investigation into the hospital in 2023. The clinic is multidisciplinary and offers detransition-related medical care to patients through age 21, along with detransition-related obstetric and gynecologic care to patients older than 21. For the first five years, services are funded by the hospital and free of charge to patients.  That investigation and the settlement followed Senate Bill 14, which took effect on September 1, 2023, and bars physicians and other providers in Texas from providing puberty blockers, hormones, and surgeries for gender transition to minors. Tracy testified before the Texas Senate in support of SB 14. We did not discuss the clinic with her during this interview, but we want to credit her role in the policy fight that led to this moment: her advocacy helped build the public record behind the law that underpins the state’s enforcement actions.

text:
Here's WHAT to EXPECT from HOU @ DAL. 🍿

Houston is 5-0, but Sengun's availability could change everything. Can Flagg and the Mavericks exploit the Rockets' depleted frontcourt?

1) Alperen Sengun's availability could determine Houston's frontcourt rotation.

Sengun is QUESTIONABLE with low back soreness after missing Wednesday's victory over Milwaukee. Marcus Smart is also QUESTIONABLE with a forearm strain, while Steven Adams and Reed Sheppard remain OUT.

With Sengun and Adams both unavailable against Milwaukee, Udoka started VanVleet, Thompson, Durant, Eason and Smith, shifting to a smaller lineup while expanding Clint Capela's responsibilities.

Dallas has its own frontcourt concerns. Dereck Lively II remains OUT following foot surgery, while Santi Aldama is DOUBTFUL. Naji Marshall is QUESTIONABLE with an illness.

2) Houston's transition offence completely overwhelmed Dallas in their first meeting.

The Rockets produced 29 fast break points in their 128-110 victory, repeatedly taking advantage of Dallas' 21 turnovers to generate easy scoring opportunities before the defence could settle.

Houston's decisive stretch came in the 2nd quarter, when it outscored Dallas 38-12 and used a 19-2 run to establish a commanding halftime lead.

Dallas has improved considerably since that defeat, but controlling turnovers remains a major priority against Houston's athletic personnel.

3) Sengun's interior creation could expose Dallas' limited traditional C depth.

Sengun has averaged 24.5/9/7 through his first 4 appearances, shooting 58.1% FG while operating as one of Houston's primary offensive initiators.

He produced 29/9/9 against Atlanta on Monday, repeatedly attacking the basket and creating opportunities for teammates from the post and elbows.

Dallas is without Lively, leaving Gafford as its primary traditional C while Washington and Morez Johnson Jr. provide additional frontcourt support.

Durant recently discussed how opponents have struggled when defending Sengun individually, joking that teams must have overlooked his offensive development.

4) Fred VanVleet could see greater offensive responsibility if Sengun remains sidelined.

VanVleet delivered his strongest scoring performance of the season against Milwaukee, finishing with 24 points on 7/14 FG and 4/9 from three.

He scored 15 consecutive Houston points during the 3rd quarter, repeatedly punishing Milwaukee's defensive coverages with perimeter shooting and aggressive shot creation.

His opportunities become particularly interesting without Sengun.

In approximately 47 minutes with Sengun OFF this season, VanVleet has recorded a 27.5 USG% and 16.9 FGA per 36.

5) Amen Thompson's paint pressure remains a major weapon against Dallas.

Thompson produced 23 points on 10/16 FG against Milwaukee, consistently finding opportunities around the basket through cuts, drives and movement without the ball.

Following the victory, Udoka explained exactly what he wants from Thompson offensively:

"If he can live in the paint, good things gonna happen for us."

The HC also highlighted the importance of recognising additional passing opportunities when opponents collapse into the paint.

6) Dallas' spot up defensive profile could favour Kevin Durant and Jabari Smith Jr.

Durant and Smith each scored 30 points in the first meeting, combining for 60 while repeatedly finding favourable scoring opportunities against Dallas.

Houston has since maintained an impressive offensive rhythm, shooting 40.4% from three through its first 5 games.

Udoka has also discussed using Houston's added depth to reduce Durant's workload, explaining that the additional personnel should help "keep him fresh."

7) Cooper Flagg's growing playmaking responsibilities could challenge Houston's defensive rotations.

Flagg has quickly established himself as Dallas' primary offensive weapon, averaging 25.3 PPG and 6.8 APG through his first 4 appearances.

He scored 32 points in the opening defeat against Houston before producing 29 points and 11 assists against Miami, followed by 26 points and 8 assists against OKC.

His development as a facilitator is becoming increasingly noticeable.

Following the OKC victory, Flagg discussed wanting to become more physical on his drives, focusing on maintaining his path toward the basket and creating contact.

8) Kyrie Irving's increased perimeter volume could exploit Houston's defensive shot profile.

Irving has averaged 18 PPG through his first 4 appearances while gradually rebuilding his rhythm following his ACL recovery.

He scored 15 points against OKC, including 3 early triples, as Dallas established an advantage from the perimeter.

May has encouraged that approach, explaining:

"We love for Kai to shoot. The ball is finding him, too."

The matchup is interesting because Houston's available L10 defensive sample shows opponents attempting 31.6 above the break threes per game, the 2nd highest in the NBA.

9) Daniel Gafford's rebounding responsibilities could become increasingly important.

Dallas has allowed opponents approximately 13.4 offensive rebounds per game in its available L10 sample, an area Houston could exploit.

The Rockets are averaging 11.6 OREB through their first 5 games, and their frontcourt has consistently generated additional possessions through physicality and activity around the basket.

Gafford has gradually increased his responsibilities, recording 9 rebounds against Miami before producing 11 rebounds and 2 blocks against OKC.

May recently praised Gafford's development, emphasising that his offensive improvement should complement his interior responsibilities rather than replace them.

Conclusion:

Houston's offensive depth, transition pressure and perimeter efficiency give the Rockets several advantages, particularly against Dallas' spot up defensive profile. However, Sengun's availability could significantly change the frontcourt matchup, while Flagg's growing playmaking role and Irving's perimeter shooting offer Dallas a credible route to a much more competitive rematch.

text:
Hollywood stars pay about 30% of every paycheck to people who can say no on their behalf. Zendaya married hers.

She described the setup this summer, sitting right next to Tom Holland. When somebody crosses a line, he shuts it down "really clearly, really strong." She's the one going "okay guys, everything's all right."

You've actually seen it on camera. In a clip that went viral in 2024, a crowd swarms their car for autographs, Zendaya stops to sign, and Tom politely steers her out of there.

That 30% is the industry standard, by the way. 10% goes to the agent, 10% to the manager, 5% to the lawyer and 5% to the business manager. A lot of what that money buys is somebody else to be the bad guy. The agent turns down the lowball offer, the studio gets mad at the agent, and the star stays lovable and still gets the call for the next movie.

And Zendaya has a lot riding on lovable.

Louis Vuitton, Lancôme and Rolex all pay her to be the person everybody likes. If someone has to be the one who shuts it down, it makes a lot more sense for it to be Tom.

Most people don't get a Tom. A study out of Notre Dame that tracked about 10,000 workers found agreeable men earned 18% less than disagreeable ones, close to $10,000 a year. That's what being the "everything's all right" person costs you when nobody's there to say no for you.

text:
“…such that, in a sense, you could say that God sees Adam or Jesus, Abel or Jesus, Moses or Jesus.”

Adam or Jesus: Adam being the first man, and Jesus Christ the second man. Hence the declaration, “Ye must be born again.” For all who are born of Adam are born into corruption, but all who are born again by the Spirit are born into newness of life, having received the incorruptible life of Christ.

Abel or Jesus: Abel’s blood cries out for vengeance, but the blood of Jesus speaks of better things. Those who approach the throne of grace must come on the basis of the blood of Jesus Christ—the blood that offers salvation, pleads for mercy, and cries, “Father, forgive them.” Where Abel’s blood cries for judgment, Christ’s blood speaks forgiveness and reconciliation.

Moses or Jesus: The law of Moses brings the knowledge of sin and condemns the transgressor, for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Yet the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus sets man free from the law of sin and death. It is no longer merely a law written upon tablets of stone, but the law of God written upon the heart, through the indwelling Spirit, bringing forth life everlasting.

Thus, in Adam there is corruption, but in Christ, incorruptible life. In Abel, blood cries for vengeance, but in Christ, blood speaks mercy. In Moses, the law exposes sin and brings condemnation, but in Christ, the Spirit brings righteousness, liberty, and eternal life.

text:
In tough times, you find out who actually stands with you.

After the Binance security incident, I noticed something interesting.
Several competing exchanges and industry leaders publicly came forward to support Binance and CZ.

Here are the ones that stood out:

WHO STOOD WITH BINANCE?
➡️ Coinbase – Brian Armstrong personally offered help.
➡️ Bybit – Ben Zhou publicly expressed support.
➡️ OKX – Star Xu called for industry-wide cooperation.
➡️ Bitget – Officially stood with Binance.
➡️ HTX / TRON – Justin Sun offered assistance.

WHO HELPED FREEZE AFFECTED FUNDS?
➡️ Tether – Paolo Ardoino
➡️ Circle – Jeremy Allaire
➡️ Ripple
➡️ World Liberty Financial

WHO REMAINED NEUTRAL?
➡️ KuCoin – Confirmed its platform was unaffected but didn't publicly offer direct support.

And an interesting moment:
CZ publicly called out Elon Musk after his emoji responses, asking him to stop trolling and offer support instead.

My personal take: Exchanges compete every day for users, liquidity and market share.
But when one of the biggest players faces a crisis, supporting the broader industry matters more than competition.

Today it's Binance. Tomorrow, it could be any other exchange.
In crypto, competition is normal. But solidarity during difficult times matters.

Who impressed you the most? And whose response disappointed you?

Your entire argument rests on the claim that Israel’s prophetic program and the kingdom offer closed permanently in a supposed “40-year transition,” so that Acts 2 is simply “the same gospel” we preach today. Scripture does not teach that.

1. The kingdom gospel and the grace gospel are not the same message
Peter in Acts 2 preaches the gospel of the kingdom to Israel:
• He calls the nation to repentance for crucifying their Messiah (Acts 2:22–23, 36–38).
• He offers the promised kingdom and the Spirit as the fulfillment of Joel’s prophecy to Israel (Acts 2:16–21, 38–39).
• Water baptism is required “for the remission of sins” in that context (Acts 2:38).
• The audience is “all the house of Israel” (Acts 2:36).

Paul’s gospel of the grace of God is different:
• It is the preaching of the cross as the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth (1 Cor. 1:18, 23–24; Rom. 1:16).
• Justification is by faith alone, without works, without water baptism, without the law (Rom. 3:24–28; 4:5; Eph. 2:8–9; Titus 3:5).
• It was a “mystery” kept secret since the world began, not revealed until Paul (Rom. 16:25; Eph. 3:1–9; Col. 1:25–27).
• Paul calls it “my gospel” (Rom. 2:16; 16:25; 2 Tim. 2:8) and distinguishes it from the gospel he previously persecuted (Gal. 1:11–12, 23).

If they were the same message, Paul’s claim of a previously hidden revelation would be false.

2. Israel’s prophetic program is postponed, not permanently closed
Romans 11 is decisive:
• “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom. 11:1).
• Israel is blinded “in part” “until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom. 11:25).
• “And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Rom. 11:26).
• The gifts and calling of God are without repentance (Rom. 11:29).

The Abrahamic, Davidic, and New Covenants are unconditional in their ultimate fulfillment to the nation. The “sheep and goats” judgment of Matthew 25 is future, at Christ’s return in glory to the earth, not a first-century closing of the program. Deuteronomy 28–32 contains both curses *and* the promise of future restoration after the curses (Deut. 30:1–10). Jesus said not one jot or tittle would pass from the law until all be fulfilled (Matt. 5:18); that includes the kingdom prophecies that remain unfulfilled.

3. The Body of Christ is not Israel’s remnant under the old program
The church which is His Body is a new creation, neither Jew nor Gentile (Eph. 2:14–16; Gal. 3:28; Col. 3:11). It was not the subject of prophecy; it was a mystery. Peter’s Acts 2 audience was still under the law, still expecting the times of restitution of all things spoken by the prophets (Acts 3:19–21). That is not the present dispensation of the grace of God (Eph. 3:2).

4. Right division is required
2 Timothy 2:15 commands us to “rightly divide the word of truth.” That means recognizing the difference between:
• Prophecy vs. mystery
• Israel vs. the Body of Christ
• The gospel of the kingdom vs. the gospel of the grace of God
• The earthly kingdom program vs. the heavenly position of the Body

Collapsing everything into one continuous “same gospel” erases the distinctive revelation given to Paul and forces the unfulfilled prophecies of Israel into the past or into spiritualization. Scripture does neither.

The old covenant system of law and temple is gone as a means of approach to God (Heb. 8–10), but God’s prophetic program for national Israel is not cancelled, it is interrupted by the present mystery dispensation. When that dispensation ends, the prophetic clock resumes.

That is the consistent Pauline, KJV, rightly divided position.

A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke for Friday October 30, 2026 (Luke 14:1-6)

The Pharisees watched Jesus at dinner on the Sabbath

Jesus healed a man with dropsy before their eyes

He challenged them to consider rescuing their own child or animal that day

This is the witness of Luke 14:1-6

Embracing the Call to Faithful Living Through Luke's Gospel

The Gospel of Luke offers a profound invitation for Catholics to deepen their relationship with Christ through its emphasis on mercy compassion and the inclusive nature of God's kingdom. As faithful practitioners we turn to these sacred words not merely for historical insight but as a living guide that shapes our prayers our actions and our hope in eternal life. Luke's narrative draws us into the story of Jesus in a way that highlights the joy found in repentance and the transformative power of encountering the divine. This reflection explores how the opening themes in Luke resonate with our call to live out the faith in everyday circumstances.

What Insights Does the Beginning of Luke Provide for Our Spiritual Journey

Luke sets the stage with a dedication to Theophilus aiming to provide an orderly account of the events that have been fulfilled among us. This structured approach reminds us that our faith is rooted in reliable testimony passed down from eyewitnesses and ministers of the word. For practicing Catholics this underscores the importance of sacred tradition and scripture as foundations that support our liturgical life and personal devotion. The careful recording of these events encourages us to approach our own spiritual reading with reverence and attention allowing the message to take root in our hearts. Such an introduction also highlights how God works through history to bring about salvation inviting us to see our lives as part of that ongoing divine plan.

How Can We Apply Luke's Focus on the Marginalized to Modern Catholic Practice

The text moves into the announcement of John the Baptist's birth which prepares the way for the Messiah in a world marked by expectation and longing. This section calls us to consider the role of prophetic voices in our communities today as we seek to live out justice and charity. Catholics are reminded through these passages that preparation for Christ involves turning away from sin and embracing humility much like the people who responded to John's message. The narrative builds a sense of anticipation that mirrors our Advent and Lenten observances where we renew our commitment to prayer and service. By reflecting on these early events we find encouragement to extend welcome to those on the edges of society just as Jesus did in his ministry.

In What Ways Does Luke Encourage Perseverance in Prayer and Trust

As the account progresses to the birth of Jesus and the shepherds' visit we witness God's revelation to the humble rather than the powerful. This choice of recipients teaches us that divine favor often comes to those who are open and attentive in their daily routines. For the faithful this means cultivating a spirit of wonder in the ordinary moments of family life work and parish involvement. The angels' message of peace on earth serves as a reminder that true harmony flows from alignment with God's will rather than worldly achievements. Such scenes invite us to trust in providence even when circumstances seem uncertain fostering a deeper reliance on the sacraments and communal worship.

Why Is Luke's Message of Mercy Essential for Our Catholic Witness Today

The reading continues with the presentation in the temple where Simeon and Anna recognize the child as the promised savior. Their faithful waiting over many years exemplifies the virtue of patience that sustains believers through trials and seasons of dryness. This part of the Gospel challenges us to examine how we recognize Christ in the Eucharist and in our neighbors calling for a response of praise and proclamation. Luke emphasizes the fulfillment of promises made to Israel while extending hope to all nations which aligns with the Church's mission of evangelization. Through these figures we learn that a life of prayer and devotion leads to joyful recognition of God's presence in our midst.

The overarching message from this portion of Luke is one of hope and invitation urging us to live as people who have encountered the living Christ. By integrating these lessons into our routines we strengthen our witness in a world that often overlooks the sacred. The Gospel encourages ongoing conversion and a commitment to love that reflects the heart of the Father. As we ponder these words may they inspire renewed fervor in our faith journey leading us ever closer to the eternal banquet.
Embracing Compassion Over Legalism: Lessons from Luke 14

Faithful Catholics find fresh motivation in the account of Jesus healing on the sabbath because it highlights mercy as the true measure of faithfulness rather than rigid rules. The passage shows how Jesus navigates a tense gathering by placing human need above custom and invites believers to do the same in their own circles. This approach encourages daily choices that reflect divine love without waiting for perfect conditions. Readers discover that small acts of kindness can bridge divides in homes workplaces and communities alike. The narrative builds toward a deeper trust in God's priorities that reshapes ordinary conversations and decisions.

How Can the Opening Scene of the Meal Inspire Family Interactions

The reading begins with Jesus entering the house of a Pharisee leader on the sabbath where observers watch him closely yet he responds to the man with dropsy by healing him. In family settings this moment encourages parents to pause household routines when a child needs emotional support instead of insisting on strict schedules. Spouses might choose to listen attentively during conflicts rather than defending positions that echo the silent critics in the story. Such actions build trust and model compassion that children absorb over time. The focus remains on immediate relief of suffering which strengthens bonds across generations.

What Does the Silent Response of the Pharisees Teach About Friendships

Jesus poses a direct question about the lawfulness of healing on the sabbath and receives no answer from the lawyers and Pharisees present. Friends often face similar moments when shared activities or opinions create unspoken pressure to conform. Catholics can draw from this by gently raising concerns about a friend's well being even if it interrupts comfortable plans. This leads to honest exchanges that prioritize care over appearances. Over repeated encounters such openness prevents resentment and fosters deeper loyalty among peers.

How Might the Healing Action Guide Relations with Neighbors

After the silence Jesus proceeds to heal the afflicted man and sends him away restored. Neighbors encounter daily opportunities to assist with practical needs such as offering help during illness or shared chores without regard for personal convenience. The example prompts Catholics to act promptly when someone nearby faces hardship rather than debating social norms. These gestures create a ripple of goodwill that turns casual acquaintances into supportive connections. The emphasis on restoration reminds believers that visible compassion speaks louder than words alone.

In What Ways Does the Final Question Apply to Co worker Dynamics

The passage closes with Jesus asking if anyone would not immediately rescue a child or ox fallen into a well on the sabbath day and the audience offers no reply. At work this challenges employees to extend flexibility when a colleague struggles with deadlines or personal matters instead of citing policies. Team members benefit when one person steps forward to lighten a load during high pressure periods. Such choices demonstrate reliability that enhances collaboration without compromising integrity. The pattern encourages workplaces where human dignity takes precedence over procedural hurdles.

Spotlight on Specific Quotes for Use in All Interactions

Several lines from the account stand out for direct application in conversations. The query Is it lawful to cure people on the sabbath or not prompts reflection on whether personal rules hinder help for others. The action of taking the man and healing him illustrates decisive kindness that families friends neighbors and co workers can emulate. A small section centers on the quote Who among you if your son or ox falls into a cistern would not immediately pull him out on the sabbath day as a reminder that urgent needs demand swift response regardless of timing. These phrases equip believers to navigate discussions with clarity and warmth drawn straight from the text.

The overall message calls Catholics to integrate mercy into every sphere of life as a living expression of faith. This consistent practice transforms routine encounters into opportunities for grace that echo the compassion shown in the reading. Readers who adopt these insights experience renewed purpose in their relationships across all contexts.

text:
Rent plus daycare for one baby: in Massachusetts, those two bills add up to about $4,043 a month. In Mississippi, it’s about $1,631. Here in Colorado, it’s about $3,570, the seventh highest in the country.

These are typical costs, combining the Census Bureau’s median rent with Child Care Aware of America’s average price for full-time infant care at a licensed center. In Colorado, that’s about $1,822 for rent and $1,748 for infant care every month.

In 21 states and D.C., infant daycare costs more than rent. Many are in the Northeast and Midwest, like Minnesota, Illinois, Wisconsin and Indiana. In much of the Sun Belt, including Florida, Texas and Georgia, rent is the bigger bill.

I’ve owned a childcare center for 11 years, so I see this from both sides. Parents are stretched thin, and many are paying as much for childcare as they do for housing. But providers aren’t getting rich either. Infant care is expensive because babies need a lot of hands. In Colorado, licensing rules require about one teacher for every five infants, and those teachers deserve fair pay. Most centers run on very thin margins just to stay open.

If a baby is on the way, here are some ways to bring the cost down:
~Use a dependent care FSA if your employer offers one. Starting in 2026, you can set aside up to $7,500 a year tax-free for childcare.
~Claim the Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit when you file.
~Check the Colorado Child Care Assistance Program, or CCCAP. Many families who qualify never apply.
~Plan ahead for Colorado Universal Preschool, which offers free preschool hours the year before kindergarten.
~Look at licensed family childcare homes, which often cost less than centers.
~Get on waitlists early. Infant spots fill fast, sometimes months before a baby arrives.

These numbers aren’t meant to scare anyone out of starting a family. They’re meant to help you plan before the first bill shows up.

I’m not a financial advisor.

Sources: U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey, Child Care Aware of America, Colorado Department of Early Childhood, IRS

#Childcare #Parenting #CostOfLiving #Colorado #WorkingFamilies

Parents, what do you pay for childcare compared with your rent or mortgage? And if you’ve found a way to make it work, like family help, a shared nanny or an FSA, share it below. Someone expecting a baby needs your tips.

From the "$200 Pyramid Trap" to attorney Dershowitz’s threat—"We will destroy those girls"—this is the true dossier of the victims: from the children who were deceived to those who met suspicious ends.

"THE VICTIMS!"

- THE VICTIMS' DOSSIER: Compiled from the U.S. Department of Justice’s 348-page Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) report (November 2020), Palm Beach police records, and court testimonies unsealed in 2024.

1. THE MECHANICS OF PREDATION: IMPOVERISHED NEIGHBORHOODS AND THE "$200 PYRAMID TRAP"

- Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell never chose their victims from the families of the wealthy elite!
- Why? Because if a child from a wealthy family went missing or was abused, the police and the media would have raised an immediate outcry!

Who Was the Target Demographic? (OPR Report, pp. 37-39):

These youths often came from divorced families, had grown up in the foster care system, faced financial hardship, or had previously been subjected to abuse.

This not only silenced them through the psychological burden of complicity but also caused the network to expand exponentially week after week. 2. "OPERATION LEAP YEAR" AND THE BETRAYAL BY THE PROSECUTOR'S OFFICE

- In March 2005, when the family of a 14-year-old girl discovered what was happening and contacted the Palm Beach Police, Police Chief Michael Reiter and Lead Detective Joseph Recarey launched an investigation.

The "Conflict of Interest" Ploy Used to Remove a Prosecutor (OPR Report, pp. 41 & 43):

- Yet, not a SINGLE person—among the kings, presidents, intelligence chiefs, and billionaires who flew those 14-year-old girls to the island and hosted them there—has ever faced a judge!

"They banked on the children’s vulnerability, poverty, and fear; but a few courageous voices that emerged from among those very children shattered the masks of trillion-dollar empires for the whole world to see!"

Hedef Kitle Kimdi? (OPR Raporu s.37-39):

 > Epstein istismar ettiği çocuğun eline 200 dolar sıkıştırırken şu teklifi yapıyordu: "Okulundan başka bir kız arkadaşını buraya getirirsen, hem ona 200 dolar vereceğim hem de sana ekstra 200 dolar komisyon ödeyeceğim!"

- Başdedektif Recarey, savcılık içinden bir köstebeğin baskını Epstein’e önceden haber verdiğini resmi tutanağa geçirdi!

Savcıyı Dosyadan Attıran Çıkar Çatışması Oyunu (OPR Raporu s.41 & s.43):

text:
There are no $300,000 starter-home subdivisions waiting to be rejected by city council. In much of Florida the starter price is already far higher. Even if one were built, not every house would be homesteaded. Investors and rental companies buy entry-level houses. Those are non-homestead. They do not get the bigger exemption. 

Furthermore, a $300,000 homestead with a $250,000 non-school exemption still has taxable value on the rest. School millage stays. Impact fees, utility charges, and special assessments still all apply. 

“Little non-school property tax” is not zero, and it is not the whole story. Amendment 3 does not mandate a council to kill starter homes or prefer apartments.

text:
Try this: The Framers who got together from 1785, onward, to reform the AC&PU gave it up as a bad job.  Total re-write from first premises required.

But, given that the states were the sovereign entities under the AC&PU - they posited everybody leaving, as the AC&PU had no equivalent to the future constitution's Art V structural change process.

No state or group of states was kicking anybody out of the union under the AC&PU; the states that voted to ratify the 1787 document were leaving that convention and forming a new one.

I maintain as a practical matter, that as an overwhelming majority of states did so (left & ratified the 1787 document), the union followed.

But you could have had a separate union of two or more hold-outs for the old system.  You could have had three confederacies of New England, the Midlands, and the South.

But nobody 'kicked' anybody out.  It was an offer of change, but any state ratifying the new structure (1787 proposal) voluntarily left to do so.  No states were harmed in the process.  That Rhode Island & North Carolina would have suffered tariffs and other economic action had they not eventually ratified and joined the new compact is 1) on them, because 2) they would have been sovereign, foreign states.

2/2

text:
Those who know me well understand that I rarely use this platform to share personal reflections or commentary on current affairs. Today, however, compels me to offer a broader observation.
It is disheartening to witness how frequently our collective discourse or shared communication on this platform descends into manufactured drama, self-absorption, and a relentless tendency to viewing every facet of existence through a political lens and then resorting to animosity. While the right to free expression and differing opinions is a cornerstone of a vibrant society—and uniformity of thought would make for a dull world indeed—as it may be-we seem to be losing sight of our shared humanity.
Strip away the labels of race, gender, identity, or socioeconomic status, and we are fundamentally the same species. Our political or religious alignments should never be the sum total of our identity or existence. We possess the capacity to disagree amicably, to listen to opposing viewpoints with genuine curiosity rather than malice, and to navigate conflict without resorting to hostility.  We possess the innate ability to do this with or without division. Ultimately, how we treat those with whom we disagree is the truest reflection of our character, who we truly are humanely. 
Much of the persistent negativity around us seems to stem from a cultural inertia which often triggers collective angst, threat, and anti-immigration or defensive attitudes—and an overabundance of idle time spent brooding over grievances rather than building something meaningful. True progress requires a conscious shift in focus. If each of us redirected that energy toward a single daily act of kindness or self-improvement, the cumulative impact would be profound.
We are each granted a finite amount of time on this earth. While a single voice cannot shift the global tide, we can choose to live deliberately and positively before our time is up. My intention is not to offend, but to remind us of what matters.
Sending warmth and grace to you all. The words above belong to the woman who birthed and raised me.  She was also a poet laureate.  Now you know precisely why I am the way I am…

text:
“Ethically, if we get offered to do this and we didn’t and someone who works for us gets COVID and dies, I don’t know how I could live with myself.”

Andy Schor holds bachelor’s degrees in political science and history from the University of Michigan. That is the medical file: a former legislative director in the Michigan Senate and House, assistant director of state and federal affairs at the Michigan Municipal League, Ingham County commissioner for a decade, state representative, and mayor of Lansing since January 2018. No M.D., no epidemiology, no immunology, no public-health degree, no clinic. The credential for taking an early dose and then requiring masks of everyone who entered a city building is two undergraduate degrees and a city hall.

In January 2021 he and roughly 200 other Lansing city employees received the COVID-19 vaccine through an invitation-only pilot at Sparrow Health System. Ingham County Health Officer Linda Vail called it an error; the employees were not in the priority groups then eligible. Schor said the doses were offered on a use-it-or-lose-it basis, that he took one of the last slots so others could go first, and that he was going to get the shot to show it was something people should be getting. He said that if the city had declined and a worker later died of COVID he did not know how he could live with himself. 

In August 2021 Schor required masks inside all city facilities for the public, regardless of vaccination status, citing rising local transmission. He said it was the best way to keep the community safe and asked everyone able to get the vaccine as soon as possible. City employees had to mask when interacting with the public or when distancing was not possible. In March 2022 he tested positive while vaccinated and boosted, reported mild cold-like symptoms, and worked from home.

He took the early dose, called it a moral necessity so that a city worker would not die, then required every visitor to mask while he was already protected. The product did not stop infection or transmission. He is still mayor. The residents who waited in the priority line while the city employees got the pilot doses, and the visitors who had to mask because the numbers were rising, did not get an apology when the shot he said he could not refuse failed the one job he assigned it.

Andy said he could not live with himself if he turned the doses down and someone died. Then he tested positive, and the narrative died.

Here's what happened.

In 1959, years before Bewitched, Dick York was filming a western with Gary Cooper. During a scene with a heavy railroad handcar, another actor grabbed the handle and about 180 pounds suddenly shifted onto York. The muscles along his back tore.

He lived in pain for the rest of his life.

On Bewitched, the writers quietly worked around it. Darrin spent a lot of scenes lying down or sitting on the couch. In season five, York collapsed on set with a high fever. He never came back.

His replacement? Dick Sargent, who had actually been offered the part first, back in 1964. He turned it down for another show.

Dick York spent his last years bedridden with emphysema in Michigan, running a charity for the homeless by phone.

Team York or Team Sargent? 👇

text:
Calculating if the pieces she had collected were numerous enough to represent Rashid’s body hadn’t been hard. She felt like she had scraped enough of Rashid together for a proper burial. How Jasmin (21) carried her little brother in Gaza. 
German books. In spite of the blockade, in spite of food shortages, in spite of almost annual Israeli invasions and other ‘mowing the lawn’ tactics, Yasmin has been obsessed with German literature. She is writing her master thesis about how German society processes the collective guilt of the Holocaust in their stories. She contrasts that with how French fiction writers depict the Holocaust. She’s fluent in the language of Rimbaud and the language of Rilke. Yasmin has always been particularly disgusted by evil. It all started when she read about Anne Frank. While reading Anne Frank’s diary at 13 Yasmin felt like the two of them could have been best friends if they had ever met. Apart from The Little Prince no book has had such a profound effect on Yasmin.

On the morning of October 7th she wasn’t celebrating in the streets, unlike what some American Twitter crusaders like to claim. She was reading Der Vorleser, by Bernhard Schlink. She had sinned, because before reading the book she had already watched the movie. Yasmin has watched almost every German movie that’s been released in the last 30 years. Her favorites are the comedy Goodbye Lenin and the thriller Das Experiment. Goodbye Lenin tells the story of a guy who wants to prevent his mum from finding out communism has fallen. He’s scared she’d get a heart attack if she did. Das Experiment is loosely based on the (in)famous Stanford prison experiment. Other favorites include Der Untergang, Gegen die Wand and Die Welle. Die Welle also deals with with an experiment gone wrong. Kinda like the oppression of her people. How far can it be taken, before something goes wrong?

Yasmin is the oldest of five. She has three sisters and one brother. Rashid. Rashid is the Benjamin of the family, meaning that he’s the youngest. He’s the youngest and he is everyone’s favorite. He was a little unexpected. Yasmin’s youngest sister is 12. Rashid is 5.

Yasmin’s father is very introverted. Obsessed with politics, but he only shares his views with his wife, his children and two friends he grew up with.

Already on October 8th her father decided the family should throw their most vital possessions into the car and start driving south. Perhaps they would be able to get into Egypt and maybe they could return later.

He told everyone to take a good look at their apartment, because he doubted Israel and its puppets – he never called them allies – would leave even one stone on top of another.

And so they did.

Yasmin had to leave her German books behind, because they were not considered vital for survival. She and her sisters searched the whole apartment for every morsel of food and rushed to the markets to buy up anything they could find. Her father gave them all the cash he could find and said: ‘Buy whatever food there is available. Pay triple the price if you must.’

They drove at night. Many people were already on the move. In the distance they could hear explosion. From time to time they could hear jets pass. All seven of them cringed every time that happened.

They reached Rafah. Life seemed to be going at the same pace as before there. Yasmin had never been to Rafah before. She tried to convince herself they were on a trip. On holiday. When she was 19 she had a boyfriend whose family was from Rafah. A car mechanic. He had spotted her walking past the car repair shop many times and had somehow figured out where she lived. He knew one of Yasmin’s classmates and he had given that one a letter for Yasmin.

It was the most romantic thing anyone had ever done for her. At first she had been delighted. She liked the way he looked at her. It made every cell in her body buzz. There were some obstacles though. He wanted to get married right away and didn’t understand why reading German books was sometimes more important than hanging out with him on the beach. Her mother had met him once and had said later: ‘He’s a nice boy, very polite, quite handsome too, but I can’t picture you with someone who thinks it’s a cute little defect that you want to read Die Blechtrommel by Günter Grass on a Sunday morning when you could be watching a Formula 1 race on your laptop.’

She still missed the way he used to look at her and she felt hot needles all over her body when she remembered his face after she had told him that she didn’t have time for a relationship right now. He hadn’t set a word. He had only nodded and had walked away. She thought that with his nod he had meant to say: I know I can’t nourish your soul. Go be nourished, I won’t stand in your way.  It’s then she realized he had probably loved her dearly, but it was too late now. They hadn’t spoken since. She started taking a different route to school.

Rashid had fallen asleep right after getting into the car. In his arms he was tightly clenching his precious Spiderman action figure. The trip had taken longer than expected. The distance was short, but with so many people on the move the roads were jammed.

Everyone got out of the car, but Rashid was still asleep. Very soon people offered to take them in. Their father didn’t want to be a burden to anyone and refused. He started asking around how one could get into Egypt. He didn’t get any optimistic answers.

Eventually they used the last money they had to buy a tent. If crossing into Egypt was not an option their father considered it to be a very bad idea to stay in an urban area.

Yasmin’s family was one of the first families to set up camp to the west of Rafah, kind of in the middle of nowhere. Soon more tents started popping up. Something like a camp emerged with a rhythm of its own. The family started making friends with other refugees. The later the people arrived the more horrible their stories became. Things were rapidly worsening all over the Gaza strip. Yasmin felt proud that her father had known how to act immediately.

In the tent camp all daytime hours were spent trying to survive. Looking for water, looking for food. People reverted to barter. Money became a little important. Yasmin heard stories about people trading a car for a bag of flour or twenty pills containing 1 gram of paracetamol. The tent camp revealed how the value of an item can be very situational.

Refugees from Gaza kept confirming to the family that it had been the right decision to leave. Her father said: ‘The international community will let Israel rage until it’s all raged out and then they will help us rebuild. First they let Israel destroy everything and then they send money to rebuild and then Israel does it again. You can’t get much more absurd than that.’

Yasmin and her sisters adapted fairly well to life in the tent camp. Her younger sisters sometimes fought over the one hair brush they all had to share. Yasmin thought it was funny that even in a war zone her sisters cared more about their hair than about anything else. She took it as a healthy sign.

Rashid had it harder. He wanted to play, he missed his toys, he missed his friends. He didn’t mind playing with his older sisters, but this was merely ersatz. He preferred to play with kids his age.

Two weeks ago Yasmin found a family with two young boys about Rashid’s age. They had a heavy rubber bowling ball and six bowling pins.

They had been bowling when the drone struck. Nobody in the camp knows why the drone targeted three kids, ages five, six and eight.

They had been playing in an empty field a few hundred yards from the nearest tent.

Yasmin is fairly certain she put only parts of Rashid in the plastic bag her mum had given her. She had carefully looked around for chunks of human bodily mass covered in blue and red. Rashid had been wearing his Barcelona shirt and blue shorts. His two friends had worn nothing but beige shorts. Locating the pieces of her brother wasn’t hard.

Calculating if the pieces she had collected were numerous enough to represent Rashid’s body hadn’t been hard. She felt like she had scraped enough of Rashid together for a proper burial. What was hard was not remembering the last thing she had said to him. What was hard was  remembering how many times she had been annoyed with him and how many times she had felt bored playing simple games with him when her school work or her social media accounts had been calling for her attention.

Already now she was scared she would never be able to recall his voice and already now she had trouble fixing his face in her mind. She desperately wanted to look at pictures of him, but she realized she didn’t have any in her phone. Her mum had plenty. She wanted to get back to her mum and she wanted to see Rashid’s picture. Smiling. Proudly kicking a ball. Before he had been turned into mush.

That’s what she did. She carried the plastic bag with Rashid to her mum. She asked to see his pictures. She stared at his smile until she felt it was burned into her forever.

The next day she convinced a stranger to drive her back to Rafah. She didn’t have much, but she had a phone and an internet connection. She started interviewing people on the street. On TikTok she started talking about what was happening around her in English, in Arabic, in German and occasionally in French. She got about 40,000 followers. She posted between 10 and 20 times a day. Three days ago an IDF sniper hit her in the chest. Four men carried her to an improvised field hospital. She couldn’t speak, but she could hear what the men were saying. They were carrying her on a door. They were using a door as a stretcher. She could hear one of the men say there was a hole the size of an orange in her chest. She felt no pain, but she felt like she could easily drink four liters of water in one go. She also felt like gravity had a bigger pull on her than on other days.

Yasmin never reached the field hospital. Her last thoughts were a mixture of imagining herself teaching at some German university, walks with her ex-boyfriend and regret for hurting him and extreme guilt for the times she had told Rashid to play by himself and leave her alone.

Her last thought was: if we meet in heaven the first thing I will do is play with him for however long he wants. Even if he wants to spend hours building a bus station using my books as building blocks.

The sniper who shot her was also 21 years old. He hadn’t read any German books, but as a teenager in school back Philadelphia he had watched the movie The Reader with Kate Winslet, based on the last book Yasmin had been reading. He had gotten a good look of her face before he shot her, the Arabic word djemile had been floating around in his head, but he forgot all about her face when his fellow soldiers had patted him on the back.

‘That’s one bitch who won’t poop out any terrorists’, his best friend had said. He hadn’t felt right about it, but he decided to think about it later, much later, when the war against the evil enemy had been won.
