text:
THE EVIDENCE™
PENTAGON REPLACES MILITARY DRONES WITH KITES TO CUT DEFENSE SPENDING
New Low-Cost Surveillance Program Promises Unlimited Flight Time, Zero Fuel Costs, and Complete Operational Dependence on the Weather

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In what Pentagon officials are describing as the greatest breakthrough in military aviation since the Wright brothers, the United States Department of Defense has announced plans to replace thousands of expensive surveillance drones with ordinary kites. The revolutionary initiative is expected to save taxpayers billions of dollars while returning American military aviation to technology that was already obsolete when Abraham Lincoln was president.

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

The program, officially designated KITE — Kinetic Intelligence and Tactical Elevation, represents a major departure from conventional military procurement. Instead of spending millions on sophisticated unmanned aircraft, the Pentagon will purchase commercially available kites, attach miniature cameras, and deploy highly trained personnel to hold the strings.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly embraced the concept after discovering that a $39.95 kite could remain airborne without consuming a single gallon of aviation fuel.

"For years, we've been spending millions of dollars putting aircraft into the sky," Hegseth supposedly explained during a fictional Pentagon briefing. "Now we've discovered that the wind will do it for free. This is the kind of military innovation taxpayers deserve."

THE ECONOMICS ARE OVERWHELMING

A conventional military surveillance drone can cost hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars, depending on its capabilities. Advanced systems require specialized maintenance, communications equipment, trained operators, replacement components, and substantial logistical support.

The Pentagon's proposed replacement requires three things: a kite, a spool of string, and somebody capable of running across an open field.

According to the entirely fictitious Defense Kite Acquisition Office, the introductory procurement package includes a $39.95 tactical kite, $8.99 worth of military-grade string, and a $4.95 plastic handle. An additional $12.50 purchases an optional reconnaissance camera mount, although officials acknowledge that the camera itself must be purchased separately.

Naturally, the Pentagon expects the complete system to cost approximately $47,000 per unit after incorporating government contracting requirements, environmental assessments, cybersecurity certification, diversity training, and a three-year feasibility study.

An additional $280 million has reportedly been allocated to determine whether red, white, and blue kites offer superior camouflage.

THE NEW AGE OF STEALTH TECHNOLOGY

Military planners believe the kite offers several advantages over conventional aircraft. Unlike drones, kites produce virtually no engine noise, generate no exhaust, and require no onboard fuel supply.

They also lack electronic guidance systems that enemy forces can jam.

Unfortunately, they lack guidance systems of any kind.

Pentagon engineers are addressing this limitation through a revolutionary flight-control technique known as Pulling the String.

A second classified maneuver, called Letting Out More String, is reportedly undergoing field testing.

Military officials have also confirmed that an experimental autonomous system is under development. The technology involves tying the kite string to a fence post and leaving it unattended.

Early trials have demonstrated promising results, provided the wind continues blowing in approximately the desired direction.

THE CHINA PROBLEM

Defense analysts acknowledge that the new system could encounter challenges during a confrontation with China, particularly over the Taiwan Strait.

Chinese military aircraft traveling at supersonic speeds might have difficulty engaging a target moving at approximately 11 miles per hour, primarily because their pilots would initially refuse to believe American military technology had deteriorated to this level.

One Pentagon strategist suggested that the psychological advantage could prove decisive.

"Imagine the confusion when Chinese radar operators report that the United States has launched 10,000 unidentified objects resembling children's birthday presents. They'll never know what hit them."

Critics immediately observed that the Chinese would probably know exactly what hit them because nothing would actually hit them.

The Pentagon has also reportedly commissioned a classified study examining whether Chinese forces could defeat the entire American surveillance network using scissors.

SPECIAL OPERATIONS GET THE DELUXE MODEL

America's elite military units will not be restricted to ordinary recreational equipment.

Navy SEALs will receive specially modified black tactical kites featuring reinforced string, night-vision-compatible fabric, and an advanced quick-release mechanism.

Army Rangers will undergo specialized training in launching kites while wearing full combat equipment.

Delta Force operators will reportedly receive exclusive access to a classified stealth model shaped like a bald eagle.

For maritime operations, the Navy is evaluating a carrier-based kite capable of remaining airborne behind an aircraft carrier traveling at 30 knots.

The principal obstacle is that the kite keeps following the ship.

Nevertheless, Pentagon officials remain optimistic that engineers can eventually teach the device to turn around.

THE AIR FORCE OBJECTS

Senior Air Force officers have reportedly expressed serious reservations about replacing sophisticated aircraft with recreational toys.

Their objections intensified when the Pentagon announced that several advanced drone squadrons would be reorganized into the newly established United States Tactical Kite Command.

Pilots who previously operated multimillion-dollar aircraft from sophisticated ground-control stations will now complete an eight-week training course covering wind direction, knot tying, string management, and avoiding power lines.

Graduates will receive the coveted Master Kite Operator qualification badge.

The Air Force Academy is reportedly considering introducing an advanced aerodynamics course entitled Why Won't This Damn Thing Fly?

Meanwhile, defense contractors are scrambling to adapt. One major aerospace manufacturer has reportedly submitted a $1.7 billion proposal for a next-generation tactical kite incorporating artificial intelligence, satellite communications, advanced composite materials, and a proprietary string.

The replacement string will cost $14,000 per spool.

THE ULTIMATE DEFENSE AGAINST DRONE WARFARE

Pentagon officials insist the new equipment offers an additional strategic benefit: enemy forces cannot electronically hijack an aircraft containing no electronics.

Unfortunately, enemy forces can simply follow the string to locate the operator.

Military planners are currently developing countermeasures, including longer strings, camouflage gloves, and instructions requiring personnel to stand behind trees.

An experimental combat version will carry miniature explosive payloads. The weapon's effectiveness remains uncertain because it cannot reliably travel toward the enemy unless the enemy happens to be downwind.

The Pentagon nevertheless describes the capability as a revolutionary development in wind-assisted precision warfare.

The program has also encountered unexpected resistance from the National Weather Service, which has declined a Pentagon request to guarantee favorable winds during major military operations.

THE VERDICT

America has spent decades developing military technology capable of operating across continents, navigating hostile airspace, collecting intelligence in real time, and striking targets with extraordinary precision.

In our imaginary Pentagon, all that technological sophistication has finally met its match: a $39.95 kite from Walmart.

The savings could be enormous. Maintenance costs would plummet. Fuel expenditures would disappear. Complex electronic systems would become unnecessary. Entire military procurement programs could be eliminated.

There would be only one operational inconvenience.

The world's most powerful military would have to postpone World War III whenever the wind stopped blowing.

And should America's adversaries decide to attack during a thunderstorm, Pentagon personnel have been instructed to bring the kites inside immediately.

On Morocco, Russia, and Western Sahara: 

Russia no longer has the strategic foothold in Syria that it once enjoyed, its old friend Gaddafi is long gone, and the fallout from Wagner has complicated Moscow's ability to pursue a coherent strategy across Africa. So yes, of course that keeping the Western Sahara conflict alive serves a larger Russian objective of obstructing U.S. influence and preventing the emergence of stronger regional partnerships that could challenge Moscow's interests.

More importantly, the Russians have also failed to appreciate how much Morocco's position has changed. The kingdom isn't simply an American ally in North Africa anymore. Morocco has become a major economic and financial power in West Africa, with Moroccan banks controlling nearly 30% of the West African banking market, and Moroccan investments spanning telecommunications, fertilizers, infrastructure, and industry. The proposed $25 billion Nigeria-Morocco Atlantic Gas Pipeline, stretching approximately 6,900 kilometers across 13 countries, could further transform the kingdom's strategic importance by connecting West African energy markets to Europe, which will inevitably make Russian gas irrelevant. 

It's safe to say that Moscow has certainly noticed this transformation, which explains why Russian diplomatic rhetoric has become increasingly accommodating toward Rabat (as I pointed out in their draft). But the underlying calculation hasn't changed since Russia still treats an abstention, rather than a favorable vote, as a diplomatic concession for which Morocco should offer something in return. That approach may have worked when Moscow enjoyed greater leverage, but Morocco's growing strategic weight has fundamentally changed the equation.

By vetoing today's resolution, Moscow apparently believed it could reaffirm its commitment to Algeria, one of its principal regional partners, while preserving its ability to bargain with Morocco. But the Russians have misread the room. Rabat now has much less reason to believe that engagement with Moscow produces meaningful diplomatic returns.

In many ways, this could be a blessing in disguise for Morocco, exposing Russia's priorities and giving Rabat every reason to deepen its alignment with Washington and Europe. Putin is accelerating the very Western alignment he wanted prevent.

🌍 BRICS+ Payment System Deemed Feasible, but Common Currency Faces Major Obstacles, New Report Finds

💳 Alternative Payment System Gains Support: A new report from BRICS+ Thinking concludes that member countries could establish a joint international payments system to reduce dependence on the U.S. dollar. The proposed mechanism would allow participating nations to conduct transactions using their national currencies while potentially lowering transaction costs and improving financial independence.

💰 Common Currency Faces Significant Barriers: Researchers warn that creating a single BRICS currency would be considerably more difficult. Such a move would require major economic reforms, including establishing a shared monetary authority, increasing central bank independence, reducing capital controls and allowing currencies to be freely exchanged internationally.

🌐 Central Banks Urged to Cooperate: The report, authored by economists Gregory Chin, Danny Quah and Jim O'Neill, emphasizes that central banks must coordinate closely to establish the infrastructure necessary for a functioning international payments network. The researchers consider this approach significantly more realistic than introducing a unified currency.

🇺🇸 Potential Challenge to U.S. Dollar Dominance: The initiative reflects growing efforts among emerging economies to reduce their reliance on American financial infrastructure. Although a BRICS payments network could gradually increase the use of local currencies in international trade, the report does not suggest that replacing the dollar as the world's dominant reserve currency is an immediate objective.

⚠️ Trump Threatens Economic Retaliation: President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened tariffs of up to 100% against BRICS countries pursuing a common currency or supporting alternatives to the dollar. Those warnings have added geopolitical complications to efforts by participating nations to develop greater financial independence.

📈 Gradual Financial Integration Seen as Most Realistic: The report concludes that connecting existing national payment networks and expanding trade settlements in local currencies offers the clearest path forward. A fully operational BRICS+ payments mechanism could strengthen economic cooperation among emerging markets, while a common currency remains a distant prospect because of political differences, economic disparities and reluctance to surrender national monetary control.

🇷🇺🇨🇩Today, Putin also held a meeting with the President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Félix Antoine Tshisekedi  on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.  Tshisekedi also received a honorary doctorate from the Peoples' Friendship University of Russia RUDN today (October 30). Tshisekedi indicated that the university must be a space for the transmission of knowledge, but also for the confrontation of ideas and the development of critical thinking. https://t.co/JpNlUi9dSw

DR Congo is the largest country in Sub-Saharan Africa (roughly the size of Western Europe, ~2.3–2.45 million km²) with a population of about 113–118 million (15th largest globally, growing ~3.2% per year)....suffering from a textbook case of "resource curse". 

DRC is one of the world’s richest countries in the universe in terms of natural resources, and yet it is among the poorest and least developed, with massive poverty, conflict, and weak institutions.

DRC has the world’s largest COBALT reserves and it is the largest Cobalt producer (~70–75% of global supply.....critical for lithium-ion batteries in EVs and electronics).  World’s second-largest producer of copper (after Chile).  Very deposits for coltan (tantalum; key for electronics), tin, tungsten, gold, diamonds, zinc, and significant lithium deposits (e.g., Manono).

World’s second-largest rainforest is in DRC,  it has vast hydropower potential (including the Inga sites), extensive arable land (mostly underutilized), and high biodiversity.

The DRC has the largest absolute number of people in extreme poverty of any country (tens of millions, cited around 70–76 million).  Approx. 70–81% of the population live below international poverty lines ($2.15 or $3/day). 

There is ongoing violence involving the Rwandan-backed M23/AFC group (which has controlled major areas including Goma and Bukavu at times), the ISIS-linked ADF, and dozens of other militias. Control of mineral-rich zones (coltan, gold, tin, etc.) fuels the conflict and smuggling. This has caused MILLIONS of internally displaced people, high civilian casualties, sexual violence, child recruitment, and a severe humanitarian crisis. 

Endless conflict deters investment, destroys livelihoods, and consumes fiscal resources on security instead of services. 

Copper and cobalt dominate Congolese exports (together usually over 90% of export value). China takes the overwhelming majority of both.

In 2024 data, China received roughly $21.6 billion of the DRC’s total exports. The main items were refined copper (~$14 billion), cobalt (~$3.02 billion), and copper ore/concentrates. 

The DRC has taken steps to reduce absolute dependence on resource extraction and export: cobalt export quotas (introduced after a temporary ban in 2025), efforts to increase sales of copper to the US, and broader talk of local processing. These have shifted some marginal volumes but have not yet changed China’s position as the primary customer.

Until here, everything above was my introduction to DRC.

Here is what Tshisekedi told Putin at the beginning of this meeting at the Kremlin (French to Russian interpretation - to English) : 

"....After the first day of the Russia-Africa Forum, you invited me to visit the exhibition . The exhibition was dedicated to the opportunities opening up in the energy sector and everything that might be of interest to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. For example, the processing of our natural resources, agriculture, and digitalization. In the area of ​​digitalization, there is a tax collection system that particularly interested us.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo is striving to diversify its economy, particularly through agriculture. I noted that there are many opportunities in this area that are of great interest, and we could renew our partnership with the Russian Federation.

For all of this to be realized, we truly need peace. For nearly 30 years now, the DRC has been facing the horrors of war in the east of our country. And we would like Russia, as a member of the G5 [UN Security Council], to help us achieve this peace. The Washington and Doha processes have been launched, but unfortunately, there have been no concrete results.

There was Resolution 2773, which remains unimplemented. Therefore, I would like to point out that this resolution demands the withdrawal of Rwandan troops, who are illegally occupying eastern DRC, an end to hostilities, respect for territorial integrity, and the restoration of the rule of law in the country. Nothing has been done, and we hope that through our relations with Russia, which we would like to intensify, we can count on Russia's support in this matter.

I would also like to note that the MONUSCO [United Nations Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo] will end on December 20. We hope that it will be resumed. We also hope for Russia's support, which should support the initiative to extend the mandate [of the mission].

We would like to confirm that the continuation of this mandate should be decided within the UN framework.

I would also like to offer you a bilateral roadmap that is agreed upon around three pillars: economic cooperation, Russian support for peace efforts, and diplomatic coordination of our efforts...."

Politico: Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine. Current U.S. policy raises the fundamental question of whether Washington understand what is at stake. The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip.

Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability.

As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake?

If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient?

Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts.

The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies.

That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today.

Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion.

Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.

Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.

On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.

The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.

The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.

This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.

If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives.

U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end.

American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment.

Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force.

Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations.

A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict.

And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians.

Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes.

History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay.

text:
Deedy Das (@deedydas) ranked where startup founders come from per 1,000 employees, and Yahoo at #3 is the most interesting line on the whole chart.

Palantir is #1 with 16.5 founders per 1,000 staff. Stanford is #2 at 14.2. Yahoo sits right behind at 10.6, with 80 alumni founders whose startups include ClickHouse at $1.1B and ElevenLabs at $792M.

Hold onto that 10.6.

Google has 488 alumni founders on the list, the most of anyone by a wide margin, and it comes out at 1.5 per 1,000 staff. Microsoft has 308 founders and lands at 1.4. A huge headcount swallows the ratio.

Yahoo went the other way on headcount. In 2008 Microsoft offered $44.6 billion for it and the board said the bid undervalued the company. Eight years later Verizon agreed to buy the core business for $4.83 billion, then shaved $350 million off after the data breaches came out. Apollo took 90% in 2021, and in 2023 Yahoo cut about 20% of its workforce.

So part of that 10.6 comes from a company that got a lot smaller. One reply under Deedy's post makes the same point about Sun Microsystems sitting at #13.

The Yahoo founder pipeline also started long before this chart.

Jan Koum and Brian Acton both worked at Yahoo. In October 2009 Acton convinced FIVE former Yahoo friends to put $250,000 into a tiny messaging app called WhatsApp. Sequoia came in with about $8 million in 2011. In February 2014 Facebook bought it for roughly $19 billion, at the time the largest acquisiton of a venture backed company in history

Funny thing is, Yahoo passed on buying Google for $1 million in 1998. Two of its own engineers later built a company Facebook paid about four times more for than Verizon paid for Yahoo's core business.

Look at the pass rate column too. OpenAI has 32 alumni founders on the list and the highest pass rate on the whole chart at 71%. Palantir is at 49%, Google at 33%.

that column is where I'd spend my time as an investor

Big companies hire great people and keep most of them. Companies in decline send a lot of them out the door with real operating scars, and some of those people end up building the next WhatsApp

NCAAB Futures: Early Sharp-Money Update

Our primary NCAAB futures report still comes ahead of March Madness, but we have some early action to share. The following futures plays are listed in order of sharp buying: Florida +700, Texas +2200, Illinois +1600, and Louisville +2500.

1. Florida +700

Pros: Florida returns an experienced frontcourt in Thomas Haugh, Alex Condon, and Rueben Chinyelu. All three earned spots on the NABC Player of the Year watch list, giving the Gators a strong foundation for a deep tournament run. Florida team notes

Cons: Depth is the early concern. Florida’s bench was outscored 61–7 across its two exhibitions, and Todd Golden identified defensive communication as another issue. With the shortest price on our list, the Gators need reliable contributions beyond their starting lineup. Florida exhibition report

2. Texas +2200

Pros: Texas has a productive interior pairing in returning center Matas Vokietaitis and TCU transfer David Punch. Vokietaitis averaged 15.6 points and 7.1 rebounds last season, while Punch led TCU in scoring, rebounding, and blocks. That provides an appealing foundation at 22-to-1. Texas team notes

Cons: Ball security and defense need watching. Texas committed 16 turnovers and allowed St. John’s to shoot 53.1% in an exhibition loss. The talent is there, but cleaner execution against quality opponents will be essential. Texas exhibition report

3. Illinois +1600

Pros: Illinois returns important pieces from its Final Four team and has already shown considerable scoring depth. Seven players reached double figures in the final exhibition against UIC, even with three key returners sitting out. Illinois team report

Cons: The early question is whether the defense can complement that offense. Illinois allowed 96 and 95 points in its first two exhibitions. Pace and preseason rotations can influence those totals, but defensive consistency remains something to monitor. Illinois preseason results

4. Louisville +2500

Pros: Louisville offers the longest price of the four, with a proven defensive anchor in Flory Bidunga. The reigning Big 12 Defensive Player of the Year averaged 9.0 rebounds and 2.6 blocks last season, bringing established rebounding and rim protection. Louisville player notes

Cons: Pat Kelsey is bringing together a roster with 11 newcomers, making chemistry and offensive execution key variables. Louisville committed 17 turnovers in its final exhibition; ball security and consistent perimeter shooting need to develop as the competition improves. Louisville exhibition report

Alabama — Off the Board

Alabama was also attracting a medium buy, but has since come off the board at multiple spots. Worth noting as getting action, tough to analyze until we see how the action responds if/when it gets back on the board.

text:
Great. Now do Utah. 

ALASKA GETS UTAHED

Except Utah’s came with an alleged $1,000 + 🥩 dinner bribe and a statewide coverup.

In Alaska, a second Dan Sullivan showed up on the ballot in what Republicans call a calculated voter-confusion play. 

In Utah, after Phil Lyman beat the convention and forced a primary against Spencer Cox, an unrelated Richard Lyman (and his mother Carol) filed as write-in candidates for governor and lieutenant governor at the absolute last minute. 

Phil’s campaign released a coworker’s affidavit and texts claiming Richard said the Cox campaign offered him $1,000 and a 🥩 dinner to run specifically “to mess with Phil Lyman’s campaign.” That is illegal under Utah law. Cox’s people called it “blatantly false.” 

Not one member of Utah GOP leadership, the federal delegation, or the legislature publicly demanded answers or an investigation; especially Mike Lee, who had already locked arms with Cox and told everyone the primary was over and it was time to unite. 

Silence.

Then the media did its part: stories about “Lyman dropping out” routinely used Phil’s photo instead of Richard’s or Carol’s. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (Cox’s running mate and the state’s chief election officer) sent the required email to registered Republicans announcing that Richard Kennedy Lyman and Carol Ann Lyman had withdrawn and that votes for them would not count. Voters flooded Phil’s campaign saying they thought he had quit. Henderson’s office clarified the obvious after the damage, but the confusion was already baked in.

Name-alike candidates + last-minute filing + alleged inducement + media sloppiness + official email that further muddied the waters + total silence from every elected Republican who could have spoken = the exact playbook used to protect the incumbent. 

The lawsuit was later dismissed on free-speech grounds without a trial on the merits. No criminal probe. No accountability. Just the same people who run the elections and the party telling everyone to move on.

text:
My guy is so inside that insiders call him an insider. 

He’s so inside that he’s on the outside. 

Trust me, he’s so inside that when the Federal Reserve was deciding whether to cut rates, he already knew the vote count, the dissenting arguments, and which governor was going to leak it to the press afterward. He was on the call. Not as a participant, obviously (those seats are reserved) but as the guy who set up the secure line and stayed on mute the whole time so he could hear everything while he fixed the projector remote.

By the time the announcement hit the wire, my guy had already moved money. Not a lot. Just enough. Enough that when the market opened green, his position was already sitting there like it had been expecting company. People started asking questions. Quiet questions. The kind that come with free dinners and very specific requests for “any other thoughts you might have.”

He started getting invited to things. Not the big rooms at first, but the rooms next to the big rooms. The ones where people speak a little more freely because they assume everyone present already knows. He didn’t correct them. He just nodded at the right moments and occasionally said something so vague it sounded profound. “Liquidity’s a feeling,” he told a hedge fund guy once. The guy wrote it down.
Within a month he had a nickname. Within two he had a second phone. Within three he was being described, in low voices, as “the one who actually knows.”

Then last Tuesday the FBI showed up at the coffee shop where he works. Turns out the secure line he set up was just the regular conference bridge the Fed uses for internal calls, and the “projector remote” he was fixing was the one from the building’s AV closet. He’d been on the call because he was the guy they sent over from facilities when the regular tech called out sick. He stayed muted because he was eating a breakfast sandwich and didn’t want anyone to hear him chewing. The money he “moved” was the $40 he’d won on a scratch-off that morning, which he used to buy the sandwich. The hedge fund guy who wrote down “liquidity’s a feeling” was the one who later called the tip line after realizing the only thing my guy had ever correctly predicted was that the coffee shop would be out of oat milk by 10 a.m.

He’s still employed. They just moved him to the loading dock. He says it’s quieter out there. More room to think.

Anyway, that’s when the raccoon that had been living in the ceiling tiles dropped down onto the table and started going through his fries. The FBI agents looked at the raccoon. The raccoon looked at the agents. One of them slowly closed his notebook and said, “We’ve been monitoring the wrong guy for six months.” The raccoon, still chewing, held up a single fry like it was making a point. Then it reached into the pocket of the tiny blazer it was wearing, pulled out a laminated badge that read “CONTRACTOR – DO NOT FEED,” and started explaining, in perfect English, that the oat milk shortage was actually a deliberate liquidity event engineered by a rival coffee chain three blocks over. It recommended shorting oat futures before the 11 a.m. rush and offered to take the agents’ order if they wanted in. My guy just sighed, took the fry back, and told them the raccoon handles the real trades now. The agents nodded like this was normal and asked if the raccoon accepted Venmo.

You really have no idea how true this story is. 

Go ahead and try to community note this.

text:
Five stories kept coming back this week, and together they showed both sides of the drone age. Ukraine got full Starshield speeds back for its drones, but the fight over who throttled them moved to Congress and the Pentagon's watchdog. Two more merchant ships went down in the Black Sea after drone attacks, including a container ship off Bulgaria that no navy was close enough to protect. At home, the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program put numbers on its plan to buy hundreds of thousands of small drones, Project Agincourt's push for an Autonomous Warfare Command drew a one-word endorsement from the Secretary of War, and the Navy and DIU opened a prize contest for drone boats that shoot down drones. The common thread was speed: who controls the networks, who can field defenses fast enough, and who can buy drones at real scale.

Ukraine's Starshield slowdown. First reported Oct. 15, the throttling of Starlink and Starshield terminals that Ukraine's drones depend on ran all week. On Oct. 23 a Ukrainian official said a 161 km/h speed cap was still in place, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal opened a probe, asking Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for answers by Nov. 5. Kyiv signed a letter of intent with Finland's ICEYE and Nokia for "sovereign" communications satellites, though ICEYE says it isn't an order and the first satellite is planned for 2028. On Oct. 24 Ukraine's Defense Ministry said Starshield was working above 400 km/h again. Elon Musk said Ukraine had broken Starlink's terms with offensive drone strikes, which Kyiv called impossible. Zelensky then said the slowdown grounded 2,000 European-funded Bars interceptor drones just after one downed a Shahed. On Oct. 28 the Pentagon's inspector general declined a bipartisan Senate request to investigate, calling it a contract matter for the Air Force and Space Force. Next to watch is the Nov. 5 deadline. https://t.co/fPbsJ9I32b

Drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The campaign against merchant ships off Romania and Bulgaria, first reported Oct. 15, turned deadlier. The bulk carrier Khoryv sank off Constanța on Oct. 23 after a suspected drone strike, with one crew member dead and three missing, and Romania's president blamed Russia. France sent an Atlantique 2 patrol plane and a U.S. Navy P-8A began patrols at Bulgaria's request. On Oct. 28 three sea drones hit the container ship Contship Jet in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. All 18 crew were rescued, but the ship sank overnight, and 20 of its 421 containers, some listing hazardous cargo, fell overboard. Bulgaria's navy chief, Rear Adm. Kiril Mihaylov, said the drones ran at about 26 knots and his forces had no way to intercept them. The French patrol plane had spotted them and warned the crew. Moscow denies involvement, and Greece's prime minister has called for a global maritime truce. The open question is whether NATO's patrols turn into real protection. https://t.co/WakwDV7act https://t.co/d5rD0a3LQ1

Drone Dominance scales up. The Pentagon's program to buy cheap attack drones in bulk, first reported Oct. 17 with the Gauntlet II results, kept growing. The Defense Innovation Unit's leaderboard lines up orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies, 30,000 each for deep strike and close-quarters battle, with Neros the only firm to place in both. Final quantities are set at contract award. On Oct. 24 the Pentagon's Owen West wrote that Drone Dominance "will soon expand in domain and size." Then DIU acting director Travis Metz gave the biggest numbers yet. He said the department expects to spend $1.1 billion on roughly 300,000 drones across all Gauntlet rounds, with Gauntlets 2.5, 3 and 4 still to come in the next year or so. He said the military needs drones "measured in hundreds of thousands just to train" and wants two to four mass producers. Gauntlet II was also the first round to bar Chinese motors and battery packs. Watch for the contract awards and the next Gauntlet. https://t.co/HcwNsTwghl

Project Agincourt and AUTOWARCOM. Project Agincourt, the Pentagon effort to build an Autonomous Warfare Command, was first reported Oct. 21, when a Department of War release and an open letter from Owen West and Senior Chief Max Strasiser laid out its roadmap. The release says the model will measure success by how fast an operational problem gets a fielded, scalable solution. On Oct. 23 West restated the goal: to "prototype the fusion of development and operations, pushing money and decisions to operational units." A day later Hegseth quoted him with a single word, "AUTOWARCOM," the clearest sign yet of top-level backing. On Oct. 25, the 611th anniversary of the 1415 battle, the project's official account pledged to "rapidly adapt, field, and scale unmanned capabilities across the joint force." The posts kept the story in front of readers all week, but no new details on how the command will be organized, staffed or funded came out. That is what to watch for next. https://t.co/cX17MzxUdO

SWAP-USV Sprint 2. First reported Oct. 17, SWAP-USV Sprint 2 is a prize challenge from the Defense Innovation Unit and the Navy's robotic and autonomous systems program office for drone boats that can shoot down drones. On Oct. 23 the Navy office said it is "scaling distributed maritime air defense." The solicitation seeks production-ready uncrewed surface vessels paired with mature counter-air weapons that can be fielded forward within 120 days. There are four weapon tracks: Hellfire or JAGM missiles, APKWS rockets, remote weapon stations with Stinger, machine guns or high-power lasers, and other mature effectors. Boats must reach 200 nautical miles of range, cruise at 10 knots and engage drones and helicopters beyond 3 nautical miles, with a human in the loop. Up to $40 million in prizes is on offer, with $200 million budgeted for follow-on deals and in-water testing planned for early 2027 at Little Creek, Va. DIU posted updated FAQs on Oct. 26. Proposals are due Nov. 30. https://t.co/Ot1vEjw9K6 https://t.co/V0zVCU3irm

Every story with its links: https://t.co/5fcCkh9lx0. Follow @autowar25 for the top 25 at 7 AM and 4 PM ET and open opportunities every Monday at noon. Tips: info@autowar25.com.

$RKLB - The launch bottleneck will be bullish for other launch providers like Rocket Lab over the next 5 years!

Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated

- Ars Technica

A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.

The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.

"What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. "What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s."

The report tallies a number of familiar factors that have gone into this crisis: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.

At a time when the supply of commercial rockets is contracting, demand for satellite launch is soaring, from megaconstellation operators such as Amazon to a flurry of small satellite startups. The report estimates the crunch will become most acute in 2028 but should then slowly improve.

"How should people react and plan around this?" Henry asked. "To be honest, I don’t have a good answer. If you haven't booked your launch already, and you need one, you’re late."

Starship's lack of a regular fairing

Henry said several key uncertainties could change the outcome. Most importantly is what SpaceX will do. The company has intensified the shortage by winding down its prolific Falcon 9 rocket program. Starship has the potential to solve the launch crisis given its massive payload capacity and potential for rapid reuse.

But SpaceX has not been aggressively selling Starship as a commercial launch option. "SpaceX has also stopped affirming Starship as a commercial launcher," the Quilty report states. And as Ars reported this week, there is no evidence that the company is putting effort into developing a conventional payload fairing door for the vehicle to accommodate traditional satellites and spacecraft. Rather, the company seems set to continue to fly the vehicle with its Starlink-optimized narrow door, which ejects satellites into space like a PEZ dispenser.

SpaceX has not offered any public commitment recently to developing a larger payload fairing door, but some of its customers have indicated they don't expect that to happen any time soon.

On Thursday, the president and chief executive of Telesat, Dan Goldberg, was asked during an earnings call about what rocket the company's future satellites might launch on. In short, to book on Starship, the company may need to build flat satellites.

"First and foremost, they'll focus on the deployment of their own satellites and their own requirements," Goldberg said of SpaceX and Starship. "Secondarily or right alongside of that, the US government will be a priority customer for them, and maybe other governments as well. I do believe that so long as our next-gen satellites are configured in a way that can go into their dispenser, the same dispenser that they'll be using to deploy their own satellites, we've got some expectation that Starship would be available to Telesat to support future missions."

What about Blue and Uncle Sam?

Another mitigating factor could be the rapid acceleration of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket launch cadence. Henry said Quilty adopted a conservative forecast, predicting eight New Glenn launches in 2028, 12 in 2029, and 16 in 2030.

"I’d be happy to be proven wrong," he said. "And Blue has been in development for so long, they could come out of the gate swinging."

Blue Origin, he noted, is building the production capacity for up to 150 upper stages annually, but it will of course take time to launch such a large rocket at a high rate.

A final wild card is the US military. The current phase of the national security launch program has two lanes. The first lane is for missions with a higher risk tolerance. Any company that has launched a rocket successfully a single time is eligible to bid on these missions. For now, this includes the Falcon rockets, New Glenn, and United Launch Alliance's Vulcan, but they should be joined by a new generation of medium lift rockets within the next year or two. Lane 2 is reserved for SpaceX and United Launch Alliance.

Earlier this year, the US Space Force announced a dramatic increase in forecast demand for both Lane 1 (from an estimated 30 to 60 launches to about 170) and Lane 2 (from 54 launches to 79 launches). These missions would be ordered between 2025 and 2029.

This surge in military launch demand was not included in Quilty's calculations, Henry said, because he believes the US military will be able to require SpaceX to perform launches it deems national priorities. Moreover, he said, SpaceX is already building a number of these satellites, such as the Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator constellation.

text:
The Ancient Echoes: how the Yayati Chronicles Position India as the Cradle of Indo European Civilization By @shreehistory

In the vast tapestry of the Mahabharata (महाभारत), few stories are as compelling for understanding ancient migration patterns as the tale of King Yayati (ययाति) and his five sons. While mainstream archaeology continues to debate the origins of Indo European peoples, the epic's detailed genealogical accounts offer a fascinating counter narrative that places India not as the destination of ancient migrations, but as their source. The story of Yayati, traditionally viewed as myth, may actually preserve the collective memory of one of history's most significant population movements.

The narrative begins with Yayati, the great king of the lunar dynasty, whose personal transgressions led to a curse that would reshape the ancient world. When Shukracharya cursed Yayati with premature old age for his betrayal of marriage vows, the desperate king turned to his five sons for salvation. Only Puru, the youngest, agreed to exchange his youth for his father's decrepitude, earning him the throne and the right to remain in the heartland of Bharatavarsha (भारतवर्ष). The other four sons faced a different fate entirely.

In his gratitude mixed with disappointment, Yayati pronounced what would become one of history's most consequential curses. Yadu (यदु), Turvasu (तुर्वसु), Druhyu (द्रुह्यु), and Anu (अनु) were condemned to leave the sacred boundaries of Aryavarta (आर्यावर्त) and establish their lineages in distant lands as mlecchas, peoples who would follow customs alien to Vedic (वैदिक) traditions. This was not merely punishment but prophecy, foretelling the great dispersal of Indo Aryan peoples across the ancient world.

The Westward Migration of the Anavas

The descendants of Anu, known as the Anavas (अनव), provide perhaps the clearest example of this outward migration. According to the Mahabharata and supporting Puranic texts, the Anavas moved systematically westward from their original territories in Kashmir and the northwestern regions of India. The Baudhayana (बौधायन) Shrautasutra (श्रौतसूत्र) specifically mentions that Amavasu (अमवसु), an early Anava leader, went west to the regions of Gandhara (गांधार), Parshu (पर्शु), and Aratta (अरत्त). From these staging areas, subsequent generations continued their westward journey into what would become Afghanistan, Central Asia, and eventually Persia.

Archaeological evidence supports this narrative in unexpected ways. The Tusharas (तुषर), prominent among the Anava tribes, are mentioned throughout the Mahabharata as fierce warriors from the northwest. Their name survives in historical records as the Tokharians of Central Asia, who by the first century CE had established the mighty Kushan (कुषाण) Empire. This empire controlled vast territories from northern India to Central Asia, dominating the Silk Road trade routes that connected East and West. The progression from Vedic Tusharas to historical Tokharians to Kushan rulers represents a clear lineage that can be traced through both textual and archaeological records.

The Linguistic and Genetic Echoes

The linguistic evidence proves equally compelling. The parallels between Vedic Sanskrit and the ancient Iranian language of the Avesta (अवस्ता) go far beyond what would be expected from mere cultural contact. Shared religious concepts, mythological figures, and even specific ritual terminology suggest a common origin rather than borrowing. The Vedic god Varuna (वरुण) and the Avestani Ahura Mazda (अहुर मज़्दा) share not only similar attributes but virtually identical hymns, while the sacred fire rituals of both traditions follow remarkably similar patterns. Such deep structural similarities point to a shared heritage that diverged when populations physically separated.

Druhyu's descendants tell a parallel story of northern migration. The Mahabharata records that this lineage moved toward what is now identified as central Europe, carrying with them the proto Indo European languages that would eventually develop into the Germanic, Celtic, and other European language families. The timing of this migration, as recorded in Puranic chronology, corresponds remarkably well with archaeological evidence for the spread of Indo European speaking peoples across Europe during the third and second millennia BCE.

The story of Yadu's descendants offers yet another piece of the puzzle. Though cursed never to rule kingdoms, the Yadavas became a powerful confederation that produced heroes like Krishna (कृष्ण) and established settlements throughout western India. Their maritime connections extended to distant shores, with Yadava trading networks reaching as far as the Mediterranean. Ancient Greek sources mention contacts with Indian peoples they called "Ethiopians of the East," descriptions that may preserve memories of these early Yadava expeditions.

Even the descendants of Turvasu, who became identified with various groups including the Yavanas (यवन), provide evidence for this outward migration theory. The term Yavana, initially referring to the descendants of Turvasu, was later applied to Greeks and other western peoples, suggesting that the original Yavanas had migrated so far west that when Greeks eventually appeared in Indian records, they were recognized as belonging to the same general category of distant western peoples.

The Chronological and Cultural Framework

The chronological framework provided by Puranic texts, while debated, offers dates for these migrations that predate the commonly accepted theories of Indo European expansion. If accurate, these accounts would push the origins of Indo European civilization back several millennia and locate its birthplace firmly within the Indian subcontinent. This would explain why the oldest and most complex forms of Indo European languages, poetry, and religious traditions are found in Vedic Sanskrit rather than in the supposed homeland of the Pontic steppes.

Furthermore, the Mahabharata's description of the technological and cultural sophistication of these migrating peoples aligns with archaeological evidence for the rapid spread of advanced metallurgy, horse domestication, and urban planning across Eurasia during the relevant time periods. The epic's detailed knowledge of distant geographical regions, from the mountains of Afghanistan to the steppes of Central Asia, suggests that these were not imaginary lands but territories familiar to the tradition's composers through historical memory.

The political implications of viewing the Yayati story as historical rather than mythological extend far beyond academic debates. If the Indian subcontinent was indeed the source rather than the destination of Indo European civilization, it would fundamentally alter our understanding of ancient cultural development and the relationships between various world civilizations. The image of India as a passive recipient of external influences would be replaced by that of an active cultural and demographic source that profoundly shaped the ancient world.

The resistance to this interpretation in mainstream scholarship often stems from methodological conservatism rather than contradictory evidence. The assumption that myth cannot preserve historical memory has led to the dismissal of valuable source material that could illuminate prehistoric population movements. Yet oral traditions worldwide have proven remarkably accurate in preserving information about ancient events, particularly those as traumatic and significant as large scale migrations and dynastic changes.

The Yayati narrative thus stands as more than just an ancient story about family conflict and divine punishment. It represents a detailed account of how populations spread from the Indian heartland to establish civilizations across the ancient world, carrying with them the languages, technologies, and cultural traditions that would shape human development for millennia. Whether viewed as myth or history, the tale offers profound insights into the interconnected nature of ancient civilizations and the continuing influence of prehistoric population movements on the modern world.

In the end, the story of Yayati and his sons challenges us to reconsider our assumptions about the direction of ancient cultural flow. Rather than viewing India as the eastern terminus of Indo European expansion, the Mahabharata invites us to see it as the dynamic center from which waves of migration carried Indian civilization to the furthest corners of the ancient world, creating the foundations upon which subsequent civilizations would build.

Sometimes I wonder if the KGB deliberately allowed the USSR to collapse in the end so that the West would lower its guard, after which they repositioned existing networks, personnel, and assets to operate inside European institutions and the U.S. Democratic Party. 

After decades of limited success with classical ideological subversion, the formal Soviet system itself had become the main liability, too rigid, too economically exhausted, and too visibly totalitarian to serve as a useful vehicle. The more practical course was to let the Union dissolve, preserve the human and operational infrastructure through the chaos of the early 1990s, and re-enter Western institutions once the end of history consensus removed most remaining scrutiny.

The 1991 collapse and the disorder that followed provided cover for retaining and relocating intelligence cadres, commercial fronts, and personal networks. Former officials, their children, and associated intermediaries could then appear in universities, media organizations, financial circles, NGOs, energy companies, and political donor networks during the period of Western complacency. European energy dependence, particularly German reliance on Russian supplies, together with the expanding EU bureaucracy, created durable points of access. In the United States, open institutional cultures and certain progressive political machines offered parallel openings, not through direct ownership of any party, but through elite capture, shared anti-nationalist framing, and reduced threat perception after the Cold War was declared finished.

Some of the documented Russian influence operations, oligarch capital flows, and interference attempts continued across this period and fit the same timeline. The later consolidation of power under Putin, a former KGB officer, then appeared as the long-term arrangement coming back into clearer view once Western societies were sufficiently distracted and internally divided. The sequence is consistent with a shift from overt confrontation to quieter, sustained access rather than a sudden invention after 1991.

Do those placements now show their effects? In the EU, authority continues to concentrate in supranational institutions while member states surrender more of their remaining sovereignty over borders, energy, industry, and speech. In the United States, Democratic leaders are openly outlining steps that would lock in permanent one-party control: granting statehood to DC and Puerto Rico to secure a lasting Senate majority, expanding mass legalization of illegal immigrants to create a permanent electoral advantage, and enlarging the Supreme Court to obtain an immediate majority. Elon just noted that a clean sweep along these lines would turn America into a permanent one-party state and end democracy in any meaningful sense, which the same pattern already visible in California. 

It is as if they are rebuilding the USSR from within in both the United States and the EU, with radical youth in recent European riots and among the American progressive left, including socialist influencers and campus-based social justice activists, now openly calling for it.

It was wonderful to visit Habitat for Humanity’s Life Advancement Center, which opened last month, in Yuba City earlier this week.  Habitat is doing encouraging work to provide a fresh start for individuals and families who have fallen into homelessness.

The center provides emergency shelter, including private rooms for families, recuperative care for patients just out of the hospital, and transitional housing.

Homelessness in California is a frustrating and wicked problem.  This comprehensive range of services the Life Advancement Center offers is an ambitious program that promises to make a real difference in Yuba/Sutter.

text: Video Transcript: [VOICEOVER] Disability Rights California. What do you wish employers knew about workers with disabilities? [ELIZABETH] I want employers to know. Number one, hiring a person with a disability is not a liability. I feel like that's a thing that for some reason, when someone, you know, like, for example, sees me with the cane, they're like, oh, my gosh, she's going to fall down because she can't see. Which we all know isn't isn't true. Right. And so, number one, like hiring a person with a disability doesn't mean you're going to have to change your office space. You're not, you know, like you might need to make some accommodations, but we're not here to disrupt anything. We're not here to turn things upside down. We're here to work just like everyone else. The second thing that I would like employers to know or consider when they are, you know, thinking about hiring someone, with a disability is. What if you took disability out of the equation? If disability wasn't a factor and you were just looking at this person for their skill sets, for the talents that they have for their background, would you hire them? And I feel like that's just a simple question that you, you know, you can ask yourself to really check your bias. Am I being biased right now? Because I know after this interview I realize this person has a disability. Now I'm changing how I view them as a candidate. So really, like if that's where you are, just take a second. And if disability weren't a factor, how would you be viewing this candidate? And a third, it doesn't cost more to have us as employees. I feel like sometimes employers misunderstand what reasonable accommodations are, you know? Not understanding that by asking for a reasonable accommodation. I'm not setting you up for a lawsuit. You know, I'm actually just trying to find a way to be able to do my job more effectively. So if employers are more aware of reasonable accommodations, how they can help their employees, then it will take some of that fear away and some of that uncertainty of like, hey, can I hire a person with a disability? Absolutely. Because as the employer, I know what reasonable accommodations I can offer because I really like this person. I think they're going to be really good at this job, and I don't want to just look past them because they have a disability. Obviously, they were able to finish college. Obviously they've had other employment. So why would I think they can't do my job? Just because I've never- I'm not familiar with their disability. And I guess lastly, like, I would like for employers to know, like, we're humans, just like everyone else. Disabled or not, people make mistakes. So although, like, you know, I'm all for, you know, people with disabilities, we try really hard, but we are going to make mistakes and we are going to maybe ask for help, but hey, like that happens with everyone, right? So for me, it's really important for employers and people to understand that things that happens with everyone, right? So for me, it's really important for employers and people to understand that things that happen to us, like leaving our keys at home or dropping something, have nothing to do with the disability. It's just because we're human like everyone else. So taking that into consideration too that, some of the things that might seem like a big deal because the person has a disability, if they didn't have a disability, you probably wouldn't think it was a big deal or a problem. [OFF CAMERA VOICE] Hell yeah! [ELIZABETH LAUGHS] [OFF CAMERA VOICE] Dude, I’m like, letting you speak. And back here I'm like, nodding so aggressively. [ELIZABETH LAUGHS]

text:
$CBRS The Cerebras Anti-Bubble: A Crushed Valuation in a Trillion-Dollar AI Buildout and A Golden Opportunity 

What Josh Brown, Scott Galloway and the frontier labs’ enormous compute commitments reveal about Cerebras’s $19.5 billion enterprise value.

After listening to "Josh Brown: If This Is A Bubble, It’s Pathetic" on Prof G Markets, I came away even more bullish on Cerebras. The episode describes extraordinary commercial growth at the frontier labs, intense competition to secure compute and an enormous infrastructure expansion still ahead. Cerebras already participates through OpenAI, with opportunities developing through $AMZ AWS, $ORCL Oracle Cloud and $CRWD CrowdStrike. At its current valuation, I think the market is dramatically underestimating what those relationships could become.

At the October 30 close, Cerebras had a market capitalization of approximately $25.9 billion and an enterprise value of roughly $19.5 billion. Its latest reported balance sheet, dated June 30, showed $6.74 billion in cash and equivalents plus $1.18 billion in investments. After accounting for approximately $1.49 billion in borrowings and operating lease liabilities, that leaves roughly $6.43 billion in net cash and investments, equivalent to almost 25% of its market capitalization.

The operating business is being valued below $20 billion as the world begins purchasing intelligence on an unprecedented scale.

One of the most revealing moments in the podcast is Scott Galloway admitting, “I wanted to hate this S1,” before saying he has almost “done a 180.” Anthropic’s financial results explain the change. First-half revenue increased from approximately $1.2 billion to $16.3 billion, representing 1,300% growth, while its operating loss narrowed to $693 million. Its filing also reports $1.6 billion in adjusted operating income. Scott calls the product “unbelievable” and emphasizes its adjusted operating income while “scaling at an unprecedented rate.”

Scott discusses a potential $200 billion revenue run rate in 2027 or 2028 and says there is a “non-zero probability that Anthropic is the most valuable company in the world” within 36 to 48 months. Those are forecasts, and they reveal how dramatically his assessment of the opportunity has changed. Josh believes Anthropic could raise another $100 billion privately “with their eyes closed.” A valuable product, rapidly expanding revenue and access to capital create powerful conditions for continued infrastructure spending.

OpenAI’s numbers make the opportunity more concrete. Its reported revenue was $5.7 billion in Q1 and $6.7 billion in Q2, or approximately $12.4 billion in the first half, alongside Anthropic’s $16.3 billion. On their respective reported accounting bases, these 2 companies generated approximately $29 billion in 6 months.

OpenAI’s subsequent figures show further acceleration. CFO Sarah Friar said its annualized revenue run rate reached $50 billion at the end of September, up 77% in 1 quarter, with its business segment doubling. She subsequently described 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users. OpenAI had already reported 2.5 million business customers in September and announced $122 billion in committed capital in March. These figures show the distribution, commercial demand and financing available to support a much larger business.

OpenAI has also connected its growth directly to compute availability. From 2023 through 2025, compute capacity increased from approximately 0.2 GW to 0.6 GW to 1.9 GW, while annualized revenue increased from $2 billion to $6 billion to more than $20 billion. Friar described compute as “the scarcest resource in AI” and said additional capacity would have allowed faster adoption and monetization. Infrastructure availability can affect how much business a frontier lab can serve.

The spending plans reveal the scale of what comes next. OpenAI reportedly plans approximately $750 billion in compute spending through 2030. Adding the purchase commitments, future leases and subsequent agreements disclosed in Anthropic’s S-1 produces roughly $850 billion in multiyear obligations, spanning different durations and contractual conditions. These are enormous commitments across the infrastructure required to train, deploy and operate increasingly capable AI.

That is why Josh’s observation matters: “if they get caught without enough compute, it’s probably worse than overcommitting.” He argues that frontier labs have a powerful incentive to “lock up as much compute as you can on a guaranteed contract basis.” Discussing Anthropic’s commitments, he makes the physical implication explicit: “that all has to get built.” He adds, “There’s a ripple effect anytime a company like Anthropic comes along and spends money the way that they’re spending.”

This is the connection to Cerebras. Anthropic demonstrates how quickly enterprises can adopt and pay for frontier intelligence. Its success increases the competitive urgency for OpenAI to deliver more capable products and win valuable workflows. OpenAI has an enormous distribution base, and Cerebras supplies technology that can help it deliver frontier intelligence faster. Cerebras’s exposure to OpenAI is direct. Its exposure to Anthropic’s growth comes through the expanding inference market and the competitive pressure that growth creates. A confirmed Anthropic supply relationship would represent an additional development.

Cerebras’s OpenAI agreement already involves substantial commitments: 750 MW of contracted capacity, with an option for another 1.25 GW through 2030, taking potential capacity to 2 GW. Cerebras reported $25.4 billion in remaining performance obligations at June 30, substantially associated with OpenAI. Those obligations are expected to convert into revenue over multiple years as the company delivers the contracted services.

The capacity commentary is especially revealing. At TechCrunch Disrupt in October, Andrew Feldman explained that the success of the initial OpenAI deployment created demand for a much wider rollout. His explanation for the constraint was explicit: “we just didn’t have the capacity for them. We didn’t have the data centers.” Separately, Cerebras CTO Sean Lie said in September that the company was “sold out of everything that we’re building.” These statements describe demand running ahead of the infrastructure available to serve it.

OpenAI confirms the practical use of that capacity. Cerebras powers GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast at advertised speeds of up to 750 output tokens per second. OpenAI describes internal use for incident response and research, including examining evidence, investigating failures, preparing fixes and accelerating experimentation. Its announcement identifies Jane Street as an early customer. Jane Street’s John Crepezzi says the speed “enables different ways of using the models.”

Speed determines how much useful work fits into the working day. A sophisticated agent may reason, retrieve information, call tools, inspect results, revise its approach and verify its answer repeatedly. Generation delays accumulate throughout that process. A developer benefits from shorter coding and testing cycles. A researcher benefits from receiving results early enough to run another experiment that afternoon. A security team needs an investigation completed while it can still act on the findings. Where model generation is a bottleneck, faster inference can shorten completion times and allow more reasoning or verification before the deadline.

Sean Lie explicitly connects inference speed with “more agentic loops” and “more intelligent agents.” OpenAI describes its own research experimentation cycles tightening enough to support multiple iterations during the workday. Its research organization also reported 3.1 agent-workdays of effort per human workday in mid-August. As organizations delegate more sustained work to agents, the machine activity associated with each employee can expand substantially.

The podcast captures the demand dynamic clearly. Josh says “the services are so popular and in so much demand that while the per token cost falls, the sheer explosion in everyday usage is rapidly outpacing that.” His discussion of people “having the machine running for 48 hours over the weekend” illustrates the emergence of sustained computational work. He raises that example while discussing spending controls, which also highlights the importance of delivering those workloads economically.

Gartner offers an important outside forecast: inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than 5× through 2028, driven by more sophisticated tasks, more reasoning and greater token consumption. Gartner emphasizes the need to manage those costs and demonstrate returns. For Cerebras, the opportunity is to supply fast inference that helps customers complete valuable work economically as the computational demands of each workflow increase.

AWS and Oracle Cloud expand the potential distribution. AWS is developing a system combining Trainium for prompt processing with Cerebras for output generation, accessible through Amazon Bedrock. Cerebras’s August update expected availability in Q1 2027. Oracle and Cerebras have also announced plans to bring Cerebras inference to OCI during 2027. Those relationships create routes to enterprises and developers already purchasing cloud services, with the potential to broaden adoption across many customers and applications.

Then consider cybersecurity, which could become an enormous source of recurring demand for fast inference.

Anthropic has documented coordinated agents conducting reconnaissance, exploitation and theft against multiple victims in parallel, with operations running for hours or days. OpenAI has called for an expansion of AI-enabled defense as AI changes the speed, scale and economics of attacks. Enterprises have a compelling reason to deploy defensive systems capable of continuously investigating threats and responding quickly.

CrowdStrike makes the operating scale tangible. In September, it said its Falcon sensor generates nearly 7 trillion security events every day. Its August threat-hunting podcast described 14 million daily detection leads, feeding a process that ultimately produced approximately 36,000 annual customer alerts and notifications. Those figures reveal the enormous volume of screening, correlation and investigation behind the findings that reach customers. The eventual LLM workload depends on how that information is filtered, grouped and routed for analysis.

CrowdStrike is introducing coordinated investigations involving multiple AI agents across endpoints, identities, SaaS applications, cloud infrastructure and networks. Agents share context, examine evidence and work toward a common conclusion. The demand for fast, capable inference can grow through both the number of investigations receiving AI assistance and the depth of reasoning performed within each investigation.

Cerebras already has a direct commercial connection through Falcon AI Detection and Response. CrowdStrike says the partnership will help it run more powerful security models at the speed required for real-time protection. Cerebras’s earnings release describes enabling inline LLM security across a large portion of enterprise traffic. That points toward recurring inference consumption as enterprise AI applications and agents operate throughout the day.

Cerebras CISO Naor Penso puts the requirement plainly: “Security cannot wait in the queue for slow AI while an attack unfolds.” In a company-reported suspicious-file analysis example, Cerebras completed the task in 58 seconds, compared with 4 minutes 43 seconds using standard processing with the same model and prompt. That saved 3 minutes 45 seconds in that particular workflow. Across an investigation involving several dependent decisions, shorter waits can give defenders more time to validate findings and act.

Gartner forecasts spending on securing AI at approximately $2.8 billion in 2026, $4.8 billion in 2027 and $7.7 billion in 2028, across categories including application security, usage controls, governance and gateways. OpenAI’s CFO also said substantial bank spending in Q3 was driven by cybersecurity as customers moved into large deployments. The commercial demand is beginning to appear in customer behavior and industry budgets.

Imagine those requirements spreading across banks, hospitals, manufacturers, cloud platforms and government systems. More enterprise agents create more activity to monitor. More automated attacks create more investigations. More capable defensive models enable deeper analysis. Faster inference helps that analysis finish within a useful response window. The scale grows across customers, systems, tasks and computational effort per task.

There is also a potential catalyst for how investors understand Cerebras’s exposure. Josh says, “Open AI will go public in Q1,” and raises January as a possibility if Anthropic’s offering receives the reception he expects. That remains his forecast. A successful Anthropic listing could establish a public valuation benchmark for frontier AI and increase attention on OpenAI’s infrastructure suppliers if OpenAI follows closely.

The market has already imposed a substantial reset. Josh calls the environment “an anti-bubble,” says investors are “factoring in growth skepticism every single day,” and points out that “we had semis down 29%.” Ed notes that Nvidia’s multiple has fallen almost 50% over the previous year. Cerebras’s market capitalization has fallen from approximately $49 billion on September 25 to $26 billion on October 30, a decline of roughly 47%.

Josh also points out that “the semiconductor industry is the largest contributor to tech earnings growth” and describes technology earnings reports as “continuing to crush.” His skepticism about the bubble narrative rests on real earnings and compressed valuations. For Cerebras, the investment question is how much of the emerging demand for fast inference it can translate into profitable revenue.

This brings me back to my earlier $250–300 billion Cerebras bull case. That framework modeled approximately 2 GW of average productive cloud capacity in 2029, generating $15–20 billion in annual core revenue per GW, or $30–40 billion in total annual revenue. At a 40% core operating margin after depreciation, that produces $12–16 billion in annual core operating profit. Applying 20× operating profit gives approximately $240–320 billion in enterprise value, centered on $280 billion. Assuming approximately zero net debt at that stage, the corresponding equity value would be similar.

The latest disclosures put that revenue target into a much more concrete context. Anthropic’s SpaceXAI arrangements alone contemplate approximately $3.1 billion per month once all contracted capacity is delivered. That represents a $37.2 billion annual spending pace with 1 supplier, subject to the agreements’ cancellation provisions. My entire Cerebras bull case assumes $30–40 billion in annual revenue in 2029-2030. Anthropic is already describing an individual supplier relationship operating at that scale.

The capacity comparison is equally revealing. On a power-capacity basis, the 2 GW in my model represents approximately 6.7% of the 30 GW buildout ambition Sam Altman outlined for OpenAI alone. Cerebras can become a very large company by earning a specialized position within a much larger infrastructure ecosystem. $NVDA Nvidia can continue supplying the largest share of that expansion.

The original model requires ambitious execution: 2 GW productive across the year, the assumed revenue per GW, substantial operating margins and disciplined financing. OpenAI’s additional 1.25 GW remains an option with deployment provisions extending through 2030. The new evidence gives the potential customer demand behind that model a much stronger commercial foundation.

At approximately $19.5 billion in enterprise value, I think this selloff may have created a golden opportunity. Cerebras has a direct OpenAI relationship, demonstrated frontier-model deployments, capacity constraints, Jane Street usage, planned AWS and Oracle distribution, and a commercial foothold in AI security through CrowdStrike.

People are underestimating how much work AI systems will perform, how continuously they will perform it, and how valuable it becomes to complete that work at the speed of the businesses relying on it. The frontier labs are already planning infrastructure spending measured in hundreds of billions of dollars. A profitable share of their most demanding inference workloads could support a company many times Cerebras’s current size.

That is the asymmetry. Wake up! (DYOR, NFA!)
